body:
# Tokamak Plasma Control: MHD Stability, Disruption Prediction, and Magnetic Confinement at Reactor Scale

## Abstract

Magnetic confinement in the tokamak rests on the axisymmetric Grad–Shafranov equilibrium, yet reactor-scale operation demands survival against kink modes, tearing modes, edge-localized modes, and disruptions that dump hundreds of megajoules and drive multi-mega-ampere halo currents into the vessel [1][2]. This thesis develops the full chain from equilibrium to catastrophe to control: the safety-factor profile *q(ψ)* and rational-surface resonances, linear and nonlinear MHD theory of ideal kinks and neoclassical tearing modes, and the empirical disruption boundary (Greenwald density, Troyon beta, *q₉₅*) against DIII-D, JET, EAST, SPARC, and ITER data [2][3]. We then treat the data-driven layer — the Fusion Recurrent Neural Network, which generalized from DIII-D training to JET plasmas, and random-forest predictors on Alcator C-Mod, DIII-D, and EAST [1][3] — and real-time control: preemptive NTM stabilization by ECCD with centimeter-accurate *q*-surface alignment [4][5] and shattered-pellet-injection mitigation for ITER and SPARC [6][7][8].

## 1 Introduction

The tokamak confines a hot plasma with a helical magnetic field: a strong toroidal field *B_φ* generated by external coils plus a poloidal field *B_θ* generated by a toroidal plasma current. The resulting field lines wind around nested toroidal flux surfaces, labeled by the poloidal flux *ψ*, on which pressure, density, and temperature are constant in equilibrium. This elegant picture is the solution of the **Grad–Shafranov equation**,

> **Theorem (Axisymmetric equilibrium):** In steady state, an axisymmetric plasma satisfies ∇*p* = **J** × **B**, and with the representation **B** = ∇*ψ* × ∇*φ* + *F*∇*φ*, the flux function obeys Δ\*ψ = −μ₀R² *dp/dψ* − *F dF/dψ*.

Here *F* = *RB_φ* is the poloidal current function and Δ\* is the Grad–Shafranov operator. Every reconstructed tokamak equilibrium — from the EFIT code used inter-shot and increasingly in real time — is a numerical solution of this equation constrained by magnetics, motional Stark effect, and kinetic measurements [5].

Equilibrium, however, is not stability. Perturbations δ**ξ** grow when the energy principle δW becomes negative, and in high-performance plasmas the free energy stored in pressure gradients and current gradients is large. The *normalized beta* β_N = β(%)·*a*(m)·*B*(T)/*I_p*(MA) is limited empirically to β_N ≲ 4*l_i* (the Troyon limit), beyond which ideal kink and ballooning modes erupt [2]. The *safety factor*,

$$q(\\psi) = \\frac{1}{2\\pi}\\oint \\frac{B_\\phi}{R B_\\theta}\\,d\\ell_{\\mathrm{pol}},$$

measures field-line pitch: where *q* = *m/n* is rational, magnetic islands (tearing modes) can reconnect and grow. Operation is therefore steered to *q₉₅* ≈ 3–4, safely above the *q* = 2 surface where the most dangerous 2/1 modes resonate [2][4].

When control fails, the plasma *disrupts*: a thermal quench (TQ) dumps the stored energy in ~1 ms, followed by a current quench (CQ) on the timescale of the vessel *L/R* time, generating halo currents that exert tens of meganewtons of force on the vessel and accelerating runaway electrons (REs) to tens of MeV [6][8]. ITER, at 15 MA and 350 MJ of thermal stored energy, can tolerate only a handful of unmitigated disruptions in its lifetime [1]. The stakes motivate the three pillars of this thesis: (i) first-principles MHD stability understanding, (ii) machine-learning disruption prediction, and (iii) real-time control and mitigation at reactor scale.

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Ideal and resistive MHD

The single-fluid MHD model couples the plasma to Maxwell's equations through Ohm's law, **E** + **v** × **B** = η**J**. In the ideal limit (η → 0), magnetic flux is frozen into the plasma and reconnection is forbidden; instability then requires bending or compressing field lines, giving rise to *kinks* (global helical displacements, e.g., the *m* = 1 internal kink driving sawteeth) and *ballooning modes* (localized on the outboard bad-curvature side). With finite resistivity, field lines can reconnect at rational surfaces, forming **magnetic islands** — the tearing mode. The stability of a tearing mode is quantified by Δ′, the jump in the logarithmic derivative of the perturbed flux across the rational surface: Δ′ > 0 implies instability in classical tearing theory.

### 2.2 Neoclassical tearing modes

In high-temperature, collisionless plasmas, the bootstrap current *j_BS* — a self-generated current proportional to the pressure gradient — introduces a *neoclassical* drive. Inside an island, fast parallel transport flattens the pressure profile, locally removing bootstrap current; the resulting helical current deficit amplifies the island. The island width *w* evolves per the generalized Rutherford equation,

$$\frac{\\tau_R}{r}\\frac{dw}{dt} = \\Delta'(w) + \\Delta_{BS}(w) + \\Delta_{GGJ}(w) + \\Delta_{pol}(w) + \\Delta_{ECCD},$$

where Δ_BS is the destabilizing bootstrap term, Δ_GGJ and Δ_pol are stabilizing curvature and polarization terms, and Δ_ECCD is the control term supplied by localized current drive [4]. Crucially, the NTM is *linearly stable but nonlinearly unstable*: a seed island (from a sawtooth crash or ELM) must exceed a threshold width before growth takes over, which is precisely why active control — shrinking the island below threshold — works so well [5].

### 2.3 The empirical disruption boundary

Decades of operation have mapped the disruption space: the Greenwald density limit *n_G* = *I_p*/(π*a*²), the Troyon beta limit, low-*q* operation (*q₉₅* < 2 invites the 2/1 external kink), impurity accumulation, and locked modes (error-field penetration braking plasma rotation). The locked-mode precursor is so reliable that the *n* = 1 radial field is a standard disruption predictor input [3].

### 2.4 Reactor design points

SPARC, the high-field compact tokamak, is designed for *Q* > 2 with β_N = 1.0, *n/n_G* = 0.37, and *q₉₅* ≈ 3.4 — a conservative point with comfortable margin to the empirical limits and low drive for NTMs at the *q* = 2 surface [2]. ITER targets *Q* = 10 at 15 MA with an ECCD-based NTM suppression system and a shattered-pellet-injection disruption mitigation system (DMS) [4][6][7].

## 3 Methodology

Our analysis proceeds in three layers, mirroring the control stack of a modern tokamak.

**Layer 1 — Equilibrium and stability analysis.** We reconstruct equilibria with a Grad–Shafranov solver (EFIT-style) and compute *q(ψ)*, magnetic shear *ŝ* = (*r/q*)(*dq/dr*), and the Mercier criterion for interchange stability. Ideal stability is assessed via the energy principle; resistive stability via Δ′ from a cylindrical tearing analysis with toroidal corrections.

**Layer 2 — Data-driven prediction.** We review two paradigms: (a) the Fusion Recurrent Neural Network (FRNN), a deep architecture combining convolutional layers (spatial profile features) with LSTM recurrence (temporal evolution), trained on >10⁴ DIII-D discharges and tested on JET — the first demonstration of cross-machine generalization of a disruption predictor [1]; and (b) random-forest classifiers trained on real-time-available scalar signals on Alcator C-Mod, DIII-D, and EAST, achieving ~80–90% shot-by-shot detection rates with interpretable feature importances [3].

**Layer 3 — Control and mitigation.** We analyze the DIII-D NTM control system — real-time *q*-surface reconstruction feeding ECCD alignment to ~1 cm accuracy, with preemptive and modulated deposition strategies [4][5] — and SPI mitigation physics: pellet shattering, impurity assimilation, radiative thermal quench, and runaway-electron suppression, as modeled by the NIMROD, M3D-C1, JOREK, and DREAM codes [6][7][8].

A compact illustration of the predictor layer in code clarifies the data flow:

```python
import numpy as np

def disruption_score(signals, model, threshold=0.5):
    """Realtime disruption score from multi-channel plasma signals.
    signals: dict of 1D arrays, e.g. locked-mode amplitude, li, q95,
             radiated power fraction, density / Greenwald fraction.
    Returns (alarm: bool, score: float, sensitivity: dict)."""
    X = np.stack([signals[k] for k in sorted(signals)], axis=-1)  # (T, C)
    score = float(model.predict_proba(X[None, -64:])[0, 1])       # last 64 ms
    alarm = score > threshold
    # sensitivity: gradient of score w.r.t. each channel (interpretability)
    sens = {k: float(np.abs(model.channel_gradient(X, k)).mean())
            for k in signals}
    return alarm, score, sens

# Example alarm logic: with ~30-50 ms warning the PCS can fire SPI [1][6]
```

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Safety factor, shear, and rational surfaces

The safety factor profile is the skeleton of tokamak stability. A monotonic *q* rising from *q₀* ≈ 1 on axis to *q₉₅* ≈ 3–4 at the edge places the *q* = 1, 3/2, and 2 surfaces at distinct radii; reversed-shear profiles (minimum *q* off-axis) can stabilize turbulence via internal transport barriers but invite double-tearing modes. Magnetic shear *ŝ* enters tearing stability directly: strong shear narrows islands, while low shear near *q_min* widens the vulnerable layer. Real-time knowledge of *q(ψ)* — from magnetics plus motional Stark effect fed to a Grad–Shafranov solver at ~ms cadence — is therefore the *sensor* on which NTM control closes the loop [5]. The DIII-D system achieves *q*-surface/ECCD alignment to order 1 cm, the tolerance required to deposit driven current inside a centimeter-scale island [5].

### 4.2 Kink, tearing, and ELM dynamics

The external kink (*m* = 2, *n* = 1) is the classic low-*q* disruption trigger: as *q₉₅* → 2, the mode couples to the wall, locks, and the plasma follows. Internal kinks (*m* = 1/*n* = 1) drive the sawtooth cycle — periodic core crashes that conveniently provide seed islands for NTMs. Tearing modes at *q* = 3/2 degrade confinement by ~30% in stored energy when they appear; at *q* = 2 they are, statistically, the single most common root cause of disruptions [4]. Edge-localized modes are the price of H-mode: the edge transport barrier steepens the pressure gradient until peeling–ballooning modes erupt quasi-periodically, ejecting ~5–10% of stored energy per ELM. In ITER, unmitigated type-I ELMs would erode the tungsten divertor, so ELM suppression by resonant magnetic perturbations (RMPs) or ELM-free regimes (QH-mode, negative triangularity) is an active frontier.

> **Theorem (Newcomb's criterion):** A cylindrical plasma is ideally stable to *m* ≥ 2 kinks iff *q(a)* > *m/n* at every rational surface inside the plasma; violation at the edge invites the external kink and, at *q* = 2, the most virulent disruption precursor.

| Instability | Drive | Timescale | Disruption role |
|---|---|---|---|
| External kink 2/1 | Current gradient, low *q₉₅* | ~100 μs (ideal) | Direct trigger, wall locking |
| NTM 3/2, 2/1 | Bootstrap current deficit | ms–s (resistive) | Confinement loss; 2/1 → disruption [4] |
| Sawtooth 1/1 | Core pressure, *q₀* < 1 | ~100 ms period | Seed island source |
| Type-I ELM | Edge pressure/current | ~ms, periodic | Divertor erosion; seed for NTMs |
| Vertical displacement | Elongation κ | ~ms (with wall) | VDE → halo currents |

### 4.3 Disruption prediction with deep learning

The FRNN result is a landmark: trained on DIII-D data, it predicted JET disruptions it had never seen, closing in on the ITER requirement of 95% true positives with <3% false alarms at ~30 ms warning time [1]. Its architecture matters — CNNs extract spatial structure from profile diagnostics while LSTMs track temporal precursors — and so does its interpretability layer: per-channel *sensitivity scores* identify *why* the alarm fired (e.g., core radiation and *q₉₅* for impurity-driven events), turning a black box into actionable guidance for the plasma control system (PCS), such as which actuator to engage [1]. Complementary random-forest studies on C-Mod, DIII-D, and EAST showed that the most predictive signals differ per machine — a cautionary result for naive transfer — yet shot-by-shot detection rates of 80–90% were achievable with real-time-capable features on all three [3]. The synthesis: deep sequence models for accuracy and transfer, shallow interpretable models for real-time deployment and physics insight.

### 4.4 Real-time control: shape, NTMs, and the PCS

Modern PCS architectures (DIII-D, EAST, KSTAR) run multiple control loops at kHz rates: vertical stabilization of elongated plasmas (κ ~ 1.8), shape/position control via poloidal-field coils, density control via gas and pellets, and rotation control via neutral beams. NTM control is the flagship *physics* loop. The DIII-D system detects the island, reconstructs the *q* = 3/2 or 2 surface in real time, and steers ECCD deposition onto the island O-point — including *modulated* ECCD synchronized to island rotation, which achieves suppression with less average power, and *preemptive* ECCD that prevents mode onset in NTM-prone scenarios [4][5]. Full suppression of the 3/2 mode was obtained robustly with ~1.5 MW of ECCD, recovering the ~30% stored-energy loss and allowing β above the original onset threshold — a factor ~2 improvement in limiting beta [5]. The 2/1 mode, more demanding, was suppressed in the low-torque ITER baseline scenario by ramping the toroidal field to walk the ECCD deposition onto the *q* = 2 surface [4]. The engineering lesson is alignment: 1-cm accuracy maintained *after* the mode disappears, so the defense persists without a target to track [5].

### 4.5 Disruption mitigation at reactor scale

When prediction fails or time runs out, mitigation must convert an unmitigated disruption into a benign one. The ITER DMS baseline is **shattered pellet injection**: a cryogenic pellet (D₂ with neon) is pneumatically launched at hundreds of m/s and shattered at the vessel entrance; the shards ablate in the plasma, radiating the thermal energy uniformly (reducing localized heat loads) while the injected deuterium raises density to collisionally suppress runaway-electron avalanches [6][8]. Three-dimensional MHD codes (NIMROD, M3D-C1, JOREK) model the assimilation and the MHD response, including thermal-quench onset criteria tied to shard arrival at the *q* = 2 surface and the critical metric of toroidal radiation peaking — asymmetric radiation that can focus heat onto wall panels [8]. For SPARC, modeling shows disruption loads comparable to or exceeding ITER's in some channels (halo currents up to ~50 MN), motivating both massive material injection and a passive runaway-electron mitigation coil that stochastically deconfines REs [2][7]. The mitigation timeline is brutal: detection to injection in tens of milliseconds, thermal quench in ~1 ms, current quench in tens of ms — which is exactly why predictors like FRNN are sized to the ITER 30-ms requirement [1][6].

## 5 Empirical Results / Formal Analysis

We consolidate the quantitative record:

- **FRNN cross-machine prediction:** trained on DIII-D, tested on JET; true-positive rate approaching the ITER target of 95% with <3% false alarms and ~30 ms warning — the first reliable prediction on an unseen device [1].
- **Random-forest predictors:** 80–90% shot-by-shot detection on Alcator C-Mod, DIII-D, and EAST using only real-time-available signals; deployed in inter-shot and real-time environments on EAST and DIII-D [3].
- **NTM suppression:** 3/2 mode fully suppressed with ~1.5 MW ECCD in DIII-D; β limit improved by nearly a factor of 2 after stabilization; 2/1 preemptive stabilization demonstrated in the low-torque ITER baseline scenario; alignment maintained to ~1 cm [4][5].
- **SPARC stability margins:** design point β_N = 1.0, *n/n_G* = 0.37, *q₉₅* ≈ 3.4 with low β_p at the *q* = 2 surface — a tearing-resilient operating space — yet unmitigated halo-current forces up to 50 MN demand mitigation hardware [2].
- **SPI mitigation modeling:** multi-injector SPI increases impurity assimilation roughly with injector count while reducing toroidal radiation peaking; injection geometry (top vs. midplane) strongly affects assimilation via driven poloidal rotation [8]. Runaway-electron modeling for ITER SPI spans the full TQ-onset criterion space (early vs. late onset) to bracket RE current conversion [6].

Formally, the control problem is a race between the Rutherford growth time of the 2/1 island (tens of ms once super-threshold) and the PCS latency (detection + actuator response). The empirical record shows the race is winnable: preemptive ECCD never lets the island nucleate [4], and FRNN-class predictors buy the tens of ms that SPI needs [1][6].

## 6 Limitations

The chain has weak links that honest reactor design must confront. **Prediction transfer** remains fragile: the random-forest study showed the most predictive signals differ markedly between C-Mod, DIII-D, and EAST [3], so FRNN's DIII-D→JET success [1] does not guarantee DIII-D→ITER transfer to a burning plasma with alpha-particle physics, tungsten walls, and ELM-suppressed regimes absent from the training distribution. **ECCD power economics** are sobering: megawatts of electron-cyclotron power spent preemptively on NTM suppression are megawatts not heating the plasma, and ITER's 2/1 stabilization at reactor β_N remains to be demonstrated at full field and current [4]. **SPI assimilation physics** carries order-unity uncertainties — fragment size distributions, drift, and TQ-onset criteria bracket rather than predict RE conversion [6][8]. **Stellarators**, the main alternative, sidestep disruptions by eliminating the plasma current (no current-driven kinks or tearing modes) but pay with 3D coil complexity and neoclassical transport challenges; the Wendelstein 7-X program is the empirical counterpoint, though a reactor-scale stellarator remains unbuilt. Finally, **burning-plasma effects** — alpha-driven Alfvén eigenmodes, self-heating nonlinearity, tritium inventory constraints — lie outside the validated domain of every predictor and controller discussed here.

## 7 Conclusion

Tokamak plasma control at reactor scale is a solved-in-principle, unfinished-in-practice engineering science. The equilibrium theory (Grad–Shafranov), the stability taxonomy (kink/tearing/ELM), and the empirical operating boundaries give us a map of where not to go; deep-learning predictors (FRNN) and interpretable classifiers give us headlights, with cross-machine generalization demonstrated but not yet proven for burning plasmas [1][3]; real-time ECCD control with centimeter-accurate *q*-surface alignment gives us steering, demonstrated to full suppression of 3/2 and 2/1 NTMs including in ITER-relevant scenarios [4][5]; and shattered pellet injection gives us airbags, designed into ITER and SPARC with 3D MHD modeling guiding injector count and geometry [6][7][8]. SPARC's conservative high-field design point [2] and ITER's integrated DMS reflect the same lesson: at reactor scale, *avoidance* (stable operating point + prediction + active control) and *mitigation* (SPI + RE control) must be layered, because no single layer meets the "handful of disruptions per lifetime" requirement alone. The next decisive experiments — SPARC's first plasma at reactor-relevant field, ITER's demonstration of ECCD NTM suppression at 15 MA, and closed-loop FRNN-to-SPI control — will determine whether the control stack scales from today's machines to the burning-plasma era.

title: Quantified Boolean Formula Solving: QCDCL, Expansion, and Dependency Schemes
abstract: Quantified Boolean formulas (QBFs) extend propositional logic with universal and existential quantification, yielding a PSPACE-complete decision problem with direct applications in planning, reactive synthesis, and bounded model checking. This thesis surveys the two dominant paradigms of modern QBF solving: **quantified conflict-driven clause learning (QCDCL)**, the search-based approach exemplified by DepQBF, and **expansion-based solving**, exemplified by RAReQS and its counterexample-guided abstraction refinement lineage. We develop the proof-theoretic foundations of both — Q-resolution and its extensions (long-distance resolution, QU-resolution) versus ∀Exp+Res and the IR-calculus family — and explain their exponential separations. We examine **dependency schemes**, which relax strict prefix ordering inside QCDCL and preprocessing, present generalized QCDCL with incompleteness-tolerant axiom rules, and treat preprocessing (blocked clause elimination in bloqqer, QRAT proof logging). A substantial section covers **strategy extraction and certificates**: how Q-resolution refutations yield decision-list strategies for universal variables, and how true instances produce Skolem certificates. body:
# Quantified Boolean Formula Solving: QCDCL, Expansion, and Dependency Schemes

## Abstract

Quantified Boolean formulas (QBFs) extend propositional logic with universal and existential quantification, yielding a PSPACE-complete decision problem with direct applications in planning, reactive synthesis, and bounded model checking. This thesis surveys the two dominant paradigms of modern QBF solving: **quantified conflict-driven clause learning (QCDCL)**, the search-based approach exemplified by DepQBF, and **expansion-based solving**, exemplified by RAReQS and its counterexample-guided abstraction refinement lineage. We develop the proof-theoretic foundations of both — Q-resolution and its extensions (long-distance resolution, QU-resolution) versus ∀Exp+Res and the IR-calculus family — and explain their exponential separations. We examine **dependency schemes**, which relax strict prefix ordering inside QCDCL and preprocessing, present generalized QCDCL with incompleteness-tolerant axiom rules, and treat preprocessing (blocked clause elimination in bloqqer, QRAT proof logging). A substantial section covers **strategy extraction and certificates**: how Q-resolution refutations yield decision-list strategies for universal variables, and how true instances produce Skolem certificates. We close with QBFEVAL competition evidence and open problems in DQBF and DQRAT verification. The central claim: no single paradigm dominates; progress depends on principled hybridisation guided by dependency analysis.

## 1 Introduction

The success of propositional SAT solvers over the past two decades has repeatedly inspired attempts to lift conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) to harder logics. The most natural first step is the *quantified* Boolean formula: variables are bound by blocks of universal and existential quantifiers in a fixed prefix, and the resulting validity problem is PSPACE-complete [8]. QBF is the canonical encoding language for problems with adversarial or uncontrollable environment behaviour — conditional planning under uncertainty [9], reactive synthesis from temporal specifications, equivalence checking of partial designs, and conformant verification tasks.

Two architectural philosophies now dominate. **QCDCL** (quantified CDCL) generalizes DPLL+CDCL: decisions must respect the quantifier prefix, propagation is QBF-aware (unit and pure literal detection), conflicts yield learned clauses via *Q-resolution*, and satisfying leaves yield learned *cubes* via dual reasoning [1,2]. **Expansion-based solving**, by contrast, eliminates universal variables by instantiation — a formula ∀u.φ(u) is equivalent to φ(0) ∧ φ(1) — producing a propositional formula handed to a SAT oracle; refinements such as counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) avoid naive exponential blowup [4,5]. The two families are not merely engineering choices: they correspond to **mutually incomparable proof systems**, Q-resolution versus ∀Exp+Res, with exponential separations in both directions established by Janota and Marques-Silva [7].

This thesis is organized as follows. Section 2 fixes notation and reviews the core calculi: Q-resolution, long-distance resolution, QU-resolution, and the expansion hierarchy (∀Exp+Res, IR-calc, IRM-calc). Section 3 describes the methodology: how the thesis was developed from solver sources, benchmarks, and proof-complexity literature. Section 4 deep-dives into QCDCL engineering (generalized axioms, dynamic blocked clause elimination), expansion solvers (RAReQS, QESTO), dependency schemes (standard, triangle, quadrangle, resolution-path), and certificates via strategy extraction. Section 5 presents empirical evidence from QBFEVAL competitions and proof-theoretic separations. Section 6 discusses limitations — preprocessing soundness under dependency schemes, certificate size blowup, and portfolio fragility. Section 7 concludes with research directions including DQBF and DQRAT-based verification.

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Syntax, semantics, and complexity

A *quantified Boolean formula* in prenex conjunctive normal form (PCNF) is written Π.φ, where Π = Q₁X₁ … QₙXₙ is the quantifier prefix (each Qᵢ ∈ {∃, ∀}) and φ is a propositional CNF matrix. Truth is defined recursively: ∃X.ψ is true iff some instantiation of X makes ψ true; ∀X.ψ is true iff ψ holds under *all* assignments to X. Deciding QBF truth is PSPACE-complete [8]; even the two-level ∃∀ fragment is Σ₂^P-complete.

For solvers, assignments must be *QCDCL assignments*: decisions follow prefix order, while propagated literals (unit/pure) may violate it [6]. A clause is *conflicting* under QBF-specific rules involving universal reduction; dually, a *cube* can be *satisfying* under symmetric conditions.

### 2.2 Q-resolution and its extensions

**Q-resolution** (Kleine Büning, Karpinski, Flögel, 1995) is the calculus underlying QCDCL, with two rules: **resolution** on an existential pivot (the resolvent must not be tautological) and **∀-reduction**, which deletes a universal literal u from a clause when every existential literal in the clause is quantified *before* u. Q-resolution polynomially simulates DPLL-based QBF search [1].

Three important extensions sharpen the picture:

1. **Long-distance resolution (LD-Q-Res)** [1,2]: resolution steps may merge complementary universal literals u, ¬u into the special literal u* when u is quantified *after* the pivot. Zhang and Malik showed this is exactly what conflict-driven learning in QBF needs [1].
2. **QU-resolution** [3]: universal variables may serve as resolution pivots. QU-Res is exponentially stronger than Q-Res, yet historically under-exploited inside QCDCL — DepQBF 6.0 harnesses it only partially via generalized axioms [3].
3. **Generalized Q-resolution axioms** [6]: instead of requiring φ[A] = ⊥ (resp. ⊤) under the current assignment, any *sound but incomplete* decision procedure may certify (un)satisfiability of φ[A], yielding a learned clause (gen-cl-init) or cube (gen-cu-init). This single mechanism integrates SAT-solver abstractions, expansion-based sub-solvers (Nenofex), and dynamic blocked clause elimination into one QCDCL loop [3,6].

### 2.3 Expansion-based proof systems

∀**Exp+Res** [7] refutes a QBF in two stages: (i) fully expand every universal variable — ∀u.φ becomes φ[u↦0] ∧ φ[u↦1] with fresh annotated copies x^α of each existential x depending on the universal assignment α; (ii) refute the resulting propositional formula by ordinary resolution. The annotation discipline is the subtle part: x^α and x^β are *distinct* variables unless the assignments α, β agree on all universals quantified before x. The **IR-calculus** (instantiation + resolution) and its merge-map extension **IRM-calc** [10] generalize this idea, allowing partial instantiations annotated with partial assignments and *merge* maps that unify compatible annotations.

> **Theorem:** (Janota–Marques-Silva [7]) ∀Exp+Res p-simulates *tree-like* Q-resolution but does *not* p-simulate unrestricted Q-resolution. Conversely, Q-resolution does not p-simulate ∀Exp+Res: parity-like formulas separate the systems.

### 2.4 Dependency schemes

The *standard* dependency relation x <_Π y declares every outer variable dependent on every inner one, but this is coarser than necessary. **Dependency schemes** compute safe over-approximations of true semantic dependence, permitting decision reordering inside QCDCL, stronger ∀-reduction, and more aggressive preprocessing.

The hierarchy runs from the **standard** and **triangle** relations (Samer–Szeider) through **quadrangle** dependencies — computable via biconnected components — up to the **resolution-path** dependency, the strongest efficiently characterizable relation [11]. In DQBF, where Henkin-style dependencies are explicit in the input, naive transplantation of QBF dependency schemes becomes *incomplete* — soundness meets incompleteness at the DQBF boundary [12].

### 2.5 Preprocessing: bloqqer, QBCE, QRAT

Modern QBF solving is unthinkable without preprocessing. **Bloqqer** implements *quantified blocked clause elimination* (QBCE): a clause C is blocked on literal l if every resolvent of C on l is a tautology; blocked clauses are satisfiability-preserving removable [13]. Bloqqer additionally performs (bounded) universal expansion, failed-literal detection, and equivalence reasoning, and it can *solve* many instances outright. Crucially, bloqqer logs **QRAT proofs** of every transformation, checkable by QRAT-trim — preprocessing is no longer a trusted black box. Its successor ideas appear in **QRATPre+** (strong redundancy via the QRAT⁺ system) and **HQSpre** [14].

---

## 3 Methodology

This thesis was developed in three passes: a literature pass over the solver lineage (Zhang–Malik [1], the DepQBF series [3,6], the expansion lineage from AReQS to RAReQS [4,5]); a proof-complexity pass (∀Exp+Res [7], IR-calc [10], strategy extraction [2], dependency schemes [11,12]); and an empirical pass over QBFEVAL reports [14] and the QBFLIB suite. Solver engineering is presented as the algorithmic shadow of a calculus, with exponential separations treated as explanations of benchmark complementarity. **Citations are primary sources only**; the empirical section synthesizes published competition data, with claims qualified by benchmark-family dependence.

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 QCDCL: the search-based engine room

QCDCL generalizes the CDCL loop with two asymmetries that have no SAT analogue [1,3,6]: decisions respect the prefix while propagation (QBCP) need not, and *both conflicts and solutions are learned* — a conflict yields a clause by Q-resolution over the implication graph, while a *solution* yields a *cube* by dual term resolution. The solver maintains a clause database *and* a cube database, terminating on the empty clause or the empty cube.

The Zhang–Malik solver introduced *long-distance* resolvents to keep learned clauses asserting, and the *symmetric* treatment of satisfaction and conflict [1]. DepQBF refined this into a full QCDCL with dependency-aware reduction: with a dependency scheme D, ∀-reduction may delete u from a clause when no existential literal *D-dependent* on u remains, which shortens learned clauses and prunes the search [3].

```python
# Sketch: QCDCL main loop with generalized axioms (after Lonsing & Egly)
def qcdcl(phi):
    A = {}            # current partial assignment (QCDCL assignment)
    while True:
        status = qbcp(phi, A)          # unit + pure literal propagation
        if status == CONFLICT:
            C = analyze_conflict(phi, A)   # Q-resolution over implication graph
            if C == EMPTY_CLAUSE: return UNSAT
            learn_clause(C); backjump(A, C)
        elif status == SOLUTION:
            K = analyze_solution(phi, A)   # dual: cube learning
            if K == EMPTY_CUBE: return SAT
            learn_cube(K); backjump(A, K)
        elif incomplete_oracle(phi, A) == UNSAT:   # generalized axiom [6]
            learn_clause(gen_cl_init(A))
            backjump(A, ...)
        elif incomplete_oracle(phi, A) == SAT:
            learn_cube(gen_cu_init(A))
            backjump(A, ...)
        else:
            decide(phi, A)             # prefix-ordered decision
```

The generalized-axiom view of DepQBF 6.0 is the most important advance: it turns QCDCL from a fixed calculus into a *framework* in which arbitrary sound oracles (SAT abstractions, Nenofex expansion calls, dynamic QBCE checks) contribute lemmas, while Q-resolution remains the glue [6].

### 4.2 Expansion-based solving: RAReQS, QESTO, and CEGAR

Expansion attacks the universal quantifiers directly. The naive rule — replace ∀u.φ by φ[u↦0] ∧ φ[u↦1] — is complete but exponential. **RAReQS** (Recursive Abstraction Refinement QBF Solver) [5] avoids full expansion via CEGAR: maintain a propositional abstraction at the outermost level, ask a SAT solver for a candidate assignment, recursively check it against the inner subformula, and refine the abstraction with each counterexample. **QESTO** [4] restructures the same idea around *clause selection variables*: one SAT formula per quantification level, with learning anchored in the SAT solver's own conflict analysis. On QBFLIB benchmarks QESTO solved 133/276 instances versus DepQBF's 128 and RAReQS's 129 under identical conditions, while dominating the 2QBF track (53/65) [4].

> **Theorem:** (Soundness of recursive CEGAR) Each refinement step of RAReQS preserves the set of winning strategies of the existential player; the algorithm terminates with a correct SAT/UNSAT verdict because every counterexample eliminates at least one candidate from a finite candidate space [5].

Expansion's Achilles' heel is formulas whose refutations inherently need *dag-like* Q-resolution reasoning (e.g., pigeonhole-style counting under quantifiers): the ∀Exp+Res lower bounds bite exactly there [7]. Conversely, parity-flavoured formulas that are exponentially hard for Q-Res fall easily to expansion — the empirical complementarity is a theorem, not an accident.

### 4.3 Dependency schemes: from prefix order to true dependence

The standard dependency relation is brutally conservative: in ∃x₁…xₙ∀z∃a₁…aₙ, every xᵢ is declared dependent on z even when the matrix never connects them. Dependency schemes recover the lost freedom. The main relations, ordered by strength (fewer declared dependencies = stronger scheme):

| Scheme | Idea | Computability |
|---|---|---|
| Standard D^std | prefix order | trivial |
| Triangle D^△ | resolution-path of length ≤ 2 (Samer–Szeider) | polytime |
| Quadrangle D^quad | biconnected-component analysis of implication structure [11] | polytime |
| Resolution-path D^rrs | full resolution-path connectivity [11] | polytime (prototype costly) |

A scheme D is *sound* for a calculus if replacing <_Π by D in ∀-reduction and decision ordering preserves refutational soundness. The resolution-path scheme is the strongest known sound relation for Q-Res; whether it admits an efficient incremental implementation remains open [11]. In DQBF (dependency QBF), where Henkin-style dependencies are explicit in the input, Beyersdorff et al. showed that naive transplantation of QBF dependency schemes becomes *incomplete* — soundness meets incompleteness at the DQBF boundary [12]. This is not a defect but a deep fact: dependency is semantic, and calculi approximate it differently.

Practically, DepQBF's dependency-aware ∀-reduction is one of its signature advantages: learned clauses shrink because universal literals with no dependent existential literals vanish [3].

### 4.4 Certificates and strategy extraction

A solver's verdict is only as trustworthy as its certificate. For *false* QBFs, Q-resolution refutations support **strategy extraction**: from a refutation π of Π.φ one computes, in time polynomial in |π|, a *winning strategy* for the universal player — a function fᵤ per universal u mapping outer existential assignments to a Boolean value [2].

> **Theorem:** (Balabanov–Jiang [2]) Given a Q-Res refutation π of a false QBF φ, there is a winning universal strategy in which each fᵤ is representable as a *decision list* of size polynomial in |π|.

Decision lists — "if t₁ then c₁ else if t₂ then c₂ …" — are a weak computational model (subsumed by small circuits), and this weakness is a *feature*: it yields proof-complexity lower bounds. If every universal winning strategy for a formula family must compute a function outside the extraction model's power (e.g., parity outside AC⁰), then no short Q-Res refutation exists. Beyersdorff, Chew, and Janota used exactly this technique to prove the exponential lower bound for parity formulas in Q-Res, separating Q-Res from ∀Exp+Res [10]. The hierarchy generalizes: C-Frege + ∀red admits extraction into C-decision lists, giving a uniform lower-bound machine for strong QBF systems [10].

For *true* QBFs the dual certificate is a set of *Skolem functions* (existential strategies). DepQBF's QRPCert pipeline extracts AIGER circuits from Q-resolution proofs and validates them with an independent checker; on QBFEVAL-derived suites, certificates were extracted for over 90% of solved instances and over 80% validated [2]. Certificate validation remains the expensive step, which motivates DQRAT-based proof logging that unifies preprocessing and solving traces [12].

### 4.5 Preprocessing as proof: bloqqer, QBCE, and QRAT

Preprocessing in QBF is far more aggressive than in SAT, because quantifiers enable simplifications with no propositional analogue. **Quantified blocked clause elimination (QBCE)** [13] removes a clause C blocked on literal l when all Q-resolvents on l are tautologies; the quantified version must additionally respect ∀-reduction side conditions. Bloqqer layers QBCE with:

- **Bounded universal expansion** (the ∀Exp rule applied to small universal blocks),
- **Failed-literal detection** (probing assignments, SAT- or abstraction-based),
- **Equivalent-literal substitution and variable elimination** adapted to prefix constraints.

The striking engineering fact is that bloqqer *solves* a large fraction of QBFEVAL instances before any solver runs. Its QRAT proof logging was pioneering: every elimination step is justified in the QRAT proof system so that QRAT-trim can independently verify the transformation chain. **QRATPre+** [14] pushes further with strong redundancy properties (QRAT⁺) orthogonal to QBCE, and experiments show preprocessing order matters: QRATPre+ *before* bloqqer outperforms the reverse on most solvers.

A subtle interaction deserves emphasis: preprocessing under *dependency schemes* can be unsound if the scheme used by the preprocessor and the solver disagree. The certification stack (QRP → QRAT → DQRAT) is the community's answer — a single proof format expressive enough to log expansion, resolution, *and* dependency-aware steps — but full solver support for advanced dependency schemes in certificates is still listed as future work [2,12].

---

## 5 Empirical Results / Formal Analysis

### 5.1 Competition evidence: QBFEVAL and the portfolio effect

The QBFEVAL series (annual since the early 2000s, using the QBFLIB suite) consistently shows **no dominant solver**. Representative data points from the published literature:

- On QBFLIB application benchmarks with bloqqer preprocessing, QCDCL with *dynamic* QBCE (eager blocked-clause elimination inside the search, implemented in DepQBF) substantially outperformed traditional QCDCL and was competitive with expansion solvers; dynamic QBCE yields a variant of cube learning exponentially stronger than the traditional method [13].
- QRATPre+ preprocessing studies on QBFEVAL'18 instances: CAQE rose from 151 to 211 solved instances with preprocessing; DepQBF from 149 to 165 — while bloqqer-first pipelines pushed CAQE to 269 [14]. The lesson is twofold: preprocessing is the largest single performance lever, and its interaction with the downstream proof system is non-trivial.
- The QESTO evaluation [4] (276 QBFLIB + 65 2QBF instances, 800 s timeout): expansion/CEGAR solvers (Qesto 133, RAReQS 129) edged QCDCL (DepQBF 128) on general instances and dominated 2QBF (Qesto 53 vs DepQBF 30) — matching the theory that low-alternation formulas favour expansion.

### 5.2 Formal separations: the proof-complexity map

The empirically observed complementarity is underwritten by theorems [7,10]:

| Separation | Witness family | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| Q-Res does not p-simulate ∀Exp+Res | parity / XOR formulas | expansion wins |
| ∀Exp+Res does not p-simulate Q-Res | pigeonhole / counting formulas | search wins |
| LD-Q-Res exponentially stronger than Q-Res | formulas needing long-distance steps | — |
| QU-Res exponentially stronger than Q-Res | universal-pivot formulas [3] | — |
| ∀Exp+Res p-simulates *tree-like* Q-Res | — | tree search ⊆ expansion |
| IR-calc / IRM-calc unify both | — | strictly stronger than each |

Strategy extraction converts these separations into *lower-bound technology* [2,10].

### 5.3 Applications

QBF solving earns its keep in domains where the ∃∀ alternation is intrinsic: **planning** (conditional/conformant planning compiles to ∃ plan ∀ contingencies; Rintanen's benchmarks remain a QBFLIB staple [9]), **reactive synthesis and verification** (strategy extraction *is* program synthesis — extracted Herbrand/Skolem functions are the controller), and **formal verification** (equivalence checking of partial designs). In each case the certificate is the deliverable, which is why the extraction machinery of Section 4.4 is not ornamental.

---

## 6 Limitations

1. **Portfolio fragility.** The state of the art is a *portfolio* of mutually incomparable solvers with heuristic per-instance selection. The exponential separations guarantee complementarity — and guarantee that any single solver family fails catastrophically on some structured family.
2. **Certificate cost.** Proof logging and validation can dominate runtime; DQRAT promises unification but solver support is incomplete, and dependency-scheme-aware certification is still future work [2,12].
3. **Preprocessing soundness under schemes.** Aggressive preprocessing interacts subtly with dependency schemes, and pipeline order (QRATPre+ vs bloqqer vs HQSpre) changes results unpredictably [14].
4. **Expansion blowup on deep prefixes.** CEGAR tames but does not eliminate exponential worst cases; dense universal blocks with many alternations still defeat RAReQS-style recursion, while QCDCL's prefix-ordered search handles them structurally.
5. **DQBF gap.** Dependency schemes sound for QBF become incomplete for DQBF [12], and certified DQBF solving is in its infancy.
6. **Benchmark bias.** QBFLIB over-represents certain encodings; solver rankings are encoding-sensitive, and preprocessing can mask the underlying calculus strength being measured.

---

## 7 Conclusion

QBF solving has matured from a single-paradigm field into a *proof-complexity-guided engineering discipline*. The central insight of the last fifteen years is that QCDCL and expansion are not competing implementations of one idea but realizations of **incomparable proof systems** — Q-resolution (with its long-distance and universal extensions) versus ∀Exp+Res and the IR-calculus family — and that their empirical complementarity on QBFEVAL benchmarks is a theorem, not an accident [7,10].

Three threads will shape the next decade. First, **dependency schemes** offer the most principled route to hybrid vigour: by computing true variable dependence, they let search-based solvers borrow expansion's freedom (out-of-order decisions, aggressive reduction) without leaving the Q-resolution proof system [3,11]. Second, **certification** must catch up with solving: DQRAT-based proof logging unifying preprocessing, expansion, and dependency-aware resolution is the prerequisite for trustworthy deployment in synthesis and verification [2,12]. Third, the **DQBF frontier** forces a re-examination of every soundness argument built on prefix order — an opportunity to rebuild QBF solving on semantic rather than syntactic foundations.

---

body:
# Oblivious Transfer Extension and Garbled Circuits: IKNP, Half-Gates, and Malicious-Secure Two-Party Computation

## Abstract

Secure two-party computation (2PC) lets two mutually distrustful parties evaluate any function over private inputs, revealing only the output. Yao's garbled circuits [1] have been the dominant constant-round approach since 1986, but practicality was long blocked by oblivious transfer (OT): each evaluator input bit required a public-key OT, and naive garbling cost four ciphertexts per gate. This thesis treats the two breakthroughs that made garbled circuits practical: **oblivious transfer extension** — IKNP [2] and KK13 [3] — which amortizes arbitrarily many OTs over a handful of base OTs using only symmetric cryptography, and the **half-gates** optimization [4], which garbles AND gates with two ciphertexts while keeping XOR gates free. We develop the IKNP matrix protocol and the half-gates construction in full technical detail, trace the ascent to malicious security through actively-secure OT extension [5, 6], authenticated garbling [7], and MASCOT [10], analyze the half-gates lower bound and its circumvention [8], and benchmark modern frameworks — demonstrating million-gate malicious-secure 2PC at seconds-scale latency.

## 1 Introduction

The problem of *secure computation* is among the oldest in modern cryptography. In 1982, Yao posed the millionaires' problem: two parties wish to determine whose fortune is larger without revealing anything else [1]. Four years later he sketched the garbled-circuit protocol — encrypt the truth table of every gate, hand the evaluator exactly the keys corresponding to the true inputs via oblivious transfer, and let the evaluator decrypt gate-by-gate toward the output. Conceptually complete, the construction languished for two decades as impractical: OT required expensive public-key operations per input bit, and the naive garbling required four ciphertexts per gate.

Two independent revolutions changed this calculus. The first, **OT extension** [2], exploited the observation that OT is *complete* for MPC yet symmetric primitives cannot realize OT alone in a black-box sense — but they *can* amplify it. IKNP showed that *k* base OTs (where *k* is the security parameter) suffice to produce *n* effective OTs for arbitrary *n*, at the amortized cost of a few hash evaluations per OT. The second revolution concerned the garbling itself: free-XOR made XOR gates costless, and half-gates [4] reduced AND gates from three ciphertexts to two — a reduction later proven optimal within the natural class of linear garbling schemes, then circumvented by slicing-and-dicing techniques that beat the lower bound [8].

This thesis is organized as follows. Section 2 establishes the foundations: Yao's protocol, point-and-permute, free-XOR, and OT. Section 3 develops the core methodology — the IKNP matrix protocol, the KK13 refinement, actively-secure variants [5, 6], and half-gates. Section 4 deep-dives into correlation robustness, the half-gates lower bound and its circumvention, the GMW-versus-garbled-circuit design space, and authenticated garbling [7] with MASCOT [10]. Section 5 presents empirical benchmarks; Sections 6–7 discuss limitations and conclude.

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Yao's Garbled Circuits

In Yao's protocol [1], the *garbler* $P_1$ associates each wire $w$ of a Boolean circuit with two random $\kappa$-bit labels $W_w^0, W_w^1$, one per semantic value. For a gate $g$ with input wires $a, b$ and output wire $c$ computing $g: \{0,1\}^2 \to \{0,1\}$, the garbler produces four doubly-encrypted ciphertexts:

$$T_{i,j} = \mathrm{Enc}_{W_a^i, W_b^j}(W_c^{g(i,j)}) \quad i, j \in \{0,1\}$$

and randomly permutes them. The evaluator $P_2$ obtains the labels for $P_1$'s input wires directly, the labels for its *own* input wires via OT, and then decrypts exactly one row per gate, propagating labels forward until the output labels are revealed and decoded. Security against a semi-honest evaluator follows from the semantic security of the encryption: exactly one row decrypts, revealing only the output label. The **point-and-permute** optimization attaches a random select bit $p_w$ to each wire; rows are ordered by permute bits so the evaluator performs exactly one decryption per gate instead of trial-decrypting four rows.

### 2.2 Free-XOR and the Cost Model

Kolesnikov and Schneider observed that if all wire labels satisfy a global relation $W_w^1 = W_w^0 \oplus R$ for a single secret offset $R \in \{0,1\}^\kappa$, then an XOR gate can be evaluated *for free*: the output labels are defined as $W_c^0 = W_a^0 \oplus W_b^0$ and $W_c^1 = W_c^0 \oplus R$, with no ciphertext transmitted and no cryptographic operation at evaluation [4]. Communication is therefore dominated by AND gates, and the entire subsequent literature is an effort to shrink the per-AND-gate cost: 4 ciphertexts (Yao) → 3 (with free-XOR) → 2 (half-gates) → $1.5\kappa + 5$ bits (Rosulek–Roy [8]).

### 2.3 Oblivious Transfer

A 1-out-of-2 OT lets a sender with messages $(x_0, x_1)$ deliver $x_b$ to a receiver holding choice bit $b$, such that the sender learns nothing about $b$ and the receiver learns nothing about $x_{1-b}$. OT is *complete* for secure computation: given OT, any efficiently computable function admits a secure protocol. Public-key OT protocols (e.g., Naor–Pinkas) cost a few modular exponentiations per transfer — acceptable for a handful of OTs, catastrophic for the millions of input labels a large garbled circuit requires. OT extension [2] resolves this by shifting the per-OT cost into the symmetric-key regime.

---

## 3 Methodology

### 3.1 The IKNP Protocol in Detail

The IKNP construction [2] is best understood as a clever matrix game. Let $\kappa$ be the computational security parameter and suppose the parties want $m$ instances of 1-out-of-2 OT on $\ell$-bit strings.

1. The **receiver** samples a random $m \times \kappa$ binary matrix $T$ and holds choice bits $r = (r_1, \dots, r_m)$. Define $t_j$ as the $j$-th column of $T$ (an $m$-bit string).
2. The **sender** samples a random $\kappa$-bit string $s = (s_1, \dots, s_\kappa)$.
3. The parties execute $\kappa$ *base OTs in the reversed direction*: in the $j$-th base OT, the receiver (acting as sender) offers the pair $(t_j,\, t_j \oplus r)$, and the sender (acting as receiver) inputs choice bit $s_j$, obtaining $q_j = t_j \oplus (r \cdot s_j)$.
4. Assemble the matrix $Q$ whose $j$-th column is $q_j$. For the $i$-th row:
   $$q_i = \begin{cases} t_i & \text{if } r_i = 0 \\ t_i \oplus s & \text{if } r_i = 1 \end{cases}$$
   where $t_i$ is the $i$-th row of $T$.
5. For the $i$-th extended OT, the sender defines its two "messages" via a correlation-robust hash $H$:
   $$y_{i,0} = H(i, q_i), \qquad y_{i,1} = H(i, q_i \oplus s).$$
   The sender masks its real inputs $x_{i,0}, x_{i,1}$ as $(x_{i,0} \oplus y_{i,0},\, x_{i,1} \oplus y_{i,1})$ and transmits both.
6. The receiver, knowing $t_i$ and $r_i$, computes $y_{i, r_i} = H(i, t_i)$ and unmasks $x_{i, r_i}$.

The crucial identity is $q_i \oplus (r_i \cdot s) = t_i$: the sender's two pads are correlated by the secret $s$, while the receiver knows exactly one of them. Security reduces to $H$ being **correlation-robust** — roughly, $H(\cdot, \cdot \oplus s)$ must look random even given oracle access — a notion weaker than a random oracle but still non-standard, discussed further in §4.1.

The amortized cost is $\kappa$ public-key base OTs plus $O(m\kappa)$ bits of communication and $O(m)$ hash evaluations — effectively a few symmetric operations per extended OT [2, 5].

### 3.2 KK13: Short Secrets and 1-out-of-$n$ OT

Kolesnikov and Kumaresan [3] observed that many applications need 1-out-of-$n$ OT (notably private set intersection) with *short* secrets. Their protocol starts from $2\kappa$ 1-out-of-2 base OTs and encodes the receiver's choice using Walsh–Hadamard (WH) codes. The WH code of length $\kappa$ has the property that distinct codewords disagree in exactly $\kappa/2$ positions, which yields 1-out-of-$n$ OTs with communication $O(m \log n)$ rather than the $O(mn)$ of the naive reduction — an asymptotic $O(\log n)$ improvement over IKNP-based approaches for short secrets, and it remains the most efficient semi-honest 1-out-of-$n$ extension known.

### 3.3 Half-Gates: Two Ciphertexts per AND

The half-gates construction [4] decomposes an AND gate $c = a \land b$ into two *half-gates* — AND gates in which the garbler knows one input. Let the global free-XOR offset be $R$, wire labels $W_a^0, W_b^0$, and permute bits $p_a, p_b, p_c$.

**Garbler half-gate.** The garbler knows $a$'s semantic value indirectly through its own choice of the output permute structure; it emits one ciphertext
$$T_G = H(W_a^0) \oplus H(W_a^1) \oplus p_b R,$$
which allows the evaluator — who knows $W_a$ (one of the two labels) — to compute $W_G = H(W_a) \oplus p_a T_G$, a label encoding $a \land p_b$.

**Evaluator half-gate.** Symmetrically, using the evaluator's known label $W_b$:
$$T_E = H(W_b^0) \oplus H(W_b^1) \oplus W_a^0 \oplus p_c R,$$
yielding $W_E = H(W_b) \oplus p_b (T_E \oplus W_a)$, encoding $p_a \land b$.

The final output label is $W_c = W_G \oplus W_E$. The evaluator performs *two* hash evaluations per AND gate instead of one — the price of the bandwidth reduction. Zahur, Rosulek, and Evans proved this optimal: any garbling scheme in the *linear* class (capturing all known practical techniques, where ciphertexts are affine combinations of hash outputs) requires $2\kappa$ bits per AND gate [4].

```python
# Half-gate garbling (simplified; H = fixed-key AES hash)
def garble_and_gate(Wa0, Wb0, pa, pb, pc, R):
    Wa1 = xor(Wa0, R); Wb1 = xor(Wb0, R)
    T_G = xor(H(Wa0), H(Wa1), mul(pb, R))          # garbler half-gate
    T_E = xor(H(Wb0), H(Wb1), Wa0, mul(pc, R))     # evaluator half-gate
    return (T_G, T_E)                              # 2 ciphertexts total

def eval_and_gate(Wa, Wb, pa, pb, T_G, T_E):
    W_G = xor(H(Wa), mul(pa, T_G))
    W_E = xor(H(Wb), mul(pb, xor(T_E, Wa)))
    return xor(W_G, W_E)
```

### 3.4 Actively-Secure OT Extension

Semi-honest OT extension is insufficient against malicious adversaries: a corrupt receiver in IKNP can choose a non-random matrix $T$ to mount *selective-failure* attacks, learning the sender's secret $s$ bit-by-bit from aborts. ALSZ13 [5] added consistency checks to IKNP, giving the first practical maliciously-secure OT extension. KOS15 [6] achieved *optimal* overhead: the sender verifies a random linear combination of the receiver's matrix rows, adding only $O(\kappa)$ communication *independent* of the number of extended OTs — now the standard substrate for malicious-secure MPC preprocessing.

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Correlation Robustness and the Random-Permutation Model

The security of IKNP-style extension and half-gates rests on the hash $H$ being *correlation-robust* (for OT) or *circular correlation-robust* (CCR, for garbling) [4]. These notions sit strictly between one-wayness and the random-oracle model: no standard-model construction from one-way functions is known, and practical deployments instantiate $H$ with fixed-key AES (the JustGarble / Bellare-Hoang-Rogaway paradigm), effectively modeling AES as an ideal cipher.

> **Theorem (informal):** If $H$ is circular correlation-robust, then the half-gates garbling scheme satisfies the standard privacy, obliviousness, and authenticity notions for garbling schemes [4].

Recent work has begun to close the foundational gap: Guo et al. showed how to instantiate half-gates in the *standard model* from indistinguishability obfuscation plus one-way functions, via a new notion of *weak* CCR — a feasibility result, but significant given the ongoing NIST effort to standardize garbling. The practical takeaway is unchanged: in the ideal-cipher model, half-gates with AES-NI is both the fastest and the most analyzed choice.

### 4.2 Beating the Lower Bound: Slicing and Dicing

The $2\kappa$ lower bound of [4] applies to *linear* garbling. Rosulek and Roy [8] circumvented it with **slicing and dicing**: wire labels are sliced into halves, and the two halves are processed through separate, carefully correlated sub-protocols. Their scheme garbles an AND gate in $1.5\kappa + 5$ bits while remaining fully free-XOR-compatible — a genuine drop-in replacement for half-gates. The cost is slightly more computation and a more intricate proof, again under CCR-like assumptions. Subsequent work (e.g., Heath's lookup-table garbling) has pushed the constant lower still, but half-gates remains the engineering default because the bandwidth savings of $1.5\kappa$ schemes rarely justify their complexity outside extreme-bandwidth regimes.

| Scheme | AND cost | XOR cost | Assumption | Optimal? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yao (point-and-permute) | $4\kappa$ | $4\kappa$ | PRF | No |
| Free-XOR | $3\kappa$ | $0$ | CCR | No |
| **Half-gates** [4] | **$2\kappa$** | $0$ | CCR | Yes (linear class) |
| Rosulek–Roy [8] | $1.5\kappa+5$ | $0$ | CCR-like | Open |

### 4.3 GMW versus Garbled Circuits: The Round–Bandwidth Tradeoff

The GMW paradigm evaluates the circuit gate-by-gate with interactive multiplication (via OT or Beaver triples), requiring rounds proportional to circuit *depth*; garbled circuits require only a constant number of rounds regardless of depth. OT extension is the hinge on which both swing: GMW consumes one OT per AND gate per evaluation *online*, while Yao's protocol consumes OTs only for the evaluator's *input labels* — the circuit itself is transferred as symmetric ciphertexts.

This yields a clean decision rule used by modern compilers:

- **Low-depth, high-volume circuits** (e.g., AES evaluation, PSI): GMW with OT-based multiplication excels, since per-gate interaction is cheap and parallelism is total.
- **Deep circuits or high-latency networks**: garbled circuits dominate; the entire circuit ships in two rounds.
- **Mixed protocols** (ABY, MOTION): the framework automatically assigns each sub-circuit to the cheaper paradigm, using OT extension as the common preprocessing substrate [5].

Silent-OT techniques such as Ferret [9] push this further: by generating *correlated* OT pseudorandomly from short seeds (a puncturable-PRF/LPN-style expansion), communication per OT drops to a handful of bits, making even GMW-style per-gate OTs affordable at scale.

### 4.4 The Ascent to Malicious Security

Semi-honest garbling is broken by a malicious garbler who garbles a *different* circuit than agreed. The classical countermeasure is **cut-and-choose**: garble $s$ copies, open a random subset for verification, evaluate the rest, and take a majority — at the cost of a statistical factor of $\approx 3s$ in communication.

Wang, Ranellucci, and Katz [7] replaced cut-and-choose with **authenticated garbling**, achieving malicious security with a *single* garbled circuit. The blueprint:

1. **Function-independent preprocessing.** The parties generate *leaky* AND triples (authenticated shares of $(a, b, ab)$) using OT extension [6], then *bucket* and combine them to eliminate leakage — exactly the SPDZ/MASCOT preprocessing paradigm [10], but over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
2. **Function-dependent phase.** The triples are consumed to produce one garbled circuit whose wire labels carry information-theoretic MACs under a global key $\Delta$ held by the evaluator.
3. **Online phase.** The evaluator evaluates as in the semi-honest protocol; any deviation by the garbler is caught by MAC verification with probability $1 - 2^{-\rho}$ for statistical parameter $\rho = 40$.

MASCOT [10] applies the same OT-based authenticated-triple machinery to *arithmetic* circuits over large fields, giving the fastest known maliciously-secure dishonest-majority MPC for arithmetic workloads. Together, [7] and [10] show that OT extension — once merely a performance trick — has become the *universal preprocessing engine* for malicious-secure MPC.

```python
# KOS-style consistency check (simplified): sender verifies receiver's matrix
def kos_check(Q_rows, s, chi):
    # Q_rows: sender's received rows q_i; chi: random coefficients
    x = xor_all(mul(chi[i], Q_rows[i]) for i in range(m))
    # receiver opens t = xor_all(chi[i] * t_i); check x == t xor (xor of chi[i]*r_i)*s
    return x
```

---

## 5 Empirical Results / Formal Analysis

We summarize published benchmarks from the primary sources, normalized to $\kappa = 128$ and $\rho = 40$ where applicable.

**Half-gates microbenchmarks** [4]. Across AES, SHA, and sorting circuits, half-gates reduced end-to-end time by up to **25%**, bandwidth by up to **33%**, and energy consumption by up to **20%** relative to the best prior free-XOR-compatible scheme — despite doubling the evaluator's hash calls per AND gate, confirming that communication, not computation, is the bottleneck.

**OT extension throughput.** IKNP with ALSZ optimizations [5] generates millions of OTs per second on commodity hardware; the malicious-secure KOS variant [6] adds only small constant overhead. Ferret's silent OT [9] further reduces communication to a few bits per correlated OT.

**Authenticated garbling end-to-end** [7]. The single-circuit authenticated protocol evaluates AES (6,800 AND gates) in the tens of milliseconds LAN setting, within a small factor of semi-honest half-gates — versus the $\approx 40\times$ blowup of naive cut-and-choose at comparable statistical security. MASCOT [10] reports triple generation at rates sufficient for large-scale arithmetic MPC, outperforming prior SHE-based SPDZ preprocessing.

| Workload | Protocol | LAN time (reported) | Communication |
|---|---|---|---|
| AES-128 (6.8k AND) | Half-gates, semi-honest [4] | ~ms | ~170 KB |
| AES-128 | Authenticated garbling [7] | tens of ms | ~1 MB |
| $2^{20}$ OTs | IKNP/ALSZ [5] | ~seconds | ~MBs |
| $2^{20}$ OTs | KOS malicious [6] | ~seconds + small const | +$O(\kappa)$ |

*Formal analysis.* The security theorems compose cleanly: IKNP is secure under correlation-robust hashing [2]; KOS adds malicious security with optimal overhead under the same assumption plus a random oracle for the check [6]; half-gates is private/authentic under CCR [4]; authenticated garbling lifts any such scheme to malicious 2PC with abort [7]. The full stack — KOS OT extension → leaky triples → bucketing → authenticated half-gates — is therefore maliciously secure in the $(\mathcal{F}_{\text{OT}}, \text{RO})$-hybrid model.

---

## 6 Limitations

**Non-standard assumptions.** Every efficiency result in this thesis — IKNP, KK13, half-gates, KOS, authenticated garbling — relies on correlation-robust or circular correlation-robust hashing, notions with no standard-model instantiation from minimal assumptions. The iO-based standard-model instantiation of half-gates is a feasibility result only; practice continues to bet on AES-as-ideal-cipher. A break of fixed-key AES indifferentiability would ripple through the entire stack.

**Post-quantum exposure.** Both OT extension and garbling are symmetric-key-heavy, but the *base OTs* and correlation-robustness reductions are not quantum-safe in deployed form. Post-quantum garbling remains an open standardization problem.

**Malicious security with fairness/guaranteed output** is not achieved: [7] and [10] provide security *with abort*, and a malicious party can deny the honest party output. Stronger notions (identifiable abort, covert security trade-offs) add further cost.

**Communication floor.** Even $1.5\kappa + 5$ bits per AND [8] is far from the intuition that one bit of functionality should cost $O(1)$ bits; whether $\kappa$-dependence per AND gate is inherent remains open.

**Implementation fragility.** The empirical wins assume AES-NI and constant-time code. Side-channel leakage of the global offset $R$ or the MAC key $\Delta$ is catastrophic — failure modes that software benchmarks understate.

## 7 Conclusion

Oblivious transfer extension and garbled circuits form the central spine of practical secure two-party computation. IKNP [2] taught us to amortize public-key cost into symmetric-key abundance; KK13 [3] and the ALSZ/KOS line [5, 6] refined extension into 1-out-of-$n$, maliciously-secure, and eventually *silent* forms [9]; half-gates [4] compressed garbling to its linear optimum of two ciphertexts per AND gate, with Rosulek–Roy [8] showing the bound itself could be sidestepped; and authenticated garbling [7] together with MASCOT [10] lifted the whole edifice to malicious security at near-semi-honest cost.

The trajectory is unmistakable: each generation converts what was once an asymptotic or public-key expense into a symmetric-key or information-theoretic one, and each conversion is then absorbed into preprocessing. The remaining challenges — standard-model correlation robustness, post-quantum garbling, and closing the gap between the $1.5\kappa$ upper bound and any fundamental lower bound — define the research frontier. For the practitioner, the conclusion is simpler: with OT extension and half-gates, malicious-secure two-party computation of million-gate circuits is no longer a research prototype but an engineering choice.

## References

[2] Extending oblivious transfers efficiently — CRYPTO 2003. https://www.iacr.org/archive/crypto2003/27290145/27290145.pdf
[3] Improved OT extension for transferring short secrets — CRYPTO 2013. https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/491
[4] Two halves make a whole: Reducing data transfer in garbled circuits using half gates — EUROCRYPT 2015. https://www.csa.iisc.ac.in/~arpita/GarblingReadingGroup/2014-756-ZRE15%20-%20Two%20Halves%20Make%20a%20Whole%20Reducing%20Data%20Transfer%20in%20Garbled%20Circuits%20using%20Half%20Gates.pdf
[5] More efficient oblivious transfer and extensions for faster secure computation — ACM CCS 2013. https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/552
[6] Actively secure OT extension with optimal overhead — CRYPTO 2015. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-47989-6_35
