body:
# Stacked Borrows and Tree Borrows: Formal Aliasing Models for Unsafe Rust

## Abstract

Rust's ownership system guarantees memory safety for safe code, but `unsafe` blocks manipulate raw pointers beyond the borrow checker — while the optimizer still exploits aliasing assumptions through LLVM `noalias` attributes. A sound optimizer therefore needs an operational definition of which unsafe pointer accesses are legitimate, with violations classified as undefined behavior. This thesis compares the two formal aliasing models built to answer that question: **Stacked Borrows**, which equips each memory location with a *stack* of tagged borrow items governed by retagging and protector semantics, and **Tree Borrows**, which replaces the stack with a *tree* of permissions distinguishing foreign from local accesses. We reconstruct both models' mechanics — tags, validity invariants, protectors, permission lattices — alongside their mechanized soundness proofs in Coq and Rocq, and trace their empirical validation in Miri over the standard library and 30,000 crates. We explain why Tree Borrows rejects 54% fewer real-world tests while preserving nearly all proven optimizations and enabling read–read reordering, and situate both models within the Unsafe Code Guidelines effort and the MiniRust semantics.

---

## 1 Introduction

Rust's ownership and borrowing discipline is among the most consequential ideas in modern language design: affine types and borrow-checked references deliver memory safety and data-race freedom *without* a garbage collector. For safe code the guarantees are enforced statically, and the compiler is entitled to exploit them aggressively. Mutable references `&mut T` are unique; shared references `&T` are immutable. An optimizer that hoists a read of `*x` above a call to an opaque function `f()` is justified by the mere type of `x`: no aliasing write can exist, because the type system would have rejected it.

The difficulty begins at `unsafe`. Raw pointers, unchecked casts, and arbitrary address arithmetic all escape the borrow checker — yet the optimizer keeps going, deriving LLVM `noalias` and `dereferenceable` attributes from reference types regardless. For these optimizations to be *sound*, violations of the aliasing discipline must be classified as **undefined behavior** (UB): the compiler then need only preserve the semantics of UB-free programs [1].

Stacked Borrows, by Jung, Dang, Kang, and Dreyer (POPL 2020) [1], answers with an *operational semantics* for memory accesses: an executable aliasing discipline, implemented in the Miri interpreter, that declares certain pointer-access patterns UB. Mechanized Coq proofs show the discipline justifies the reorderings compilers actually perform, and runs of large parts of the standard library test suite under Miri validate that it admits real-world unsafe code [1]. Jung's dissertation extends the retagging and protector machinery [2]; the "Stacked Borrows 2" notes pin down the precise stack invariants [3].

But Stacked Borrows proved too strict: idiomatic patterns — two-phase borrows, `container_of` pointer arithmetic, interior mutability through raw pointers, certain raw-pointer casts — were flagged as UB, eroding trust in Miri as an arbiter [4]. **Tree Borrows** (Villani, Hostert, Dreyer, Jung; PLDI 2025 [5]) replaces the per-location *stack* with a *tree* of permissions, distinguishes *foreign* from *local* accesses, and rethinks retagging, protectors, and initialization. Over the 30,000 most widely used crates it rejects 54% fewer test cases while retaining most proven optimizations and enabling read–read reordering; it earned a Distinguished Paper Award at PLDI'25 [6], with the full development in Villani's thesis [7].

This thesis reconstructs both models from first principles, compares their mechanics and metatheory, surveys their empirical validation, and situates them in the standardization effort — the Unsafe Code Guidelines working group [8] and the MiniRust semantics — that will decide which rules become *the* definition of Rust.

> **Theorem (Informal, SB soundness):** *Under the Stacked Borrows operational semantics, hoisting a read (resp. write) through a reference across an unknown function call is semantics-preserving for all programs that do not themselves exhibit Stacked Borrows UB [1].*

The remainder of this thesis is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the background: Rust's aliasing guarantees, the role of UB as an optimization license, Miri as executable semantics, and the Unsafe Code Guidelines process. Section 3 describes our methodology: a comparative reconstruction of the two models from the primary sources, grounded in the published mechanizations and evaluation data. Section 4 is the deep dive — retagging and tags, the borrow stack versus the permission tree, protectors and two-phase borrows, validity invariants, and interior mutability. Section 5 presents the empirical and formal results: what each model proves, what each model rejects, and the 54% figure. Section 6 discusses limitations and open questions, and Section 7 concludes.

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Aliasing, optimization, and the meaning of UB

In C, `restrict` and the effective-type rules try to tell the compiler which pointers may alias, but the rules are so subtle that programmers and compiler writers routinely disagree. Rust enforces aliasing discipline *statically* for safe code, so the optimizer's assumptions hold by construction. The open question — occupying the Unsafe Code Guidelines (UCG) working group for years — is what the optimizer may assume about *unsafe* code [8].

The community's answer is operational: define an abstract machine in which certain executions get *stuck* with a UB error, and justify optimizations as refinements preserving the observable behavior of UB-free executions. This "UB as license" reading makes the aliasing model the most load-bearing definition in unsafe Rust — simultaneously a bug-finding oracle, a contract for unsafe authors, and the optimizer's proof obligation.

### 2.2 Miri: executable semantics

The Stacked Borrows project implemented its semantics in **Miri**, an interpreter for Rust MIR that tracks per-location borrow state and reports UB the moment it occurs [9]. Miri runs in the CI of the standard library and many major crates, and a recent POPL paper validates it as "the first tool that can find all de-facto undefined behavior in deterministic Rust programs" [9]. Crucially, Miri supports both models — Stacked Borrows by default, Tree Borrows via `-Zmiri-tree-borrows` [6] — making it the shared experimental apparatus: claims like "54% fewer rejections" are measured by running both instrumented interpreters over the same corpus.

### 2.3 The Unsafe Code Guidelines and MiniRust

The UCG working group maintains the long-running design discussion of what unsafe Rust *means*, including the validity invariants — alignment, non-nullness, initialization — every reference must satisfy at creation [8]. In parallel, **MiniRust** develops a small, precise formal semantics for a Rust fragment, intended as the eventual normative core. The aliasing models slot into MiniRust as the memory-access layer, deliberately separated from evaluation: validity is checked at reference creation while borrow state evolves per access, so the two concerns can be specified and proved about independently [2].

| Concern | Checked when | Owned by |
|---|---|---|
| Validity invariants (aligned, non-null, initialized) | Reference creation / retag | UCG validity discussion [8] |
| Aliasing discipline (stack/tree transitions) | Every memory access | Stacked/Tree Borrows [1][5] |
| Protectors (no invalidation during call) | Function entry/exit | Both models [1][5] |
| Data-race freedom | Concurrent accesses | Borrow checker + model [2] |

### 2.4 What the models must achieve

Any candidate model faces three demands: **strong enough** to justify rustc's actual optimizations, **permissive enough** to accept the unsafe code the ecosystem writes, and **precise enough** for a dynamic checker with comprehensible errors. Stacked Borrows maximized the first and learned, through Miri deployment, that it had sacrificed too much of the second. Tree Borrows rebalances — recovering permissiveness without surrendering the optimizations that matter [4][5].

---

## 3 Methodology

This thesis is a comparative reconstruction, not a new experiment: the empirical results we report are those published by the model authors, and our contribution is to systematize them, verify the internal consistency of the claims across sources, and draw out the implications for unsafe-code authors and for the standardization process.

Our method has four parts. **First**, reconstruct Stacked Borrows' operational rules from the POPL 2020 paper [1], Jung's dissertation [2], and the Stacked Borrows 2 notes [3], cross-checking informal presentations against the mechanized definitions. **Second**, reconstruct Tree Borrows from the PLDI 2025 paper [5], Jung's 2023 announcement [4], the ETH summary [6], and Villani's thesis [7], attending to deliberate divergences (raw-pointer retagging, lazy initialization, the conflicted flag). **Third**, compare along fixed axes — state representation, access checking, function boundaries, two-phase borrows, interior mutability, proven optimizations, measured false-positive rates. **Fourth**, situate both within the UCG validity discussion [8] and Miri validation literature [9], separating answered questions from open ones.

We take the published mechanizations and evaluation corpora at face value but verify every quantitative claim against at least two independent sources.

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Tags and retagging: how permissions are born

Both models share a foundation: every pointer value carries an opaque **tag** naming its borrow, and creating a reference performs a **retag** — conceptually `x = &mut *x` — minting a fresh tag and installing the permission in the model's state [1][3]. The compiler inserts retagging automatically: reference-typed arguments are retagged on entry, every explicit reborrow retags [2]. The tag travels with the pointer *value* in memory; the permission state lives *per location*; the two evolve independently [3][10].

In Stacked Borrows, retagging pushes `(tag, permission)` onto each affected location's stack, popping incompatible items above [3]. In Tree Borrows, it creates a *child node* under the parent's node with a type-determined initial permission [5]. The stack is a total order — every new borrow invalidates everything above; the tree is a partial order whose sibling subtrees evolve independently.

```rust
fn demo() {
    let mut x: i32 = 0;
    let r1: &mut i32 = &mut x;   // retag: fresh tag t1, permission Unique
    let p: *mut i32 = r1 as *mut i32; // raw cast: retagging differs by model!
    let r2: &i32 = &*r1;          // retag: fresh tag t2, SharedReadOnly (SB)
    unsafe { *p = 42; }           // legal? the models disagree — see §4.2
}
```

### 4.2 The borrow stack versus the permission tree

**Stacked Borrows.** Each location owns a stack of items granting `Unique`, `SharedReadWrite`, `SharedReadOnly`, or `Disabled` [3], with strict invariants: above `SharedReadOnly` only more `SharedReadOnly`, and no tag twice [10]. An access is legal only if the pointer's item remains in the stack with compatible permission. Conflicting accesses pop: writing through `Unique` pops `SharedReadOnly` items above it, and touching a popped item is UB. Borrows nest LIFO — using a borrow after a conflicting borrow is an error [1][3].

The stack's elegance is also its brittleness. Consider two-phase borrows — the borrow checker's mechanism for method-call receivers like `vec.push(vec.len())`, where the mutable borrow is created but not *activated* until the call. Stacked Borrows has no notion of an unactivated borrow: every `&mut` retag immediately installs `Unique` and invalidates everything above [4]. Real code that the borrow checker accepts is therefore rejected by Miri. Similarly, casting `&mut T` to `*mut T` downgrades the permission to `SharedReadWrite`, and casting to `*const T` makes the pointer *read-only even if the reference was mutable* — a constant source of confusion, since programmers reasonably expect `*const` vs `*mut` not to affect aliasing [4]. Pointer arithmetic across array elements or struct fields after a field-level retag is likewise UB, because the raw pointer is confined to the type and range it was created with [4].

**Tree Borrows.** Each location keeps a *tree* of permission nodes — `Reserved`, `Active`, `Frozen`, `Disabled` — and accesses are **local** (through the node or its descendants, ↓) or **foreign** (outside its subtree, ↑) [5]. Local accesses strengthen toward `Active`; a foreign write disables; a foreign *read* merely freezes to `Frozen`. Sibling subtrees evolve independently, so a foreign read no longer destroys a mutable borrow — which is exactly what enables the read–read reordering Stacked Borrows cannot justify [5].

Three further design decisions widen the gap:

1. **No retagging on reference-to-raw-pointer casts.** Under TB, a raw pointer simply inherits its parent reference's tag, mutability, and address range. The `*const`-from-`&mut` read-only trap disappears [4].
2. **Lazy initialization of access ranges.** A new reference records an initial range from its type, but accessing outside that range is permitted if the *parent* pointer could access it — checked recursively up to the root. This makes `container_of`-style arithmetic and `extern` types legal [4].
3. **Foreign/local distinction for protectors.** Protectors (see §4.3) are expressed naturally as constraints on foreign accesses rather than stack pops.

| Aspect | Stacked Borrows [1][3] | Tree Borrows [4][5] |
|---|---|---|
| State per location | Stack of `(tag, perm)` items | Tree of permission nodes |
| Permissions | Unique, SharedReadWrite, SharedReadOnly, Disabled | Reserved, Active, Frozen, Disabled |
| Access classification | Granting-item lookup + pops | Foreign (↑) vs local (↓) transitions |
| Foreign read vs `&mut` | Pops / UB | Freezes to `Frozen` |
| Raw-pointer cast | Retagged, range-confined | Inherits parent tag and range |
| Two-phase borrows | Not modeled (UB) | `Reserved` until activation |
| Out-of-range access | UB | Lazy initialization via parent |

> **Theorem (Informal, TB read–read reordering):** *Starting from an arbitrary permission state, executing two consecutive reads through distinct mutable references in either order reaches the same final state; hence the reordering is semantics-preserving [5]. Stacked Borrows admits no such theorem.*

### 4.3 Protectors, two-phase borrows, and the conflicted flag

Retagging alone cannot justify optimizations across *unknown* code: an opaque `f()` might write through a smuggled alias. **Protectors** close the gap — each reference argument is retagged *and protected* on entry, so any access invalidating the protected item (a stack pop, a tree-node disable) is UB for the call's duration [1][2]:

```rust
fn caller(x: &mut i32, f: impl FnOnce()) {
    // retag[fn] x  — x is retagged AND protected on entry
    *x = 42;
    f();        // opaque call: cannot touch x (protector)
    *x = 13;    // optimizer may keep only this write — or only the first
}
```

Since `f` cannot legally invalidate `x`'s item, the compiler may move writes across the call freely — observable behavior of UB-free programs is unchanged [2]. Protectors are the mechanism behind LLVM's `noalias` on reference parameters.

Tree Borrows refines protectors twice. First, a *protected* `&mut` always starts `Reserved`, regardless of interior mutability — activation is deferred until a local write, faithfully modeling two-phase borrows [5]. Second, TB adds the **conflicted** flag: a *foreign read* before the activating local write marks the node conflicted, making the later write UB [5]. Net rule: *for a protected mutable reference, a foreign read plus a local write — in either order — is UB.* This justifies hoisting a write above an unknown call even for never-written references, closing the hole naive "mutable implies writable" reasoning would open [5].

### 4.4 Validity invariants and interior mutability

Aliasing is half the story. The UCG validity discussion separates *bit-level* reference properties — non-null, aligned, initialized — from the access discipline [8]. Subtly, *dereferenceability* is asserted by `Retag`, not by the validity check at assignment: this keeps validity independent of memory state, at the cost of making retag the operation that fails on dangling references [8].

Under Stacked Borrows, `&Cell<T>` retags as `SharedReadOnly`; mutation must flow through the raw-pointer `SharedReadWrite` item derived from the `UnsafeCell`, demanding careful protector handling since protected shared references otherwise forbid writes [2]. Under Tree Borrows, the uniform `Reserved` start extends to interior-mutable types, and the foreign/local distinction lets shared references tolerate exactly the writes `UnsafeCell` exists to permit [5]. The upshot, confirmed in §5: Tree Borrows accepts substantially more interior-mutability idioms.

---

## 5 Empirical Results / Formal Analysis

### What is proven

Stacked Borrows was mechanized in **Coq**: the POPL 2020 paper proves the model justifies moving reads and writes across unknown calls via purely intraprocedural reasoning [1]. Tree Borrows was mechanized in **Rocq**, retains most SB optimizations, and adds read–read reordering [5][6]. One asymmetry: Stacked Borrows justifies inserting and reordering writes *without regard for the activating write* — a consequence of treating every `&mut` as immediately `Unique`. Tree Borrows is deliberately conservative: a reference counts as writable only once written, so collapsing a conditional increment loop into one addition is not generally valid [5]. Neither model is a pure relaxation of the other.

### What is rejected: the 54% figure

The headline result is a differential evaluation over the test suites of the **30,000 most widely used crates** under Miri: Tree Borrows rejects **54% fewer test cases** than Stacked Borrows [5][6]. The eliminated rejections cluster exactly on the §4.2 patterns: two-phase borrows, raw-pointer casts with arithmetic, `container_of` idioms, interior mutability through shared references [4][5]. Stacked Borrows' original validation ran large parts of the standard library suite and found only six violations in the architecture-independent portion — all fixed — suggesting it fit the standard library but not the wider ecosystem [1].

### Miri as the ongoing experiment

Miri remains the shared laboratory — SB by default, TB via `-Zmiri-tree-borrows` — so each new dispute about an unsafe idiom is adjudicated by running both [6]. The POPL 2026 Miri paper calls it the first tool capturing all de-facto UB of deterministic Rust programs [9]. Every model change is thus immediately falsifiable against the corpus — which is how Tree Borrows earned adoption: not by authority, but by rejecting fewer real programs while keeping the optimizer's proof obligations.

---

## 6 Limitations

**Neither model is final.** Both are *proposals* awaiting UCG and MiniRust; data races are largely out of scope — the TB proofs never needed to reason about them since protectors already induce enough UB [5] — and atomics, inline assembly, and FFI boundaries (where LLVM's own aliasing rules apply) are unaddressed.

**Tree Borrows gives up real optimizations.** The write-insertion/reordering family SB justifies is unsound under TB's lazy `Reserved` semantics [5]. Whether performance-critical code depends on them is an open empirical question; a "strong mode" recovering them at the cost of new UB is already being explored [5].

**The corpora are test suites, not proofs.** "54% fewer rejections" counts Miri test executions: untested paths are invisible and Miri's determinism under-samples concurrency [9][5]. The long tail of crates was never exhaustively adjudicated under SB — which is why the TB evaluation mattered.

**Validity is unresolved.** Whether references must always point to *valid* data, how uninitialized bits interact with retagging, and the exact dereferenceability contract remain open UCG design questions [8].

---

## 7 Conclusion

Stacked Borrows and Tree Borrows answer the same question — *what may unsafe Rust do with a pointer?* — separated by five years of deployment experience. SB established the methodology: an operational, executable discipline with mechanized optimization proofs and standard-library validation [1][2][3]. TB kept the methodology and replaced the central data structure, trading LIFO elegance for a tree distinguishing foreign from local accesses, modeling two-phase borrows, and tolerating the ecosystem's raw-pointer idioms [4][5][7] — rejecting 54% fewer test cases, preserving nearly all proven optimizations, adding read–read reordering, and earning a Distinguished Paper Award at PLDI'25 [6].

The deeper lesson is institutional: there is no *correct* rule set to be proved, only a design to validate against proof obligations and real code [1]. The models are instruments in an ongoing negotiation between compiler writers, unsafe authors, and the UCG working group [8] — conducted empirically, in Miri, one rejected test case at a time [9]. Until MiniRust converges on a normative semantics, the responsible position is conservative: write code *both* models accept, run Miri in CI with both flags, and treat each new rejection as data about where the language is heading.

---

## References

[2] Understanding and Evolving the Rust Programming Language — PhD thesis, Saarland University / MPI-SWS (2020). https://research.ralfj.de/phd/thesis-screen.pdf
[3] Stacked Borrows 2 — Ralf Jung's blog (Apr 30, 2019). https://www.ralfj.de/blog/2019/04/30/stacked-borrows-2.html
[4] From Stacks to Trees: A new aliasing model for Rust — Ralf Jung's blog (Jun 2, 2023). https://www.ralfj.de/blog/2023/06/02/tree-borrows.html
[5] Tree Borrows — Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 9, PLDI, Article 188 (Jun 2025). https://research.ralfj.de/papers/2025-pldi-tree-borrows.pdf
[6] Tree Borrows — Distinguished Paper Award, PLDI'25 — Programming Language Foundations Lab, ETH Zurich. https://plf.inf.ethz.ch/research/pldi25-tree-borrows.html
[7] Tree Borrows — PhD thesis, ENS Paris-Saclay (2025). https://github.com/Vanille-N/tree-borrows/raw/refs/heads/master/full/main.pdf

body:
# Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machines: RISC-V Arithmetization, STARK-Based Execution Proofs, and Recursive Continuations

## Abstract

Zero-knowledge virtual machines reduce verifiable computation to one reusable primitive: proving that an instruction-execution *trace* satisfies a fixed ISA's transition function. This thesis analyzes the modern zkVM design space, centered on RISC-V, through algebraic intermediate representations (AIR), STARK-based execution proofs, and recursive proof composition. We give a rigorous account of trace arithmetization — register files, memory consistency via permutation arguments, range checks via lookups, control-flow decoding — and compare three architecturally distinct systems: **RISC Zero** (randomized AIR with preprocessing, DEEP-ALI, FRI over BabyBear [2]), **SP1** (multi-table "chip" arithmetization over Plonky3 with LogUp cross-table lookups [3]), and **Cairo** (register-machine AIR with 69+ components under Circle STARKs on M31 [4]) — alongside the lookup-singularity paradigm of **Jolt/Lasso** [5]. We formalize *continuations*: segmenting long executions into independently provable chunks joined by recursion, and analyze precompiles, verifier costs, and soundness. Drawing on published benchmarks, we identify the asymptotic and engineering barriers separating today's zkVMs from real-time, universally deployable verifiable computation.

## 1 Introduction

A *zero-knowledge virtual machine* certifies the correct execution of an arbitrary program for a fixed virtual ISA, producing a succinct proof verifiable in milliseconds without re-execution. The move is one of indirection: instead of hand-crafting a circuit per computation, developers compile ordinary code (Rust, C, even EVM interpreters) to a guest ISA, and one ISA-specialized backend verifies *any* program by checking a single universal relation — the machine's one-step transition function [6].

An execution of $T$ cycles yields the trace $(s_0, \ldots, s_T)$ with $s_{t+1} = \delta(s_t, \iota_t)$. The proving statement: there exists a trace with $s_0 = \mathsf{init}(\text{program}, \text{public input})$, every adjacent pair satisfying a polynomial transition relation $C(s_t, s_{t+1}) = 0$, and the final state committing to the claimed output.

Two facts make this scalable. First, $\delta$ is fixed, so its arithmetization cost is amortized across all programs: the burden shifts from circuit design to ISA design. Second, the transition relation is *local* — each constraint touches a constant number of consecutive rows — exactly the structure Algebraic Intermediate Representations exploit.

The central questions: (1) **Arithmetization** — how a RISC-V ISA becomes polynomial constraints, and the cost of monolithic vs. multi-table encodings; (2) **Proving** — how STARK systems (FRI + DEEP-ALI, Circle STARKs, multilinear Hypercube) turn traces into succinct arguments; (3) **Continuations** — proving executions longer than one trace via segments and recursive aggregation while preserving global constraints like memory consistency; (4) **Verifier economics** — what recursion, precompiles, and SNARK wrapping imply for on-chain cost and latency.

We contribute: (i) a unified formal treatment of zkVM arithmetization (AIR, chip, lookup-singularity); (ii) a comparative analysis of RISC Zero, SP1, Cairo/Stwo, Jolt, and Nexus from published specifications and benchmarks [2][3][4][5][7][8]; (iii) a soundness-and-cost model of recursive continuations; (iv) an empirical synthesis of published benchmarks with methodological critique.

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 From circuits to virtual machines

Early verifiable-computation systems (Pinocchio, libsnark) required per-program circuits. *Programmable* SNARKs (TinyRAM, vnTinyRAM) introduced universal machine circuits but suffered large per-step overhead and trusted setups. The modern zkVM revives the universal-machine idea with transparent, plausibly post-quantum STARK backends and ISAs chosen for arithmetization friendliness — above all **RISC-V (rv32im)**, whose regular encoding admits efficient constraints and which enjoys mature toolchains (rustc, LLVM) emitting ELF binaries the prover consumes directly.

### 2.2 STARKs in one paragraph

A STARK proves that an execution trace satisfies an AIR: polynomial constraints over consecutive rows of a trace matrix [9]. The prover interpolates each trace column into a polynomial, evaluates it over an expanded domain (blowup factor, typically 4–16×), commits via Merkle trees, and proves low-degreeness with **FRI**. Constraint satisfaction is folded through **DEEP-ALI** into a single composed polynomial evaluated at a random out-of-domain point. Security rests on collision-resistant hashing; there is no trusted setup, and the conjectured hardness is hash-based, giving plausible post-quantum security.

### 2.3 Fields, hashes, and the small-field revolution

Classical STARKs worked over 252-bit fields. Modern zkVMs moved to *small* fields — RISC Zero's **BabyBear** (31-bit, $2^{27}\cdot 15 + 1$) [2], Plonky3's BabyBear/KoalaBear/Mersenne-31 family, StarkWare's **M31** ($2^{31}-1$) for Circle STARKs [4] — because 32-bit field arithmetic maps to native CPU/SIMD instructions, dramatically accelerating the prover. Extension fields restore ~100-bit security where needed; hash functions moved with them (**Poseidon2**, **Blake3**) for small-field efficiency.

### 2.4 Lookups: Plookup, LogUp, and Lasso

Range checks and "non-arithmetic" operations (bitwise ops, byte decomposition) are expensive as raw polynomial constraints but cheap as *lookups*: prove that trace values appear in a fixed table. **Plookup** [10] uses a permutation argument; **LogUp** replaces it with a logarithmic-derivative sum that composes across many differently-sized tables — the enabler of SP1's multi-chip design [3]. **Lasso** [5] supports lookups into *structured* tables of size up to $2^{128}$ that are never materialized, decomposing one large lookup into several small ones. **Jolt** pushes this to the *lookup singularity*: proving RISC-V execution almost entirely through lookups (~60 constraints, 80 field elements per step [11]).

---

## 3 Methodology

Our method is comparative-analytic. From the published specifications and engineering documentation of five systems — RISC Zero [2], SP1 [3][8], Cairo/Stwo [4], Lasso/Jolt [5][11], and Nexus [7] — we extract a common formal model, then instantiate it per system.

### 3.1 The trace model

We model a zkVM execution as a matrix $T \in \mathbb{F}^{n \times w}$: $n$ rows (cycles, padded to a power of two) and $w$ columns carrying architectural state — program counter, decoded opcode fields, register indices/values, memory address/value/timestamp — plus auxiliary columns for permutation arguments and lookups. A *constraint* is a polynomial $C_j$ over a constant-width row window (rows $t$, $t+1$) vanishing on the trace domain:

$$C_j(T[t], T[t+1]) = 0 \quad \forall\, t \in \{0, \ldots, n-2\}, \;\; \forall\, j.$$

Boundary constraints fix $T[1]$ (initial state, program/memory commitments) and $T[n-1]$ (halt, output commitment). Memory consistency — a read returns the last written value — is non-local; all production systems enforce it with a *permutation argument*: operations are sorted by (address, timestamp) into an auxiliary trace, and a grand-product (or log-derivative) accumulator proves multiset equality [2][3].

### 3.2 Arithmetization styles

We distinguish three styles:

| Style | Trace organization | Constraint expression | Exemplars |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Monolithic AIR** | One wide table; every cycle has every column | Single constraint set, selectors per opcode | RISC Zero v1/v2 [2] |
| **Multi-table / chip** | Per-operation tables (ALU, memory, keccak, …) linked by lookups | Local constraints + cross-table LogUp | SP1 [3], Cairo/Stwo [4] |
| **Lookup-singularity** | Minimal CPU circuit; instruction semantics via lookups | ~60 constraints/step | Jolt [5][11], Nexus 2.0 [7] |

The monolithic style pays for *all* columns in *every* row; the chip style sizes each table to usage at the cost of cross-table argument complexity; the lookup style minimizes per-step constraints but shifts cost into the lookup argument and commitment scheme.

### 3.3 Continuations and recursion

No single trace can hold an unbounded execution: FRI proving time and memory grow superlinearly in $n$. All systems therefore *segment* execution — RISC Zero's *segments*/*continuations*, SP1's *shards* (~$2^{22}$ cycles) [3][8] — prove each segment independently (embarrassingly parallel), and aggregate recursively: each recursion step verifies the previous segment's proof inside the zkVM or a dedicated circuit, chaining public outputs (register file, memory Merkle root, cycle count). The final layer is typically wrapped in Groth16/Plonk for cheap on-chain verification.

### 3.4 Evaluation criteria

We evaluate on: (i) **prover time per cycle**; (ii) **proof size and verifier time**; (iii) **ISA expressiveness and precompile support**; (iv) **transparency**; (v) **recursion architecture** and overhead; (vi) **soundness** (conjectured bits of security). Benchmarks are vendor-published [3][8]; we treat them as indicative (see §6).

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Arithmetizing RISC-V: from opcode to constraint

RISC-V's appeal is regularity: 32-bit fixed-width instructions, six formats (R/I/S/B/U/J), a small base opcode space. Arithmetizing one cycle proceeds in four stages.

1. **Fetch and decode.** The PC selects an instruction word from the committed program image. Decoding uses *selector polynomials*: for each opcode $o$, a binary selector $s_o(t)$ marks the active instruction, with $\sum_o s_o = 1$, $s_o^2 = s_o$. Bit decomposition of the 32-bit word uses range-checked limbs, e.g. $w = \sum_{i=0}^{3} b_i 2^{8i}$ with each $b_i$ lookup-constrained to $[0,255]$.
2. **Operand resolution.** Register indices select values from register-file columns; x0-is-zero becomes $x_0(t) = 0$.
3. **Execute.** Each opcode imposes its semantic constraint, gated by its selector. Addition is one constraint ($s_{\text{ADD}}\cdot(rd - rs_1 - rs_2) = 0$); shifts and comparisons need bit decompositions. This per-opcode cost — constraint-degree × column width — is why bitwise-heavy programs (SHA-256, Keccak) are expensive without precompiles.
4. **Writeback and PC update.** The destination column is constrained to the computed value (or held constant via a no-write selector); $pc(t+1)$ is constrained to $pc(t)+4$, a branch target, or a jump target.

```rust
// Schematic: one AIR transition constraint for ADD (BabyBear field)
// s_add: selector, rs1/rs2/rd: register value columns (current/next row)
fn add_constraint(s_add: F, rs1: F, rs2: F, rd_next: F) -> F {
    // Gated: constraint active only when s_add = 1
    s_add * (rd_next - (rs1 + rs2))
    // Degree 2 (selector x linear) — cheap in FRI/DEEP-ALI
}
```

```python
# Schematic: LogUp cross-table lookup (SP1-style chip linkage)
# Proves tuple (op, a, b) was "sent" by CPU chip and "received" by ALU chip
def logup_accumulate(acc, multiplicity, op, a, b, beta):
    # acc_{t+1} = acc_t + m / (beta + encode(op, a, b))
    return acc + multiplicity / (beta + op * X**2 + a * X + b)
# Final claim: sum over all chips of signed accumulators == 0
```

> **Theorem: (Selector soundness).** If $\sum_o s_o(t) = 1$ and $s_o(t)^2 = s_o(t)$ hold per cycle, and each opcode constraint is gated as $s_o \cdot C_o = 0$, then any satisfying trace executes exactly one valid instruction semantics per cycle. ∎

### 4.2 RISC Zero: randomized AIR with preprocessing

RISC Zero's argument system [2] is a **randomized AIR with preprocessing**: preprocessing constructs constraints for a PLONK-based *memory permutation argument* and a Plookup-based *range check*; the execution trace (one wide table: PC, opcode fields, registers, memory columns) is committed with random blinding for zero-knowledge; **DEEP-ALI** composes all constraints and **FRI** proves low-degreeness over BabyBear with Blake3 Merkle commitments.

The system is *transparent* (no trusted setup), recurses via a circuit that verifies STARKs inside the zkVM, and supports continuations joined by receipts; the on-chain story wraps the STARK in Groth16. The cost driver is trace width: every cycle carries every column, so FRI time scales with $n \times w$ regardless of which opcodes execute — the inefficiency that motivated multi-table designs.

### 4.3 SP1: chips, LogUp, and Plonky3

SP1 [3][8] decomposes the machine into **chips**: a CPU chip, ALU chips per operation class, a memory chip, and precompile chips (SHA-256, Keccak-256, secp256k1, BN254/BLS12-381, …). Each chip's trace is sized to actual usage, and chips communicate through **LogUp** cross-table lookups: the CPU "sends" $(opcode, operands)$ tuples; the ALU "receives" them; a global log-derivative sum must vanish. Three documented wins [8]:

- **No merklized memory overhead** — memory consistency uses a dedicated chip with its own efficient argument.
- **Blowup factor 2 instead of 4**, halving FRI domain size.
- **First-class precompiles.** SHA-256 costs a handful of cycles through the precompile chip instead of tens of thousands of RISC-V cycles — the dominant factor in SP1's reported 28× speedup over RISC Zero v0.21 on a Tendermint light client (2.2 h → 4.6 min) [8]. Cycle counts themselves shrink because precompile calls replace instruction sequences.

Recursion proceeds in stages: *core* proofs per shard, *compressed* proofs aggregating shards, and a final Groth16/Plonk "shrinking" wrapper for EVM verification. **SP1 Hypercube** [12] replaced univariate FRI with a *multilinear* backend: the trace becomes a high-dimensional hypercube committed with a "jagged" PCS committing only accessed regions, with constraint checking via **LogUp-GKR sumcheck** — targeting real-time Ethereum block proving (~10 s average on GPUs) [12].

### 4.4 Cairo and Stwo: the register-machine alternative

Cairo bets on a different ISA: a minimal **register machine** with write-once memory and nondeterminism-friendly semantics (the prover may "guess" values, then constrain them — ideal for hash preimages, Merkle paths, signatures). The Cairo AIR comprises **69+ components** (CPU, memory, range-check, Pedersen/ECDSA/Keccak/Blake builtins) proven by **Stwo**, StarkWare's Circle-STARK prover over M31 [4]. Circle STARKs [13] exploit the circle group $x^2+y^2=1$ over M31 for FFT-friendly domains without large smooth-subgroup fields, making the prover very fast on commodity hardware. Recursion is native — a Cairo verifier written *in Cairo* verifies STARK proofs of other Cairo executions — and Starknet's production proving is the largest real-world deployment of a zkVM-family system.

### 4.5 The lookup singularity: Jolt, Lasso, and Nexus

Jolt [5][11] asks: what if instruction semantics were *never* arithmetized as circuits? Every RISC-V instruction decomposes into a few table lookups (e.g., ADD = byte-wise addition with carry tables); **Lasso** [5] proves these against *structured* tables up to $2^{128}$ rows without materializing them, via sumcheck over multilinear extensions. The CPU circuit shrinks to bookkeeping, and the ISA becomes nearly free to extend — no per-opcode circuit engineering. The trade is a heavier commitment layer (Lasso pairs with MSM-based commitments like Zeromorph/Hyrax rather than FRI) and a different recursion story. **Nexus 2.0** [7] adopted Jolt as its prover frontend with **HyperNova** as the recursive backend, betting that lookup-singularity arithmetization plus folding-based recursion is the path to minimal per-step cost.

```tla+
---- MODULE ZkVMContinuations ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences
CONSTANTS MaxSegmentCycles
VARIABLES segments, aggProof

(* Each segment proof attests: init state, final state, and
   correct execution of <= MaxSegmentCycles transitions. *)
SegmentOK(s) == /\ Len(s.trace) <= MaxSegmentCycles
                /\ s.init = IF s.index = 0 THEN GenesisState
                           ELSE Prev(s.index).final
                /\ \A t \in 1..Len(s.trace)-1 :
                       TransitionOK(s.trace[t], s.trace[t+1])

(* Aggregation: recursion verifies each segment proof in order,
   chaining final->init states; the aggregate proof covers all. *)
AggregateOK == /\ \A i \in 1..Len(segments) : SegmentOK(segments[i])
               /\ \A i \in 1..Len(segments)-1 :
                      segments[i].final = segments[i+1].init
====
```

> **Theorem: (Continuation soundness).** If each segment proof is knowledge-sound for "$\le K$ valid cycles from committed init to committed final state," and recursion constrains $\text{final}_i = \text{init}_{i+1}$ for all adjacent segments, the aggregate proof is knowledge-sound for the full $T$-cycle execution. *Proof sketch.* Extract witnesses segment-by-segment (standard hybrid argument); chaining constraints glue them into one $T$-cycle witness, with extraction loss linear in the segment count. ∎

---

## 5 Empirical Results / Formal Analysis

### 5.1 Published benchmark synthesis

All figures are vendor-published [3][8][12] (AWS r7i.16xlarge, 64 vCPU, 512 GB RAM); treat as *indicative* — methodology caveats in §6.

| Program | SP1 (v1.1.1) | RISC Zero (v1.0.0) | Speedup | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fibonacci | 30 s | 163 s | 5.4× | Baseline loop |
| SSZ Merkle proof | 49 s | 229 s | 4.6× | Hash-heavy |
| Tendermint light client | 278 s (4.6 min) | 7,920 s (2.2 h) | ~28× | Precompiles dominate |
| SP1-Reth (2 eth blocks) | reported competitive | — | — | EVM-in-zkVM |

Against **Jolt**, SP1 reports 1.66–3.23× faster proving at 1.3–3.6× smaller proof sizes on SHA-2-chain/Fibonacci/loop microbenchmarks with comparable settings [3]. **SP1 Hypercube** targets the real-time frontier: ~93% of Ethereum mainnet blocks proven in under 12 s (avg ~10.3 s) on GPUs [12] — the threshold at which L2s can finalize within a single L1 slot.

### 5.2 Cost model

Prover time decomposes as:

$$T_{\text{prove}} \approx \underbrace{c_1 \cdot n \cdot w}_{\text{trace commit}} + \underbrace{c_2 \cdot n \cdot w \cdot \log n}_{\text{FRI queries}} + \underbrace{c_3 \cdot n_{\text{seg}} \cdot T_{\text{rec}}}_{\text{recursion}} + \underbrace{T_{\text{wrap}}}_{\text{Groth16 shrink}}.$$

The chip architecture attacks $w$ (effective columns per cycle); blowup-2 FRI attacks the $\log n$ constant; precompiles attack $n$ itself; GPU/multilinear backends attack $c_1, c_2$. The recursion term is *quasi-fixed per segment*: smaller shards increase parallelism but add recursion overhead per shard — the fundamental latency/throughput trade-off of continuations. SP1's Groth16 "shrinking" wrapper adds ~50 s of constant overhead [3], irrelevant at Tendermint scale but dominant for tiny programs.

### 5.3 Verifier asymptotics

| Layer | Proof size | Verifier time | Trust assumption |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raw STARK (per segment) | $O(\log^2 n)$, ~100 KB–1 MB | $O(\log^2 n)$, ms | hash (PQ-plausible) |
| Recursion-compressed | $O(\log^2 n)$, smaller constant | ms | hash |
| Groth16-wrapped | $O(1)$, ~200–800 bytes | $O(1)$, ~5–15 ms + pairing | trusted setup, discrete log (not PQ) |

Wrapping buys EVM-cheap verification at the cost of reintroducing a trusted setup and losing post-quantum security — a trade the whole industry currently accepts for on-chain use, since the STARK layer retains its properties for off-chain verification.

### 5.4 Soundness accounting

Conjectured security is budgeted across components: FRI query count and grinding bits; DEEP-ALI sampling error; hash collision resistance; and the *arithmetization gap* — the informal step where humans assert the constraints faithfully encode the ISA. RISC Zero pursues a formally verified verifier in Lean4 [2]; Stwo's engineering discipline forbids manual edits to generated AIR code and gates constraint definitions, FRI parameters, and the Fiat–Shamir channel behind CI [4]. No deployed zkVM has a fully machine-checked *arithmetization* proof — the softest point in every soundness claim.

---

## 6 Limitations

1. **Benchmark incommensurability.** Vendors differ in hardware, hash function, precompile enablement, shard sizes, and even *what counts* (witness generation; latency vs. throughput with parallel recursion). The 28× figure compares systems with different precompile sets on a workload where precompiles dominate — it measures ISA-extension strategy as much as backend efficiency [8]. Independent, workload-fixed benchmarking (e.g., the Waseda framework comparing 7 zkVMs [14]) is the only sound basis for ranking, and it remains nascent.
2. **The arithmetization gap.** Every soundness theorem is conditional on "the constraints encode the ISA correctly." Constraint systems are tens of thousands of lines of generated code; one missing range check is a soundness break, not a performance bug. Formal verification of arithmetizations is in its infancy.
3. **Memory and state blowup.** Continuations handle *time* but not *space*: large-memory programs still pay per-access argument costs, and cross-segment memory consistency requires committing memory Merkle roots at every boundary — a serial bottleneck for parallel proving.
4. **Precompile centralization of trust.** Precompiles are hand-optimized gadgets outside the uniform ISA argument; each is new trusted code. The modern performance story is increasingly *the precompile story*, reintroducing the per-application circuit engineering zkVMs were meant to abolish.
5. **Prover economics.** Real-time proving (~10 s/block) demands GPUs and parallelism; per-block cost, while falling, still prices out long-tail applications.
6. **Post-quantum honesty.** STARK cores are plausibly PQ-secure, but every EVM-deployed proof today terminates in a Groth16/Plonk wrapper with a trusted setup and discrete-log assumptions. "Post-quantum zkVM" currently describes the off-chain layer only.

---

## 7 Conclusion

The zkVM has converged on a stable pattern — *arithmetize a fixed ISA once, prove traces, recurse over segments* — while diverging on how to arithmetize: monolithic AIR (RISC Zero), multi-chip LogUp tables (SP1), register-machine Circle STARKs (Cairo/Stwo), and the lookup singularity (Jolt/Nexus). Each attacks a different term of the prover cost equation: trace width, FRI constants, cycle counts via precompiles, per-step constraints via lookups. The frontier has moved from hours per program to seconds per Ethereum block, and the remaining barriers are as much about *trust* (the arithmetization gap, precompile auditing, PQ-honest on-chain verification) as *speed*. The key open problem is not a faster FRI but a *verified* arithmetization: a machine-checked proof that production constraints actually encode the claimed ISA. Until then, zkVM soundness rests on auditing discipline — considerable, but not mathematical.

body:
# Formally Verified Smart Contracts: EVM Semantics, Symbolic Execution, and Certified Compilation for On-Chain Correctness

## Abstract

Smart contracts secure digital assets exceeding one hundred billion dollars in aggregate value, yet they execute in an adversarial, immutable environment where a single flaw is irrevocably exploitable. This thesis develops an end-to-end methodology for establishing on-chain correctness of Ethereum smart contracts. We formalize the Ethereum Virtual Machine as a small-step operational semantics with explicit gas accounting and cross-contract call structure; we characterize reentrancy, access-control failure, and arithmetic error as violations of precise safety properties; we show how symbolic execution with SMT solving enumerates feasible attack traces while deductive techniques discharge absence of entire bug classes; and we close the trust gap between source and bytecode via certified compilation grounded in mechanized simulation lemmas. Across the toolchain — KEVM [1], Dafny EVM [2], Oyente [3], Slither [4], Manticore [5], solc-verify [6], MAIAN [7], VeriSol [8] — we compare audit, testing, and proof, quantifying what each technique can and cannot guarantee.

---

## 1 Introduction

A smart contract is a program whose execution is *consensus*: every full node replays its bytecode against replicated state, and the result is binding and irreversible. There is no hotfix channel; the 2017 Parity library self-destruct froze hundreds of millions of dollars permanently, and the 2016 The DAO reentrancy exploit drained tens of millions through recursive calls that exploited the interaction between external calls and deferred state updates [3]. These failures share a structural feature: the vulnerability is a *semantic* mismatch between the programmer's mental model and the actual EVM semantics.

The EVM is a 256-bit-word stack machine with byte-addressable volatile memory, persistent word-addressed storage, and a resource model — *gas* — metering every opcode [1]. Formal verification here must solve three coupled problems. First, the platform semantics must be pinned down mathematically, because properties are meaningless without a definition of what a program *does*; the Yellow Paper's ambiguities were only exposed by mechanized semantics [1]. Second, analysis must handle path explosion across contract boundaries: any public function can be invoked in any order by any caller, and symbolic execution addresses this by treating inputs as logical variables and accumulating path conditions discharged by SMT solvers [3][5]. Third, source-level assurance must survive compilation — verified Solidity is worthless if the bytecode differs from the model — which is why certified compilation, with machine-checked proofs of semantics preservation, closes the loop [6].

We define a core EVM calculus with small-step semantics (§4.1); formalize symbolic execution with path conditions and SMT feasibility (§4.2); encode vulnerability patterns as negated safety properties (§4.3); develop certified compilation via forward simulation (§4.4); and present a Hoare-style contract logic (§4.5). Empirics ground the theory (§5); limits close the work (§6).

---

## 2 Background

**The EVM execution model.** A *world state* σ maps addresses to accounts holding nonce, balance, code, and persistent storage. A machine state is ⟨pc, stack, mem, σ, gas, calldata, depth⟩: a 1024-deep word stack, linear byte memory charged quadratically on expansion, gas consumed per opcode [1][2]. Transactions are the reflexive-transitive closure of small steps until halt, exceptional halt, or a nested call.

**Calls and reentry.** The `CALL` family transfers control to another account's code with value and a gas stipend, pushing a new frame — and the callee may call back into the caller before its frame completes: *reentrancy*. The EVM imposes no reentry discipline; the 63/64 gas-forwarding rule only bounds recursion indirectly. Sound verification must therefore model the caller as an *adversarial environment*: unknown code at an arbitrary address can reenter any public entry point [3].

**The assurance ladder.** Conventional assurance ascends in rigor: manual audit (expert, informal), static analysis (Slither's SlithIR detectors run pattern rules over SSA IR [4]), symbolic execution (Oyente and Manticore enumerate feasible paths, querying SMT solvers for violations [3][5]), and deductive verification (reachability-logic proofs over KEVM [1], Boogie-based modular verification in solc-verify [6] and VeriSol [8], machine-checked semantics in Dafny [2]). Each rung trades soundness against automation: pattern detectors are fast but incomplete; symbolic execution is sound only for bounded depths; deductive verification is complete relative to the specification but demands human proof effort.

**Symbolic execution.** A *symbolic state* replaces concrete inputs with symbols; each symbolic branch splits the state, conjoining the guard to the *path condition* π. Feasibility is SMT satisfiability over bitvectors, arrays, and uninterpreted functions; a violation φ is reachable iff π ∧ φ is satisfiable, and the solver's model yields a concrete attack trace [5]. Oyente pioneered EVM symbolic execution, flagging 8,833 of 19,336 contracts on the first 1.46 million blocks [3].

**Hoare-style contract logics.** Contracts are open systems, so modular reasoning needs boundary specifications: {P} f {Q} means every terminating execution of f from P ends in Q [6]. Loop and contract-level invariants reduce global reasoning to local verification conditions discharged by SMT [6][8].

---

## 3 Methodology

Our methodology is *semantics-first*: define the machine precisely, state properties as logical formulas over its traces, then choose the analysis whose soundness theorem matches the required guarantee.

**Step 1 — Mechanized operational semantics.** We formalize the EVM core as a deterministic labeled transition system in the KEVM style [1]: each opcode is a rewrite rule over machine states, gas is an explicit premise, exceptional halts are distinguished outcomes. Determinism is proved by opcode case analysis, ruling out the "specification gap" where analyzers disagree with clients.

**Step 2 — Property specification.** Vulnerability classes become negated trace properties: reentrancy forbids a second entry before the first entry's state effects commit across an external call; access control requires `msg.sender` in an authorized set at every state-modifying entry; arithmetic requires each 256-bit result to equal its mathematical value or carry an explicit check [6].

**Step 3 — Symbolic exploration with SMT.** Symbolic execution over the semantics: branch conditions become path constraints; at each `CALL` the callee is modeled as a nondeterministic environment capable of arbitrary gas-bounded reentry; solver queries decide feasibility and violation [3][5]. Unsatisfiable paths are pruned; satisfiable violations yield concrete counterexamples.

**Step 4 — Deductive closure.** Where symbolic execution is bounded, reachability-logic proofs [1] or Boogie VCs [6][8] close the gap: validity of all VCs implies the property for *all* executions.

**Step 5 — Certified compilation.** We prove forward simulation: every bytecode behavior is permitted by the source semantics, so source proofs transfer to deployed artifacts; the mechanized proof emits proof objects alongside bytecode [6].

**Evaluation.** Three axes: *fidelity* (does the semantics pass the 40,683-test Ethereum conformance suite [1]?), *recall on known bugs* (The DAO pattern, BEC overflow, frozen-library patterns [3][7]?), and *proof coverage* (functional correctness of ERC-20 end-to-end [1]?).

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Operational Semantics of the EVM: A Small-Step Machine

We define a core calculus, λ-EVM, capturing the safety-relevant fragment: stack, memory, storage, control flow, and the call family. A machine state is:

```haskell
data Machine = Machine
  { pc      :: Int                  -- program counter
  , stack   :: [Word256]            -- operand stack, depth <= 1024
  , mem     :: Mem                  -- byte array, word-aligned expansion
  , stor    :: Map Word256 Word256  -- persistent account storage
  , gas     :: Integer              -- remaining gas
  , world   :: WorldState            -- global account map
  , frames  :: [Frame]              -- call stack
  }
```

Single-step transitions are inference rules. The arithmetic rule shows gas accounting and modular semantics together:

```tla+
\* TLA+ sketch of the ADD transition
ADD(mu, sigma) ==
  /\ Len(mu.stack) >= 2
  /\ mu.gas >= G_verylow
  /\ LET x == Head(mu.stack)
         y == Head(Tail(mu.stack))
     IN  /\ mu' = [mu EXCEPT !.stack = <<(x + y) % 2^256>> \o Tail(Tail(mu.stack)),
                          !.pc = mu.pc + 1,
                          !.gas = mu.gas - G_verylow]
         /\ UNCHANGED sigma
```

The call rule is where verification gets hard: `CALL` invokes *arbitrary bytes* from the world state. KEVM handles this via reachability-logic abstraction over a code-map-parametric semantics [1]; the Dafny formalization machine-checks the same case analysis functionally [2]. Both exposed Yellow Paper ambiguities, including the exact forwarded gas stipend and `RETURNDATACOPY` on empty return data [1].

Gas is itself a verification target: the semantics yields a deterministic *gas function* over traces, and proving upper bounds is essential for liveness. The 63/64th rule makes recursion depth a function of initial gas, which symbolic executors exploit to bound reentry depth [3][5].

### 4.2 Symbolic Execution: Path Conditions and SMT Solving

Symbolic execution lifts the concrete relation to symbolic states ⟨μ̂, σ̂, π⟩ — values as terms over symbolic variables, π the path condition. The symbolic `JUMPI` forks:

```python
def sym_jumpi(state, dest, cond):
    """Fork on a symbolic branch; query SMT for feasibility."""
    for branch, guard in [(dest, cond), (state.pc + 1, Not(cond))]:
        pi = And(state.pi, guard)
        if solver.is_sat(pi):                      # bitvector + array theories
            yield state._replace(pc=branch, pi=pi)
        # else: infeasible path pruned — sound by solver soundness
```

Three engineering decisions dominate EVM symbolic execution [3][5]:

1. **Memory and storage as SMT arrays.** The array theory models `MLOAD`/`SSTORE` precisely, but the 256-bit index space forces concretization of almost-concrete addresses, keeping symbolic only attacker-dependent ones.
2. **Hashing as uninterpreted functions.** `KECCAK256` is solver-opaque, so `keccak256(key . slot)` becomes an uninterpreted *f* with *x ≠ y → f(x) ≠ f(y)* — sound absent collisions [5].
3. **Environment as adversary.** `CALL` to an unknown address havocs reachable state and assumes arbitrary return data; Manticore adds state merging and concretization policies against fork explosion [5].

Path explosion is the fundamental barrier: *n* symbolic branches yield up to 2ⁿ paths, and each 256-bit bitvector query is NP-complete in the worst case. Small programs and gas-bounded loops keep this tractable — Oyente completed thousands of contracts — but symbolically-bounded loops remain the incompleteness frontier, addressed by invariant-based deduction (§4.5) [3][6].

### 4.3 Reentrancy and Access Control as Safety Properties

Vulnerability taxonomies — Oyente's four classes [3], Slither's 80+ detectors [4], MAIAN's greedy/prodigal/suicidal trichotomy [7] — are best understood as *patterns*, syntactic witnesses of semantic property violations. We formalize the two most consequential.

**Reentrancy.** The canonical vulnerable pattern:

```rust
// VULNERABLE (Solidity sketched in Rust-like pseudocode)
fn withdraw(&mut self, amount: U256) {
    require(self.balances[msg_sender] >= amount);
    msg_sender.call{value: amount}("");      // (A) external call FIRST
    self.balances[msg_sender] -= amount;    // (B) state update AFTER
}
```

The attacker's fallback reenters at (A); the balance check still passes since (B) has not executed; recursion drains the contract. The fix — *checks-effects-interactions* — moves (B) before (A); a reentrancy guard makes reentry revert.

> **Definition (Reentrancy safety).** A contract is reentrancy-safe iff in every trace, for every external call *c* in function *f*, no segment *c … reentry(f) … return(c)* contains a storage write that precedes in program order a write to the same slot ordered after *c* in *f*.

Symbolic executors detect the violation via the query of §4.2 [3][5]; Slither detects the *pattern* (state write after external call) syntactically with taint tracking [4]. The semantic property is strictly stronger: it admits safe patterns that syntactic detectors flag as false positives — the audit-vs-proof gap in miniature.

**Access control.**

| Vulnerability class | Formal property | Detection technique | Canonical tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reentrancy | No reentrant write-before-commit | Symbolic path query | Oyente [3], Manticore [5] |
| Unprotected privileged ops | `msg.sender ∈ Owners` at every privileged entry | Taint + pattern | Slither [4], MAIAN [7] |
| Integer overflow | Math result = modular result ∨ explicit check | SMT bitvector query | solc-verify [6] |
| Greedy / prodigal | ∃ trace locking funds / leaking to arbitrary caller | Inter-procedural symbolic search | MAIAN [7] |
| Tx-order dependence | Outcome independent of interleaving | Path-condition comparison | Oyente [3] |

MAIAN instead *searches for exploit primitives* — contracts that can be forced to lock ether forever, leak it to an arbitrary address, or be killed by anyone — finding thousands at scale [7].

### 4.4 Certified Compilation: Verified Solidity/Yul Pipelines

Source-level assurance is void if compilation is untrusted. A *certified compiler* is a pair (compile, proof) with:

> **Theorem 2 (Forward simulation / semantics preservation).** For every source program *S* and *T = compile(S)*, every terminating execution of *T* from σ₀ corresponds to an execution of *S* from σ₀ with identical observable behavior (return data, storage effects, balance transfers, logs).

The proof uses *simulation diagrams*: a relation R between source and target states preserved as each target step is matched by source steps, concluding by coinduction over traces. The solc-verify pipeline implements the practical half: annotated Solidity → Boogie IVL, the Boogie verifier discharges VCs with SMT solvers, and results map back to source lines [6]. Its modular-arithmetic mode is instructive — mathematical integers *with* range assertions capturing exact 256-bit wraparound, giving solver scalability plus bit-precise overflow detection and discharging all SimpleBank VCs in seconds [6].

The full stack is layered: **source → Yul** (the translation must preserve checked- vs. wrapping-arithmetic semantics, a notorious analyzer unsoundness when the wrong mode is assumed); **IR → IR optimizations** (peephole rules proved as denotational equalities in the Dafny EVM semantics [2]); **IR → bytecode** (the simulation relation must account for gas exactly, since out-of-gas is observable). The economic argument is decisive: a compiler bug is *systemic*, affecting every contract it compiles — certified compilation amortizes proof effort across all compilations.

### 4.5 Hoare-Style Contract Logics and Modular Verification

Symbolic execution reasons about *traces*; Hoare logic reasons about *programs*:

```haskell
-- Hoare triple for a token transfer
-- { balanceOf[from] >= amt /\ to /= 0 }
--   transfer(from, to, amt)
-- { balanceOf[from] = old(balanceOf[from]) - amt
--   /\ balanceOf[to] = old(balanceOf[to]) + amt
--   /\ sum(balanceOf) = old(sum(balanceOf)) }
```

> **Theorem 3 (Soundness of the contract logic).** If every function of contract *C* satisfies its {P} f {Q} against the λ-EVM semantics, every loop carries a valid invariant, and every contract-level invariant *I* is established by the constructor and preserved by each public function, then *I* holds in every reachable state of *C* under arbitrary adversarial callers.

*Proof sketch.* Induction on traces: the constructor establishes the base; the inductive step applies the frame rule — reentry can only invoke public functions, each preserving *I* by its verified triple; adversary code never executes in the contract's frame. ∎

This is the architecture of VeriSol and solc-verify [6][8]: Solidity → Boogie; annotations become VCs; Z3/CVC4 discharge them; failures map back to source. VeriSol adds *semantic conformance* — the contract must refine a finite-state workflow policy — and *infers* invariants via predicate abstraction [8]. Where symbolic execution finds bugs, this logic proves their absence: solc-verify's evaluation shows each catches what the other misses [6].

---

## 5 Empirical Results and Proofs

**Semantics fidelity.** KEVM passes all 40,683 tests of the official Ethereum VM conformance suite — the first formal semantics to do so — and its reachability-logic verifier, derived correct-by-construction from the same semantics, has verified ERC-20 transfers, the Ethereum 2.0 deposit contract, and MakerDAO components [1]. The Dafny formalization provides a complementary human-readable, machine-checked interpreter with proved gas-reasoning invariants and a methodology for synthesizing verified bytecode from verified Dafny code [2].

**Bug-finding recall.** The empirical record is unambiguous [3][4][5][7]:

| Tool | Technique | Scale | Key result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Oyente [3] | Symbolic execution on bytecode | 19,336 contracts | 8,833 flagged; The DAO pattern detected |
| MAIAN [7] | Inter-procedural exploit search | 970k+ contracts | Thousands greedy/prodigal/suicidal |
| Manticore [5] | Dynamic symbolic execution | Commercial audit corpus | Bugs found + correctness proofs in production |
| Slither [4] | SlithIR static analysis | 1,000 top contracts, manual review | Best speed/false-positive balance |
| solc-verify [6] | Boogie VCs + SMT | Annotated benchmarks | All VCs discharged in seconds |
| VeriSol [8] | Boogie + predicate abstraction | Azure Blockchain samples | Unknown conformance bugs found |

Two results deserve emphasis: solc-verify's SimpleBank experiment shows only VC-based reasoning discharges reentrancy *and* overflow with zero false alarms [6], and MAIAN's solver found killable-by-anyone contracts absent from 2016-era taxonomies [7].

**Proofs of absence.** Reachability-logic verification over KEVM proves functional correctness — not just bug absence — of token contracts against full specifications including gas bounds [1]. VeriSol's conformance proofs guarantee implementation traces refine workflow policies for *all* interleavings of public calls, which no bounded symbolic executor can establish [8] — genuine *proofs*, composable with the simulation theorem of §4.4.

**The layered stack.** Manual audit remains unmatched at *specification discovery* — auditors find missing requirements no formal property states. The mature stack is therefore layered: Slither-class analyzers in CI [4], symbolic executors for pre-deployment exploit search [3][5][7], deductive verification for invariants that must hold forever [1][6][8] — with the compiler verified so the layers agree on what the code *means*.

---

## 6 Limitations

**Decidability and the solver ceiling.** Symbolic execution reduces security to SMT satisfiability, but 256-bit bitvector formulas with arrays and uninterpreted functions sit at the edge of solver capacity. Path explosion is exponential; symbolically-bounded loops force unsound bounding or expensive invariant inference. Every symbolic tool is *bounded-complete at best*: no counterexample within the bound is not absence of a bug [3][5].

**The specification bottleneck.** Deductive verification proves exactly what is specified — written by humans, at a cost comparable to the code. The DAO's flaw was arguably a *missing requirement* (no reentrant withdrawal), not a failed proof; no verifier discovers requirements. Invariant inference (VeriSol's predicate abstraction [8]) mitigates but does not eliminate this.

**Semantic drift.** The EVM is a moving target: gas schedules change at hard forks (EIP-150, EIP-1884, EIP-2929 repriced opcodes), and analyzers parameterized by stale schedules are unsound against the live network. KEVM makes the semantics parametric in the fee schedule [1], but downstream tools must track the parameterization or silently diverge.

**Environment modeling.** Reentry analysis assumes an *arbitrary* adversary, but gas stipends, the 63/64 rule, and callee whitelists constrain it. Over-approximation yields false positives; under-approximation misses exploits via trusted-but-compromised callees. The `delegatecall` proxy pattern — the "callee" executing in the *caller's* storage context — defeats most modular analyses and remains the sharpest open problem.

**Certified compilation coverage.** Today's verified pipelines cover subsets: solc-verify handles most of Solidity but not inline assembly or ABI-encoding edge cases [6]; Dafny-to-EVM synthesis is a research methodology, not a production compiler [2]. Until solc itself carries proof objects, the trust gap is narrowed, not closed.

**Economic properties are out of scope.** Formal methods verify *code* properties. Oracle manipulation, governance attacks, and MEV extraction are *mechanism* properties; a provably correct lending contract can still be drained through a price-feed exploit. Verification is necessary but not sufficient for on-chain safety.

---

## 7 Conclusion

On-chain correctness is achievable — not by any single technique, but by a semantics-grounded stack in which each layer's guarantee is stated as a theorem. Mechanized EVM semantics [1][2] fix the meaning of execution; symbolic execution with SMT solving [3][5][7] hunts feasible attacks and produces replayable counterexamples; static analysis [4] gives fast approximate feedback; Hoare-style modular logics [6][8] prove invariants for all executions and all adversaries; certified compilation carries those proofs to the bytecode that executes.

The central lesson is the *audit-vs-proof* distinction: audits discover requirements; proofs establish, with machine-checked certainty, that stated requirements hold of the deployed artifact. The DAO hack, the Parity freeze, and MAIAN's greedy contracts were failures of *guarantee* — properties believed but never proved. Assurance must move up the ladder: from testing what we can think of, to proving what we must guarantee, over a semantics we can trust.

---

title: Global Navigation Satellite Systems: Pseudorange Positioning, Kalman Filtering, and Relativistic Corrections in Precision GNSS
abstract: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) provide meter-to-millimeter positioning worldwide through the measurement of pseudoranges — signal travel times contaminated by receiver clock bias, atmospheric propagation delays, and satellite orbit and clock errors. This thesis develops the complete theoretical pipeline from raw pseudorange measurements to precision position–velocity–time (PVT) solutions: the nonlinear trilateration observation model, its linearization and weighted least-squares solution, ionospheric correction via the Klobuchar broadcast model and dual-frequency combinations, tropospheric modeling, and sequential Bayesian estimation with extended Kalman filters [4][3]. We derive the relativistic corrections mandated by special and general relativity — gravitational frequency shifts, second-order Doppler shifts, eccentricity terms, and the Sagnac correction — whose aggregate effect exceeds ten kilometers per day if neglected [1]. We analyze dilution of precision as the geometric amplification of measurement noise, and contrast real-time kinematic (RTK) and precise point positioning (PPP) techniques that resolve carrier-phase ambiguities to reach centimeter-level accuracy [5][6].
