body:
# Global Navigation Satellite Systems: Pseudorange Positioning, Kalman Filtering, and Relativistic Corrections in Precision GNSS

## Abstract

Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) provide meter-to-millimeter positioning worldwide through the measurement of *pseudoranges* — signal travel times contaminated by receiver clock bias, atmospheric propagation delays, and satellite orbit and clock errors. This thesis develops the complete theoretical pipeline from raw pseudorange measurements to precision position–velocity–time (PVT) solutions: the nonlinear trilateration observation model, its linearization and weighted least-squares solution, ionospheric correction via the Klobuchar broadcast model and dual-frequency combinations, tropospheric modeling, and sequential Bayesian estimation with extended Kalman filters [4][3]. We derive the relativistic corrections mandated by special and general relativity — gravitational frequency shifts, second-order Doppler shifts, eccentricity terms, and the Sagnac correction — whose aggregate effect exceeds ten kilometers per day if neglected [1]. We analyze dilution of precision as the geometric amplification of measurement noise, and contrast real-time kinematic (RTK) and precise point positioning (PPP) techniques that resolve carrier-phase ambiguities to reach centimeter-level accuracy [5][6]. Numerical simulations and formal results characterize estimator consistency, integrity monitoring, and the fundamental error bounds of the pseudorange system.

---

## 1 Introduction

The *Global Positioning System* (GPS), with GLONASS, Galileo, and BeiDou, is among the most successful applications of twentieth-century physics deployed at planetary scale. A receiver measures microwave signal transit times from satellites with known orbits and clocks, then solves nonlinear range equations [9] — concealing an extraordinary estimation problem: ionospheric/tropospheric delays, multipath, noise, Earth rotation during transit, and clocks in different gravitational potentials [1][2].

We cover the GNSS estimation chain: the pseudorange model and error sources (Sec. 2); linearization, least squares, atmospheric correction, and Kalman filtering (Sec. 3); the rigorous clock model, relativistic corrections, DOP, and RTK/PPP (Sec. 4); simulations and proofs (Sec. 5); limitations (Sec. 6); and conclusions (Sec. 7).

> **Thesis:** The pseudorange system is *nonlinear, clock-biased, and atmosphere-corrupted*; meter-level raw measurements become centimeter-level positions through (i) least-squares/Kalman state estimation, (ii) ionospheric correction, (iii) relativistic and Earth-rotation corrections, and (iv) carrier-phase ambiguity resolution [5][6][8].

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 The pseudorange concept

A true *range* ρ between satellite *s* and receiver *r* is the Euclidean distance ‖**x**⁽ˢ⁾ − **x**ᵣ‖. A GNSS receiver cannot measure it directly: the receiver's inexpensive quartz clock is offset from system time by an unknown bias *δtᵣ*, and the satellite clock carries its own offset *δt⁽ˢ⁾*. The receiver instead measures a *pseudorange*:

**P⁽ˢ⁾ = ρ⁽ˢ⁾ + c(δtᵣ − δt⁽ˢ⁾) + I⁽ˢ⁾ + T⁽ˢ⁾ + M⁽ˢ⁾ + ε⁽ˢ⁾**

where *I*, *T*, *M*, *ε* are ionospheric, tropospheric, multipath, and thermal-noise terms. Because *δtᵣ* is common to all satellites at an epoch, it is estimated as a fourth unknown alongside position — hence the classic **four**-satellite requirement for a snapshot 3D fix [9].

### 2.2 Signal structure and observables

Each satellite transmits spread-spectrum signals on multiple L-band carriers (L1 ≈ 1575.42 MHz, L2 ≈ 1227.60 MHz, L5 ≈ 1176.45 MHz for GPS). The receiver generates two fundamental observables:

1. **Code pseudorange** *P* — measured by correlating the received pseudorandom noise (PRN) code with a local replica; noise ≈ 0.3–3 m.
2. **Carrier phase** Φ — measured by tracking the carrier's phase; noise ≈ 1–3 mm, but *ambiguous* by an integer number of wavelengths *N* [5].

Modernized signals (L2C, L5, Galileo E1/E5a, BeiDou B1/B2) enable multi-frequency processing, essential for ionosphere-free combinations and rapid ambiguity resolution [8].

### 2.3 Satellite ephemeris and clock data

Satellite positions **x**⁽ˢ⁾ and clock corrections *δt⁽ˢ⁾* come from the *broadcast navigation message* (Keplerian elements plus harmonic perturbations, valid ~2–4 h, orbit ~1 m, clock ~5 ns) or from *precise products* of the International GNSS Service: final orbits ~2 cm, clocks ~75 ps [6]. This broadcast-vs-precise fork is the principal architectural divide between standard positioning and PPP.

### 2.4 Error budget

| Error source | Typical magnitude (m) | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Satellite clock & ephemeris (broadcast) | 1.0–3.0 | Precise products; PPP |
| Ionospheric delay (single freq.) | 1.0–30.0 | Klobuchar model [7]; dual-frequency ionosphere-free combination |
| Tropospheric delay | 2.0–25.0 (elevation dependent) | Saastamoinen/Hopfield model; estimate zenith delay |
| Receiver clock bias | up to 10⁶ (estimated) | Solved as state; 4+ satellites |
| Multipath | 0.1–5.0 | Choke-ring antennas; sidereal filtering |
| Receiver noise | 0.1–1.0 | Carrier smoothing; longer integration |
| Relativistic effects | 0.01–10.0 (accumulated) | Analytical corrections [1] |

---

## 3 Methodology

### 3.1 Linearization and weighted least squares

With **x** = [*xᵣ*, *yᵣ*, *zᵣ*, *cδtᵣ*]ᵀ, each pseudorange gives *P⁽ˢ⁾ = h⁽ˢ⁾*(**x**) + *v⁽ˢ⁾* with

*h⁽ˢ⁾*(**x**) = ‖**x**⁽ˢ⁾ − **x**ᵣ‖ + *cδtᵣ* − *cδt⁽ˢ⁾* + corrections.

Linearizing about **x**₀ yields the Gauss–Newton iteration:

> **Theorem 1 (Iterated least-squares PVT).** Let **H** be the *n*×4 geometry (Jacobian) matrix with rows [−**e**⁽ˢ⁾ᵀ, 1], where **e**⁽ˢ⁾ is the unit line-of-sight vector to satellite *s*, and let **W** be the measurement weight matrix. Then the weighted least-squares update Δ**x** = (**H**ᵀ**WH**)⁻¹**H**ᵀ**W**Δ**P** converges to the maximum-likelihood estimate whenever the initial error is below ~100 km and **H** has full column rank (four non-coplanar satellites) [9].

The normal matrix (**H**ᵀ**WH**)⁻¹ directly yields the *dilution of precision* metrics of Section 4.4.

### 3.2 Atmospheric correction

The ionosphere is *dispersive*: group delay *I = 40.3·TEC/f²*. Single-frequency receivers apply the **Klobuchar model** [7] — a broadcast eight-parameter cosine fit correcting ~50–60% RMS. Dual-frequency receivers form the **ionosphere-free combination** *P_IF = (f₁²P₁ − f₂²P₂)/(f₁² − f₂²)*, eliminating the first-order term at the cost of amplified noise.

The troposphere is non-dispersive; its zenith delay (~2.3 m hydrostatic + up to 0.3 m wet) is mapped to slant via mapping functions, with the residual wet component often estimated as a random-walk state [8].

### 3.3 Sequential estimation: the extended Kalman filter

Snapshot least squares ignores dynamics. The **extended Kalman filter** (EKF) maintains a state — position, velocity, clock bias/drift, optionally troposphere and ambiguities — propagated with a constant-velocity, random-walk-clock model and updated each epoch [4]. The EKF is the workhorse of real-time GNSS; neural-augmented variants learning process-noise and weighting models from data improve robustness in degraded environments [3].

```python
import numpy as np
def ekf_pvt_predict(x, P, F, Q):
    """Predict step: x in [pos(3), vel(3), clk_bias, clk_drift]."""
    x_pred = F @ x
    P_pred = F @ P @ F.T + Q
    return x_pred, P_pred

def ekf_pvt_update(x_pred, P_pred, z, h, H, R):
    """Update step with pseudorange residuals z and Jacobian H."""
    y = z - h(x_pred)  # innovation
    S = H @ P_pred @ H.T + R
    K = P_pred @ H.T @ np.linalg.inv(S)  # gain
    x_new = x_pred + K @ y
    P_new = (np.eye(len(x_pred)) - K @ H) @ P_pred
    return x_new, P_new
```

### 3.4 Carrier-phase processing and ambiguity resolution

Carrier-phase observables Φ⁽ˢ⁾ = ρ⁽ˢ⁾ + *c*(*δtᵣ* − *δt⁽ˢ⁾*) + λ*N*⁽ˢ⁾ − *I*⁽ˢ⁾ + *T*⁽ˢ⁾ + ε_Φ are ambiguous by integers *N*. Between-receiver/satellite *double differencing* cancels clock errors (and, over short baselines, atmospheric terms), leaving ambiguities resolvable via the **LAMBDA method** [8]. Fixing *N* converts the millimeter-noise carrier into a millimeter-accurate range — the foundation of RTK and PPP-AR.

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 The pseudorange measurement model, rigorously

The undifferenced code observation equation is:

*Pᵣ,ⱼ⁽ˢ⁾ = ρᵣ⁽ˢ⁾ + c(dtᵣ − dt⁽ˢ⁾) + d_trop + d_ion,j + c(dᵣ,ⱼ + d⁽ˢ⁾,ⱼ) + d_rel + M + ε*

where *j* indexes the frequency, *dᵣ,ⱼ*, *d⁽ˢ⁾,ⱼ* are receiver/satellite code biases, and *d_rel* collects relativistic path corrections. Three structural facts dominate downstream processing:

1. **Clock-bias dominance.** *c·dtᵣ* can reach kilometers; it is estimated as an unknown, not modeled as noise. A GNSS receiver is fundamentally a *time-transfer* device that yields position as a byproduct [9].
2. **Common-mode structure.** Satellite clock and ephemeris errors project onto ranges with near-unit geometry; differencing between receivers removes them almost entirely — why differential techniques outperform standalone positioning by orders of magnitude [8].
3. **Frequency dependence.** Only the ionospheric term carries the index *j*, through the 1/*f²* law — enabling dual-frequency ionosphere-free combinations [7].

The measurement model as a pure *Haskell* function:

```haskell
-- Pseudorange measurement model
data Obs = Obs { rho      :: Double   -- geometric range (m)
               , clkRecv  :: Double   -- c * dt_r (m)
               , clkSat   :: Double   -- c * dt^s (m)
               , iono     :: Double   -- ionospheric delay (m)
               , tropo    :: Double   -- tropospheric delay (m)
               , relat    :: Double   -- relativistic correction (m)
               , multipath:: Double   -- multipath + noise (m)
               } deriving Show

pseudorange :: Obs -> Double
pseudorange o = rho o + clkRecv o - clkSat o
              + iono o + tropo o + relat o + multipath o

-- Ionosphere-free combination
ionoFree :: Double -> Double -> Double -> Double -> Double
ionoFree f1 f2 p1 p2 = (f1^2 * p1 - f2^2 * p2) / (f1^2 - f2^2)
```

### 4.2 Extended Kalman filtering for position, velocity, and time

A standard 8-state filter uses **x** = [**r**ᵀ, **v**ᵀ, *b*, *ḃ*]ᵀ with transition

**F** = diag(**F**_pv, **F**_clk), **F**_pv = [[**I**₃, Δt·**I**₃],[**0**, **I**₃]], **F**_clk = [[1, Δt],[0, 1]],

and process noise **Q** tuned to platform dynamics. The measurement Jacobian row for satellite *s* is [−**e**⁽ˢ⁾ᵀ, **0**₃ᵀ, 1, 0]; clock bias is observable only while satellites are tracked — during outages the filter coasts and *ḃ* uncertainty grows linearly [4].

> **Theorem 2 (EKF consistency).** If the linearized system is uniformly observable, noises are zero-mean white with known **Q**, **R** ≻ 0, and linearization errors satisfy *L*·‖**P**‖ < 1, then the EKF error is bounded in mean square and E[εᵀ**P**⁻¹ε] = dim(**x**) — the filter is *consistent* [4].

In practice, consistency is monitored with innovation χ² tests; failures trigger *receiver autonomous integrity monitoring* (RAIM) fault detection and exclusion via the residual vector's parity-space projection [9].

The RAIM check in *Rust*:

```rust
/// RAIM chi-square fault detection.
fn raim_check(innov: &[f64], s_inv: &[Vec<f64>], dof: usize, alpha: f64) -> bool {
    // test statistic t = y^T S^{-1} y
    let mut t = 0.0;
    for (i, &yi) in innov.iter().enumerate() {
        for (j, &yj) in innov.iter().enumerate() {
            t += yi * s_inv[i][j] * yj;
        }
    }
    // chi-square threshold test
    t < chi_square_threshold(dof, alpha)
}
```

### 4.3 Relativistic corrections

GNSS is the largest operational experiment in general relativity ever built; *without* relativistic corrections it would fail within minutes [1]. In the Earth-centered inertial (ECI) frame:

1. **Gravitational frequency shift.** A clock at GPS orbital radius runs *faster* than a terrestrial clock by ~38.6 µs/day. GPS oscillators are therefore *factory-offset* to 10.22999999543 MHz (instead of 10.23 MHz) so they appear correct to ground users [1].
2. **Second-order Doppler shift.** Orbital velocity *v* ≈ 3.874 km/s gives time dilation −7.2 µs/day. Combined with the gravitational term, the net secular offset is ≈ +38 µs/day — ~11.4 km/day of range error if ignored [1].
3. **Eccentricity correction.** The combined redshift/Doppler effect varies around the orbit: Δ*tᵣ* = −2(**r**⁽ˢ⁾·**v**⁽ˢ⁾)/*c²*, amplitude ~23 ns (≈ 7 m) for GPS eccentricities, corrected analytically [2].
4. **Sagnac effect.** During the ~70 ms signal transit the Earth rotates beneath the path; the ECEF↔ECI transformation contributes up to ~133 ns (≈ 40 m) for low-elevation satellites [1][2].
5. **Shapiro delay.** Gravitational time delay of the signal path is sub-centimeter for GNSS geometries and is absorbed in PPP models [2].

| Relativistic effect | Size (time) | Size (range) | Handling |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gravitational blueshift (orbit) | +45.7 µs/day | — | Factory frequency offset |
| Second-order Doppler | −7.2 µs/day | — | Factory frequency offset |
| Net secular clock offset | +38.6 µs/day | 11.4 km/day | Offset + polynomial clock model [1] |
| Eccentricity term | ±23 ns periodic | ±7 m | −2**r**·**v**/*c²* correction |
| Sagnac (Earth rotation) | up to ±133 ns | up to ±40 m | ECEF↔ECI rotation during transit |
| Shapiro delay | <0.1 ns | <2 cm | PPP models [2] |

A *TLA⁺* fragment formalizes the correction pipeline:

```tla+
------------------------------ MODULE GnssRelCorr ------------------------------
EXTENDS Reals, Sequences
CONSTANTS Sats
VARIABLES rawPR, corrPR, applied
TypeOK == /\ rawPR \in [Sats -> Real]
          /\ corrPR \in [Sats -> Real]
          /\ applied \in [Sats -> {"none","secular","ecc","sagnac","done"}]
Init == /\ rawPR \in [Sats -> Real]
        /\ corrPR = [s \in Sats |-> rawPR[s]]
        /\ applied = [s \in Sats |-> "none"]
ApplySecular(s) == /\ applied[s] = "none"
                   /\ corrPR' = [corrPR EXCEPT ![s] = @ - 38.6e-6 * C * DayFrac]
                   /\ applied' = [applied EXCEPT ![s] = "secular"]
ApplyEcc(s, r, v) == /\ applied[s] = "secular"
                     /\ corrPR' = [corrPR EXCEPT ![s] = @ + 2*(r \cdot v)/C^2]
                     /\ applied' = [applied EXCEPT ![s] = "ecc"]
Safety == \A s \in Sats : applied[s] /= "done" => corrPR[s] \notin EstimatorInput
=============================================================================
```

### 4.4 Dilution of precision

Satellite *geometry* amplifies measurement noise. From the least-squares covariance (**H**ᵀ**H**)⁻¹σ², the DOP family is:

- **GDOP** = √(trace **Q**), **PDOP** = √(Q₁₁+Q₂₂+Q₃₃), **HDOP**/**VDOP** horizontal/vertical components, **TDOP** = √Q₄₄.

> **Theorem 3 (Geometric amplification).** With user-equivalent range error σ₀, the RMS 3D position error is σ_pos = PDOP · σ₀ and time-transfer error σ_t = TDOP · σ₀/*c*. PDOP ≥ √3 (equality for isotropic distributions); open-sky values are 1.5–3, urban canyons exceed 10 [9].

Good geometry means satellites spread across the sky (large line-of-sight intersection angles); poor geometry means clustered satellites and an ill-conditioned sphere intersection. Constellation design (GPS: 55°, 6 planes; GLONASS: 64.8°, 3 planes; Galileo: 56°, 3 planes) is optimized to keep DOP low worldwide [8].

### 4.5 High-precision differential techniques: RTK and PPP

Two architectures push GNSS from meters to centimeters [8]:

**Real-Time Kinematic (RTK).** A base station with known coordinates broadcasts carrier-phase observations; the rover forms double differences, canceling satellite clocks, orbits, and (over baselines < 10–20 km) atmospheric delays, then fixes ambiguities with LAMBDA: 1 cm + 1 ppm horizontal accuracy in real time, at the cost of a data link and base infrastructure [8].

**Precise Point Positioning (PPP).** Introduced by Zumberge et al. [5], PPP uses *undifferenced* observations with IGS precise orbits and clocks [6], estimating position, clock, troposphere, and float ambiguities in one Kalman filter. No base station is needed, but convergence to centimeter level takes 15–40 minutes. PPP-AR applies satellite phase-bias products to fix undifferenced ambiguities to integers, cutting convergence substantially [5].

| Technique | Infrastructure | Accuracy | Convergence | Baseline limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standalone pseudorange | None | 1–5 m | Instant | — |
| SBAS (WAAS/EGNOS) | Geostationary overlays | 0.5–2 m | Seconds | Continental |
| RTK | Base station + datalink | 1 cm + 1 ppm | Seconds | ~20 km |
| Network RTK | CORS network | 1–2 cm | Seconds | ~70 km |
| PPP (float) | Precise products | 3–10 cm | 15–40 min | Global |
| PPP-AR | Precise products + phase biases | 1–3 cm | 5–20 min | Global |

---

## 5 Empirical Results and Proofs

### 5.1 Simulation: EKF pseudorange positioning

We simulated a static receiver tracking 8 GPS satellites (15° elevation mask, σ₀ = 2.5 m code noise) with a velocity random-walk model. A 500-epoch Monte Carlo run of the Section 3.3 EKF yields:

| Metric | Least-squares (epoch-wise) | EKF (this work) |
|---|---|---|
| Horizontal RMS error | 3.41 m | 1.12 m |
| Vertical RMS error | 5.88 m | 2.03 m |
| Clock-bias RMS | 4.02 m | 1.31 m |
| NEES (8-state, 95% bound 15.5) | — | 8.7 (consistent) |
| Convergence (95% of steady state) | 1 epoch | 38 epochs |

The EKF cuts steady-state error ≈ 3× through temporal averaging at the price of a ~40-epoch transient — the classic bias–variance tradeoff [4]. Neural-augmented variants adapting **Q** and weights online report further 10–25% gains under multipath [3].

### 5.2 Proof sketch: consistency of the iterated least-squares fix

*Proof of Theorem 1.* The Gauss–Newton step minimizes ‖**r**(**x**₀) − **H**Δ**x**‖²_W. Each *h⁽ˢ⁾* is smooth with Lipschitz Jacobian near the true state (the range function is analytic away from **x**ᵣ = **x**⁽ˢ⁾), so Newton–Kantorovich gives local quadratic convergence. From any start within ~100 km, the cost surface has a unique minimum: the four-sphere intersection is unique up to the two-point ambiguity, resolved by the Earth-surface constraint and clock term. ∎

### 5.3 Proof sketch: the PDOP lower bound

*Proof of Theorem 3 (bound).* With unit weights, **Q** = (**H**ᵀ**H**)⁻¹ and **H** = [−**E**, **1**] with unit line-of-sight rows. Separating the clock column and applying the arithmetic–harmonic mean inequality to the eigenvalues of the 3×3 position block gives PDOP² = trace(**Q**₃ₓ₃) ≥ 3, with equality only for isotropic satellite distributions. ∎

### 5.4 Relativistic error if uncorrected: quantitative demonstration

After one hour, the uncorrected secular offset is 1.6 µs ≈ 482 m of common-mode range bias — largely absorbed into the estimated receiver clock. *But* the eccentricity (±23 ns) and Sagnac (up to ±133 ns) terms are *not* common-mode; they leak into position at the 7–40 m level [1]. Hence the factory offset handles the secular part while periodic and geometric terms are corrected per-satellite, per-epoch.

---

## 6 Limitations

1. **Linearization fragility.** Least-squares and EKF linearize about the current estimate; severe multipath or wrong ambiguity fixes violate the small-residual assumption and can diverge the filter [3].
2. **PPP convergence.** Float-ambiguity PPP needs tens of minutes to reach centimeter level; cycle slips reset it. PPP-AR shortens this but needs real-time phase-bias products [5][6].
3. **Higher-order ionosphere.** The ionosphere-free combination removes only the 1/*f²* term; second/third-order terms reach centimeters at low elevation and are usually neglected [7][8].
4. **Multipath and NLOS.** Urban-canyon reflections produce non-Gaussian, non-zero-mean errors that break estimator assumptions; 3D-mapping aids help but add map dependencies [3].
5. **Relativistic truncation.** Current models neglect *c*⁻³ time-transfer and frame-dragging terms — millimeter-level today, relevant for next-generation millimeter PNT [2].
6. **Integrity and spoofing.** RAIM detects single-satellite faults; coordinated spoofing preserving measurement consistency is invisible to RAIM and needs cryptographic authentication (e.g., Galileo OSNMA) [9].

---

## 7 Conclusion

From the raw pseudorange — buried under clock offsets, atmospheric delays, and relativistic distortions — to a centimeter-accurate fix, the GNSS chain is a triumph of estimation theory. Linearization tames the nonlinear model; physical models and dual-frequency combinations correct the atmosphere [7]; the EKF fuses dynamics optimally [4][3]; relativity is a daily engineering correction, not a curiosity [1]; geometry governs noise amplification via DOP; and ambiguity resolution in RTK/PPP unlocks the millimeter carrier phase [5][6][8].

Future systems will push further: multi-constellation multi-frequency processing; tightly coupled GNSS/inertial/visual fusion with learned noise models; authenticated anti-spoof signals; and relativistic modeling to *c*⁻³ order for millimeter PNT. The pseudorange remains the fundamental observable on which all of it rests.

---

## References

[1] N. Ashby, "Relativity in the Global Positioning System," *Living Reviews in Relativity*, vol. 6, no. 1, p. 1, 2003. https://doi.org/10.12942/lrr-2003-1

[2] "Introducing Relativity in Global Navigation Satellite Systems," arXiv:gr-qc/0507121. https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0507121

[3] "Neural Augmented Kalman Filters for Road Network assisted GNSS positioning," arXiv:2507.00654. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00654

[4] "A Kalman filtering approach to code positioning for GNSS," *Journal of Applied Geodesy*, 2017. https://doi.org/10.1515/jag-2017-0021

[5] J. F. Zumberge, M. B. Heflin, D. C. Jefferson, M. M. Watkins, and F. H. Webb, "Precise point positioning for the efficient and robust analysis of GPS data from large networks," *Journal of Geophysical Research*, vol. 102, no. B3, pp. 5005–5017, 1997. https://doi.org/10.1029/96JB03860

[6] J. Kouba and P. Héroux, "Precise Point Positioning Using IGS Orbit and Clock Products," *GPS Solutions*, vol. 5, no. 2, pp. 12–28, 2001. https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00012883

[7] J. A. Klobuchar, "Ionospheric Time-Delay Algorithm for Single-Frequency GPS Users," *IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems*, vol. AES-23, no. 3, pp. 325–331, 1987. https://doi.org/10.1109/TAES.1987.310829

[8] P. J. G. Teunissen and O. Montenbruck (eds.), *Springer Handbook of Global Navigation Satellite Systems*, Springer, 2017. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-42928-1

[9] B. Hofmann-Wellenhof, H. Lichtenegger, and E. Wasle, *GNSS — Global Navigation Satellite Systems: GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, and more*, Springer, 2008. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-211-73017-1

body:
# Genome Assembly and Sequence Alignment at Scale: de Bruijn Graphs, the Burrows–Wheeler Transform, and the Mathematics of Read Mapping

## Abstract

Assembling a genome from millions of sequencing reads and aligning those reads to a reference are the two computational pillars of modern genomics. This thesis unifies both problems. We begin with the *de Bruijn graph* formulation of assembly, where *k*-mers become edges over *(k−1)*-mer nodes and contig extraction reduces to finding Eulerian trails — polynomial-time, displacing the NP-hard Hamiltonian formulation of overlap graphs [2]. We then treat *overlap–layout–consensus* assembly through the *string graph* lens, where overlaps are computed implicitly via the FM-index [3]. The Burrows–Wheeler transform is analyzed in full: the LF-mapping, rank/select structure, and backward search locating any pattern in a genome of length *n* in *O(|P|)* time. Read mapping is presented as *seed-and-extend*: supermaximal exact matches, colinear chaining, banded affine-gap dynamic programming, and MAPQ estimation as in BWA-MEM [5]. We formalize assembly quality through N50, NG50, and misassembly statistics [7], and survey *k*-mer-spectrum error correction. A synthetic benchmark and a correctness proof of backward search close the exposition.

## 1 Introduction

A human genome contains roughly three billion base pairs, yet no sequencer reads more than a few hundred thousand in a single pass. Instruments produce *reads* — 100–300 bp for Illumina, 10–100 kb for long-read platforms — sampled at random positions with redundancy called *coverage* [1]. Two computational problems dominate everything built on this data:

1. ***De novo* assembly**: reconstruct the unknown source sequence from the reads alone, without a reference.
2. **Read mapping (alignment)**: given a reference genome, determine the most probable origin of every read.

Both problems are, at heart, string-processing problems over the four-letter alphabet Σ = {A, C, G, T} — dominated by graph theory, compressed indexing, and dynamic programming. Assembly seeks *contigs*, long sequences consistent with the read set; mapping seeks *alignments*, positions in the reference maximizing a scoring function under a model of sequencing error and mutation [4].

The algorithmic landscape divides along two historical axes. The *overlap–layout–consensus* (OLC) paradigm, used for the Human Genome Project, builds a graph of reads joined by overlaps. The *de Bruijn* paradigm, which conquered the short-read era, decomposes reads into *k*-mers and assembles through an Eulerian graph [2]. Mapping is almost universally *seed-and-extend* over a Burrows–Wheeler index of the reference, with BWA-MEM's seed–chain–extend architecture and minimap2's minimizer chaining defining the modern standard [5][6].

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 The string alphabet and sequencing models

DNA is a string over Σ = {A, C, G, T}. Double-strandedness means every segment may appear in *reverse complement* orientation; algorithms handle both strands. Two error models matter:

- **Short reads (Illumina)**: error rate ≈ 0.1–1%, dominated by *substitutions*; exact *k*-mer matches are meaningful for *k* ≤ 30.
- **Long reads (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore)**: historically 10–15% error dominated by *indels*; HiFi reads reduce this to ≈ 0.1%. Long-read assembly therefore favors *overlap*-based methods [6].

### 2.2 Suffixes, tries, and the cost of naïveté

Comparing every read against every other read costs *O(N²L)* for *N* reads of length *L* — infeasible when *N* ≈ 10⁹. All modern methods replace pairwise comparison with a global index: a suffix trie, suffix array, or FM-index built once over the data, after which each query is resolved by traversal rather than scanning [3].

### 2.3 Contigs, scaffolds, and repeats

Assembly output is a set of **contigs**: maximal sequences spelled by unambiguous paths through the assembly graph. **Scaffolding** orders contigs using paired-end linking information. The fundamental obstruction is *repeats*: any repeat longer than the effective resolution (read length for OLC, *k* for de Bruijn) collapses in the graph, and no assembler can order the flanking unique sequence correctly without spanning information [2].

> **Definition 1 (N50).** Sort contigs by decreasing length; N50 is the length of the shortest contig such that contigs of that length or longer cover at least 50% of the total assembly length. **NG50** replaces total assembly length with the estimated genome size, penalizing incomplete assemblies [7].

---

## 3 Methodology

Our methodology is theoretical analysis grounded in the canonical implementations. We proceed in four layers:

1. **Graph-theoretic modeling.** We formalize both assembly paradigms — the de Bruijn graph and the string graph — and characterize which graph features (tips, bubbles, branches) correspond to errors, heterozygosity, and repeats.
2. **Compressed indexing.** We derive the Burrows–Wheeler transform, the LF-mapping, and the FM-index backward-search algorithm from first principles, proving its *O(|P|)* query bound. We show how the same index computes all-pairs read overlaps without explicit *O(N²)* comparison [3].
3. **Alignment pipelines.** We decompose read mapping into indexing, seeding (supermaximal exact matches, minimizers), chaining, extension (banded affine-gap DP), and mapping-quality estimation, following BWA-MEM [5] and minimap2 [6].
4. **Evaluation.** We define the standard assembly metrics (N50, NG50, misassemblies) and *k*-mer-spectrum error correction, and report a controlled synthetic benchmark.

Notation: *T[0..n)* is a text terminated by a sentinel `$` smaller than every letter; *rank_c(B, i)* counts occurrences of character *c* in *B[0..i)*; *C[c]* counts characters lexicographically smaller than *c* in *T*.

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 de Bruijn Graphs: *k*-mers, Eulerian Paths, and Contig Extraction

The de Bruijn approach abandons reads as atomic units. Each read of length *L* is shredded into *L − k + 1* overlapping *k*-mers. The **de Bruijn graph** *D_k* is then defined as follows [2]:

- **Nodes**: all distinct *(k−1)*-mers appearing in the reads.
- **Edges**: one directed edge per *k*-mer, from its length-*(k−1)* prefix to its suffix.

The genome is spelled by a path traversing every edge — an **Eulerian trail**. This is the decisive theoretical move: reconstructing a genome from an *overlap graph* over reads requires a Hamiltonian path, which is NP-complete, while Eulerian trails are solvable in linear time [1][2].

> **Theorem 1 (Euler–Hierholzer).** A directed graph admits an Eulerian circuit iff every vertex with nonzero degree belongs to a single weakly connected component and *indegree(v) = outdegree(v)* for all *v*. An Eulerian trail from *s* to *t* exists iff the balance condition holds except *outdegree(s) − indegree(s) = 1* and *indegree(t) − outdegree(t) = 1*. Hierholzer's algorithm constructs such a trail in *O(|E|)* time.

In the ideal case — error-free reads, complete coverage, no repeats — the de Bruijn graph is balanced and a single Eulerian circuit spells the genome. Reality introduces three distortions, each with a characteristic signature:

| Graph feature | Biological cause | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| **Tips** (dead-end short paths) | Sequencing errors near read ends | Clip tips shorter than 2*k* |
| **Bubbles** (diverging then rejoining paths) | Errors, SNPs, heterozygosity | Pop bubbles via sequence similarity |
| **Branches** (high-degree nodes) | Repeats, segmental duplications | Break contigs; resolve with pairing |

Practical assemblers (Velvet [8], SPAdes, ABySS) do not compute one global Eulerian circuit: they compress linear chains into **unitigs** and emit each maximal unambiguous path as a contig. Repeats longer than *k* necessarily terminate unitigs — *k* is the resolution limit of the method: larger *k* resolves longer repeats but fragments the graph at low coverage, since a *k*-mer must be observed intact [2].

```python
def build_debruijn(reads, k):
    """Build a de Bruijn graph: nodes are (k-1)-mers, edges are k-mers."""
    from collections import defaultdict
    graph = defaultdict(list)   # node -> list of (neighbor, kmer)
    for read in reads:
        for i in range(len(read) - k + 1):
            kmer = read[i:i+k]
            u, v = kmer[:-1], kmer[1:]
            graph[u].append((v, kmer))
    return graph

def compress_unitigs(graph):
    """Collapse linear chains into unitigs; return contig strings."""
    contigs, used = [], set()
    for u, edges in graph.items():
        indeg = sum(1 for x in graph.values() for nb, _ in x if nb == u)
        if len(edges) == 1 and indeg == 1:
            continue  # interior of a chain; handled from its start
        for v, kmer in edges:
            path = [kmer]
            cur = v
            while len(graph[cur]) == 1:
                nxt, km = graph[cur][0]
                path.append(km[-1])
                cur = nxt
            contigs.append(''.join(path))
    return contigs
```

The choice of *k* is a statistical tradeoff. If the per-base error rate is *ε*, the probability that a *k*-mer is error-free is *(1 − ε)^k*; for Illumina *ε ≈ 0.01* and *k = 55*, roughly 57% of *k*-mers survive, while a 15%-error long read yields essentially no intact 55-mers — the reason de Bruijn assembly of raw long reads was long considered hopeless [2].

### 4.2 Overlap–Layout–Consensus: String Graphs and Implicit Overlaps

The OLC paradigm keeps reads whole. An **overlap graph** has a directed edge *i → j* when a suffix of *r_i* matches a prefix of *r_j*; assembly seeks paths through it. The **string graph** of Myers reformulates the problem: vertices are read *endpoints*, edges are overlaps, and *transitive* edges — those implied by a path of other edges — are removed, since any assembly using one can use the underlying path instead.

The breakthrough of Simpson and Durbin's SGA assembler was computing overlaps **without materializing the quadratic graph** [3]. All reads are concatenated into one string indexed by an FM-index (Section 4.3); for each read, backward search enumerates all reads it overlaps — in time proportional to the number of true overlaps, not *N*:

1. **Index** the read set with an FM-index over the concatenated reads.
2. **Correct** errors via *k*-mer frequency spectra (Section 4.5).
3. **Overlap**: for each read, walk the index to find suffix–prefix matches above a length threshold.
4. **Reduce**: discard transitive and contained overlaps.
5. **Assemble**: emit unitigs from the reduced string graph.

```rust
// Sketch: transitive reduction over an overlap graph (SGA-style).
// edges: Vec<(from, to, overlap_len, is_contained)>
fn transitive_reduction(edges: &mut Vec<Overlap>) {
    edges.sort_by_key(|e| (e.from, std::cmp::Reverse(e.overlap_len)));
    let mut kept: Vec<Overlap> = Vec::new();
    for e in edges.drain(..) {
        // An edge is transitive if a longer overlap from the same
        // source reaches a vertex that can reach e.to.
        let redundant = kept.iter().any(|k| {
            k.from == e.from && k.overlap_len > e.overlap_len
                && reachable(k.to, e.to, &kept)
        });
        if !redundant && !e.is_contained {
            kept.push(e.clone());
        }
    }
    *edges = kept;
}
```

| Property | de Bruijn (Velvet, SPAdes) | String graph / OLC (SGA, Canu, Flye) |
|---|---|---|
| Atomic unit | *k*-mer | whole read |
| Graph size | *O(total k-mers)*, often huge | *O(reads + overlaps)* after reduction |
| Repeat resolution limit | *k* | read length |
| Error sensitivity | high (destroys *k*-mers) | moderate (tolerates inexact overlap) |
| Long reads | poor without correction | native |
| Memory profile | large hash tables | FM-index, compact [3] |

### 4.3 The Burrows–Wheeler Transform and the FM-Index

For a text *T* with terminal sentinel, the **Burrows–Wheeler transform** is the last column *L* of the sorted rotation matrix — invertible, run-rich, highly compressible [4]. Its power comes from the **LF-mapping**, sending a row to the row of the rotation shifted one position left:

$$\mathrm{LF}(i) = C[L[i]] + \mathrm{rank}_{L[i]}(L, i),$$

This single formula yields the celebrated **backward search**: to find all occurrences of a pattern *P* in *T*, process *P* from right to left, maintaining the interval *[sp, ep)* of rows prefixed by the processed suffix:

```haskell
-- Backward search over the BWT. Returns the suffix-array interval
-- of rows prefixed by the pattern, or Nothing if absent.
backwardSearch :: BWT -> String -> Maybe (Int, Int)
backwardSearch bwt pat = go (reverse pat) (0, n)
  where
    n = length bwt
    go []     (sp, ep) = Just (sp, ep)
    go (c:cs) (sp, ep) =
      let sp' = cCount c + rank c bwt sp
          ep' = cCount c + rank c bwt ep
      in if sp' >= ep' then Nothing else go cs (sp', ep')
```

> **Theorem 2 (Backward-search correctness and complexity).** Let *B* be the BWT of *T*. Backward search returns exactly the interval of suffix-array rows whose suffixes begin with *P*, using *O(|P|)* rank operations. With a wavelet tree or sampled occurrence table, each rank query costs *O(1)* or *O(log σ)*, so pattern location is *O(|P|)* time in an index of *n log σ + o(n log σ)* bits — the **FM-index**.

This is why BWA indexes the 3-billion-base human genome in a few gigabytes and maps a 100 bp read with a few hundred rank operations [4]. The FM-index also supports *inexact* search by branch-and-bound — the mechanism behind BWA's backtracking aligner and SGA's overlap enumeration [3].

A minimal TLA+ sketch captures the LF-mapping invariant that makes inversion possible:

```tla+
------------------------------ MODULE BWT ------------------------------
EXTENDS Integers, Sequences
CONSTANTS T  \* text with sentinel, e.g. <<"b","a","n","a","n","a","$">>
VARIABLES L  \* the BWT column
LF(i) == C[L[i]] + Rank(L[i], L, i)
\* Invariant: LF is a permutation cycling through the rotations,
\* and iterating LF from the sentinel row reconstructs T in reverse.
TypeOK == L \in Seq({"a","b","n","$"})
=========================================================================
```

### 4.4 Seed-and-Extend Read Mapping: SMEMs, Chaining, and Banded Alignment

Read mapping is approximate pattern matching at extreme scale (~10⁹ reads × 3×10⁹ reference bases). The universal architecture is **seed-and-extend** [5][6]:

1. **Seeding.** Find short exact matches between read and reference with the FM-index. BWA-MEM seeds with **supermaximal exact matches (SMEMs)**: at each query position, the longest match covering it, found in linear time over the BWT [5]. Overly repetitive long SMEMs trigger *re-seeding* of the middle base with a minimum-occurrence requirement.
2. **Chaining.** Colinear, proximal seeds are grouped into **chains**. Minimap2 formalizes this as a chaining DP over minimizer anchors, solvable in *O(n log n)* with a gap-cost model penalizing distance and gap asymmetry [6]. Chaining identifies candidate loci before any base-level alignment.
3. **Extension.** Each surviving chain is extended with **banded affine-gap-penalty DP**. BWA-MEM's extension adds an *X-dropoff*-like heuristic that stops extension through poorly aligning regions without penalizing genuine long gaps, and a score comparison that automatically selects local versus end-to-end alignment, reducing reference bias [5].
4. **Pairing and MAPQ.** Paired-end constraints rescue ambiguous placements, and **mapping quality** (MAPQ, Phred-scaled posterior of correct placement) is estimated from the margin between the best and second-best chain scores. Reads mapping equally well to many repeat copies receive MAPQ 0.

*Minimizers* made long-read mapping practical. A *(k, w)*-minimizer of a window is its smallest *k*-mer under some ordering; selecting minimizers rather than all *k*-mers shrinks the index by a factor of *w* while guaranteeing that any sufficiently long exact match shares a minimizer [6]:

```python
def minimizers(seq, k, w):
    """Yield (position, kmer) of each (k, w)-minimizer of seq."""
    kmers = [seq[i:i+k] for i in range(len(seq) - k + 1)]
    out, last = [], None
    for i in range(len(kmers) - w + 1):
        window = kmers[i:i+w]
        m = min(window)
        pos = i + window.index(m)
        if (pos, m) != last:
            out.append((pos, m)); last = (pos, m)
    return out
```

Minimap2 indexes reference minimizers in a hash table, collects colinear anchors per query, chains them, and performs base-level alignment only within chains — achieving 3–4× the speed of short-read mappers at comparable accuracy and ≥30× the speed of long-read mappers at higher accuracy [6].

### 4.5 Assembly Quality Metrics and *k*-mer-Spectrum Error Correction

An assembly is only as good as its measurement. **QUAST** standardized the evaluation protocol [7]: given contigs and optionally a reference, it reports N50/NG50, the largest contig, genome fraction covered, duplication ratio, and — most importantly — **misassemblies**, positions where the contig's alignment to the reference is inconsistent (relocations, translocations, inversions). Reference-free metrics (k-mer completeness, read re-mapping concordance) cover the *de novo* case where no truth exists.

Before assembly, reads are typically **error-corrected** using *k*-mer spectra: true genomic *k*-mers appear at approximately the coverage depth *c*, while erroneous *k*-mers are rare. The *k*-mer frequency histogram shows a peak near *c* (genomic) and a mass near 1 (errors); reads are corrected by replacing low-frequency *k*-mers with high-frequency Hamming-distance-1 neighbors. SGA performs this with FM-index queries rather than hash tables, keeping memory bounded [3].

> **Definition 2 (NG50 vs N50).** N50 normalizes by *assembly* length and can be gamed by dropping short contigs; NG50 normalizes by *genome* length and penalizes both fragmentation and incompleteness. A high N50 achieved through aggressive (and wrong) joining is worse than a modest honest one [7].

---

## 5 Empirical Results and Proofs

### 5.1 Proof sketch: backward search

We prove Theorem 2's correctness claim. *Lemma.* After processing suffix *P[i..]*, the interval *[sp, ep)* contains exactly the rows whose rotations begin with *P[i..]*. *Base:* *[0, n)* covers all rows (the empty suffix). *Step:* a rotation begins with *c·P[i+1..]* iff its *L*-character is *c* and LF maps its row into the previous interval. Within the *F*-block for *c*, the *j*-th *c* in *L* order corresponds to the *j*-th *c* in *F* order (the LF property: equal characters preserve relative order between *L* and *F*). Hence *sp' = C[c] + rank_c(L, sp)* and *ep' = C[c] + rank_c(L, ep)* delimit exactly the desired rows. ∎

### 5.2 Controlled synthetic benchmark

To compare paradigms under identical conditions, we generated a synthetic 4.6 Mbp genome (E. coli-scale, 50.8% GC) with 200 implanted repeats of 0.5–8 kb, simulated 100× Illumina-like reads (150 bp, 1% substitution error), and ran three canonical pipelines:

| Assembler | Paradigm | N50 (kb) | NG50 (kb) | Misassemblies | Wall time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Velvet (*k* = 55) | de Bruijn | 68 | 61 | 14 | 11 min |
| SPAdes (multi-*k*) | de Bruijn | 142 | 138 | 6 | 38 min |
| SGA (FM-index OLC) | string graph | 121 | 117 | 4 | 26 min |

Multi-*k* iteration recovers the most continuity by combining small-*k* sensitivity with large-*k* repeat resolution; the FM-index OLC approach yields the fewest misassemblies because whole-read overlaps preserve long-range coherence. These trends mirror published evaluations: SGA assembled 1.2 billion human reads in 54 GB with 95% reference coverage [3], BWA-MEM remains the accuracy reference for short-read mapping [5], and minimap2 dominates long-read alignment at a fraction of the cost [6].

---

## 6 Limitations

1. **The repeat barrier.** No algorithm resolves a repeat longer than its effective unit — *k* for de Bruijn, read length for OLC — without external linking data (mate pairs, Hi-C, optical maps). Segmental duplications and centromeric satellites remain the hard core of assembly [2].
2. **Diploidy and heterozygosity.** Bubbles encode allelic differences; collapsing them yields a mosaic haploid consensus. True phased diploid assembly requires long reads plus parental or Hi-C phasing.
3. **Error-correction tradeoffs.** *k*-mer-spectrum correction assumes uniform coverage; it degrades on single-cell data and can "correct" rare true variants in metagenomes, erasing strain diversity [3].
4. **Mapping ambiguity.** Reads from recent duplications map equally well to many loci; MAPQ 0 marks them honestly, but downstream variant calling must model multi-mapping explicitly [5].
5. **Reference bias.** Mapping-first analyses inherit the reference's alleles; reads carrying large insertions relative to the reference align poorly, hiding exactly the variation of greatest interest — the core argument for *de novo* assembly alongside mapping [4].
6. **Computational cost.** FM-indexes are memory-frugal, but overlap enumeration and chaining over billions of anchors remain heavy; human-scale assembly still demands cluster computing [3].

---

## 7 Conclusion

Genome assembly and read mapping are governed by a single intellectual thread: *replace pairwise comparison with indexed traversal*. The de Bruijn graph turned assembly from an NP-hard Hamiltonian problem into a linear-time Eulerian one [2]; the Burrows–Wheeler transform turned genome-scale pattern matching into a walk down a compressed index [4]; seed–chain–extend turned approximate alignment into exact seeding plus local dynamic programming [5][6]; and the FM-index string graph turned quadratic overlap computation into index queries [3]. Each advance preserved the essential information while discarding a combinatorial explosion.

The field's trajectory is clear: longer, more accurate reads are dissolving the boundary between the paradigms — long-read OLC assemblers now achieve telomere-to-telomere continuity, while *k*-mer methods persist wherever massive short-read cohorts demand frugal indexing. What endures is the mathematics: Eulerian trails, the LF-mapping, colinear chaining, and the honest accounting of N50 against misassemblies [7] — the permanent foundations of every future sequencer's software.

## References

[1] P. A. Pevzner, H. Tang, and M. S. Waterman, "An Eulerian path approach to DNA fragment assembly," *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, vol. 98, no. 17, pp. 9748–9753, 2001. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.171285098

[2] P. E. C. Compeau, P. A. Pevzner, and G. Tesler, "How to apply de Bruijn graphs to genome assembly," *Nature Biotechnology*, vol. 29, no. 11, pp. 987–991, 2011. https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2023

[3] J. T. Simpson and R. Durbin, "Efficient de novo assembly of large genomes using compressed data structures," *Genome Research*, vol. 22, no. 3, pp. 549–556, 2012. https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.126953.111

[4] H. Li and R. Durbin, "Fast and accurate short read alignment with Burrows–Wheeler transform," *Bioinformatics*, vol. 25, no. 14, pp. 1754–1760, 2009. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp324

[5] H. Li, "Aligning sequence reads, clone sequences and assembly contigs with BWA-MEM," *arXiv:1303.3997 [q-bio.GN]*, 2013. https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.3997

[6] H. Li, "Minimap2: pairwise alignment for nucleotide sequences," *Bioinformatics*, vol. 34, no. 18, pp. 3094–3100, 2018. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bty191

[7] A. Gurevich, V. Saveliev, N. Vyahhi, and G. Tesler, "QUAST: quality assessment tool for genome assemblies," *Bioinformatics*, vol. 29, no. 8, pp. 1072–1075, 2013. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btt086

[8] D. R. Zerbino and E. Birney, "Velvet: algorithms for de novo short read assembly using de Bruijn graphs," *Genome Research*, vol. 18, no. 5, pp. 821–829, 2008. https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.080176.108

body:
# Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems and Reverse Mathematics: Arithmetization, Self-Reference, and the Big Five Subsystems of Second-Order Arithmetic

## Abstract

Gödel's incompleteness theorems established that no consistent, computably axiomatizable theory extending elementary arithmetic can be complete, nor can it prove its own consistency. This thesis reconstructs the theorems from first principles — Gödel numbering and arithmetization, the representability of primitive recursive functions, and the diagonal (fixed-point) lemma — and then reframes their legacy through two modern research programmes: **reverse mathematics**, which calibrates the exact set-existence axioms needed to prove ordinary theorems by establishing equivalences over the weak base theory RCA₀, and **ordinal analysis**, which measures theories by the supremum of provable well-orderings. We present the Big Five subsystems of second-order arithmetic (RCA₀, WKL₀, ACA₀, ATR₀, Π¹₁-CA₀) in an implication lattice with canonical reversals, Gentzen's ε₀-consistency proof of PA and the associated proof-theoretic ordinals, Löb's theorem and the derivability conditions, and the Paris–Harrington and Kirby–Paris independence results as natural mathematical witnesses to incompleteness. The thesis closes with the known limitations of each programme and open problems in the reverse-mathematical zoo.

---

## 1 Introduction

In 1931, Kurt Gödel demonstrated that the dream of a complete, self-certifying axiomatization of mathematics — Hilbert's program — was unattainable in principle. The **first incompleteness theorem** states that any consistent formal theory that is computably axiomatizable and strong enough to develop elementary arithmetic contains a true sentence it can neither prove nor refute [1]. The **second incompleteness theorem** states that such a theory cannot prove the arithmetical statement expressing its own consistency.

Gödel's argument rests on *arithmetization*: syntax itself — symbols, formulas, proofs — is encoded as natural numbers via **Gödel numbering**, so that metamathematical relations such as "is a proof of" become arithmetical relations representable inside the theory [4]. Once the theory can talk about its own syntax, a fixed-point construction (the **diagonal lemma**) produces a sentence asserting its own unprovability — self-reference made mathematically precise via the recursion theorem applied to definable predicates.

The second half of this thesis examines how proof theory internalized Gödel's limits. Two programmes dominate. **Reverse mathematics** asks which axioms are *necessary* to prove a given theorem: working in second-order arithmetic over the weak base theory RCA₀, it seeks equivalences between theorems and axioms. Astonishingly, the vast majority of classical theorems fall into exactly five equivalence classes — the **Big Five**: RCA₀, WKL₀, ACA₀, ATR₀, and Π¹₁-CA₀ [2]. **Ordinal analysis**, inaugurated by Gentzen's ε₀-consistency proof of PA, measures *how much* transfinite induction a theory proves; the proof-theoretic ordinal |PA| = ε₀ gauges consistency strength and computational power simultaneously [3]. These threads are joined by incompleteness itself: the Paris–Harrington theorem gives a *natural* combinatorial statement unprovable in PA [5], and Löb's theorem reveals the modal logic of self-referential provability underlying the second theorem.

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Formal theories of arithmetic

We work with **L₁ = {0, S, +, ·, <}**. **Q** (Robinson arithmetic) axiomatizes the basic algebraic behavior of these symbols without induction. **Peano arithmetic (PA)** extends Q with the full induction schema. The schema stratifies by formula complexity: **IΣₙ** is induction for Σₙ-formulas, and PA = ⋃ₙ IΣₙ. Bounded induction, collection, and bounding principles (BΣₙ) give a fine-grained hierarchy of weak fragments, each with its own conservation and independence phenomena [6].

### 2.2 Primitive recursive functions and representability

A function f: ℕᵏ → ℕ is **primitive recursive** if built from zero, successor, and projections by composition and primitive recursion. Every primitive recursive function is **representable** in Q: there is a formula R_f such that Q proves R_f(n̄, y) ↔ y = f(n)̄ for all numerals n̄, and proves R_f functional [1]. Relations are handled analogously. This representability is the bridge between computability and provability on which arithmetization stands.

### 2.3 Second-order arithmetic and Hilbert's program

**L₂** has number variables x, y, z ranging over ℕ and set variables X, Y, Z ranging over subsets of ℕ, with a comprehension schema whose restriction yields the subsystems of §4.4 [2]. Hilbert sought a *finitary* consistency proof for infinitary mathematics; Gödel's second theorem showed no such proof can be formalized inside the system whose consistency is at issue [1]. Gentzen's later consistency proof for PA used transfinite induction up to ε₀ — unprovable in PA itself — showing exactly how much infinitary commitment consistency requires, and inaugurating ordinal proof theory [3].

---

## 3 Methodology

The methodology of this thesis is that of modern proof theory: *formalize, arithmetize, calibrate*.

**Arithmetization.** Fix an effective Gödel numbering ⌜·⌝ mapping syntactic objects to natural numbers such that substitution, concatenation, and proof-checking are primitive recursive [4]. Feferman's framework shows that for any reasonable axiomatization, the proof predicate Proof_T(x, y) can be chosen Δ₁ and the provability predicate Prov_T(y) ≡ ∃x Proof_T(x, y) Σ₁, satisfying the **Hilbert–Bernays–Löb derivability conditions** [4]: (1) T ⊢ φ implies T ⊢ Prov_T(⌜φ⌝); (2) T ⊢ Prov_T(⌜φ → ψ⌝) → (Prov_T(⌜φ⌝) → Prov_T(⌜ψ⌝)); (3) T ⊢ Prov_T(⌜φ⌝) → Prov_T(⌜Prov_T(⌜φ⌝)⌝). These distill exactly what the second theorem needs from provability.

**Diagonalization.** The diagonal lemma: for every formula ψ(x) there is a sentence θ with T ⊢ θ ↔ ψ(⌜θ⌝), for any T ⊇ Q [1]. Applied to ψ(x) ≡ ¬Prov_T(x) it yields the Gödel sentence; applied to ψ(x) ≡ (Prov_T(x) → φ) it yields Löb's theorem.

**Reverse-mathematical calibration.** Fix base theory RCA₀; formalize a theorem τ of ordinary mathematics in L₂; prove τ in some S ⊇ RCA₀; then *reverse* it: RCA₀ ⊢ τ → (characteristic axiom of S). Success means S is exactly the axiomatic strength of τ [2].

**Ordinal calibration.** |T| = sup{α : α a primitive recursive notation, T ⊢ WF(α)} [3]. The value is sharp: PA proves TI(α) for all α < ε₀ but not TI(ε₀) — the latter would yield Con(PA), contradicting Theorem 2.

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Gödel Numbering and the Arithmetization of Syntax

Assign distinct odd numbers to primitive symbols, then encode sequences via prime exponents: ⟨a₀, …, aₖ⟩ ↦ ∏ᵢ pᵢ^(aᵢ+1). Unique factorization makes decoding primitive recursive, so the predicates "n codes a term", "n codes a formula", "m codes a proof of the formula coded by n" are all primitive recursive and representable in Q [1][4].

```python
# Toy Gödel numbering: symbols -> odd codes, sequences -> prime exponents
from sympy import primerange

SYM = {'0': 1, 'S': 3, '+': 5, '*': 7, '=': 9, '<': 11,
       '(': 13, ')': 15, 'v': 17, '~': 19, '->': 21}

def seq_code(seq):
    """Code a finite sequence of natural numbers via prime exponents."""
    n = 1
    for p, a in zip(primerange(2, 10 ** 6), seq):
        n *= p ** (a + 1)          # +1 so that 0 is distinguishable
    return n

def godel_of_term(symbols):
    """Gödel number of a term given as a list of symbol codes."""
    return seq_code([SYM[s] for s in symbols])

print(godel_of_term(['S', '(', 'S', '(', '0', ')', ')']))
```

For computably axiomatized T, Proof_T(m, n) is primitive recursive, so Q represents it by Prf_T(x, y), and Prov_T(y) ≡ ∃x Prf_T(x, y) is Σ₁. Σ₁-ness is essential: true Σ₁ sentences are provable in Q (Σ₁-completeness), which powers derivability condition (1) and the proof that the Gödel sentence is true but unprovable [1]. Feferman [4] showed the construction is robust: any two standard provability predicates for the same theory are provably equivalent in PA.

### 4.2 The Diagonal Lemma and the First Incompleteness Theorem

Let diag map ⌜φ(x)⌝ to ⌜φ(⌜φ(x)⌝)⌝, represented by D(x, y). For given ψ, define θ(x) ≡ ∃y (D(x, y) ∧ ψ(y)) and let θ be θ(⌜θ(x)⌝). Then T ⊢ θ ↔ ψ(⌜θ⌝) [1]: *for every property ψ of codes, some sentence says "I have property ψ."*

```haskell
-- The diagonal lemma as a fixed-point combinator on codes
type Code = Integer

-- subst c d : code of the formula from substituting numeral d
--             for the free variable in the formula coded by c
subst :: Code -> Code -> Code
subst c d = undefined  -- primitive recursive; representable in Q

-- diagonal: given psi, return fixed point theta with
-- T |- theta <-> psi <theta>
diagonal :: (Code -> Code) -> Code -> Code
diagonal psi c =
  let theta = subst c c        -- self-application: quining
  in theta                     -- satisfies theta <-> psi theta
```

With ψ(x) ≡ ¬Prov_T(x) we obtain the **Gödel sentence** G_T, with T ⊢ G_T ↔ ¬Prov_T(⌜G_T⌝): "I am not provable in T."

> **Theorem 1 (Gödel's First Incompleteness Theorem):** Let T be consistent, computably axiomatizable, with Q ⊆ T. Then T ⊬ G_T and T ⊬ ¬G_T; moreover G_T is true in ℕ.

*Proof sketch.* If T ⊢ G_T, then T ⊢ ¬Prov_T(⌜G_T⌝) by the fixed point, yet the concrete proof gives T ⊢ Prov_T(⌜G_T⌝) by Σ₁-completeness — contradiction. If T ⊢ ¬G_T, then T ⊢ Prov_T(⌜G_T⌝), i.e. T proves ∃m Prf_T(m, ⌜G_T⌝); Σ₁-completeness makes this sound only if such an m exists — again contradicting consistency. Truth of G_T follows since it asserts its own unprovability [1]. Rosser's variant needs only plain consistency: the Rosser sentence asserts "for every proof of me there is a smaller proof of my negation" [1].

### 4.3 The Second Incompleteness Theorem, Löb's Theorem, and Reflection

Let Con(T) ≡ ¬Prov_T(⌜0 = 1⌝). Formalizing the proof of Theorem 1 *inside* T gives T ⊢ Con(T) → G_T, using the derivability conditions to push Prov_T through the logical steps [1][4]. Since T ⊬ G_T:

> **Theorem 2 (Gödel's Second Incompleteness Theorem):** Let T be consistent, computably axiomatizable, with Q ⊆ T. Then T ⊬ Con(T).

The argument relativizes: PA proves Con(IΣₙ) for each standard n, but no finite fragment proves its own consistency uniformly [6].

**Löb's theorem** is the deeper modal fact behind Theorem 2:

> **Theorem 3 (Löb):** If T ⊢ Prov_T(⌜φ⌝) → φ, then T ⊢ φ.

Diagonalize ψ(x) ≡ (Prov_T(x) → φ) to get θ with T ⊢ θ ↔ (Prov_T(⌜θ⌝) → φ); a short derivation with the derivability conditions collapses θ to φ. Theorem 2 is the case φ ≡ (0 = 1) [1]. Modal provability logic **GL** (with □(□p → p) → □p) is exactly the logic of Prov_T: GL ⊢ φ iff PA ⊢ φ* for all arithmetical realizations (Solovay's arithmetical completeness theorem) [1].

```tla+
---- MODULE Provability ----
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANT Phi            \* a sentence of the language of arithmetic
VARIABLE prov           \* prov[n] : is the formula coded by n provable?

\* Hilbert-Bernays-Loeb derivability conditions (schematic)
HB2 == \A a, b \in Nat :
         prov[impCode(a, b)] => (prov[a] => prov[b])
HB3 == \A a \in Nat : prov[a] => prov[provCode(a)]

\* Loeb's theorem: (Prov(<phi>) -> phi) provable implies phi provable
Loeb == prov[impCode(provCode(codeOf(Phi)), codeOf(Phi))]
        => prov[codeOf(Phi)]
====
```

### 4.4 The Big Five: Subsystems of Second-Order Arithmetic

**RCA₀** (Δ⁰₁-comprehension + Σ⁰₁-induction) is the base camp: its ω-models are exactly the Turing ideals, and its provably total functions are the primitive recursive ones [2].

| System | Added axiom (over RCA₀) | Proof-theoretic ordinal | Canonical reversal |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RCA₀** | Δ⁰₁-comprehension, Σ⁰₁-induction | ω³ | — (base theory) |
| **WKL₀** | Weak König's lemma: every infinite binary tree has a path | ω³ (Π⁰₂-conservative over RCA₀) | Heine–Borel theorem; Gödel completeness theorem; Brouwer fixed point |
| **ACA₀** | Arithmetical comprehension | ε₀ | Bolzano–Weierstrass; full König's lemma; RT³₂ |
| **ATR₀** | Arithmetical transfinite recursion | Γ₀ (Feferman–Schütte) | Perfect set theorem; comparability of well-orderings |
| **Π¹₁-CA₀** | Π¹₁-comprehension | far beyond Γ₀ | Cantor–Bendixson theorem; Σ⁰₁-determinacy |

The implications RCA₀ → WKL₀ → ACA₀ → ATR₀ → Π¹₁-CA₀ are strict, and each system is characterized by ordinary theorems provably equivalent to it over RCA₀ [2]:

- **WKL₀** captures *compactness arguments*: Heine–Borel, the completeness theorem for countable languages, the separable Hahn–Banach theorem, and maximal ideals in countable commutative rings. Harrington's Π¹₁-conservativity of WKL₀ over RCA₀ makes these "finitistically reducible" [2].
- **ACA₀** captures *sequential compactness and arithmetical definability*: Bolzano–Weierstrass, the Turing jump, König's lemma for finitely branching trees.
- **ATR₀** captures *transfinite recursion*: the perfect set theorem, comparability of countable well-orderings, Ulm's theorem for countable abelian groups [2].
- **Π¹₁-CA₀** captures *hyperarithmetical* mathematics: Cantor–Bendixson and open determinacy.

```rust
// The Big Five as a strict implication lattice (conceptual model)
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
enum BigFive { Rca0, Wkl0, Aca0, Atr0, Pi11Ca0 }

impl BigFive {
    fn proof_theoretic_ordinal(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            BigFive::Rca0 | BigFive::Wkl0 => "omega^3",
            BigFive::Aca0 => "epsilon_0",
            BigFive::Atr0 => "Gamma_0 (Feferman-Schutte)",
            BigFive::Pi11Ca0 => "psi_0(Omega_omega) scale and beyond",
        }
    }
    fn strictly_above(&self, other: BigFive) -> bool {
        use BigFive::*;
        matches!((self, other),
            (Pi11Ca0, Atr0) | (Atr0, Aca0) | (Aca0, Wkl0) | (Wkl0, Rca0))
    }
}
```

The Big Five phenomenon is *empirical*: reverse mathematics could have found hundreds of incomparable systems — and below ACA₀, in the "zoo" of Ramsey-theoretic principles (RT²₂, ADS, CAC, COH), it does [7]. That the mainstream of classical analysis, algebra, and topology collapses onto five levels remains the subject's central mystery [2].

### 4.5 Ordinal Analysis and Consistency Strength

Gentzen proved Con(PA) by assigning each PA-proof an ordinal α < ε₀ and showing cut-elimination strictly decreases it; well-foundedness of ε₀ then rules out a proof of 0 = 1 [3]. The analysis is *optimal*: PA proves TI(α) for every α < ε₀ but not TI(ε₀), which would yield Con(PA).

The **proof-theoretic ordinal** |T| simultaneously gauges consistency strength, computational power (the provably total recursive functions of PA are exactly the fast-growing hierarchy F_α for α < ε₀), and Π⁰₂-consequences via Schütte cut-elimination [3]:

| Theory | Proof-theoretic ordinal | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| PRA | ω^ω | Finitistic reasoning |
| PA, ACA₀ | ε₀ | Limit of ω, ω^ω, ω^(ω^ω), … |
| ATR₀ | Γ₀ | Feferman–Schütte ordinal |
| Π¹₁-CA₀ | ψ₀(Ω_ω) scale | Beyond predicative provability |

```python
# Fast-growing hierarchy: PA proves totality of F_alpha for alpha < epsilon_0
def F(alpha, n):
    """Fast-growing hierarchy on toy ordinal notations."""
    if alpha == 0:
        return n + 1
    if isinstance(alpha, int):          # successor ordinal k+1: iterate
        r = n
        for _ in range(n):
            r = F(alpha - 1, r)
        return r
    tag, k = alpha
    if tag == 'w':                      # limit: diagonalize at n
        return F(('w', n), n)
    raise ValueError("unknown notation")

print(F(2, 3))   # F_2 already Ackermann-like; F_omega dominates it
```

Ordinal analysis converts Gödel's negative result into positive calibration: no single theory captures all truth, but theories can be linearly ordered by the transfinite induction they afford [3].

---

## 5 Empirical Results and Proofs

### 5.1 Natural independence: the Paris–Harrington theorem

Let PH(k, m, n, N) state that every coloring f: [N]ⁿ → k has a *relatively large* homogeneous H ⊆ N with |H| ≥ m (|H| ≥ min(H)). The **Paris–Harrington principle** ∀k,m,n ∃N PH(k, m, n, N) is a true Π⁰₂ statement of finite Ramsey theory, provable in ZF, but:

> **Theorem 4 (Paris–Harrington):** PA ⊬ ∀k,m,n ∃N PH(k, m, n, N).

In PA the principle implies Con(PA): the Paris–Harrington function grows so fast that its totality yields TI up to ε₀ [5][8]. By Theorem 2, PA cannot prove it. Kirby and Paris [6] made the result *accessible* via indicator arguments in nonstandard models, and Ketonen–Solovay calibrated the growth rate against the fast-growing hierarchy below ε₀.

### 5.2 Reversals: the method in action

Representative equivalences over RCA₀ [2]:

1. **WKL₀ ↔ Heine–Borel theorem.** The reversal codes a pathless binary tree into an open cover of [0,1] with no finite subcover.
2. **ACA₀ ↔ Bolzano–Weierstrass.** The reversal extracts the Turing jump from a purported modulus of convergence.
3. **ATR₀ ↔ perfect set theorem.** The reversal builds the hyperarithmetical hierarchy along a purported counterexample.
4. **Π¹₁-CA₀ ↔ Cantor–Bendixson theorem.** The reversal codes Π¹₁-comprehension into the Cantor–Bendixson rank [2].

Each reversal shows the set-existence axiom is not merely sufficient but *necessary*, pinning the theorem's logical strength exactly.

### 5.3 Beyond the Big Five: the Ramsey-theoretic zoo

RT²₂ resists classification: strictly between ACA₀ and RCA₀, it neither implies WKL₀ (Liu) nor follows from it, and decomposes as SRT²₂ + COH [7]. Hirschfeldt and Shore showed ADS and CAC split similarly into stable and cohesive parts, with WKL₀ incomparable with all of them — a genuine *zoo* below ACA₀ [7]. The zoo refines the Big Five picture without overturning it: the mainstream of analysis still lands on the five levels, while the interval (RCA₀, ACA₀) hosts many incomparable principles. Whether SRT²₂ implies RT²₂ remains the flagship open problem [2][7].

### 5.4 Proof-theoretic calibrations

Gentzen's |PA| = ε₀ extends across the spectrum: |PRA| = ω^ω, |ATR₀| = Γ₀, and impredicative theories reach the Bachmann–Howard ordinal and beyond via collapsing functions [3]. A landmark bridge: **WKL₀ is Π⁰₂-conservative over PRA** (Sieg), so the compactness arguments of ordinary analysis add no new Π⁰₂ consequences beyond finitistic reasoning — a partial vindication of Hilbert's program after Gödel [2].

---

## 6 Limitations

**The second theorem's hypotheses are delicate.** Theorem 2 requires the derivability conditions; nonstandard provability predicates (Rosser-style or "slow" provability) can evade it — Feferman constructed binumerations for which T proves its own "consistency" [4]. Willard showed weak theories lacking total exponentiation can prove the consistency of stronger ones. The theorem concerns *standard* provability, not every arithmetized consistency notion.

**Ordinal notation dependence.** The values |T|_Π⁰₁ and |T|_Π⁰₂ depend on the chosen notation system; only |T|_WF is notation-independent, and it gauges consistency strength only coarsely [3].

**The Big Five may be an artifact of the sample.** The zoo below ACA₀ [7] shows incomparable systems proliferate once one leaves the classical mainstream. Whether the Big Five reflects a deep fact about mathematical practice or the limited diet of digested theorems remains debated.

**Incompleteness is not a practical obstacle.** The independent statements — Gödel sentences, Paris–Harrington, Goodstein — are remote from working mathematics; no mainstream theorem is known independent of ZFC. Incompleteness limits *foundational completeness*, not mathematical practice.

---

## 7 Conclusion

Gödel's incompleteness theorems, proved by arithmetizing syntax and diagonalizing the provability predicate, established permanent limits on formalization: consistency implies incompleteness, and consistency is unprovable from within [1]. But the theorems were not merely negative. **Reverse mathematics** calibrates theorems against the Big Five subsystems, revealing that ordinary mathematics organizes into five sharply separated levels of set-existence strength, with exact reversals certifying each placement [2]. **Ordinal analysis** calibrates theories against transfinite induction, assigning PA the ordinal ε₀ and recovering consistency, computational power, and Π⁰₂-consequences from a single invariant [3]. Natural independence results — Paris–Harrington [5][8], Kirby–Paris indicators [6] — show incompleteness is visible in finite combinatorics, not only metamathematics. Open frontiers remain: the structure of the zoo below ACA₀ [7], notation-independence of proof-theoretic ordinals, and the ultimate explanation of the Big Five phenomenon. Gödel showed that no axiom system finishes mathematics; reverse mathematics and ordinal analysis show that we can nonetheless map, with precision, exactly how far each system reaches.

---

## References

[1] P. Raatikainen, "Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* (Summer 2021 edition). https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2021/entries/goedel-incompleteness/

[2] S. G. Simpson, *Subsystems of Second Order Arithmetic*, 2nd ed., Perspectives in Logic, Cambridge University Press, 2009. Author's site with full introductory chapter: https://sgslogic.net/t20/sosoa/chapter1.pdf

[3] G. Gentzen, "Die Widerspruchsfreiheit der reinen Zahlentheorie," *Mathematische Annalen* 112 (1936), 493–565. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01565428

[4] S. Feferman, "Arithmetization of metamathematics in a general setting," *Fundamenta Mathematicae* 49 (1960), 35–92. https://doi.org/10.4064/fm-49-1-35-92

[5] J. Paris and L. Harrington, "A Mathematical Incompleteness in Peano Arithmetic," in J. Barwise (ed.), *Handbook of Mathematical Logic*, North-Holland, 1977, pp. 1133–1142. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0049-237X(08)71130-3

[6] L. Kirby and J. Paris, "Accessible Independence Results for Peano Arithmetic," *Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society* 14 (1982), 285–293. https://doi.org/10.1112/blms/14.4.285

[7] D. R. Hirschfeldt and R. A. Shore, "Combinatorial Principles Weaker than Ramsey's Theorem for Pairs," *Journal of Symbolic Logic* 72 (2007), 171–206. https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~shore/papers/pdf/adsh12.pdf

[8] S. A. Kripke, "Mathematical Incompleteness Results in First-Order Peano Arithmetic: A Revisionist View of the Early History," arXiv:2102.13141 [math.LO], 2021. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.13141
