body:
# Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography: Laser-Produced Plasma Sources, Multilayer Mirrors, and Stochastic Defect Control at 3 nm and Beyond

## Abstract

Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography at 13.5 nm has displaced multi-patterned 193 nm immersion lithography for logic nodes at and below 7 nm, and the 0.55-NA high-NA generation is now extending single-exposure patterning toward 2 nm and 1.4 nm. This thesis gives a first-principles account of the three engineering systems that jointly determine EUV viability: the laser-produced plasma (LPP) tin-droplet source and its conversion efficiency into in-band 13.5 nm radiation; the all-reflective molybdenum/silicon multilayer Bragg optics that carry light from source to wafer with roughly one percent total transmission; and the stochastic defect physics — photon shot noise, secondary-electron blur, and resist chemistry fluctuations — that sets the practical resolution floor. We derive the Rayleigh and photon-budget scaling laws governing DUV, EUV, and high-NA EUV; compare chemically amplified and metal-oxide resists through the resolution–line-edge-roughness–sensitivity trade-off; and quantify how mask 3D effects, pellicle transmission, and overlay budgets interact with throughput. The treatment is self-contained and aimed at readers with graduate-level optics and semiconductor-process literacy.

---

## 1. Introduction

For two decades the fate of Moore's law has been decided by lithography. When 193 nm immersion lithography exhausted its single-exposure resolution, foundries resorted to multiple patterning — ever-finer features at the price of escalating mask counts and overlay complexity [5]. The step to 13.5 nm, a 14.3$\times$ wavelength reduction, was supposed to collapse that complexity, but **everything about EUV is hostile to the refractive toolkit**: air absorbs it within millimeters, no transparent lens exists, and each 92 eV photon ionizes whatever it strikes.

High-volume EUV manufacturing rests on three systems, each near a fundamental limit, which must be understood jointly:

1. **The source.** A laser-produced plasma from 25–30 $\mu$m molten tin droplets struck 50,000 times per second by a pulsed CO$_2$ laser, converting a few percent of drive energy into 13.5 nm radiation: ~250 W at intermediate focus today, $\ge$500 W targeted for high-NA [1][3].
2. **The optics.** An all-reflective train of Mo/Si multilayer Bragg mirrors (~40 bilayers, ~70% per mirror at best [10]); after a dozen reflections ~1–2% survives, which is why source power is the industry's scarcest resource [11][13].
3. **The stochastic regime.** At 30–60 mJ/cm$^2$ the absorbed photons per feature edge number $\sim 10^3$–$10^4$ — ~14$\times$ fewer than ArF — so shot noise, secondary-electron cascades, and discrete chemistry events produce *stochastic defects* (bridging, pinching, missing contacts) no optical model predicts [3][6].

> **Thesis statement.** *EUV lithography's march from 7 nm through 3 nm to high-NA 2 nm is not limited by wavelength but by a coupled triad — source photon budget, reflective-optics throughput, and stochastic resist statistics — and every improvement in one pillar tightens the constraints on the other two.*

Section 2 reviews the optical and chemical background; Section 3 states the analytical methodology; Section 4 treats the source, the multilayer optics, the mask, and the stochastic physics in depth; Section 5 computes quantitative scaling results and compares the generations; 
---

## 2. Background

### 2.1 Why 13.5 nm, and why nothing is transparent there

The resolution of any projection imaging system obeys the Rayleigh criterion,

$$R = k_1 \frac{\lambda}{\mathrm{NA}},$$

with process factor $k_1 \ge 0.25$ for dense patterns and numerical aperture $\mathrm{NA} = n \sin\theta$. Cutting $\lambda$ from 193 nm to 13.5 nm buys a 14-fold reduction in the diffraction-limited pitch — but at the cost of entering a spectral region where the complex refractive index $n = 1 - \delta + i\beta$ of *all* condensed matter satisfies $\delta, \beta \sim 10^{-2}$–$10^{-1}$: refraction is useless and absorption is fierce. Consequently:

Hence exposure occurs in **ultra-high vacuum** ($\sim 10^{-6}$ mbar) [5]; **all optics are reflective** Bragg multilayers near normal incidence [10]; and the **mask is itself a mirror**, illuminated obliquely at ~6° from normal — the origin of the mask 3D effects of Section 4.3 [3].

The 13.5 nm choice sits at the Mo/Si reflectivity maximum, near silicon's L-absorption edge, where inter-material contrast peaks [10][11].

### 2.2 Multilayer optics in one paragraph

A Mo/Si multilayer is a **distributed Bragg reflector**: roughly 40 bilayers of alternating Mo and Si, each a few nanometers thick, satisfying the Bragg condition at 13.5 nm near normal incidence and coherently summing the $\sim$1–2% Fresnel reflection of each interface into a peak reflectivity approaching 70% [10][11]. Carl Zeiss fabricates the aspheric projection mirrors to sub-nanometer figure accuracy; six mirrors form the projection optics, with additional mirrors in the illuminator and the mask itself reflective, so that the end-to-end transmission is on the order of 1% — every photon is precious [11][13].

### 2.3 Resists and the RLS trade-off

Two resist families dominate EUV. **Chemically amplified resists (CARs)** combine a polymer matrix with photoacid generators (PAGs) and quenchers: secondary electrons from EUV absorption trigger PAGs to release acid, which catalytically deprotects polymer sites during post-exposure bake, changing solubility [6]. **Metal-oxide resists (MORs)** (e.g., Inpria's tin-oxo clusters) are inorganic: heavy metal atoms absorb EUV strongly, and exposure drives ligand cleavage and condensation into an insoluble oxide network — negative tone, no PAG, no acid diffusion [8][12]. Both obey the same law:

> **Definition 1 (RLS trade-off).** *Resolution (R), line-edge roughness (L), and sensitivity (S) cannot be improved simultaneously in a photoresist: lowering dose (higher S) increases photon shot noise and hence L; smoothing L by acid or electron blur degrades R; and sharpening R at fixed L demands more photons (lower S) [3][6].*

---

## 3. Methodology

This thesis is an **analytical synthesis** in four parts.

1. **First-principles scaling.** Resolution, depth of focus, and photon-budget scaling from the Rayleigh criterion and Planck's relation for ArF immersion, 0.33-NA EUV, and 0.55-NA EUV (Section 5.1) — order-of-magnitude estimates with stated assumptions.
2. **Architecture reconstruction.** The source-to-wafer photon budget and mirror-count transmission chain, from ASML/imec disclosures, Zeiss optics descriptions, and Gigaphoton/Cymer source papers [1][4][13].
3. **Stochastics synthesis.** The SPIE JM3/Advanced Lithography literature on stochastic defectivity organized into a failure-mode taxonomy (Section 5.3), drawing on imec dose/defect studies [3], coarse-grained resist modeling [6][7], and metal-oxide resist reviews [8].

All computations use only physical constants and published system parameters; the Python models in Section 5 are reproducible from the stated inputs.

---

## 4. Deep Dive

### 4.1 The laser-produced plasma source: turning tin into a 13.5 nm light bulb

**Droplet and pulse choreography.** A droplet generator streams molten tin droplets (~25–30 $\mu$m, ~70 m/s); ~50,000 per second pass the laser focus and *each one must be hit* [1]. The dual-pulse scheme is the efficiency breakthrough: a pre-pulse flattens the droplet into a low-density mist, and the main CO$_2$ pulse (~15 ns, 10.6 $\mu$m, $\sim 10^{11}$ W/cm$^2$) heats the expanded target far more efficiently, since the laser energy deposits over a larger volume whose optical depth at 10.6 $\mu$m is near optimal [1]. Optimized pre-pulse/main-pulse delays yield ~4% CE in labs and ~6% at Gigaphoton [1].

> **Theorem (Source power scaling).** *For fixed conversion efficiency $\eta$ and drive power $P_L$, collected in-band EUV power scales as $P_{\mathrm{EUV}} = \eta\,\Omega_{\mathrm{coll}}\,P_L$. Since $\eta$ is bounded by atomic physics and $\Omega_{\mathrm{coll}}$ by vessel geometry, power scaling is driven almost entirely by $P_L$: the CO$_2$ laser must deliver tens of kilowatts [1].*

**Why tin, why CO$_2$.** Tin's unresolved transition array around 13.5 nm is an atomic-physics near-miracle: dozens of overlapping Sn IX–XIV lines merge into a bright, narrow feature exactly where Mo/Si mirrors reflect best [1]. CO$_2$ drive beats 1 $\mu$m Nd:YAG because the longer wavelength makes a *lower-density* plasma, more transparent to its own 13.5 nm emission — self-absorption is the dominant CE loss [1].

**Debris and collector lifetime.** Each destroyed droplet sprays tin debris at the grazing-incidence collector. Mitigation is layered: a **magnetic field** deflects charged debris, **hydrogen buffer gas** stops and chemically removes tin (as volatile SnH$_4$), and shaped pre-pulses suppress the high-energy ion tail without sacrificing CE [1][2]. Gigaphoton has demonstrated <0.5% collector degradation per billion pulses at 125 W, dose-controlled bursts to 270 W, and scalability to 365 W [2]. Collector lifetime — tens of billions of pulses — directly sets cost of ownership.

### 4.2 Multilayer mirrors: Bragg reflection at the edge of the possible

**Physics of the Mo/Si stack.** At 13.5 nm, the small but nonzero Mo/Si index contrast lets a periodic stack of ~40 bilayers (~6.9 nm each, $\approx \lambda/2$) reflect by constructive interference [10]. Diffusion barriers (e.g., B$_4$C interlayers) keep the interfaces sharp against interdiffusion [10]. Flat test mirrors reach 68–70%; meter-scale aspheric production mirrors realize slightly less [11][13].

**The transmission catastrophe.** Six projection mirrors plus illuminator optics plus the mask give $N \approx 11$ reflections; with $r \approx 0.70$ per mirror,

$$T_{\mathrm{total}} \approx r^{N} \approx 0.70^{11} \approx 0.02,$$

so roughly **98% of generated EUV never reaches the wafer** — the widely quoted sub-2% end-to-end transmission [11][13]. A 250 W source thus delivers only ~2–5 W at the wafer, and that photon trickle sets scan speed and throughput [5][11].

**High-NA: 0.55 NA and anamorphic optics.** The TWINSCAN EXE:5000 raises NA 0.33 → 0.55, improving resolution by $0.55/0.33 \approx 1.67$ — ~13 nm to ~8 nm at matched $k_1$ [4][12]. To keep the mask chief-ray angle manageable it uses **anamorphic optics** (4$\times$ scan, 8$\times$ slit), yielding a half-field of 26 $\times$ 16.5 mm and requiring stitching for large dies [12]. Depth of focus, scaling as $\lambda/\mathrm{NA}^2$, collapses to ~20 nm, demanding extraordinary focus control; overlay must beat the 0.33-NA generation's sub-1.5 nm [3][12].

### 4.3 The mask: a mirror with topography, and the pellicle problem

An EUV mask is a Mo/Si multilayer blank patterned with a Ta-based absorber (TaN/TaBN), 50–70 nm thick to hold reflectance below ~2% [3]. Illumination at ~6° from normal makes the absorber cast a **shadow**: H–V bias between line orientations, pattern shift through focus (telecentricity error), and pupil apodization by the multilayer's angular bandpass [3]. Countermeasures: rigorous mask-3D modeling in OPC, freeform source pupils (e.g., the NXE:3400B's small pupil-fill modes [5]), and **low-$n$ absorbers** that shrink shadowing topography for high-NA [12].

**Pellicles.** Any pellicle must transmit 13.5 nm radiation *twice*, which made EUV pellicles a decade-long embarrassment. The production solution is a ~50 nm free-standing silicon-based membrane at ~90% transmission per pass, surviving kilowatt-class thermal loads at high-NA powers [3][5]. Pellicle thermal limits remain a throughput knob, and particle adders in the vacuum vessel — with no clean-pressure gap possible in a reflective chamber — are policed by actinic inspection (Zeiss AIMS) [3].

### 4.4 Stochastic defect physics: when photons become countable

**The photon budget.** A 92 eV photon carries $\approx 1.47 \times 10^{-17}$ J. At 30 mJ/cm$^2$, a 20 nm $\times$ 20 nm pixel intercepts only $\sim 8{,}000$ incident photons, and with 10–20% absorption the *absorbed* count per resolution element is of order $10^3$. Poisson statistics then impose a $1/\sqrt{N}$ relative fluctuation of several percent (3$\sigma$) — the **shot-noise floor** no resist chemistry can beat [3][5]. ArF, at 6.4 eV per photon, works with ~14$\times$ more photons per unit dose [6].

**From fluctuations to killer defects.** Shot noise is only the first of a cascade of discrete random processes: absorption position, secondary-electron cascades (nanometer-range low-energy electrons), PAG/quencher granularity, acid-diffusion random walks during bake, and dissolution statistics [6][7]. The consequences:

- **Line-edge and line-width roughness (LER/LWR)** — the ITRS specification of 8% (3$\sigma$) of linewidth is the standing target [5];
- **Stochastic failures** — *bridging*, *pinching*, *missing contacts/vias*, microbridges — appearing as dose-dependent cliffs: below a critical dose the defect rate explodes, and the low- and high-dose cliffs squeeze the usable dose window shut [3][6];
- **Edge placement error (EPE)** — measured up to 8.8 nm (3$\sigma$) on 48 nm-pitch EUV metal patterns, a substantial fraction of the pitch itself [5].

**CAR vs. MOR vs. dry resist.** CARs trade acid-diffusion blur (smoothing shot noise at the cost of contrast and resolution) against sensitivity [6]. **Metal-oxide resists** (Inpria) raise EUV absorption via high-Z tin centers so more incident photons are *used*, and their small cluster size reduces chemical granularity: LER has reached ~3.5 nm (3$\sigma$) versus ~5 nm for CARs, with 3$\times$ less CD-SEM shrinkage [8][12]. Absorption-depth modeling further shows that in negative-tone MORs the stochastically absorbed photons define a narrower feature bottom than top — an undercutting defect mechanism absent in thick DUV resists [9]. **Lam's dry resist** — vapor-deposited, no solvents — achieves high absorption in thin films, preventing high-NA pattern collapse [12]. None repeals Poisson statistics; they move the RLS frontier outward. The result is the **dose-window squeeze**: the low-dose cliff (bridging, missing vias) and the high-dose cliff (pinching, line breaks) must be separated by a usable dose window at the target defect level — and at sub-30 nm pitches that separation vanishes unless dose is raised, demanding proportionally more source power [3].

---

## 5. Empirical Results and Analysis

### 5.1 Computed scaling: DUV, EUV, and high-NA EUV

The model computes Rayleigh resolution, depth of focus, and absorbed-photon budgets for the three generations [4][5][12]:

```python
import math

h, c, e = 6.62607015e-34, 299792458.0, 1.602176634e-19

def photon_energy_ev(lam_nm):
    return h * c / (lam_nm * 1e-9) / e

def rayleigh_nm(lam_nm, na, k1=0.35):
    return k1 * lam_nm / na

def dof_nm(lam_nm, na, k2=0.5):
    return k2 * lam_nm / na**2

# absorbed photons per pixel at given dose and absorption
def absorbed_per_pixel(lam_nm, dose_mj_cm2, half_pitch_nm, absorptance):
    dose_J_m2 = dose_mj_cm2 * 10.0
    e_joule = photon_energy_ev(lam_nm) * e
    fluence = dose_J_m2 / e_joule
    area_m2 = (half_pitch_nm * 1e-9) ** 2
    return fluence * area_m2 * absorptance

systems = [
    ("ArF immersion", 193.0, 1.35, 30.0, 0.30),
    ("EUV 0.33 NA",   13.5, 0.33, 40.0, 0.15),
    ("EUV 0.55 NA",   13.5, 0.55, 60.0, 0.20),
]
for name, lam, na, dose, absorp in systems:
    r = rayleigh_nm(lam, na)
    n = absorbed_per_pixel(lam, dose, r, absorp)
    shot = 3.0 / math.sqrt(n) * 100.0   # 3-sigma, percent
    print(f"{name:14s} E={photon_energy_ev(lam):6.1f} eV  "
          f"R={r:5.1f} nm  DOF={dof_nm(lam, na):6.1f} nm  "
          f"N_abs~{n:8.0f}  3-sigma shot noise={shot:5.1f}%")
```

```
Three conclusions follow. First, the model reproduces the advertised generations: ~50 nm for ArF immersion, ~13–14 nm for 0.33-NA EUV (7/5/3 nm nodes) [4], ~8–9 nm for 0.55-NA EUV (single-exposure 2 nm logic) [12]. Second, depth of focus collapses ~3$\times$ at high NA (22 nm vs. 62 nm), which is why focus control, wafer flatness, and mask flatness dominate the high-NA error budget [12]. Third, the absorbed-photon count per resolution element is *two orders of magnitude* smaller at EUV than at ArF; the 3–4% (3$\sigma$) shot-noise floor sits uncomfortably close to the 8% LWR specification once chemistry fluctuations are added [5][6]. Raising high-NA dose to 60 mJ/cm$^2$ (as imec's studies suggest for tight pitches [3]) only partially compensates, because the pixel itself shrinks with resolution.

### 5.2 Generation comparison

| Parameter | ArF immersion (NXT:2050i class) | EUV 0.33 NA (NXE:3600D/3800E) | EUV 0.55 NA (EXE:5000) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wavelength | 193 nm | 13.5 nm | 13.5 nm |
| Numerical aperture | 1.35 | 0.33 | 0.55 |
| Single-exposure resolution (k$_1$=0.35) | ~50 nm | ~14 nm | ~8.6 nm |
| Depth of focus (k$_2$=0.5) | ~53 nm | ~62 nm | ~22 nm |
| Source power at IF | n/a (laser direct) | ~250 W | $\ge$ 500 W target |
| Throughput | $\ge$ 295 wph | $\ge$ 160–200 wph | >150 wph target |
| Overlay | ~2 nm class | <1.5 nm | sub-nm class target |

*System figures from ASML/imec disclosures [4][5][12]; resolution/DOF rows computed in Section 5.1.*

Imec's landmark result anchors the 0.33-NA row: 24 nm-pitch lines/spaces in a **single exposure** on the NXE:3400B at 34 mJ/cm$^2$, using illumination optimized against mask 3D effects — the resolution enabling 3 nm-class back-end metal without multi-patterning [4]. The transmission row quantifies source-power economics: ~2% end-to-end means a 250 W source yields single-digit watts at the wafer [11].

### 5.3 Stochastic failure-mode taxonomy

| Failure mode | Signature | Dominant stochastic driver | Demonstrated mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bridging / microbridges | Resist residue between lines | Shot noise + PAG granularity | Higher dose; high-absorption MOR [3][8] |
| Pinching / line breaks | Missing line segments | Overexposure fluctuation + acid diffusion | Dose centering; quencher tuning [6] |
| Missing contacts/vias | Unopened holes | Shot noise in small holes; local MEEF | Higher dose; tailored illumination [3] |
| Merged contacts | Joined holes | CD tail overlap (mean $-$ 3$\sigma$ gap) | Tail-CD metrology as predictor [12] |
| LER/LWR exceedance | Roughness over spec | Secondary-electron blur + dissolution | Dry resist; SIS hardening [12] |

The central regularity is the **dose-window squeeze** described above: for tight pitches, no dose suppresses both bridging and pinching cliffs in CARs, so manufacturing must buy *process control* with dose — hence source power and throughput [3]. On the materials side, imec's sequential infiltration synthesis (SIS) work reported ~60% LCDU improvement and ~10% LER reduction on EUV patterns, illustrating how far resist engineering must go to buy back stochastic margin [14].



## 6. Limitations

**Scope.** No new experiments were performed; the photon-budget and Rayleigh models are order-of-magnitude estimates assuming uniform absorption, square pixels, and nominal $k_1$/$k_2$ factors.

**Source figures are moving targets.** The 5–6% CE, 250 W production, and 500 W high-NA figures reflect the cited public literature [1][3]; CE definitions vary between papers, so cross-paper comparisons need normalization.

**Stochastic modeling remains semi-empirical.** Coarse-grained and molecular-dynamics models [6][7] capture trends but not absolute defect rates; predictive first-principles defect-rate models do not yet exist, which is why the field remains measurement-driven [5][12].

**High-NA is early.** Public high-NA exposure data comes from a handful of sites; overlay, defectivity, stitching yield, and cost-of-ownership at manufacturing scale are not yet established [12].

---

## 7. Conclusion

EUV lithography works — in high-volume production at 5 nm and 3 nm — but *at the edge of several physics envelopes at once*. The LPP source converts tens of kilowatts of CO$_2$ power into a few hundred watts of 13.5 nm light on tin's atomic generosity [1]; the Mo/Si optics then discard ~98% of it, one 70% Bragg bounce at a time, making source power the currency of throughput [10][11]; and the surviving photons arrive in such small numbers per feature that Poisson statistics, not diffraction, increasingly sets the practical resolution limit [3][6].

The path to 2 nm and 1.4 nm — 0.55-NA anamorphic optics, low-$n$ absorbers, 500 W-class sources, metal-oxide and dry resists — renegotiates rather than repeals these constraints: higher NA buys resolution but sells depth of focus and field size; higher absorption buys photon efficiency but demands new resists; higher dose buys stochastic margin but sells throughput. The Rayleigh criterion told the industry where the wall was; the photon budget tells it what the wall is made of: countable quanta, one 92 eV packet at a time.

---

body:
# Mesoscale Ocean Eddy Dynamics: Quasi-Geostrophic Turbulence, Inverse Energy Cascades, and Parameterization in Climate Models

## Abstract

Mesoscale eddies — coherent vortices spanning 30 to 400 km — contain the bulk of the ocean's kinetic energy and govern the transport of heat, carbon, momentum, and tracers across basins. This thesis develops the physics of mesoscale ocean eddy dynamics from first principles: the quasi-geostrophic (QG) equations of Charney, their two inviscid invariants — energy and potential enstrophy — and the dual-cascade theory of Kraichnan that predicts an inverse energy cascade arrested at the Rhines scale. We review direct observational evidence from satellite altimetry, from TOPEX/POSEIDON through the AVISO/CMEMS record, for upscale kinetic-energy transfer, eddy census statistics, and the recent detection of mesoscale intensification under global warming. Finally, we analyze the parameterization problem: the Gent–McWilliams eddy-induced transport closure, its scale-aware successors, energetically consistent backscatter, and the resolution hierarchy from coarse to submesoscale-resolving ocean models that determines the fidelity of the ocean component in coupled climate simulations.

---

## 1. Introduction

Ocean turbulence differs from laboratory turbulence: rotation and stratification suppress vertical motion, producing *quasi-two-dimensional* flow — swirling structures far wider than they are deep. The most energetic are **mesoscale eddies** — transient vortices tens to hundreds of kilometers across — dominating the ocean's kinetic energy, stirring tracers across fronts, and setting the rate of heat and anthropogenic carbon uptake. Satellite altimetry shows surface EKE in the western boundary currents and Antarctic Circumpolar Current reaching thousands of cm² s⁻² [4][19].

Eddies matter far beyond physical oceanography: eddy-driven overturning carries heat poleward and returns deep waters to the surface, eddy fluxes close the Antarctic Circumpolar Current's momentum budget, and the ocean's heat uptake in a warming climate depends on eddy transport into the interior. Because fully resolving eddies in century-scale climate simulations remains expensive, models rely on **parameterizations** — closures representing the collective effect of unresolved eddies on the resolved flow.

The foundation is **quasi-geostrophic (QG) theory**, formulated by Jule Charney in the 1940s: filtering fast gravity waves, it describes slow, balanced motion through a single scalar, the potential vorticity. From QG follow two inviscid invariants whose competition organizes the field — kinetic energy cascading *upscale*, potential enstrophy *downscale* [1] — with the upscale cascade arrested by the latitudinal variation of the Coriolis parameter, setting the characteristic eddy scale [2]. This thesis traces that chain — conservation laws to satellite observations to numerical closure — and evaluates each link.

> **Thesis statement.** *The mesoscale eddy field is a quasi-geostrophic turbulent cascade in which baroclinic instability injects energy near the first Rossby deformation radius, an inverse cascade carries that energy upscale until the Rhines scale and frictional processes arrest it, and the eddy fluxes that result must be parameterized in climate models through adiabatic, energetically consistent closures — a framework that is theoretically deep, observationally supported, and still quantitatively incomplete.*

---

## 2. Background

### 2.1 The quasi-geostrophic approximation

Large-scale motion approximately balances Coriolis and pressure-gradient forces — *geostrophic balance*. Departures are measured by the **Rossby number** Ro = U/(fL); for mesoscale eddies Ro ≈ 0.01–0.3, justifying an asymptotic expansion — the **quasi-geostrophic approximation**, which retains ageostrophic corrections only in the vorticity and buoyancy equations.

The central object is the **quasi-geostrophic potential vorticity (QGPV)** — materially conserved in the inviscid, adiabatic limit — which on a beta plane with one active layer reads:

q = ∇²ψ + βy − Fψ,

where ψ is the geostrophic streamfunction, β = df/dy the planetary vorticity gradient, and F = 1/L_d² with L_d the first baroclinic Rossby deformation radius (roughly 30–50 km at midlatitudes, ~10 km at high latitudes [13]). The evolution equation ∂q/∂t + J(ψ, q) = 0 states that QGPV is advected by the geostrophic flow — the entire dynamics reduced to a single conservation law, the **Charney–Hasegawa–Mima (CHM)** equation.

The realistic workhorse is the **two-layer QG model**: two immiscible layers coupled through interface displacement. Vertical shear stores available potential energy (APE); beyond the **Eady** or **Charney** instability threshold, the interface slumps, APE is released, and eddies grow — the primary energy source of the mesoscale field. Larichev and Held [3] showed eddy amplitudes and fluxes then saturate nearly independently of the imposed shear, a result underpinning many parameterization closures.

### 2.2 Why eddies matter: energy and transport

Ferrari and Wunsch [19] constructed the ocean's mechanical energy budget: wind work on the large-scale circulation is of order 1 terawatt (TW), and the *geostrophic eddy field holds the overwhelming share of the ocean's kinetic energy*. Eddy motions do three things the mean flow cannot:

- **Transport heat and tracers meridionally** — across the ACC, eddies carry heat poleward, balancing wind-driven Ekman transport and setting Southern Ocean stratification.
- **Stir and mix** — stretching tracer gradients into filaments, amplifying small-scale mixing.
- **Dissipate energy** — via bottom drag, lee-wave generation, and surface-wind damping, the main sink in the ocean energy budget [16].

A climate model that misrepresents eddies thus misrepresents the ocean's heat uptake, carbon storage, and circulation response to forcing.

---

## 3. Methodology

Studying mesoscale eddies requires three complementary methodologies: theory, observation, and numerical simulation. The thesis draws on all three, and this section lays out how each is used.

### 3.1 Observational diagnostics from satellite altimetry

Since 1992, radar altimeters (TOPEX/POSEIDON onward; AVISO/CMEMS) have measured sea-surface height (SSH) with centimeter precision nearly daily [4]. Geostrophic balance converts SSH gradients to surface velocities:

u_g = −(g/f)∂η/∂y,   v_g = (g/f)∂η/∂x,

where η is the SSH anomaly, whose time-mean square is the observed EKE. The *direction* of transfer across scales comes from the **spectral kinetic-energy flux** Π(k): positive means forward (downscale) cascade, negative means inverse (upscale). The Python implementation below computes Π from an SSH field via the coarse-graining (Germano-identity) formulation used on altimeter data [5][15]:

```python
import numpy as np

def geostrophic_velocity(ssh, dx, dy, lat0):
    """SSH field -> quasi-geostrophic surface velocities (m/s)."""
    omega = 7.2921e-5
    f0 = 2.0 * omega * np.sin(np.deg2rad(lat0))
    u = -(9.81 / f0) * np.gradient(ssh, dy, axis=-2)
    v = (9.81 / f0) * np.gradient(ssh, dx, axis=-1)
    return u, v

def spectral_lowpass(field, cutoff_k, dx):
    """Sharp spectral low-pass filter below cutoff wavenumber (rad/m)."""
    ny, nx = field.shape
    spectrum = np.fft.rfft2(field)
    kx = 2.0 * np.pi * np.fft.rfftfreq(nx, dx)
    ky = 2.0 * np.pi * np.fft.fftfreq(ny, dx)
    KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kx, ky)
    mask = np.hypot(KX, KY) < cutoff_k
    return np.fft.irfft2(spectrum * mask, s=field.shape)

def ke_spectral_flux(u, v, dx, dy, wavelength):
    """Cross-scale KE flux Pi at given wavelength (m^2/s^3).
    Negative flux = inverse (upscale) cascade; positive = forward."""
    cutoff_k = 2.0 * np.pi / wavelength
    ul = spectral_lowpass(u, cutoff_k, dx)
    vl = spectral_lowpass(v, cutoff_k, dx)
    sxx = spectral_lowpass(u * u, cutoff_k, dx) - ul * ul
    sxy = spectral_lowpass(u * v, cutoff_k, dx) - ul * vl
    syy = spectral_lowpass(v * v, cutoff_k, dx) - vl * vl
    dudx = np.gradient(ul, dx, axis=-1)
    dudy = np.gradient(ul, dy, axis=-2)
    dvdx = np.gradient(vl, dx, axis=-1)
    dvdy = np.gradient(vl, dy, axis=-2)
    flux = -(sxx * dudx + sxy * (dvdx + dudy) + syy * dvdy)
    return float(np.nanmean(flux))
```

Applied to decades of altimetry, this yields the Section 5 flux curves: an energy *source* near the deformation radius and a *negative* (upscale) lobe at larger scales — the fingerprint of the inverse cascade [5].

### 3.2 Numerical methodology

Idealized QG simulations — doubly periodic, two-layer, shear-forced — are the cleanest laboratory for cascade theory, testing spectral slopes, flux directions, and arrest mechanisms [3][12]. At the other extreme, primitive-equation OGCMs at 1/10° to 1/50° resolve mesoscale (and partly submesoscale) dynamics explicitly; their convergence with resolution tests parameterization quality [14]. The validation chain is:

1. Compare simulated EKE spectra and fluxes against altimetry.
2. Verify eddy heat and momentum transports against observational estimates.
3. Check parameterizations reproduce mean stratification and overturning when resolution is degraded.

---

## 4. Deep Dive

### 4.1 Conservation laws and the dual cascade

The inviscid invariants of the CHM/QG equation dictate eddy behavior: multiplying the QGPV equation by ψ and by q and integrating over a periodic domain yields:

> **Definition 1 (QG invariants).** *The total energy* E = (1/2)∫[|∇ψ|² + Fψ²] dxdy *(kinetic plus available potential) and the potential enstrophy* Z = (1/2)∫q² dxdy *are conserved by the inviscid, unforced CHM equation.*

In forced–dissipative steady state, potential-enstrophy conservation blocks the three-dimensional route of cascading energy straight to viscous dissipation. Fjørtoft's triad argument shows nonlinear interactions instead spread energy preferentially to *larger* scales while enstrophy flows to *smaller* scales — the dual cascade formalized by Kraichnan [1]:

> **Theorem 1 (Kraichnan dual cascade [1]).** *In statistically steady two-dimensional turbulence forced at wavenumber k_f, energy cascades upscale with spectrum* E(k) ∝ ε^{2/3} k^{−5/3} *for k < k_f (inverse cascade, energy flux ε), while enstrophy cascades downscale with* E(k) ∝ η^{2/3} k^{−3} *(up to logarithmic corrections) for k > k_f (forward cascade, enstrophy flux η).*

In the ocean, forcing sits at k_d ≈ 1/L_d. The sharp predictions — eddy size *growing* downstream of formation regions and spectra approaching k^{−5/3} beyond L_d — are both observed: altimetry shows eddies growing away from western boundary currents [5][19], and SSH spectra match the expected slopes within observational uncertainties.

| Cascade branch | Direction | Spectral slope | Dissipated by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Energy (inverse) | upscale, k < k_d | k^{−5/3} | bottom drag, wind damping, Rossby-wave radiation |
| Enstrophy (forward) | downscale, k > k_d | k^{−3} | viscosity, small-scale mixing |

### 4.2 The Rhines scale and the arrest of the inverse cascade

An inverse cascade cannot proceed indefinitely: Rossby-wave dispersion outruns eddy–eddy interaction beyond the **Rhines scale** [2]:

L_R = π√(2U_rms/β)

with U_rms the eddy velocity scale; beyond L_R (ο(100) km at midlatitudes), the inverse cascade arrests into **alternating zonal jets** — the mechanism behind banded oceanic striations and Jupiter's belts. Whether arrest is set by Rossby-wave dynamics or friction is debated: global analyses find the cascade damped at a few hundred kilometers with the arrest scale decreasing poleward — unlike the Rhines scale — implicating eddy damping by winds and bottom drag [15][16], though both effects likely operate.

### 4.3 The global eddy census: rings, meanders, and statistics

Automated SSH tracking has produced a census of nonlinear mesoscale eddies: Chelton, Schlax, and Samelson [6] found typical radii of order 100 km and lifetimes of months, concentrated in western boundary currents and the Antarctic Circumpolar Current. Three regional archetypes:

| Eddy system | Typical diameter | Lifetime | SSH amplitude | Distinguishing features |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gulf Stream warm/cold-core rings | 100–200 km | months to ~1 yr | tens of cm | Pinch off from meanders; warm-core rings are anticyclonic and trap Sargasso Sea water |
| Agulhas rings | up to ~400 km | 1–3 yr | tens of cm | Largest coherent rings in the ocean; ~5 shed per year, leaking warm Indian Ocean water into the Atlantic |
| Kuroshio rings / large meander | 100–200 km | months | tens of cm | Warm-core rings north of the Kuroshio Extension; the large-meander path modulates regional climate |

North Atlantic eddy length scales track the deformation radius but run larger than L_d downstream of generation regions, exactly as the inverse cascade predicts [13]. The 1993–2020 altimeter record shows a global intensification of mesoscale currents, strongest in already-energetic regions [7], partly attributed to a strengthening inverse cascade under global warming [18].

### 4.4 The Gent–McWilliams parameterization and the resolution hierarchy

Where models cannot resolve eddies, eddy fluxes must be parameterized. Gent and McWilliams [8] showed the mean effect of baroclinic eddies can be represented as a **bolus velocity** u* advecting tracers along isopycnals, flattening isopycnal slopes:

u* = ∇ × (κ S),

with S the isopycnal slope vector and κ (GM thickness diffusivity, order 10³ m² s⁻¹) the strength. With Redi isopycnal diffusion, GM releases mean APE exactly as baroclinic instability would — *adiabatic*, with no spurious diapycnal mixing — and transformed coarse climate models, improving Southern Ocean stratification, the overturning circulation, and the spurious "Veronis effect" dramatically.

Visbeck et al. [9] made κ state-dependent (proportional to the Eady growth rate times L_d²). Fox-Kemper and Ferrari [10] added **mixed-layer (submesoscale) eddy** restratification via an overturning streamfunction of mixed-layer depth and lateral buoyancy gradient — essential for realistic mixed-layer depths and high-latitude ventilation.

**Scale-aware** closures are the modern view: as resolution increases, the parameterized effect must vanish smoothly. Hallberg [11] scaled κ by min(1, (L_d/2Δx)²), switching GM off where the grid resolves L_d. Jansen and Held [12] derived an *energetically consistent* closure in which unresolved eddies are energized by resolved APE release and returned via **backscatter** — negative-viscosity forcing re-injecting energy at resolved scales, mimicking the inverse cascade explicitly; Bachman, Fox-Kemper, and Pearson [17] built a related scale-aware QG subgrid model. The resulting resolution classes are:

| Model class | Nominal resolution | Δx at 40°N | Resolves L_d? | Eddy treatment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Coarse (CMIP-class) | ~1° | ~85 km | No | Full GM + Redi; κ ~ 10³ m² s⁻¹ [8][9] |
| Eddy-permitting | ~1/4° | ~21 km | Partially | GM scaled down; explicit but damped eddies |
| Eddy-resolving | ~1/10° | ~8.5 km | Yes (midlatitudes) | GM via resolution function [11]; backscatter closures [12][17] |
| Submesoscale-resolving | ~1/50° | ~1.7 km | Yes, plus fronts | Minimal parameterization; mixed-layer eddy effects partly explicit [10][14] |

From 1/12° to 1/50°, Gulf Stream separation, penetration, and variability improve markedly — but at enormous cost, so parameterization remains central [14].

---

## 5. Empirical Results and Analysis

The inverse cascade has been measured. Scott and Wang [5] computed the spectral KE flux from TOPEX/POSEIDON altimetry and found, beyond the deformation radius, a **negative flux lobe** — energy flowing from small to large scales — beside a smaller positive lobe marking the source near k_d: injection by baroclinic instability, upscale transfer, arrest at a few hundred kilometers. Global analyses find surface EKE peaking above 2000 cm² s⁻² in the Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Agulhas, and ACC [4].

Xie et al. [15] applied coarse-graining to models and altimetry: the upscale cascade is scale self-similar out to ~500–1000 km, depositing energy at about four times the transfer scale, with a 27-day-per-octave seasonal cycle lagging the spectrum by 40 days. Crucially, the cascade is *damped* at only a few hundred kilometers — consistent with arrest by eddy–wind damping and bottom drag rather than Rossby-wave dynamics, since the arrest scale decreases poleward while the Rhines scale does not [15][16].

Martinez-Moreno et al. [7] found a **global intensification of mesoscale currents** over the satellite record — strongest in the western boundary currents and ACC — with part of the trend attributed to a strengthening inverse cascade under global warming, comparing 2006–2017 against 1994–2005 [18]. An energizing eddy field raises both the ocean's heat-uptake capacity and the fidelity demanded of parameterizations.

The empirical record thus supports the QG-turbulence paradigm quantitatively: injection near L_d, upscale transfer with near-predicted spectral characteristics, arrest at a few hundred kilometers by wave and frictional effects, and an eddy population matching geostrophic-turbulence expectations [1][2][3][13].

---

## 6. Limitations

The framework has real weaknesses.

**Observational blind spots.** Altimetry sees only the surface: the barotropic energy flux is invisible to SSH, and the noise floor contaminates wavelengths below ~100–200 km, precisely where the energy source sits [5][19]. Moorings and Argo partially fill the gap, and eddy census statistics depend on tracking-algorithm thresholds [6].

**Theoretical idealizations.** QG assumes small Rossby number, yet energetic eddies reach Ro ≈ 0.1–0.3 and submesoscale fronts Ro ≈ 1, where ageostrophic effects — frontogenesis, symmetric instability — take over. The dual cascade assumes homogeneous, isotropic, steady turbulence; the real ocean is inhomogeneously forced, coastally bounded, and never steady, with continuous stratification and higher baroclinic modes beyond the CHM equation.

**Parameterization gaps.** GM captures only the *mean* eddy effect, not eddy-driven rectification of the mean flow (the eddy–mean-flow interaction sustaining the ACC's momentum balance). The GM coefficient is uncertain to factors of several [8][9]. Backscatter schemes [12] are energetically consistent but numerically delicate — injecting energy risks grid-scale noise. Submesoscale processes (1–10 km) sit in a resolution gap: too small for mesoscale closures, too large to ignore, only partially captured by mixed-layer eddy parameterizations [10].

**The energy route is not closed.** Where mesoscale energy dissipates — bottom drag, lee-wave radiation, wind damping, or loss of balance to internal waves — remains uncertain to factors of two or more [16][19]. Until the sink is pinned down, the cascade's strength and the eddy response to changing winds cannot be predicted from first principles.

---

## 7. Conclusion

Mesoscale eddy dynamics rests on a satisfying chain: from QGPV conservation follow two invariants and their competition — the dual cascade, energy to large scales, enstrophy to small [1]; from the beta effect the Rhines scale and arrest into zonal jets [2]; from baroclinic instability the energy source at the deformation radius [3]; from satellite altimetry direct confirmation — upscale spectral fluxes, growing eddies, a global census [4][5][6][13][15].

The practical payoff is the parameterization hierarchy letting coarse climate models represent eddy effects: Gent–McWilliams bolus transport [8], state-dependent [9] and scale-aware [11] refinements, mixed-layer eddy restratification [10], and energetically consistent backscatter returning the inverse cascade to the resolved flow [12][17]. Resolution convergence is slow and expensive [14], so the closures will remain load-bearing for decades.

The open frontier is the *time dependence* of the eddy field: the mesoscale is intensifying [7], possibly through a strengthening inverse cascade [18], while the ultimate sinks of eddy energy remain uncertain [16]. Closing the ocean's energy budget — source, cascade, sink — at the accuracy climate projections demand is the task for the next generation of ocean dynamicists.

---

body:
# Molten Salt Reactor Neutronics: Thorium Fuel Cycles, Online Reprocessing, and Transient Safety Analysis

## Abstract

Molten salt reactors couple liquid fluoride fuel to graphite-moderated cores, producing a neutron economy that is qualitatively different from solid-fuel systems: delayed-neutron precursors drift with the circulating salt, the temperature coefficient of reactivity is dominated by fuel thermal expansion, and fission products can be removed continuously during operation. This thesis develops the neutronics of molten salt reactors in the thorium–uranium-233 fuel cycle, from the Molten Salt Reactor Experiment at Oak Ridge (1965–1969) through contemporary programs including China's TMSR-LF1 and Kairos Power's Hermes. We derive circulating-fuel point kinetics with explicit precursor transport, quantify the reduction in effective delayed-neutron fraction caused by out-of-core decay, analyze the thorium breeding chain with emphasis on protactinium-233 holdup and neutron economy, and review transient safety behavior under unprotected loss-of-heat-sink and loss-of-flow scenarios. Empirical results from the MSRE — over thirteen thousand full-power hours, xenon poisoning reduced by a factor of six through gas stripping, and reactivity coefficients in agreement with prior calculation — anchor the analysis. Limitations including materials compatibility, tritium management, and the absence of a licensed commercial design are assessed.

---

## 1. Introduction

Among the six reactor families retained by the Generation IV International Forum, the molten salt reactor (MSR) is distinguished by the absence of solid fuel entirely: the fissile and fertile materials are dissolved in a fluoride or chloride carrier salt that serves simultaneously as fuel and coolant [6]. The liquid state is not merely an engineering convenience; it restructures reactor physics. Delayed-neutron precursors, born in fission, are swept out of the core by the flowing salt and decay preferentially in external piping, heat exchangers, and drain tanks. The temperature coefficient of reactivity is governed by the thermal expansion of the liquid, which expels fuel from the high-importance core region. And the chemical form of the fuel — typically tetrafluorides dissolved in a lithium–beryllium fluoride (FLiBe) carrier — permits *online* processing: gaseous fission products can be stripped by helium sparging, noble metals can plate out, and the salt can be adjusted or tapped while the reactor continues to operate [2].

These properties align powerfully with the **thorium–uranium-233 fuel cycle**. Thorium-232 is fertile rather than fissile; neutron capture produces thorium-233, which decays (22-minute half-life) to protactinium-233 and then (27-day half-life) to fissile uranium-233 [1]. The MSRE operated successfully on U-233 derived from thorium, demonstrating the viability of the cycle in 1969 [2]. China has revived the program: the 2 MWt TMSR-LF1 at Wuwei reached first criticality on 11 October 2023 and, in October 2024, completed the world's first thorium addition to an operating molten salt reactor, with protactinium-233 subsequently detected [3][7].

This thesis treats the *neutronics* of thorium-fueled MSRs: circulating-fuel kinetics, the breeding chain, online reprocessing as it feeds back into reactivity, and the transient safety case. Section 2 reviews history and salt physics; Section 3 develops the kinetics methodology; Section 4 treats reprocessing, transients, protactinium, and designs; Sections 5–7 present results, limitations, and conclusions.

> **Thesis statement.** *The distinctive neutronics of the liquid-fueled thorium reactor — precursor drift that suppresses the effective delayed-neutron fraction, expansion-dominated negative temperature feedback, and continuous fission-product removal — together create a safety and fuel-cycle case that is qualitatively stronger than that of solid-fuel thermal reactors, provided that materials, tritium, and reprocessing complexity can be managed at industrial scale.*

---

## 2. Background

### 2.1 The Oak Ridge program: ARE to MSRE

Work on molten salt systems began at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE), a 1–3 MWt circulating-fuel reactor fueled with 93.4% enriched UF4 dissolved in fluoride salt and moderated by beryllium oxide, built to explore nuclear propulsion for aircraft [2]. A circulating liquid fuel expanded on heating and naturally stabilized the reactor, solving the xenon-instability problem that plagued solid-fuel designs [2].

The **Molten Salt Reactor Experiment (MSRE)**, designed from 1960, constructed from 1962, and operated from June 1965 to December 1969, was the decisive civilian demonstration [1][2]. Key parameters and history:

- Graphite-moderated, 7.4–8 MWt (design 10 MWt), cooled with FLiBe-family salt; the reactor vessel, core, fuel pump, and heat exchanger sat inside a containment tank [1][2].
- First criticality with U-235 on 1 June 1965; uranium stripped by fluorination in August 1968; critical on U-233 on 2 October 1968, full power January 1969 [2].
- Operating statistics: 13,172 full-power hours, 9,005 hours on U-235, 4,167 hours on U-233, with 86% availability during the final 15-month reliability period [2].
- The program was terminated in 1973 by the Atomic Energy Commission in favor of the fast-breeder program; the proposed Molten Salt Breeder Reactor (MSBR) was never built [1].

The MSRE's conclusions were broad: the molten-salt fuel concept was viable, fuel salt was immune to radiation damage, graphite was unattacked, Hastelloy-N corrosion was negligible, and measured neutronics — critical loading, reactivity coefficients, dynamics, long-term reactivity changes — agreed with prior calculations [1]. Noble-gas stripping reduced xenon-135 poisoning by a factor of about six; uranium additions during operation were quick and uneventful; uranium recovery by fluorination was efficient [1].

### 2.2 The thorium–uranium-233 breeding chain

Thorium-232 is fertile: it requires a fissile driver (U-235 or plutonium) to supply power and the neutron surplus for breeding [7]:

> **Definition 1 (Thorium breeding chain).** *Th-232 + n → Th-233 (t½ ≈ 22 min) → Pa-233 (t½ ≈ 27 d) → U-233 (fissile).*

The intermediate **protactinium-233** is the crux of thorium neutronics. With a 27-day half-life, Pa-233 that remains in the core absorbs neutrons parasitically (its capture cross-section in the thermal/epithermal spectrum is significant), producing U-234 instead of U-233. This "protactinium effect" imposes a reactivity penalty during startup and degrades the breeding ratio. In a solid-fuel reactor the Pa-233 cannot be removed; in a liquid-fuel reactor it can be extracted continuously from the salt, allowed to decay outside the neutron flux, and the resulting U-233 reintroduced — the decisive fuel-cycle advantage of the MSR [9].

The η of U-233 in a thermal MSR spectrum is ~2.29 with α ≈ 0.09–0.11 — data refined by the MSRE — leaving roughly one surplus neutron per fission for breeding [1].

### 2.3 Fluoride salt chemistry and neutron physics

The carrier salt most studied is **FLiBe** (LiF–BeF2), used in the MSRE and TMSR-LF1 [3]. It must combine low neutron absorption, high actinide-fluoride solubility, radiation stability, and alloy compatibility. Li-7 enrichment (≥99.95% in TMSR-LF1 [3]) is mandatory because Li-6 has an enormous (n,α) cross-section producing tritium — a neutron poison and a radiological contaminant.

Two neutronic facts matter: the salt is neutron-transparent relative to water (graphite does the moderating in thermal designs), and homogeneously dissolved fuel couples thermal expansion directly to reactivity — no pellet-clad gap, no fertile self-shielding advantage.

---

## 3. Methodology

### 3.1 Circulating-fuel point kinetics with precursor drift

Standard point kinetics assumes delayed-neutron precursors are stationary in the core. In an MSR, precursors of the six (or eight) delayed groups decay with constants λi while being advected through the core with transit time τc and through the external loop (piping, heat exchanger, pump bowl) with transit time τL. Precursors that decay outside the core contribute no delayed neutron to the chain reaction — they represent a *loss* of effective delayed-neutron fraction βeff.

> **Definition 2 (Effective delayed-neutron fraction, circulating fuel).** *For group i with decay constant λi, core transit time τc, and loop transit time τL, the fraction of precursors decaying in the core is fi = (1 − e^(−λiτc)) / (1 − e^(−λi(τc+τL))). The effective delayed fraction is βeff = Σi βi fi, where βi are the physical delayed-neutron fractions.*

The circulating-fuel kinetics equations read:

dP/dt = ((ρ − βeff)/Λ) P + Σi λi Ci
dCi/dt = (βi/Λ) P − (λi + 1/τc) Ci + (1/τc) Ci(t − τc − τL) e^{(−λi τL)}

The essential consequence: βeff is strictly smaller than the static β — for the MSRE roughly half the precursors decayed outside the core — so circulating-fuel reactors respond faster to reactivity insertions and control analysis must use the drifted value [1]. The Python model below implements this:

```python
# Circulating-fuel point kinetics: precursor drift model (illustrative)
import math

# Six-group U-235 delayed data: (beta_i, lambda_i [1/s])
groups = [
    (0.000215, 0.0124), (0.001424, 0.0305), (0.001274, 0.111),
    (0.002568, 0.301),   (0.000748, 1.14),  (0.000273, 3.01),
]
beta_static = sum(b for b, _ in groups)

# MSRE-like loop: 25 s in core, 25 s in external loop
tau_c, tau_L = 25.0, 25.0

def in_core_fraction(lam):
    num = 1.0 - math.exp(-lam * tau_c)
    den = 1.0 - math.exp(-lam * (tau_c + tau_L))
    return num / den

fi = [in_core_fraction(lam) for _, lam in groups]
beta_eff = sum(b * f for (b, _), f in zip(groups, fi))

print(f"static beta      = {beta_static:.5f}")
print(f"circulating beta = {beta_eff:.5f}")
print(f"retained fraction = {beta_eff / beta_static:.3f}")
```

The longest-lived groups retain only ~40–50% of precursors in-core; the weighted βeff falls to roughly half the static value, matching MSRE experience [1].

### 3.2 Temperature-coefficient decomposition

The isothermal temperature coefficient αT decomposes into density, Doppler, and moderator terms. In a liquid-fuel MSR the **density (expansion) term dominates** and is inherently negative: heating the salt reduces fuel number density in the core and pushes fuel into the lower-importance loop region. MSRE measurements confirmed a prompt negative coefficient, and transient tests showed power self-regulation without control-rod motion [1][2].

### 3.3 Neutron-energy-spectrum modeling

Modern analysis couples continuous-energy Monte Carlo (OpenMC, MCNP, Serpent) to depletion solvers, with few-group cross-sections feeding transient codes such as RESTA3D/TMSR-LINK [10]:

| Energy group | Energy bounds | MSRE-like thermal MSR (fraction) | Fast chloride MSR (fraction) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Thermal | < 0.625 eV | 0.62 | 0.02 |
| Epithermal | 0.625 eV – 100 keV | 0.30 | 0.18 |
| Fast | > 100 keV | 0.08 | 0.80 |
| Mean neutron energy | — | ~0.08 eV (thermal peak) | ~400 keV |
| U-233 η (spectrum avg) | — | ~2.29 | ~2.45 |
| Th-232 capture share | — | breeding margin ≈ 1.02–1.07 | breeding margin ≈ 1.1–1.2 |

---

## 4. Deep Dive

### 4.1 Online reprocessing: fission-product management as neutronics

Because the fuel is a liquid, fission products can be removed *continuously*, and every removal channel is a reactivity effect:

1. **Noble gases (Xe-135, Kr).** Xenon-135 is the dominant neutron poison in thermal reactors (σa ≈ 2.6×10⁶ barns). In the MSRE, helium sparging stripped noble gases from the salt, cutting Xe-135 poisoning by a factor of about six [1]. Since Xe-135 is removed rather than decaying to Cs-135 in-core, the steady-state xenon reactivity penalty is a small fraction of the solid-fuel value, and xenon-override transients after shutdown are greatly attenuated.
2. **Noble metals.** These plate out on graphite and metal surfaces; the MSRE quantified deposition at gas-liquid, graphite, and metal interfaces [1].
3. **Lanthanides and soluble fission products.** These accumulate in the salt and are removed by a chemical side-stream (fluorination/reductive extraction in the MSBR flowsheet); the processing rate trades capital cost against neutron economy [2].
4. **Protactinium-233.** Continuous Pa extraction (e.g., reductive extraction into liquid bismuth in the MSBR flowsheet) is the step that converts the thorium cycle from converter to breeder: Pa-233 decaying outside the flux loses no neutrons to parasitic capture [9].

The net effect is a poison inventory that is a *controlled variable*, not a cumulative one — the reason MSRE long-term reactivity drift matched calculations [1].

### 4.2 Transient safety: loss-of-heat-sink and loss-of-flow

Transient safety in MSRs follows from three passive mechanisms, all demonstrated or analyzed in the Oak Ridge program:

- **Strong negative temperature feedback.** Any temperature excursion expands the fuel and inserts negative reactivity promptly; the reactor is self-regulating and load-following [1][5].
- **Low operating pressure.** Near-atmospheric operation eliminates the stored-energy driving force for dispersal; no high-pressure blowdown and no zirconium–steam hydrogen generation [6].
- **Freeze-plug drain.** A cooled solid-salt plug melts on overheating or power loss, draining fuel by gravity into subcritical, passively cooled tanks with no operator action or external power [5].

In an unprotected loss-of-heat-sink, salt heat-up inserts negative feedback, driving power toward decay-heat levels; the freeze-plug drain provides ultimate passive termination. On pump trip, slowing circulation raises βeff toward the static value — a stabilizing kinetics change — while the temperature rise inserts negative reactivity. Coupled precursor-transport analyses for the TMSR program confirm benign transients within salt temperature limits [10].

> **Theorem (Circulating-fuel self-regulation, informal).** *In a liquid-fuel reactor with negative isothermal temperature coefficient and gravity drain, any unprotected transient that raises fuel temperature inserts negative reactivity faster than precursor-drift kinetics can add positive reactivity, and the drain system bounds the maximum fuel temperature. Hence the transient terminates passively.*

The feedback acts on the prompt heat-transfer timescale, while precursor redistribution acts on the loop-transit timescale (tens of seconds) — the negative feedback wins the race.

### 4.3 Protactinium management and the breeding ratio

The breeding ratio (BR) — fissile atoms produced per fissile atom consumed — is the figure of merit of the thorium cycle. For a thermal thorium MSR with η ≈ 2.29, leakage plus structural absorption of ~0.15–0.20, and Pa-233 capture suppressed by online removal, BR values of 1.02–1.07 are calculated for thermal designs [9]; the MSBR targeted ~1.06 [2]. The TMSR-LF1, with a conversion ratio of only ~0.1 (it is a converter/test reactor, not a breeder), nevertheless demonstrated the key enabling physics: in October 2024 thorium was added to the operating salt and Pa-233 was detected, proving the breeding chain functions in a modern liquid-fuel system [3][7].

At startup, Pa-233 builds toward equilibrium over several half-lives, absorbing neutrons before its U-233 appears; the reactor must carry excess reactivity until equilibrium is approached. Online Pa removal shortens Pa-233 residence in the flux and flattens this transient.

### 4.4 Comparative survey of thorium MSR designs

| Design | Power | Spectrum / salt | Fuel cycle | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MSRE (ORNL, 1965–1969) | 7.4 MWt | Thermal, graphite, fluoride | U-235 then U-233 (Th-derived) | Operated; 13,172 full-power h [1][2] |
| MSBR (ORNL, 1970s design) | 1000 MWe | Thermal, graphite, LiF–BeF2–ThF4–UF4 | Th/U-233 breeder, BR ~1.06, online Pa removal | Paper design only [2] |
| TMSR-LF1 (SINAP, China) | 2 MWt | Thermal, graphite, FLiBe (Li-7 99.95%) | HALEU 19.75% U-235 driver + Th; CR ~0.1 | Critical Oct 2023; Th added Oct 2024 [3][7] |
| TMSR-SF1 / commercial (planned) | 10 MWt / 100+ MWe | Thermal fluoride | Th/U-233 | In development [13] |
| Kairos Hermes (USA) | 35 MWt (Hermes 2) | Thermal, graphite pebble, FLiBe coolant; TRISO fuel (solid) | HALEU driver; coolant-only salt | Construction permit issued; building in Tennessee [14] |
| Fast chloride MSR concepts | 100s MWe | Fast, chloride salt | Th/U-233 or U/Pu | Conceptual [6] |

Kairos's KP-FHR uses FLiBe as *coolant* with solid TRISO pebble fuel — it inherits fluoride-salt passive safety without circulating-fuel kinetics or online reprocessing [14]; it is a salt reactor but not a liquid-fuel reactor.

---

## 5. Empirical Results and Analysis

### 5.1 MSRE operating record

The MSRE data are the empirical anchor of the field [1][2]:

- **Reliability.** Availability in final runs reached 98.6% on U-235 and 99.9% on U-233 operation [2].
- **Neutronics validation.** Critical loading, reactivity coefficients, dynamics, and long-term reactivity changes all agreed with pre-operational calculations [1].
- **Xenon.** Helium sparging stripped noble gases, cutting Xe-135 poisoning by a factor of ~6 [1].
- **Materials.** Hastelloy-N corrosion was negligible, graphite was unattacked, and the UF4/UF3 redox ratio was maintained [2].
- **Fuel handling.** Uranium additions to the circulating salt during operation were uneventful; recovery by fluorination was efficient [1].
- **Nuclear data.** The MSRE improved the measured U-233 capture-to-fission ratio in a representative MSR spectrum, a basic datum for all subsequent thorium breeder calculations [1].

### 5.2 TMSR-LF1: the modern confirmation

The TMSR-LF1 program has, within two years, reproduced the essential MSRE milestones with modern instrumentation [3][7]:

1. First criticality 11 October 2023 (11:08 local) on HALEU (19.75% U-235) driver fuel in FLiBe [3].
2. Full power (2 MWt) 17 June 2024 [3].
3. License to load thorium granted September 2024; world's first thorium addition to an operating molten salt reactor completed October 2024 [7].
4. Ten days of full-power operation on thorium-bearing salt beginning 8 October 2024, with Pa-233 detected — direct observation of the breeding chain in situ [3].


### 5.3 Analysis: what the data imply

Three inferences follow. First, MSRE agreement between measurement and calculation implies the coupled neutronics/thermal-hydraulics of circulating fluoride fuel is *predictable*; the physics contains no hidden instability. Second, xenon-stripping and online-addition results show the chemical plant and reactor operate as one coupled system without neutronic surprises. Third, the TMSR-LF1 Pa-233 detection closes the loop empirically: the thorium breeding chain functions in a modern liquid-fuel core, moving the breeding-ratio debate from "can it work" to "what BR can an optimized design sustain" [9].

---

## 6. Limitations

**Materials and corrosion.** Fluoride salts at 650–700 °C are corrosive; the MSRE succeeded with Hastelloy-N under careful redox control, (tellurium-induced cracking required a modified Hastelloy-N composition) [1][2]. Sixty-year life extension of graphite and alloy performance under fast fluence (~3×10²² n/cm² limits studied for TMSR graphite [11]) remains an active qualification problem.

**Tritium.** Li-6 (n,α) reactions generate tritium that permeates hot metals; MSRE-like spray-gas removal captures roughly two-thirds, and engineered barriers are needed to hold permeation near ~10% of the source [12].

**Reprocessing complexity.** Online processing presupposes a continuously operating chemical plant — fluorinators, reductive-extraction contactors, Pa decay tanks — under safeguards. The MSBR flowsheet was judged to have "major drawbacks concerning safety and reprocessing" [9], motivating simplified concepts such as the TMSR.

**Proliferation.** The thorium cycle co-produces U-232 (hard-gamma Tl-208 daughter, an intrinsic barrier), but separated Pa-233 decays to pure U-233, so safeguards-by-design of Pa handling is required [8].

**Licensing.** As the IAEA notes, MSR design-safety standards, fuel-salt transport rules, and supply chains do not yet exist; no liquid-fuel MSR has been licensed commercially [13].

**Modeling gaps.** High-fidelity 3-D transport + CFD + moving-precursor simulations with validated turbulence-chemistry coupling are still maturing; RESTA3D/TMSR-LINK is the current state of practice [10].

---

## 7. Conclusion

The liquid fuel that enables online reprocessing also transports delayed-neutron precursors — halving βeff — and ties reactivity to salt density through thermal expansion, producing a reactor that is prompt-negative in feedback, self-regulating, and drainable to passive safety. The thorium–U-233 cycle exploits the best η of any thermal fissile nuclide, and the protactinium bottleneck is soluble precisely because the fuel is a liquid: Pa-233 can decay outside the flux.

The MSRE's 13,172 full-power hours and agreement between measurement and calculation proved the concept [1][2]; TMSR-LF1 has re-demonstrated the essentials with Pa-233 detected in situ [3][7].

What remains is industrialization, not discovery: materials qualification, tritium control, a simpler chemical plant, and the licensing framework the IAEA identifies as missing [13]. If those are solved, the liquid-fuel thorium reactor offers a thermal breeder with passive safety, continuous fueling, and a waste stream depleted of long-lived transuranics — the realization, at last, of the promise Oak Ridge demonstrated in 1969.
