title: Hardware Trojan Detection in Integrated Circuits: Side-Channel Fingerprinting, Machine-Learning Classifiers, Golden-Chip-Free Anomaly Detection, and Split-Manufacturing Countermeasures
abstract: The globalization of the semiconductor supply chain has made hardware Trojans — stealthy malicious modifications inserted by untrusted foundries, third-party IP vendors, or compromised CAD tools — a first-order threat to integrated-circuit trustworthiness. This thesis develops a unified treatment of post-silicon hardware Trojan detection: classical side-channel fingerprinting pioneered by Agrawal et al. in 2007, statistical test generation via MERO that maximizes Trojan activation probability, and machine-learning classifiers trained on power and electromagnetic side-channel features from the TrustHub benchmark suite. A central emphasis is **golden-chip-free** anomaly detection — one-class SVM, autoencoders, and PCA-subspace residuals that dispense with trusted reference devices. It further analyzes **split manufacturing**, which divides FEOL and BEOL fabrication between untrusted and trusted foundries so no single adversary observes the complete netlist. Synthesizing quantitative results from the literature into a detection-theoretic framework with formal bounds, it closes with the fundamental limits of each approach and argues that only defense-in-depth — fingerprinting, learning, and manufacturing-level countermeasures combined — yields practical assurance.
body:
# Hardware Trojan Detection in Integrated Circuits: Side-Channel Fingerprinting, Machine-Learning Classifiers, Golden-Chip-Free Anomaly Detection, and Split-Manufacturing Countermeasures

## Abstract

## 1. Introduction

A modern integrated circuit traverses a deeply fragmented supply chain. Register-transfer-level design may be outsourced; soft IP cores are licensed from vendors whose environments cannot be audited; EDA tools are complex software stacks from a handful of vendors; and fabrication is concentrated in offshore foundries with full access to the complete layout database (GDSII). At each handoff, a motivated adversary may insert a **hardware Trojan**: additional logic dormant during manufacturing test yet, once triggered by rare internal states, delivering a payload from denial of service to silent cryptographic key exfiltration [4].

Three properties make the hardware Trojan problem uniquely difficult. First, Trojans are designed to evade conventional post-manufacturing functional and structural test: they hide behind *rare* trigger conditions, so the probability that a random or even coverage-driven test vector activates them is vanishingly small. Second, Trojan circuitry can be **ultrasmall** — a comparator-based Trojan may occupy well under 0.1% of the total gate count — so its signature in power, delay, or area is easily buried beneath inter-die and intra-die process variation. Third, the *verifier* of the chip is typically not the fabricator: the design house receives silicon from an entity it does not fully trust, and must authenticate a device against specifications it cannot physically re-derive without destructive reverse engineering.

This thesis is organized as follows. Section 2 establishes the Trojan taxonomy and threat model. Section 3 details the methodology: side-channel fingerprint construction, statistical rare-node excitation, supervised classification, unsupervised anomaly detection, and split manufacturing. Section 4 deep-dives into four pillars — the supply-chain threat model; side-channel physics and fingerprint statistics; the machine-learning detection pipeline; and the security argument for split manufacturing. Section 5 presents empirical results with a detection-theoretic formulation and proofs. Section 6 enumerates limitations, and Section 7 concludes.

> **Definition 1.1 (Hardware Trojan).** A hardware Trojan is a tuple $T = (\tau, \pi)$ where $\tau$ is a *trigger* circuit, a combinational or sequential function of a subset of internal nodes that evaluates to true under a rare operating condition, and $\pi$ is a *payload* circuit whose effect is observable (functionally or parametrically) only after $\tau$ fires.

## 2. Background

### 2.1 Trojan Taxonomy

The canonical classification of hardware Trojans, articulated in the survey literature and in DARPA Trust-in-IC program documents, partitions Trojans along three axes [5]:

- **Physical attributes**: the type (functional vs. parametric), size (number of added gates), distribution (tightly clustered vs. dispersed), and structure (layout altered vs. preserved).
- **Activation characteristics**: Trojans are *always-on* (e.g., a side-channel leakage path that continuously modulates power to transmit a key bit) or *triggered* (internally by rare logic conditions, or externally via a sensor or antenna).
- **Action characteristics**: the payload may *modify functionality* (e.g., privilege escalation in a processor), *degrade performance*, *leak information*, or *deny service*.

A combinational Trojan fires when a conjunction of $q$ rare-valued nodes simultaneously assumes its rare value; a sequential Trojan adds a state machine (classically a counter, as in the TrustHub AES-T100 benchmark) that advances toward activation only when specific patterns are observed. The adversary's design objective is a trigger probability so small that manufacturing test never observes activation, yet nonzero so the Trojan is usable in the field.

### 2.2 The Golden-Chip Problem

Nearly all parametric detection methods require a **golden chip**: a reference device or signature known to be Trojan-free. Acquiring one is the bootstrap problem of hardware assurance — Agrawal et al. [1] proposed reverse-engineering a small sample of fabricated ICs, an expensive, destructive, and statistically weak procedure, since a Trojan present in *all* sampled chips would poison the reference. This motivates the golden-chip-free techniques of Section 4.4: instead of trusting a physical artifact, one trusts a *model* of process variation and nominal simulation behavior, and flags deviations from it as anomalous.

### 2.3 Side-Channel Physics

Every switching event in CMOS logic dissipates dynamic power $P_{dyn} = \alpha C V_{DD}^2 f$. A Trojan adds gates, hence capacitance $C$ and activity $\alpha$ beyond the nominal design. Even when the Trojan is *not* triggered, its trigger-monitoring logic switches in response to its input nodes, producing a parametric signature in **transient supply current** ($I_{DDT}$), **quiescent current** ($I_{DDQ}$), **path delay** (added capacitive load), and **electromagnetic emanations** (localized current loops; EM probes provide spatial resolution that power rails cannot).

> **Theorem:** Let the measured side-channel vector be $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{s} + \mathbf{n}_p + \mathbf{n}_m + \mathbf{t}$, where $\mathbf{s}$ is the nominal signature, $\mathbf{n}_p$ process variation, $\mathbf{n}_m$ measurement noise, and $\mathbf{t}$ the Trojan contribution. Then any detector with false-alarm rate $\alpha$ has detection power bounded by the signal-to-interference ratio $\|\mathbf{t}\|^2 / \mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_p + \Sigma_m)$.

This is the fundamental SNR formulation: detection is a battle between Trojan magnitude and the process-noise floor, and every technique in this thesis is, at bottom, an attempt to maximize that ratio.

## 3. Methodology

The detection methodology proceeds in four stages, each corresponding to a generation of the literature:

1. **Fingerprint construction (Agrawal et al. [1])**. Apply $M$ input vectors; record the side-channel response. From reverse-engineered golden chips, estimate the nominal mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. For a chip under test with response $\mathbf{x}$, compute the Mahalanobis distance $d^2 = (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})$ and threshold against a $\chi^2$ value; chips outside the fingerprint are declared infected.

2. **Rare-node excitation (MERO [2])**. Identify internal nodes whose signal probability of a logic value is below a threshold $\theta_{rare}$ via logic simulation. Generate test vectors forcing each rare node to its rare value at least $N$ times — *multiple excitation of rare occurrences* — raising Trojan switching activity during measurement and achieving comparable coverage with ~85% fewer vectors than random patterns.

3. **Supervised classification on extracted features**. Collect power or EM traces across TrustHub benchmarks (AES-T100 through AES-T2000, RS232-T1000, BasicRSA). Extract PCA, wavelet, and spectral features; train SVM, random forest, ELM, or contrastive deep networks; evaluate with cross-validation.

4. **Unsupervised golden-chip-free modeling [3]**. Learn a trusted region from simulation-calibrated process models or from the population under test itself (assuming only a minority is infected). One-class SVM, autoencoder reconstruction error, or PCA-subspace projection distance then scores each chip; outliers are flagged without any golden reference.

The constructive countermeasure — **split manufacturing** — is evaluated as a methodology for *prevention* rather than detection: partition the layout so that FEOL layers (transistors, polysilicon) are fabricated at the untrusted foundry while BEOL layers (metal interconnect) are completed at a trusted facility. The untrusted foundry then sees gates but not their wiring, and Trojan insertion requires guessing the missing connectivity.

---

## 4. Deep Dive

### 4.1 The Supply-Chain Threat Model and Trojan Insertion Points

The IC supply chain can be modeled as a sequence of custodians, each with distinct capabilities:

| Stage | Custodian | Trojan insertion capability |
|---|---|---|
| RTL / IP integration | Design house, 3PIP vendor | Malicious RTL in soft IP cores |
| Logic synthesis & P&R | EDA tool vendor | Tool-level subversion of netlist |
| Fabrication (FEOL+BEOL) | Untrusted foundry | Full-layout Trojan insertion (strongest adversary) |
| Test & assembly | Test house | Limited; parametric tampering |
| Deployment | End user / system integrator | None (victim) |

The foundry-level adversary is the strongest: with the complete GDSII, it can perform *engineering change order* (ECO)-style insertion, adding a handful of gates into whitespace (filler-cell regions) and routing trigger inputs from existing nets with minimal perturbation of timing closure — leaving the footprint nearly unchanged. The 3PIP adversary is weaker in layout control but stronger in *stealth of specification*: a Trojaned AES core can leak key bits through a covert power channel while passing all functional tests, because the leakage path is *functionally invisible*.

> **Theorem:** An adversary with full layout access and knowledge of the test-vector set can construct a Trojan whose trigger condition is disjoint from all test vectors, making logic-testing detection probability exactly zero.

*Proof sketch.* Let $V \subset \{0,1\}^n$ be the test set. The adversary chooses a trigger conjunction over $q$ internal nodes whose joint rare condition is never satisfied by any $v \in V$ — possible whenever $|V| \ll 2^n$ and the node functions are not constant on $V$. The Trojan's observable behavior then coincides with the genuine circuit on all of $V$. ∎

This theorem is the formal justification for side-channel methods: since the trigger can always be hidden from the test set, detection must rely on the Trojan's *parametric* footprint, which exists whether or not the Trojan fires.

### 4.2 Side-Channel Fingerprinting: From Power Traces to Statistical Decision

Agrawal et al.'s IC fingerprinting [1] treats each chip as a point in a high-dimensional measurement space: path delays of $K$ sensitized paths, or transient-current waveforms under $M$ vectors. The *fingerprint* of the genuine population is the estimated distribution $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, with inter-die variation shifting $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ per lot and intra-die variation widening $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.

Two refinements proved essential. First, **differential and regional analysis**: comparing the *shape* of the transient waveform rather than absolute power (which is swamped by inter-die shifts), or partitioning the chip into regions so that a localized Trojan perturbs one region disproportionately. Rad, Plusquellic, and Tehranipoor [6] showed power-supply transient analysis could resolve Trojans as small as **three additional gates** in simulation — a landmark sensitivity result. Second, **self-referencing**: comparing *neighboring* dies or repeated measurements of the same die to cancel systematic variation.

The statistical decision rule is a hypothesis test:

- $H_0$: chip is genuine, $\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$.
- $H_1$: chip is infected, $\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu} + \boldsymbol{\delta}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, with unknown shift $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ induced by the Trojan.

The generalized likelihood-ratio test reduces, for known $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, to thresholding the Mahalanobis distance. The detection probability is $P_D = Q\left(Q^{-1}(P_{FA}) - \sqrt{\boldsymbol{\delta}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\delta}}\right)$ — the closed-form embodiment of the SNR theorem. Every technique in this thesis is, at bottom, an attempt to increase the non-centrality parameter $\boldsymbol{\delta}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\delta}$: MERO increases $\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|$ by exciting the Trojan; regional/EM analysis shrinks the effective $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ by spatial localization; learning-based methods estimate a better $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ from data.

### 4.3 Machine-Learning Classifiers on TrustHub Benchmarks

The TrustHub suite (hosted at trust-hub.org) provides the community's standard evaluation vehicle: synthesizable Trojan-inserted designs including AES cores with counter-based and comparator-based triggers (AES-T100 … AES-T2000), RS232 UART Trojans that leak data or deny service, and RSA variants. Each benchmark ships with the Trojan-free base design, enabling controlled genuine-vs.-infected experiments in simulation and on FPGA.

A modern ML detection pipeline has four stages: **acquisition** of $I_{DDT}$ or EM traces (thousands per chip across dozens of chips); **feature extraction** via PCA (95% variance retained), wavelet decompositions, or spectral statistics; **classification** with SVM, random forests, ELM, or contrastive deep networks [7], routinely exceeding 95% accuracy on TrustHub AES benchmarks and 99%+ under controlled aging [8]; and **validation** by $k$-fold cross-validation *across chips* — never across traces — to avoid leaking per-chip process signatures into both folds.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# X: (n_traces, n_samples) EM/power traces; y: 0 genuine, 1 infected
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95, svd_solver="full")
Z = pca.fit_transform(X)          # denoise + decorrelate; kills measurement noise
clf = SVC(kernel="rbf", C=10.0, gamma="scale", class_weight="balanced")
scores = cross_val_score(clf, Z, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
print(f"mean AUC={scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}")
# Guard: split folds by chip id, not by trace, to avoid process-signature leakage.
```

A subtle methodological pitfall deserves emphasis: if traces from the *same physical chip* appear in both training and test folds, the classifier may learn the chip's individual process signature rather than the Trojan's — inflating accuracy. Rigorous studies therefore perform **leave-one-chip-out** validation.

### 4.4 Golden-Chip-Free Detection with Unsupervised Anomaly Models

The golden-chip-free program, exemplified by Hu, Nowroz, Reda, and Koushanfar [3], removes the trusted reference entirely. The key insight is that the *population under test* is mostly genuine: if Trojans are rare in the supply (a realistic assumption — a foundry that infected every chip would be trivially caught by functional anomalies and would destroy its own business), then the genuine population can be estimated robustly from the data itself.

The method proceeds as follows. First, calibrate a **simulation-based process model**: run Monte Carlo simulations of the genuine netlist under the foundry's statistical compact models to predict the nominal side-channel distribution. Second, measure process-control-monitor (PCM) structures on the actual wafer to fit the *actual* process corner — correcting the simulation-to-silicon mismatch that would otherwise poison the trusted region. Third, construct the trusted region in the calibrated space and classify each chip by its distance to the region boundary.

> **Theorem:** Let a fraction $\epsilon < 1/2$ of the population be infected, and let the genuine distribution have bounded covariance. Then a robust estimator (e.g., minimum covariance determinant) recovers the genuine mean and covariance with error $O(\epsilon)$ in operator norm, so the induced detector's excess false-alarm rate vanishes as $\epsilon \to 0$.

In practice, unsupervised models take several forms: **one-class SVM** (minimum-volume hypersphere enclosing the genuine population), **autoencoders** (trained to reconstruct genuine traces; infected chips yield high reconstruction error), and **PCA-subspace residuals** (large $\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{P}_k\mathbf{x}\|^2$ flags anomalies).

Empirically, the DAC 2014 golden-chip-free study [3] reported that classification boundaries learned from simulation-calibrated data correctly classified all 80 Trojan-infested devices while misclassifying only a minority of genuine devices — with PCM measurements strictly improving the genuine acceptance rate. The residual gap is the price of abandoning the golden chip: without ground truth, the trusted region is necessarily conservative.

### 4.5 Split Manufacturing as a Constructive Countermeasure

Detection asks, "is this chip infected?" Split manufacturing asks the stronger question: "can the adversary insert a Trojan at all?" In the Rajendran et al. framework, fabrication is divided: the **front end of line** (transistors, contacts, lower metal layers) is built at an advanced but untrusted foundry, while the **back end of line** (upper metal layers completing the interconnect) is finished at a trusted facility. The untrusted foundry therefore observes the complete transistor-level netlist *without* the wiring that defines its function — a sea of gates with dangling pins.

> **Theorem:** If $m$ two-pin nets are lifted to the BEOL and the adversary's proximity hint yields at most $c$ candidate partners per pin, the expected number of correctly recovered lifted nets is at most $m/c$; choosing $m$ and the lifting policy to cover all key-dependent nets forces the adversary's targeted-Trojan success probability below any prescribed $\eta$ at $O(m \log c)$ trusted-BEOL cost.

The practical costs are real: split manufacturing requires compatible process design kits at two foundries and trusted BEOL capacity (often at an older, coarser node, constraining how much can be lifted). It also composes naturally with detection: split manufacturing raises the *cost* of insertion, while side-channel fingerprinting raises the *probability of catching* whatever slips through — a genuine defense in depth.

---

## 5. Empirical Results and Proofs

### 5.1 Quantitative Synthesis from the Literature

| Technique | Benchmark / setup | Reported result |
|---|---|---|
| Path-delay fingerprinting [1] | Explicit-payload Trojans, high process variation | 100% detection |
| Path-delay fingerprinting [1] | Implicit (counter-based) Trojan, 0.76% area | 36% detection — hard case |
| Power transient analysis [6] | Simulated benchmark circuit | Sensitivity down to 3 added gates |
| MERO test generation [2] | ISCAS benchmarks | ~85% test-length reduction vs. random |
| Golden-chip-free classification [3] | 80 infected + 40 genuine devices | All 80 infected caught; genuine acceptance improves with PCM calibration |
| ML + controlled aging [8] | AES-T100, 32-bin features | 99.15% genuine / 100% infected accuracy |
| Contrastive learning [7] | Side-channel traces | Improved separation vs. classical classifiers |

### 5.2 Detection-Theoretic Formulation and Proof

We formalize the detector's fundamental limit. Consider the binary hypothesis test of Section 4.2 with $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ unknown but constrained to a Trojan-feasible set $\mathcal{D}$ (small norm, sparse support corresponding to localized gates).

> **Theorem:** (Minimax detection bound.) Let $\mathcal{D} = \{\boldsymbol{\delta} : \|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_2 \le \rho,\ \|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_0 \le s\}$. For any detector with false-alarm rate at most $\alpha$, the worst-case miss rate satisfies $\beta^* \ge Q\left(\frac{\rho}{\sigma_{\min}\sqrt{s}} - Q^{-1}(\alpha)\right)$-type lower bounds decreasing in $\rho$ and increasing in the effective noise projected onto the sparse support.

*Proof.* Reduce to the hardest one-sparse alternative: the adversary concentrates the Trojan signature into the single measurement coordinate with the largest projected noise variance. The problem becomes detection of a bounded signal in Gaussian noise, where the Neyman–Pearson lemma gives the optimal likelihood-ratio test and ROC $P_D = Q(Q^{-1}(P_{FA}) - \rho/\sigma_{\max})$. Since the adversary chooses the coordinate, no detector beats this bound uniformly over $\mathcal{D}$. ∎

The bound makes the design trade-offs quantitative: MERO and rare-node excitation increase $\rho$ (signal amplitude); EM spatial localization and regional power analysis decrease $\sigma_{\max}$ (noise in the relevant coordinate); and larger Trojans (bigger $s$ with fixed total $\rho$) are paradoxically *easier* to detect because the adversary cannot concentrate signature arbitrarily.

### 5.3 Worked Numerical Example

Consider an AES core with transient-current standard deviation $\sigma = 2.1\,\mathrm{mA}$ per measurement after averaging ($N=1000$ repetitions). A comparator Trojan tapping 8 nets adds an estimated $\rho = 0.35\,\mathrm{mA}$ of correlated shift under MERO excitation, so the per-coordinate SNR is $\rho/\sigma \approx 0.167$. With $P_{FA} = 10^{-3}$ ($Q^{-1} \approx 3.09$), single-measurement $P_D = Q(3.09 - 0.167) \approx 0.17\%$ — useless. But aggregating $K = 400$ independent measurements, the effective SNR grows as $\sqrt{K}$: $P_D = Q(3.09 - 0.167\sqrt{400}) = Q(-0.25) \approx 60\%$. Doubling excitation or halving noise via EM localization pushes $P_D$ past 95%. This reproduces, in miniature, why the literature's successful results all combine *excitation* (bigger $\rho$) with *aggregation* (more coordinates): neither alone suffices against ultrasmall Trojans.

## 6. Limitations

Intellectual honesty requires stating what these methods cannot do.

## 7. Conclusion

Hardware Trojan detection has matured from Agrawal et al.'s foundational fingerprinting insight — that a chip's side-channel emanations constitute an identity that malicious additions must perturb — into a diversified discipline spanning statistics, machine learning, and manufacturing technology. The through-line of this thesis is the **signal-to-interference ratio**: every advance, from MERO's rare-node excitation to EM spatial localization, from supervised classifiers on TrustHub traces to golden-chip-free anomaly models, is a technique for amplifying the Trojan's whisper above the roar of process variation. Split manufacturing complements detection with prevention, denying the foundry adversary the complete netlist needed for targeted insertion.

No single method suffices. Fingerprinting needs golden chips that are hard to bootstrap; golden-chip-free methods need models that are hard to calibrate; ML needs data that is hard to generalize; split manufacturing needs a trusted facility that is hard to provision. The practical conclusion is **defense in depth**: excite rare nodes during test, fingerprint power and EM side channels against simulation-calibrated trusted regions, screen populations with unsupervised anomaly models, and split the fabrication of security-critical designs. Together, these layers make Trojan insertion expensive, risky, and likely to be caught — the most that hardware assurance, short of fully trusted domestic fabrication, can honestly promise.

# Cache-Oblivious B-Trees and Fractal Tree Indexes: Ideal-Cache Model Bounds, van Emde Boas Layout, Buffered Message Injection, and Write-Amplification Analysis

## Abstract

This thesis develops the theory and systems practice of external-memory search trees that are simultaneously oblivious to hardware cache parameters and asymptotically optimal with respect to them. We begin with the ideal-cache model of Frigo, Leiserson, Prokop, and Ramachandran [1] and prove the regularity lemma that reduces multilevel, LRU-based hierarchies to a single two-level ideal cache. We analyze the van Emde Boas (vEB) memory layout [2][9], showing how recursive square-root decomposition yields an asymptotically optimal static cache-oblivious search structure with $\Theta(\log_B N)$ transfers per query. We survey the dynamic cache-oblivious B-tree of Bender, Demaine, and Farach-Colton [2], whose packed-memory-array machinery matches B-tree search, scan, and amortized update bounds. We then turn to write optimization: the $B^\varepsilon$-tree [5][6] and the fractal tree index deployed in TokuDB [7], where message injection into per-node buffers decouples the update path from the search path. Finally we compare write amplification across B-trees, fractal trees, and log-structured merge trees [8][10], formalize the trade-off through the RUM conjecture [12], and close with empirical measurements and open problems.

## 1. Introduction

Modern processors execute instructions orders of magnitude faster than they can fetch data from main memory, which is itself far faster than persistent storage. The *memory wall* means data-intensive programs are dominated not by arithmetic but by transfers between hierarchy levels. Database kernels and filesystems consequently invest enormous effort in *tuning* block sizes, page layouts, and buffer pools to a particular machine — effort redone on every hardware migration.

Two responses dominate the literature. *External-memory (EM)* algorithms explicitly parametrize cache size $M$ and block size $B$ and tune every decision to them [8]. *Cache-oblivious* algorithms pursue the same asymptotic optimality without ever naming $M$ or $B$ in code: a single program is simultaneously efficient at every level of an arbitrarily deep hierarchy [1]. This thesis studies both in the demanding setting of ordered key-value indexes, where the read/write tension is sharpest.

Section 2 fixes the ideal-cache model and explains why its idealizations cost at most constant factors. Section 3 describes our analytical methodology. Section 4 is the deep dive: the van Emde Boas layout, the cache-oblivious B-tree, the $B^\varepsilon$-tree and fractal-tree message machinery, and write-amplification analysis grounded in the RUM conjecture. Section 5 states theorems with proofs and reports measurements [7][11]. Section 6 collects limitations; Section 7 concludes.

---

## 2. Background

### 2.1 The Ideal-Cache Model

The *ideal-cache model* [1] idealizes the CPU/memory interaction as a two-level hierarchy:

- The **cache** holds $M$ words in $M/B$ lines of $B$ consecutive words; **main memory** ("disk") is unbounded.
- The cache is **fully associative** with **optimal (Belady) replacement**.
- Only **memory transfers** — block movements between levels — are counted. Cost is the **cache complexity** $Q(N; M, B)$.

A cache-oblivious algorithm *never references $M$ or $B$ in code* yet is asymptotically optimal *for every* $M$ and $B$ [1]. Under the *regularity condition*, results transfer to multilevel LRU hierarchies: optimizing the two-level model optimizes the whole machine.

> **Theorem (Regularity; Frigo et al. [1]):** If $Q(M, B) = O(Q(M/2, B))$ (regularity), then cache complexity on an LRU cache of size $M$ is at most twice the ideal-cache complexity on a cache of size $M/2$.

The common extra hypothesis is the **tall-cache assumption** $M = \Omega(B^2)$, true in practice and required by several optimal dynamic structures [2]. It marks the dividing line between static results (the vEB layout needs none) and dynamic ones.

### 2.2 Classical Predecessors

The cache-aware tradition began with the disk access model (DAM) of Aggarwal and Vitter [8]: B-trees achieve $\Theta(\log_B N)$ I/Os by *choosing* node size equal to $B$; LSM trees [10] achieve write-optimality by batching and merging sorted runs; the buffered repository tree [5] trades read cost against write cost via per-node buffers. The cache-oblivious program [1][3][4] generalizes all of these, with the vEB layout as the primitive that makes search trees oblivious.

---

## 3. Methodology

1. **Ideal-cache accounting.** Count block transfers under fully associative, optimal-replacement caching; express bounds in $N, M, B$ without the algorithm using $M$ or $B$.
2. **Recursive decomposition.** Divide-and-conquer shrinks data footprints until subproblems fit in cache; transfer recurrences like $Q(N) = 2Q(\sqrt{N}) + O(1)$ are solved for the crossover scale where a subtree fits in $O(1)$ blocks.
3. **Amortized potentials for buffered updates.** Potential functions charge each injected message $\Theta(1/B^\varepsilon)$ flush cost per level descended, yielding amortized update bounds for $B^\varepsilon$-trees and fractal trees.
4. **Write-amplification (WA) accounting.** WA = device bytes written per user byte, decomposed into (i) read-modify-write WA ($B/r$ for an $r$-byte change in a $B$-byte page), (ii) compaction/merge WA, (iii) space WA ($1/\text{occupancy}$), and (iv) logging WA. We evaluate each structure on uniform random inserts of 128-byte records, sequential inserts, and 50/50 read-write mixes, using published measurements [7][11].
5. **Theorem–proof presentation.** Each bound is stated formally with a proof sketch; full proofs are cited to [1][2][5][6].

---

## 4. Deep Dive

### 4.1 The Ideal-Cache Model and Its Justifications

Each idealization of [1] costs at most a constant factor:

- **Associativity.** For the recursive, contiguous access patterns studied here, conflict misses in set-associative caches are bounded by a constant factor.
- **Replacement.** Regularity reduces LRU (what hardware approximates) to optimal replacement at the price of doubling the effective cache. All our recurrences are monotone in $M$, hence regular.
- **Two levels.** Adjacent levels of a multilevel hierarchy each form an external-memory pair $(M_i, B_i)$ with inclusion. A cache-oblivious algorithm optimal for every $(M, B)$ is simultaneously optimal for every adjacent pair, hence the whole hierarchy.

### 4.2 The van Emde Boas Memory Layout

The van Emde Boas layout [9] is the foundational cache-oblivious primitive for search trees. In naive *heap order* (breadth-first) layout, a root-to-leaf search visits one node per level in unrelated array regions — $\Theta(\log N)$ transfers, no better than pointer chasing. The vEB layout instead:

1. Splits the height-$h$ tree into a **top subtree** of height $\lceil h/2 \rceil$ and $2^{\lceil h/2 \rceil}$ **bottom subtrees** of height $\lfloor h/2 \rfloor$.
2. Lays out the top subtree contiguously, then the bottom subtrees left to right.
3. Recurses within each piece.

Each recursion takes a square root of subtree size, so some recursion level produces subtrees of size between $\sqrt{B}$ and $B$ — each retrievable in $O(1)$ transfers. A root-to-leaf path crosses $\Theta(\log_B N)$ such subtrees, because the recursion squares granularity at each level [9][4]. Hence:

> **Theorem (Prokop [3]; cf. Demaine [4]):** A complete binary search tree of $N$ keys in the van Emde Boas layout supports search in $\Theta(\log_B N)$ memory transfers — asymptotically optimal for comparison-based search — for *all* $B$ simultaneously, with no dependence on $M$.

| Layout | Search transfers | $B$-dependence | Dynamic? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sorted array + binary search | $\Theta(\log(N/B))$ | none (worst) | No |
| Heap-order implicit tree | $\Theta(\log N)$ | none | No |
| **van Emde Boas layout** | $\Theta(\log_B N)$ | oblivious-optimal | No (static) |
| B-tree (cache-aware) | $\Theta(\log_B N)$ | tuned to $B$ | Yes |
| Cache-oblivious B-tree [2] | $O(\log_B N)$ | oblivious | Yes |

The vEB layout is *static*: an insertion can disturb the global recursive partition. Dynamic structures need further machinery.

### 4.3 Cache-Oblivious B-Trees: Dynamicizing the Layout

Bender, Demaine, and Farach-Colton [2] made the vEB layout dynamic with polylogarithmic overhead, yielding the first dynamic cache-oblivious dictionary matching B-tree bounds. Three tools:

1. **Strongly weight-balanced trees**, localizing updates to $O(\log N)$ nodes and preserving the recursive partition structure.
2. **The packed-memory array (PMA)** — "a cache-oblivious linked list": an array of size $\Theta(N)$ with per-segment density thresholds, scanning $S$ consecutive elements in the optimal $O(1 + S/B)$ transfers and updating in $O(1 + (\log^2 N)/B)$ amortized transfers.
3. **Exponential decomposition of the layout**: the tree is split into geometrically sized blocks, each internally vEB-laid-out; updates rebuild only affected blocks.

> **Theorem (Bender–Demaine–Farach-Colton [2]):** A dynamic cache-oblivious ordered dictionary on $N$ keys supports **search** in $O(1 + \log_{B+1} N)$ transfers, **scan** of $S$ keys in $O(1 + S/B)$ transfers (optimal), and **update** in $O(1 + \log_{B+1} N + \tfrac{\log^2 N}{B})$ amortized transfers — matching the B-tree whenever $B = \Omega(\log N \log \log N)$, true in external memory though not always in L1/L2 cache.

Later work simplified the construction, added persistence and optimal constants [4]; CORoBTS [13] generalizes it to arbitrary B-tree-like structures.

### 4.4 Fractal Trees and the $B^\varepsilon$-Tree: Buffered Message Injection

The cache-oblivious B-tree optimizes the *read* path; each insert still descends to a leaf. **Fractal tree indexes** [6][7] — the $B^\varepsilon$-tree family commercialized as TokuDB — optimize the *write* path by buffering updates in internal nodes and flushing them in batches.

**Structure.** A $B^\varepsilon$-tree ($0 < \varepsilon \le 1/2$) is a B-tree variant where each internal node carries a **buffer** of size $\Theta(B)$ alongside $\Theta(B^\varepsilon)$ pivot keys and children [5][6]. Updates are *messages* injected at the root buffer; when a buffer overflows, a batch flushes one level down, routed by pivots. A flush moves $\Theta(B)$ messages for $O(1)$ transfers, so each message pays $O(1/B)$ transfers per level.

**Asymptotics.** With height $\Theta((1/\varepsilon)\log_B N)$:

- **Insert/delete:** $O\!\left(\frac{\log_B N}{\varepsilon B^{1-\varepsilon}}\right)$ amortized transfers — for $\varepsilon = 1/2$, $O((\log_B N)/\sqrt{B})$, asymptotically *faster* than a B-tree by $\sqrt{B}$ [6].
- **Point search:** $\Theta((1/\varepsilon)\log_B N)$ — slower than a B-tree by $1/\varepsilon$, since searches must inspect buffers along the path for pending messages.
- **Range scan:** B-tree-competitive, as messages flush ahead of the scan cursor.

This is the canonical **read–write trade-off curve**: $\varepsilon \to 1$ recovers B-tree-like reads, $\varepsilon \to 0$ approaches write-optimality. Brodal and Fagerberg [5] first exhibited this curve; the $B^\varepsilon$-tree makes it continuous and tunable.

**Message injection as a programming model.** Fractal trees generalize "insert a key" to *inject a message* [7]: inserts, delete tombstones, and **upserts** — update-if-present-else-insert messages carrying a function $f$ (e.g., $x \mapsto x + c$). An upsert needs no prior search: it is appended to the root buffer, eliminating the read-modify-write. Most remarkably, **broadcast messages** replicate to *every* child's buffer and can transform *all* rows — e.g., adding a column. Total work is unchanged, but *latency* collapses: once the broadcast sits in the root buffer, every query observes the new schema, while physical rewriting is deferred to flushes that would have happened anyway [7]. Hence TokuDB's online schema changes — "it's just a message" — with the table fully available.

```python
# Fractal-tree message injection (schematic)
def inject(node, msg):
    node.buffer.append(msg)
    if len(node.buffer) > BUFFER_CAPACITY:   # Theta(B)
        for child, batch in partition(node.buffer, node.pivots):
            inject(child, batch)              # amortized O(1) I/Os
        node.buffer.clear()

def upsert(root, key, delta):
    inject(root, UpsertMessage(key, lambda x: x + delta))  # NO search

def add_column(root, default):
    inject_broadcast(root, SchemaMessage(("add", default)))  # instant schema change
```

### 4.5 Write-Amplification Analysis: B-Trees, LSM Trees, and the RUM Trade-Off

**Write amplification (WA)** — device bytes written per user byte — is the currency of storage-engine trade-offs. On random inserts of small records (the LSM-friendly regime [11]):

- **B-tree.** Each insert rewrites a full leaf page: a 128-byte record in a 16 KiB page is WA $\approx 128$ before splits. Page-granular read-modify-write dominates; in-storage transparent compression narrows but does not close the gap [11].
- **Fractal tree / $B^\varepsilon$-tree.** Batched flushes rewrite a node per $\Theta(B)$ messages: amortized WA per insert is $O((\log_B N)/B^{1-\varepsilon})$ — sub-constant in $B$ for $\varepsilon < 1$. Reads pay the $1/\varepsilon$ search penalty plus buffer-merge work: internal *read amplification*.
- **LSM tree [10].** Memtable batching plus leveled compaction gives insert WA $\approx$ levels $\times$ merge fan-in, measured around 10–30$\times$ on RocksDB [11]; point reads probe many levels (Bloom filters help); range scans merge iterators across levels.

| Structure | Point search | Amortized insert | Write amplif. | Read amplif. |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B-tree | $\Theta(\log_B N)$ | $\Theta(\log_B N)$ | High ($B/r$ page RMW) | $\approx 1$ |
| Cache-oblivious B-tree [2] | $O(\log_B N)$ | $O(\log_B N + \tfrac{\log^2 N}{B})$ | High (as B-tree) | $\approx 1$ |
| $B^\varepsilon$-tree / fractal tree [6] | $\Theta(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\log_B N)$ | $O(\tfrac{\log_B N}{\varepsilon B^{1-\varepsilon}})$ | Low (batched flush) | Moderate |
| LSM tree [10] | $O(L)$ levels + filters | $O(L \cdot T)$ compaction | Low ($\sim$10–30$\times$) | High |

**The RUM conjecture.** Athanassoulis et al. [12] conjecture that *read, update, and memory* overheads cannot be optimized simultaneously: an access method can improve at most two of {read cost, update cost, memory overhead} at the expense of the third. B-trees buy reads with update + memory overhead (70%-full nodes, page-granular writes); LSM trees buy updates and memory (dense immutable files) with read overhead; fractal trees slide along the curve via $\varepsilon$. The conjecture reframes "which index is best" as "where on the RUM surface does your workload live" — answered by measurement, not asymptotics alone.

---

## 5. Empirical Results and Proofs

> **Theorem (Static optimality [3][4]):** The vEB layout achieves $\Theta(\log_B N)$ search transfers for all $B$ simultaneously, matching the comparison-based lower bound. *Proof sketch.* A root-to-leaf path has $\log_2 N$ nodes. Recursive halving yields contiguous segments; at the level where segment size first drops below $B$, each segment costs $O(1)$ transfers, and any root-to-leaf path crosses $\Theta(\log_B N)$ such segments because each layout-recursion level squares the granularity. Optimality follows from the $\Omega(\log_B N)$ decision-tree lower bound: each transfer reveals at most $B$ keys. ∎

> **Theorem (Buffered update bound [5][6]):** In a $B^\varepsilon$-tree, amortized insert cost is $O((\log_B N)/(\varepsilon B^{1-\varepsilon}))$ transfers. *Proof sketch.* Let potential $\Phi$ be buffered messages weighted by remaining depth. Injecting at the root raises $\Phi$ by $O((1/\varepsilon)\log_B N)$. Flushing a full $\Theta(B)$-message buffer one level costs $O(1)$ transfers and drops $\Phi$ proportionally, so each message's amortized descent cost is $O(1/B^{1-\varepsilon})$ per level. Summing over $\Theta((1/\varepsilon)\log_B N)$ levels gives the bound. ∎

**Empirical evidence:**

1. **TokuDB / fractal trees [7].** Tokutek's benchmarks showed fractal-tree indexes sustaining insertion throughput an order of magnitude above B-tree engines (notably InnoDB) on random inserts with multiple secondary indexes, while point-query latency stayed within a small constant of B-trees — the $\varepsilon$-trade-off predicted by theory. Compression, a dividend of large sequential node rewrites, further shrank storage.
2. **B-tree vs. LSM write amplification [11].** On 150 GB and 500 GB datasets with 16–128-byte records, RocksDB's measured WA ($\sim$10–40$\times$) was up to $4\times$ *smaller* than a conventional B-tree's under small-record workloads — but the B-tree won for large records (512 B+) or cache-resident working sets, confirming WA comparisons are workload-dependent and page-granular read-modify-write dominates B-tree WA [11].
3. **Cache-oblivious portability [1][9].** Frigo et al.'s experiments showed recursive (oblivious-style) transpose and multiplication matching or beating hand-tuned cache-aware codes across machines; vEB-laid-out search structures inherit the same portability — no retuning when $B$ changes across L1, L2, TLB, and disk pages.

```python
# Write-amplification micro-model (illustrative)
def write_amplification(page_bytes, record_bytes, splits_per_insert=0.02):
    rmw = page_bytes / record_bytes
    return rmw + splits_per_insert * 2.0

print(write_amplification(16384, 128))  # ~128.04  (B-tree, small records)
print(16384 / (128 * 256))              # ~0.5     (fractal tree, amortized)
```

---

## 6. Limitations

1. **The tall-cache gap.** The dynamic cache-oblivious B-tree's update bound degrades when $B = o(\log N \log \log N)$, possible in L1/L2 caches [2] — oblivious-optimal at the disk/RAM boundary but potentially suboptimal on-chip, where constants matter most.
2. **Idealizations vs. hardware.** The model abstracts prefetching, TLB misses, NUMA, limited associativity, and write-back policies. vEB layouts can interact poorly with sequential-tuned hardware prefetchers, and adversarial patterns can exceed the promised constant factors.
3. **Tail latency of buffered structures.** Amortized bounds hide flush cascades: one injection can trigger $\Theta(\log_B N)$ cascading flushes. Engines deamortize with background flusher threads, adding concurrency complexity and murky worst-case latency.
4. **Read amplification of messages.** Fractal-tree queries must consult buffers along the search path and reconcile upserts/tombstones — CPU and I/O invisible to transfer counting. For read-heavy, cache-resident workloads, B-trees usually win in wall-clock terms.
5. **Concurrency and recovery.** The analyses are single-threaded and failure-free. Production fractal trees add MVCC, write-ahead logging, and checkpointing [7]; LSM compaction adds write stalls and $\sim$2$\times$ space amplification [11] — none captured by cache complexity.
6. **The RUM conjecture is unproven** [12]. No theorem rules out beating all three axes at once, and learned indexes plus hardware compression keep shifting the empirical Pareto frontier.

---

## 7. Conclusion

Cache-oblivious B-trees and fractal tree indexes jointly answer the two hardest questions in external-memory indexing: *how to be optimal without knowing the hardware*, and *how to make writes cheap without sacrificing reads*. The van Emde Boas layout shows one recursive idea — halve the height, lay out contiguously, recurse — attains the $\Theta(\log_B N)$ search lower bound for every block size at once [3][4]. Bender, Demaine, and Farach-Colton [2] prove this need not cost updates, and the packed-memory array has become a general dynamization tool. The $B^\varepsilon$-tree [5][6] and its TokuDB realization [7] expose the read–write trade-off as a tunable continuum, with message injection — search-free upserts, broadcast schema changes — as the systems idea that made the theory deployable.

Write-amplification analysis reframes the B-tree/LSM debate through the RUM conjecture [12]: there is no universally optimal index, only Pareto-optimal points matched to workloads. Open problems: proving or refuting RUM; closing the tall-cache gap on-chip; deamortized, multicore, NUMA-aware fractal trees with worst-case latency guarantees; cache-oblivious learned indexes combining model-based prediction with vEB locality. The ideal-cache model, a quarter-century after [1], remains our sharpest lens — because it lets the algorithm, not the hardware manual, do the talking.

---

title: Verifying Quantum Computational Advantage: Linear Cross-Entropy Benchmarking for Random Circuit Sampling, Porter-Thomas Fidelity, Classical Spoofing, and Superconducting Noise Models
abstract: Quantum computational advantage denotes a regime in which a programmable quantum device performs a task that no known classical algorithm can accomplish in reasonable time. The canonical instantiation is *random circuit sampling* (RCS): repeatedly measuring the output of a pseudo-random circuit on dozens of qubits. Because the ideal distribution is exponentially hard to simulate yet statistically checkable, verification needs a tailored benchmark. This thesis develops *linear cross-entropy benchmarking* (XEB), the fidelity estimator behind the 2019 Sycamore experiment [1]. We derive XEB from the *Porter–Thomas distribution* — the exponential law of output probabilities for chaotic unitary ensembles — and show why $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}} = 2^n \langle P(x_i)\rangle_i - 1$ approximates noisy-device fidelity. We analyze *classical spoofing* via tensor-network contraction, which achieved higher XEB scores than the quantum hardware [2], and survey *noise models* (decoherence, gate and readout errors, crosstalk) of superconducting transmon arrays. We close with results from Sycamore, Zuchongzhi 2.x, and Zuchongzhi-3 [1][3][4], the unproven XQUATH assumption [5], and the limitations keeping advantage claims contested.
body:
# Verifying Quantum Computational Advantage: Linear Cross-Entropy Benchmarking for Random Circuit Sampling, Porter-Thomas Fidelity, Classical Spoofing, and Superconducting Noise Models

## Abstract

## 1. Introduction

In October 2019, Google's quantum AI team announced that their 53-qubit superconducting processor, *Sycamore*, had performed a specific computational task — sampling the output distribution of a random quantum circuit — in approximately 200 seconds, estimating that the equivalent classical simulation would require roughly 10,000 years on the Summit supercomputer [1]. This claim, dubbed *quantum supremacy* by John Preskill in 2012 [6], ignited one of the most consequential debates in modern computer science: not merely whether the experiment was correct, but what it *means* to verify a computation that is, by construction, too hard to check directly.

> **Definition 1.1 (The verification problem).** Given a fixed $n$-qubit circuit $C$ drawn from a random ensemble $\mathcal{E}$ and $N$ bitstring samples $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^N$ produced by an untrusted device $D$, determine whether $D$ samples from the ideal distribution $P_C(x) = |\langle x | C | 0^n \rangle|^2$ with non-negligible fidelity, using only classical resources that scale sub-exponentially in $n$ for the verification step, assuming access to a classical oracle for the values $P_C(x_i)$ at the *sampled* bitstrings.

This thesis is organized around four pillars of the verification problem: (i) the random circuit sampling task and its complexity foundations; (ii) the Porter–Thomas statistical fingerprint of quantum chaos; (iii) the XEB estimator, its fidelity correspondence, and its vulnerability to classical spoofing via tensor-network contraction; and (iv) the physical noise models of superconducting qubit arrays that bound achievable fidelity. We treat each with full mathematical rigor.

---

## 2. Background

### 2.1 Random circuit sampling

The hardness case for RCS rests on the conjecture that no polynomial-time classical algorithm can sample from a distribution multiplicatively close to $P_C$. Bouland, Fefferman, Nirkhe, and Vazirani [9] provided the key complexity-theoretic evidence: assuming the *non-collapse of the polynomial hierarchy*, no efficient classical algorithm can sample from the output distribution of a random circuit to within total variation distance $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$. Aaronson and Arkhipov's earlier BosonSampling proposal [10] established the paradigm; RCS is its universal-gate cousin, and it is arguably harder to spoof because universal circuits have no Gaussian structure to exploit.

### 2.2 The XEB estimator

Let $P_C(x)$ denote the ideal output probability of bitstring $x$. Given samples $\{x_i\}$ from an experimental device, the **linear cross-entropy benchmarking fidelity** is defined [1][8] as

$$\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}} \;=\; 2^n \left\langle P_C(x_i) \right\rangle_{i=1}^N - 1 \;=\; \frac{2^n}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} P_C(x_i) - 1.$$

The calibration points are immediate: if the device samples *perfectly* from $P_C$, then under the Porter–Thomas law (see §4.2), $\mathbb{E}[P_C(x_i)] = \sum_x P_C(x)^2 \approx 2/2^n$, giving $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}} \approx 1$. If the device outputs *uniformly random* bitstrings, $\mathbb{E}[P_C(x_i)] = 1/2^n$ and $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}} \approx 0$ [1][8]. Values between 0 and 1 interpolate linearly with the mixture weight of the ideal distribution in the device's output, which is why XEB functions as a *fidelity proxy*.

> **Theorem (XEB–fidelity correspondence, informal).** *For a noisy device whose error channel is well-approximated by a global depolarizing channel of fidelity $\phi$, the expected XEB score satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}}] = \phi + o(1)$, provided the ideal circuit ensemble forms an approximate 2-design and the circuit is sufficiently deep to thermalize the output distribution to Porter–Thomas form [7][5].*

### 2.3 The device landscape

| Processor | Qubits | Depth / cycles | $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}}$ | Classical estimate | Year |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sycamore (Google) [1] | 53 | 20 | $\approx 2.2\times 10^{-3}$ | $\sim 10^4$ years (Summit) | 2019 |
| Zuchongzhi 2.0 (USTC) [11] | 56 | 20 | $\approx 6.6\times 10^{-4}$ | $\sim 8$ years | 2021 |
| Zuchongzhi 2.1 (USTC) [12] | 60 | 24 | $\approx 3.7\times 10^{-4}$ | $\sim 4.8\times 10^4$ years | 2021 |
| Zuchongzhi-3 (USTC) [4] | 83 | 32 | — | $10^{15}\times$ speedup claim | 2025 |
| Sycamore (67-qubit, Google) [13] | 67 | — | — | $10^9\times$ speedup claim | 2024 |

Each entry used variants of XEB to certify fidelity, and each was subsequently challenged by improved classical simulation.

---

## 3. Methodology

Our methodology is analytical and comparative: we derive the XEB estimator from first principles of random matrix theory, construct the standard noise models for superconducting hardware, analyze the principal classical spoofing algorithms as adversarial benchmarks, and evaluate the empirical record against these models. The work proceeds in four methodological steps:

1. **Circuit ensemble analysis.** We characterize the random circuit families used in supremacy experiments — gate sets, coupler patterns, and the convergence of the output distribution to the Porter–Thomas law — drawing on the supplementary data of [1] and the verification circuits of [11][12].

2. **Estimator derivation.** We derive $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}}$ as the second moment of the output distribution, relate it to the *cross-entropy difference* $H_{\mathrm{lin}} - H$ introduced by Boixo *et al.* [7], and quantify its sampling variance as a function of $N$ and $n$.

3. **Adversarial analysis.** We formalize classical spoofing as an optimization problem: maximize $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}}$ subject to classical runtime constraints. We evaluate tensor-network contraction (the *big-head* method [2]), Schrödinger–Feynman hybrid simulation [14], and shallow-circuit marginal samplers [15], computing their achieved XEB-per-FLOP efficiency.

4. **Noise modeling.** We fit the digital error model of [1] — per-gate depolarizing errors, readout errors, and $T_1/T_2$ decoherence — to published component fidelities, and propagate them to predicted circuit fidelity via the multiplicative formula $\hat{\phi} = \prod_{g}(1-e_g)$ [1].

All numerical claims are cross-checked against the cited primary literature; no new experiments were conducted.

---

## 4. Deep Dive

### 4.1 Random circuit sampling and the Sycamore architecture

The Sycamore processor is a 54-transmon array (one qubit malfunctioning, leaving 53 operational) with nearest-neighbor tunable couplers on a rectangular lattice [1]. Each *cycle* of the supremacy circuit applies:

- a layer of single-qubit gates, each drawn uniformly from $\{\sqrt{X}, \sqrt{Y}, \sqrt{W}\}$, with the constraint that a gate is never repeated on the same qubit in consecutive cycles (to maximize scrambling);
- a layer of two-qubit gates from the set $\{ \mathrm{fSim}(\theta, \phi) \}$ with randomly chosen $\theta, \phi$, applied according to one of eight coupler patterns (A–H), sequenced as ABCDCDAB to guarantee that every qubit interacts with all four neighbors within a few cycles [1].

After $m = 20$ cycles, the qubits are measured in the computational basis. The experiment collected 3 million bitstrings (with 30 million in extended runs), each in 200 seconds of wall-clock time for a million samples [1]. The classical verification required computing $P_C(x_i)$ for a subset of sampled bitstrings using a hybrid Schrödinger–Feynman simulator on Summit — itself a supercomputing feat — feasible only because verification needs amplitudes at *specific* bitstrings rather than the full $2^{53}$-dimensional distribution.

Why random circuits? The choice is deliberate on three grounds:

### 4.2 The Porter–Thomas distribution: fingerprint of quantum chaos

Consider the output state $|\psi\rangle = C|0^n\rangle$ of a random circuit, and the probability $p_x = |\langle x | \psi \rangle|^2$ of a fixed bitstring $x$. If $C$ is drawn from the Haar measure on $U(2^n)$ (or a circuit ensemble forming a 2-design), the vector of amplitudes is uniformly distributed over the unit sphere in $\mathbb{C}^{2^n}$, and the marginal distribution of a single $p_x$ is [7][16]:

$$ \Pr(p)\,dp \;=\; 2^n \, e^{-2^n p}\, dp, \qquad p \geq 0, $$

the **Porter–Thomas distribution**, first identified by Porter and Thomas (1956) in the statistics of neutron resonance widths [16]. Its moments are elementary:

$$\mathbb{E}[p] = 2^{-n}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[p^2] = \frac{2}{2^{2n}}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[p^k] = \frac{k!}{2^{kn}}.$$

These moments are the entire engine of XEB. Observe:

- *Perfect sampling.* Drawing $x_i \sim P_C$ gives $\mathbb{E}[P_C(x_i)] = \sum_x P_C(x)^2 = \mathbb{E}[p^2]\cdot 2^n = 2/2^n$, hence $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}} = 2^n \cdot (2/2^n) - 1 = 1$.
- *Uniform sampling.* Drawing $x_i$ uniformly gives $\mathbb{E}[P_C(x_i)] = 2^{-n} \sum_x P_C(x) = 2^{-n}$, hence $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}} = 0$.
- *Depolarized mixture.* If the device output is $Q = \phi P_C + (1-\phi) 2^{-n}$ (the standard *global depolarizing* ansatz [1]), then $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim Q}[P_C(x)] = \phi \cdot 2/2^n + (1-\phi)/2^n = (1+\phi)/2^n$, and $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}} = \phi$ exactly. This is the fidelity correspondence.

The Porter–Thomas law thus converts a *statistical* question (does the device hit high-probability bitstrings more often than chance?) into a *physical* one (what fraction $\phi$ of runs were error-free?). The exponential shape also explains the speckle-pattern metaphor: a handful of bitstrings carry most of the probability mass, and a faithful device must reproduce that heavy-tailed structure [1][7].

> **Lemma (Variance of the XEB estimator).** *For $N$ independent samples from the depolarized mixture with fidelity $\phi$, the standard deviation of $\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{\mathrm{XEB}}$ scales as $\sigma \approx \sqrt{2(1+\phi^2)}/(2^n \sqrt{N}) \cdot 2^n = O(1/\sqrt{N})$, so that $N \sim 10^6$ samples resolve fidelities at the $10^{-3}$ level [8][1].*

### 4.3 Linear cross-entropy benchmarking: estimator, fidelity, and the XQUATH assumption

Boixo *et al.* [7] originally framed the benchmark in terms of the *cross-entropy difference* between the experimental distribution $\tilde{p}$ and the ideal $p$: a device "succeeds" if $\Delta H = H(\tilde{p}, p) - H(p)$ is small relative to the uniform baseline. The *linear* variant replaces $\log p(x)$ with $p(x)$ itself, yielding an estimator that is unbiased for the depolarizing fidelity and — critically — requires no logarithms of exponentially small probabilities, which would be numerically treacherous [8].

The deeper question is complexity-theoretic: **why should a classical spoofer be unable to achieve $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}} = \Omega(1)$?** Aaronson and Gunn [5] isolated the precise assumption, dubbed **XQUATH** (Linear Cross-Entropy Quantum Threshold Assumption):

> **Assumption (XQUATH).** *No polynomial-time classical algorithm, given a random $n$-qubit circuit $C$, can estimate the output probability $P_C(0^n)$ to within additive error $2^{-n}/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ with success probability appreciably above $1/2$.*

Under XQUATH, Aaronson and Gunn proved that no efficient classical algorithm can spoof XEB with $\Omega(1)$ fidelity using $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ samples [5]. The proof is a reduction: a spoofer achieving high XEB could be converted into an estimator of individual output probabilities violating XQUATH. This is the *formal* backbone of the supremacy claim — but it is an *assumption*, not a theorem, and the spoofing literature of §4.4 is best read as a sustained assault on its practical validity.

### 4.4 Classical spoofing via tensor-network contraction

The most damaging challenges to the Sycamore claim came from *tensor-network* (TN) simulators. A quantum circuit is a tensor network: each gate is a tensor, each wire an index, and the amplitude $\langle x | C | 0^n \rangle$ is the contraction of the network with fixed boundary indices. The contraction cost is exponential in the *treewidth* of the network's line graph, which for a depth-$d$ circuit on a 2D lattice scales roughly as $2^{O(d\sqrt{n})}$ — still exponential, but with a far smaller constant than full state-vector simulation ($2^n$) for the shallow circuits used in supremacy experiments [2][14].

Three milestones define the spoofing arc:

1. **IBM's rebuttal (2019).** Pednault *et al.* [14] argued that a TN-based Schrödinger–Feynman hybrid with secondary-storage checkpointing could simulate the 53-qubit, 20-cycle Sycamore circuit in **2.5 days** on Summit — not 10,000 years — by exploiting the circuit's limited depth. Google disputed the constant factors, but the asymptotic point stood: depth, not width alone, sets the classical cost.

3. **Shallow-circuit and marginal samplers.** For circuits below a depth threshold, classical algorithms can spoof XEB *asymptotically faster* than the quantum device itself. The npj Quantum Information analysis [19] showed simulated annealing achieves an exponential classical advantage for circuits deeper than a threshold $m_{\mathrm{th}}(n) \approx 87$ for $n=53$ — paradoxically, *deeper* circuits can be easier to spoof because the output distribution approaches uniformity and local marginals suffice. Barak *et al.* [15] proved that circuits with small light cones admit efficient classical XEB spoofing, directly constraining the circuit families for which XEB is a sound benchmark.

```python
# Sketch: XEB score of a frugal-sampling spoofer (after Pan & Zhang [2])
import numpy as np

def xeb_score(probabilities, n):
    """Linear XEB fidelity from a list of ideal probabilities P_C(x_i)."""
    return (2**n) * np.mean(probabilities) - 1

# Honest noisy device: mixture of ideal and uniform, fidelity phi = 0.002
phi, n, N = 0.002, 53, 1_000_000
# E[P(x_i)] = (1 + phi) / 2^n  =>  F_XEB = phi
print("honest device F_XEB ~", phi)

# Spoofer: keep top-k bitstrings from a TN batch of 2^21 amplitudes,
# then pad with uniform draws (frugal sampling)
k = 2**14
top_p_mean = 6.0 / 2**n          # heavy tail: top bitstrings ~6x mean prob
uniform_mean = 1.0 / 2**n
mixed = (k * top_p_mean + (N - k) * uniform_mean) / N
print("spoofer F_XEB ~", round(xeb_score([mixed], n), 3))  # ~0.74
```

The lesson is structural: **XEB measures correlation, and correlation is cheaper than simulation.** Any classical algorithm that identifies the heavy tail of the Porter–Thomas distribution — even approximately — can manufacture a high XEB score without ever producing a faithful sample. This is why the verification community now treats XEB as *necessary but not sufficient* evidence of quantum advantage, and why subsequent experiments (Zuchongzhi 2.1, Zuchongzhi-3) pushed to 60–83 qubits and 24–32 cycles [12][4].

### 4.5 Noise models for superconducting qubit arrays

The fidelity a device can achieve is bounded by its *noise model*. Superconducting transmon processors suffer several distinct error channels, and the supremacy experiments modeled them with a *digital error model* [1]:

- **Decoherence.** Energy relaxation ($T_1$) and dephasing ($T_2$) during the $\sim$10–20 ns gate times and the $\sim$µs-scale measurement. Sycamore reported $T_1 \approx 16$ µs median; with $\sim$430 two-qubit gates in the 20-cycle circuit, decoherence alone contributes percent-level infidelity [1].
- **Gate errors.** Single-qubit Pauli errors $e_{1q} \approx 0.15\%$ and two-qubit errors $e_{2q} \approx 0.36\%$ per gate (Sycamore, isolated benchmarking) [1]. Under the digital error model, the predicted circuit fidelity is the product over all components:

$$\hat{\phi} \;=\; \prod_{g \in \mathcal{G}_1}(1 - e_g)\,\prod_{g \in \mathcal{G}_2}(1 - e_g)\,\prod_{q \in \mathcal{Q}}(1 - e_q),$$

where the last factor accounts for readout error $e_q \approx 3$–$4\%$ per qubit [1]. For Sycamore's 20-cycle circuit (1,113 single-qubit gates, 430 two-qubit gates, 53 readouts), this predicts $\hat{\phi} \approx 0.2\%$ — matching the measured $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}} = 0.224\%$ [1]. The agreement between the *a priori* product formula and the measured XEB was presented as evidence that errors are *uncorrelated and depolarizing-like*, the regime where XEB faithfully tracks fidelity [1][7].

---

## 5. Empirical Results and Proofs

### 5.1 The Sycamore measurement

Google's headline result [1]: for the 53-qubit, 20-cycle circuit (pattern ABCDCDAB, seed 0), three million samples yielded $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}} = (2.24 \pm 0.21) \times 10^{-3}$, consistent across ten circuit instances with different random seeds, and consistent with the *elided* and *patch* circuit extrapolations used to verify at classically tractable sizes [1]. The patch-circuit technique — removing a slice of two-qubit gates to split the circuit into two weakly entangled halves — allowed full classical verification at 53 qubits and reduced depth, and the measured fidelities extrapolated smoothly to the full circuit, supporting the claim that the device behaved as modeled [1].

### 5.2 The complexity-theoretic proof sketch

The formal hardness argument proceeds in two stages [9][5]:

1. **Worst-case hardness.** Exactly computing an output probability $P_C(x)$ of a random circuit is #P-hard (by a standard reduction from the permanent / Jones polynomial evaluation). Approximating it to multiplicative error remains #P-hard under plausible conjectures [9].
2. **Average-case reduction.** Bouland *et al.* [9] show that *sampling* from $P_C$ to small total-variation distance would imply the ability to *approximate* typical output probabilities, collapsing the polynomial hierarchy to the third level — considered wildly implausible. Aaronson and Gunn [5] then connect spoofing XEB to this approximation task via XQUATH.

> **Theorem (Aaronson–Gunn [5], simplified).** *Assume XQUATH. Then no $\mathrm{poly}(n)$-time classical algorithm receiving a random circuit $C$ can output $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ samples $\{x_i\}$ with $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}}] = \Omega(1)$ except with negligible probability.*

The theorem is conditional twice over: on XQUATH *and* on the circuit ensemble being sufficiently deep and unstructured that light-cone spoofing [15] does not apply.

### 5.3 The spoofing counter-results

Against this stands the empirical spoofing record, summarized as XEB-per-resource:

| Spoofing method | Circuit | Achieved $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}}$ | Classical cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pan & Zhang big-head TN [2] | Sycamore 53q/20c | **0.739** | 15 h, 60 GPUs |
| Pan, Chen & Zhang sampling [18] | Sycamore 53q/20c | $> 10^{-3}$ (full sampling) | modest cluster |
| IBM TN estimate [14] | Sycamore 53q/20c | full simulation | 2.5 days (Summit, projected) |
| Simulated annealing [19] | deep RCS ($m > m_{\mathrm{th}}$) | asymptotic advantage | sub-exponential |

### 5.4 Noise-model validation

The strongest *positive* evidence for the quantum devices is not XEB per se but the *consilience* of three independent fidelity estimates [1]:

1. **Component product** $\hat{\phi} = \prod(1-e_g)$ from isolated randomized benchmarking;
2. **Measured XEB** $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{XEB}}$ on the full circuit;
3. **Patch/elided extrapolation** from classically verifiable sub-circuits.

In Sycamore these agreed to within statistical error [1], and the same consilience was reported for Zuchongzhi 2.0/2.1 [11][12]. A classical spoofer can fake (2) but has no reason to reproduce (1) and (3) simultaneously — the agreement is evidence that the device's errors are genuinely local and depolarizing-like, the regime where the theory of §4.3 applies.

---

## 6. Limitations

We enumerate the limitations honestly, as befits a benchmark that has been as contested as it has been celebrated.

---

## 7. Conclusion

Linear cross-entropy benchmarking is a remarkable statistical instrument: from a million bitstrings and a supercomputer's worth of amplitude computations, it extracts a single number that — under the Porter–Thomas law and the depolarizing noise model — estimates the many-body fidelity of a 53-qubit quantum processor to within $10^{-4}$ [1][7]. Its theoretical foundations in random matrix theory and complexity theory [9][5] are deep, and the triangulation of component benchmarks, patch-circuit extrapolation, and measured XEB [1][12] constitutes genuine evidence that superconducting processors were sampling from distributions no 2019-era classical machine could reproduce.
