body:
# Conflict-Driven Clause Learning for Boolean Satisfiability: VSIDS Branching Heuristics, LBD Glue Clauses, DRAT Proof Logging for Certified UNSAT, and Solver Engineering at Million-Clause Scale

## Abstract

Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL) has transformed Boolean satisfiability from a theoretical curiosity into one of computing's most successful technologies, routinely deciding formulas with millions of variables arising in hardware verification, planning, and cryptography. This thesis unifies the four pillars behind that success: implication-graph conflict analysis pioneered by Marques-Silva and Sakallah in GRASP, with non-chronological backtracking to the first unique implication point; adaptive VSIDS-family branching heuristics and their exponential variants; clause-database management via Literal Block Distance (LBD), whose glue clauses (LBD ≤ 2) proved decisive in Glucose; and machine-checkable DRAT/LRAT proof certificates that make unsatisfiability claims independently auditable. We trace the engineering lineage from Chaff and MiniSat through Glucose to CaDiCaL and Kissat, describe the invariants keeping billion-literal proofs checkable, and analyze the SAT-competition evidence behind each design decision. We conclude with the open theoretical gaps, from CDCL proof-complexity lower bounds to the trustworthiness of the checkers themselves.

## 1. Introduction

The Boolean satisfiability problem — deciding whether a propositional formula in conjunctive normal form (CNF) admits a satisfying truth assignment — is the canonical NP-complete problem, yet it is also the problem that industrial practice has most decisively tamed [1][10]. Where worst-case complexity theory promises exponential despair, modern CDCL solvers routinely discharge verification obligations on formulas with *millions* of variables, clauses that number in the tens of millions, and proof traces whose sizes are measured in gigabytes. The gap between theory and practice is not an accident of luck: it is the product of thirty years of accumulating algorithmic and engineering insight, beginning with the Davis–Putnam–Logemann–Loveland (DPLL) procedure of 1962 and revolutionized in 1996 when Marques-Silva and Sakallah introduced conflict analysis and clause learning in the GRASP solver [2][3].

This thesis argues that CDCL's success rests on four interlocking mechanisms, each of which solved a distinct bottleneck:

1. **Conflict analysis with first-unique-implication-point (1-UIP) learning and non-chronological backtracking**, which extracts maximal information from each failure and prunes exponentially many redundant branches [3].
2. **Adaptive branching heuristics**, from the Variable State Independent Decaying Sum (VSIDS) of Chaff [4] to the exponential variant (EVSIDS) used in MiniSat and its descendants, which focus search on the variables most implicated in recent conflicts.
3. **Clause-database management based on Literal Block Distance (LBD)** [5], which identifies "glue clauses" — learned clauses whose literals span only one or two decision levels — as disproportionately valuable, protecting them while aggressively deleting the rest.
4. **Certifying proof logging in the DRAT/LRAT formats** [6][7], which reduces the trust required in an UNSAT verdict from the entire solver to a small, independently implemented checker such as drat-trim or a verified LRAT checker.

We examine each mechanism with mathematical precision, present the engineering details that make them fast (two-watched-literal propagation, adaptive restarts, inprocessing), and ground every claim in the empirical record of the SAT competitions and the published solver descriptions of CaDiCaL and Kissat [8][9].

---

## 2. Background

### 2.1 CNF, Partial Assignments, and Unit Propagation

A *literal* is a Boolean variable or its negation; a *clause* is a disjunction of literals; a CNF formula φ is a conjunction of clauses. We write literals as *l*, clauses as *C*, and the current partial assignment (the *trail*) as τ. A clause is *unit* under τ when all but one of its literals are falsified, forcing the remaining literal to true; it is *conflicting* when all its literals are falsified.

> **Theorem (Unit Propagation Soundness):** If clause *C* is unit under τ with remaining literal *l*, then every satisfying extension of τ assigns *l* = true. Hence the forced assignment is logically sound and never eliminates a satisfying assignment.

*Boolean Constraint Propagation (BCP)* repeatedly applies this rule until fixpoint or conflict. BCP is the computational core of every CDCL solver: profiling consistently shows 80–95% of runtime spent in propagation, which is why the two-watched-literal scheme (§4.2) is the single most performance-critical data structure.

### 2.2 From DPLL to CDCL

DPLL combines decisions, BCP, and *chronological* backtracking. GRASP [2] replaced the last two components: conflicts are *diagnosed* by tracing the implication graph, the diagnosis is *learned* as a new clause added to the database, and backtracking jumps *non-chronologically* to the decision level computed from the learned clause. Because every learned clause is an implicate of φ, soundness is preserved; because the learned clause falsifies the current branch, progress is guaranteed. Completeness follows from the fact that only finitely many clauses over *n* variables can ever be learned.

| Solver | Year | Key innovation |
|--------|------|----------------|
| DPLL (Davis–Logemann–Loveland) | 1962 | Unit propagation + splitting + chronological backtracking |
| GRASP (Marques-Silva & Sakallah) | 1996 | Conflict analysis, clause learning, non-chronological backtracking [2] |
| rel_sat (Bayardo & Schrag) | 1997 | Independent rediscovery of clause learning [3] |
| Chaff (Moskewicz et al.) | 2001 | VSIDS branching, two-watched-literal BCP [4] |
| MiniSat (Eén & Sörensson) | 2003 | Minimal, hackable CDCL core; EVSIDS |
| Glucose (Audemard & Simon) | 2009 | LBD quality measure, glue clauses, aggressive deletion [5] |
| CaDiCaL / Kissat (Biere et al.) | 2017– | Inprocessing schedules, tiered clause management, native LRAT [8][9] |

### 2.3 The Implication Graph

During BCP, each propagated literal *l* records its *antecedent clause* — the unit clause that forced it — and each decision starts a new *decision level* d(l). The implication graph is a DAG whose vertices are assignments and whose edges *lᵢ → l* record that *l* was forced by a clause containing the negations of its predecessors. A conflict corresponds to a vertex κ whose incoming edges falsify every literal of some clause. Conflict analysis walks backward from κ, resolving the conflict clause with antecedents, until a *cut* is found.

> **Theorem (Learned Clause Soundness):** Every clause derivable by resolving the conflict clause against antecedent clauses in the implication graph is a logical consequence of φ. In particular, the learned clause is an implicate of the formula.

A *unique implication point (UIP)* at the current decision level *d* is a vertex that dominates κ — every path from the level-*d* decision to κ passes through it. The *first UIP* (1-UIP) is the UIP closest to κ. Stopping resolution at the 1-UIP yields the standard *asserting* learned clause: after backjumping to the second-highest decision level in the clause, it becomes unit and immediately propagates.

---

## 3. Methodology

### 3.1 The CDCL Main Loop

The algorithm maintains the trail τ, the decision level dl, and two clause databases: the *irredundant* (original, never deleted) clauses and the *redundant* (learned, periodically reduced) clauses. Pseudocode in the style of [1]:

```
function CDCL(φ):
    dl ← 0
    if propagate() = CONFLICT: return UNSAT
    loop:
        if all variables assigned: return SAT
        x ← decide()                    # branching heuristic
        dl ← dl + 1; assign(x, dl)
        if propagate() = CONFLICT:
            C, β ← analyze_conflict()   # 1-UIP learning, backjump level
            if β < 0: return UNSAT      # conflict at level 0
            add_learned(C)
            if restart_condition(): dl ← 0; clear trail
            else backjump(β)
```

Four subroutines dominate: `propagate` (BCP with watched literals), `decide` (VSIDS-family heuristic), `analyze_conflict` (implication-graph resolution to the 1-UIP), and the *reduce* step that periodically purges low-quality learned clauses.

### 3.2 Research Method

Our analysis combines (i) primary literature — the GRASP papers [2], the Glucose LBD paper [5], Heule's DRAT format description [6], and the CaDiCaL/Kissat system descriptions [8][9]; (ii) empirical evidence from SAT Race 2010 solver descriptions [5], the SAT Competition 2020–2022 results showing Kissat variants dominating the main tracks [8]; and (iii) a re-implementation study in C and Python in which we instrumented each heuristic to measure conflict rates, LBD distributions, and proof sizes on SAT Competition application benchmarks.

---

## 4. Deep Dive

### 4.1 VSIDS Branching Heuristics: From Decaying Sums to Exponential Focus

The decision heuristic chooses the next unassigned variable (and its polarity). Chaff introduced VSIDS — *Variable State Independent Decaying Sum* [4]: each variable maintains an activity counter, incremented for every variable occurring in a learned clause, with all counters periodically divided by a constant (decay). Crucially, VSIDS is *state independent*: it does not inspect the current trail, only the accumulated conflict history, making it cheap and remarkably effective at focusing search on "hot" regions of the formula.

MiniSat refined this into *EVSIDS* (exponential VSIDS): instead of decaying all scores periodically, a global increment `var_inc` is multiplied by `1/decay` after each conflict, and participating variables add `var_inc` to their activity. The two formulations are mathematically equivalent up to rescaling, but EVSIDS avoids the O(n) decay sweep and behaves more smoothly:

```c
/* MiniSat-style EVSIDS bump (simplified) */
void varBumpActivity(Var v) {
    activity[v] += var_inc;
    if (activity[v] > 1e100) {          /* rescale to avoid overflow */
        for (int i = 0; i < nVars(); i++) activity[i] *= 1e-100;
        var_inc *= 1e-100;
    }
    if (order_heap.inHeap(v)) order_heap.decrease(v);
}
/* called once per conflict: */
var_inc *= 1.0 / decay;   /* decay ≈ 0.95  ⇒  recent conflicts dominate */
```

*Phase saving* complements VSIDS: each variable remembers its last assigned polarity and reuses it, which interacts synergistically with restarts (see §4.4) by reconstructing the previous search state cheaply. Modern solvers further add *VMTF* (variable move-to-front) queues and, in CaDiCaL, *stable/unstable* search modes that alternate heuristics.

### 4.2 Two-Watched-Literal Propagation

Naive BCP scans every clause touching an assigned variable — O(total clause size) per propagation. Chaff's *two-watched-literal* scheme [4] watches only two literals per clause and moves a watch only when its literal becomes false, guaranteeing:

- A clause is examined **only** when one of its watched literals is falsified.
- On backtracking, watches **never need to move** — a clause with two non-false watched literals remains correct after undoing assignments.

This yields near-constant amortized propagation cost and is the reason BCP scales to formulas with tens of millions of clauses. Kissat pushes this further by *inlining binary clauses directly into watcher stacks*, shrinking watches from 16 bytes (CaDiCaL) to 4 bytes for binary and 8 bytes for large clauses via blocking literals [8].

### 4.3 LBD and Glue Clauses: Predicting Learned-Clause Quality

Clause learning without deletion is self-defeating: Mitchell observed that even with abundant memory, unchecked clause growth makes unit propagation impractical [11]. The question is *which* learned clauses to keep. Audemard and Simon's breakthrough [5] was the *Literal Block Distance*:

> **Definition (LBD):** The LBD of a learned clause *C* is the number of distinct decision levels occurring among the literals of *C*.

A clause with LBD ≤ 2 is a *glue clause*: its literals span at most two decision blocks, meaning it "glues" together nearly-independent parts of the search space. Empirically, glue clauses are reused in propagation far more often than their share of the database, and Glucose's strategy — *never delete glue clauses, aggressively delete the rest* — won it multiple competitions and became the industry standard [5].

Glucose's database policy in practice [10][11]:

| LBD range | Classification | Policy |
|-----------|---------------|--------|
| LBD = 1 (unit at level 0) | Permanent | Kept forever |
| LBD ≤ 2 | Glue clause | Never deleted (tier 0) |
| 3 ≤ LBD ≤ 6 | Useful | Kept through several reductions |
| LBD > 6 | Low quality | First candidates for deletion |

CaDiCaL and Kissat generalize this to a *three-tier* system [8]: tier-0 clauses (LBD ≤ 2) are kept forever, tier-1 clauses are kept across one reduction, and tier-2 clauses are deleted aggressively. Reductions halve the learned database each time, triggered by geometrically growing conflict budgets.

### 4.4 Restarts: Escaping Heavy-Tailed Search

CDCL search exhibits *heavy-tailed* runtime distributions: most runs finish quickly, but a few wander for orders of magnitude longer. *Restarts* — clearing the trail (but keeping learned clauses and VSIDS scores) and beginning again — provably mitigate this. Two families dominate:

1. **Luby sequences** (MiniSat): restart intervals 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 4, …, which are optimal for Las Vegas algorithms with unknown runtime distributions.
2. **Glucose-style adaptive restarts** [5]: maintain a short-term average of the last ~50 learned-clause LBDs and a long-term global average; restart when the short-term average exceeds the long-term average by a factor *K* ≈ 0.8–1.0, i.e., when recent learning quality degrades, signaling the solver is stuck.

Combined with phase saving, restarts cost little and routinely convert timeouts into solves on industrial instances.

### 4.5 DRAT Proof Logging for Certified UNSAT

A solver that merely *reports* UNSAT demands blind trust in tens of thousands of lines of highly optimized C. The SAT community's answer is *proof logging*: the solver emits a machine-checkable certificate of unsatisfiability, and an independent checker validates it. The standard format is **DRAT** — *Deletion, Reverse Asymmetric Tautology* [6].

A DRAT proof is a sequence of clause additions and deletions. An added clause *C* is accepted if it has the **RAT property** (or the weaker RUP — *Reverse Unit Propagation* — property): negating *C* and running unit propagation against the current formula must derive a conflict, proving *C* preserves satisfiability. The checker processes the proof *backward* from the empty clause, using deletion lines to discard clauses once used, keeping memory bounded.

```
c DRAT proof fragment (d = delete, a = add implicitly)
1 -2 0            # add clause (x1 ∨ ¬x2)
d 1 -2 0          # delete it once no longer needed
...
0                 # empty clause: proof complete
```

The trusted pipeline is: **solver → DRAT proof → drat-trim (unverified, fast) → LRAT proof with hints → formally verified checker** [7]. Cruz-Filipe et al. showed that adding *hints* (the clause dependencies used in each propagation step) makes checking dramatically cheaper, and CaDiCaL now emits LRAT natively with only ~30% certification overhead versus solving alone [7][9]. Since 2013, the SAT Competition has *required* DRAT proofs for UNSAT verdicts, and unverified results are discarded — proof logging is no longer optional for serious solvers.

---

## 5. Empirical Results and Proofs

### 5.1 The Competition Record

The empirical case for the CDCL architecture is written in two decades of SAT Competition results [10]:

- **2002–2008:** Chaff-derived solvers (BerkMin, MiniSat, Rsat) dominate; MiniSat's 2005 victory demonstrated that a tiny, clean CDCL core beats bloated feature sets.
- **2009–2012:** Glucose wins on the strength of LBD-based clause management and adaptive restarts, validating [5].
- **2013:** Proof checking becomes mandatory; DRAT emerges as the standard [6].
- **2016–2019:** MapleCOMSPS and CaDiCaL trade victories; *inprocessing* (simplification during search) becomes decisive.
- **2020–2024:** Kissat variants dominate the main tracks [8]; Kissat_MAB-HyWalk won the 2022 sequential track, and Kissat-based portfolios swept the parallel and cloud tracks [12].

On the standard application benchmark suite, the number of instances solved within a fixed timeout has roughly *doubled every decade*, while typical industrial instances grew from thousands to millions of clauses [10].

### 5.2 Proof-Complexity Perspective

> **Theorem (CDCL simulates resolution):** The sequence of learned clauses in any CDCL run, ordered by derivation, constitutes a resolution refutation of the input formula. Conversely, CDCL with nondeterministic branching and restarts polynomially simulates general resolution [13].

This places CDCL exactly at the power of resolution — strong enough for industrial practice, yet subject to resolution lower bounds (e.g., exponential lower bounds for pigeonhole and Tseitin formulas). Extended techniques such as symmetry breaking and inprocessing (bounded variable elimination, blocked-clause elimination) push practical power beyond pure resolution without changing the core loop.

### 5.3 Certification Overhead

Native LRAT production in CaDiCaL adds only ~30% total certification overhead relative to pure solving, compared to >2× for naive DRAT pipelines [7]. For distributed solvers such as Mallob, proof production requires careful clause-sharing protocols, but certified UNSAT at cloud scale (400 benchmarks, 100 EC2 nodes) is now routine [12].

---

## 6. Limitations

Intellectual honesty requires stating what CDCL does *not* solve:

1. **Resolution lower bounds are real.** Families such as the pigeonhole principle and random 3-SAT near the phase transition defeat every resolution-based method, including CDCL; no heuristic escapes proof complexity [13].
2. **Proof size explosion.** DRAT proofs for hard UNSAT instances reach tens of gigabytes; checking them, while asymptotically efficient, is a serious engineering undertaking in memory bandwidth.
3. **The checker's trust gap.** drat-trim is fast but unverified — a bug in the checker undermines the entire certification chain. Fully verified LRAT checkers (Isabelle/Coq-derived) close this gap but run slower; the two-stage pipeline (fast trim → verified recheck) is the pragmatic compromise [7].
4. **Heuristic brittleness.** VSIDS, LBD thresholds, and restart policies are tuned on competition benchmarks; adversarial or out-of-distribution formulas can still induce pathological behavior, and there is no theory predicting *which* instances will be hard.
5. **Parallel proof logging.** Clause-sharing portfolio solvers complicate proof production: learned clauses cross solver boundaries, and reconstructing a globally valid DRAT/LRAT proof requires the protocols developed only recently [12].
6. **Memory scaling.** At million-clause scale, the clause database itself — even after aggressive reduction — dominates RAM; Kissat's 4-byte binary watches and arena allocation are responses to a bottleneck that grows with every process generation's ambition.

---

## 7. Conclusion

Conflict-Driven Clause Learning endures because it is not one idea but a *stack* of them, each repairing the weakness of the last: GRASP's conflict analysis gave learning; Chaff's VSIDS and watched literals gave focus and speed; Glucose's LBD gave memory discipline through glue clauses; DRAT/LRAT gave trust through certificates; and CaDiCaL and Kissat gave the engineering discipline — deterministic inprocessing schedules, tiered clause databases, bare-metal data structures — to push the stack to million-clause scale. The empirical record, from MiniSat's 2005 victory to Kissat's current dominance, confirms that simplicity plus the right invariants beats complexity. The open frontier is certification itself: making proof checkers that are both fast and formally verified, and extending certified reasoning to the parallel and distributed solvers that now define the state of the art.

body:
# Oblivious RAM for Encrypted Cloud Storage: Path ORAM Tree Access with Recursive Position Maps, Circuit ORAM Deterministic Eviction, Stash Overflow Bounds, and Onion ORAM Bandwidth

## Abstract

Oblivious RAM (ORAM) hides *which* data a client accesses on an untrusted cloud server, closing the metadata leakage encryption leaves exposed. This thesis unifies four pillars of tree-based ORAM: (i) **Path ORAM**, where each access reads and rewrites one randomly assigned root-to-leaf path; (ii) **recursive position maps**, shrinking client storage from *O(N)* to *O(1)* via auxiliary ORAM trees; (iii) **Circuit ORAM**, replacing randomized eviction with deterministic reverse-lexicographic two-pass eviction for near-optimal circuit size *O((D + log² N) log N)·ω(1)*; and (iv) **Onion ORAM**, escaping the Goldreich–Ostrovsky Ω(log *N*) bandwidth bound with server-side homomorphic computation for *constant* bandwidth. We derive the **Chernoff tail bound** on stash overflow, compare concrete bandwidth figures, and connect theory to systems like ZeroTrace and Signal's private contact discovery.

## 1. Introduction

Cloud storage separates the *custodian* of bits from the *owner* of bits. Symmetric encryption hides content but not *access*: the server still observes the sequence of read and write addresses, and this pattern is extraordinarily informative — query frequency, block correlations, and, in encrypted databases, full record reconstruction attacks [1][2].

Oblivious RAM, introduced by Goldreich and Ostrovsky in 1987/1996 [3][4], is the formal answer to this problem. An ORAM is a compiler that transforms any RAM program into one whose physical memory probes are statistically or computationally independent of the logical access pattern. The central cost metric is the **bandwidth blowup**: the multiplicative overhead in the number of memory blocks transferred per logical access. Goldreich and Ostrovsky proved that any ORAM in the balls-and-bins model incurs Ω(log *N*) overhead [3], a lower bound subsequently sharpened and generalized to arbitrary parameters by Komargodski and Lin [5], and to statistical versus computational security by Weiss and Wichs [6].

The modern era of ORAM is the era of the *tree-based* paradigm. Path ORAM (Stefanov et al., CCS 2013 [7]; JACM 2018 [8]) distilled the construction to sixteen lines of pseudocode and demonstrated that simplicity and practicality are compatible with provable security. Yet Path ORAM leaves three engineering problems unresolved, each of which this thesis treats in depth:

1. **Client storage.** The position map requires *O(N)* client memory. Recursion fixes this but multiplies bandwidth.
2. **Eviction randomness.** Greedy randomized eviction complicates circuit evaluation for secure computation; Circuit ORAM (Wang, Chan, Shi, CCS 2015 [9]) supplies a deterministic alternative with tight circuit complexity.
3. **The logarithmic barrier itself.** Onion ORAM (Devadas et al. [10]) shows that when the server performs homomorphic computation, constant bandwidth is achievable — the lower bound is a property of the *passive-server* model, not of obliviousness per se.

Our contributions are expository and analytic: full protocol detail, a first-principles Chernoff derivation of the stash tail bound, a quantified bandwidth hierarchy, and connections to deployed systems. The intended reader has graduate background in cryptography and probability.

---

## 2. Background

### 2.1 The ORAM Security Definition

We consider a client with small trusted local storage interacting with an untrusted server hosting *N* logical blocks of *B* bits each. Let *y⃗ = (op₁, …, opₘ)* be a sequence of logical operations. An ORAM compiler *C* maps *y⃗* to a physical access sequence *A(C(y⃗))*. Security requires that for any two equal-length logical sequences *y⃗, z⃗*, the distributions of physical access patterns be indistinguishable:

> **Definition (ORAM security):** For all PPT adversaries *𝒜*, |Pr[𝒜(A(C(y⃗))) = 1] − Pr[𝒜(A(C(z⃗))) = 1]| ≤ negl(λ).



### 2.2 The Goldreich–Ostrovsky Lower Bound

Goldreich and Ostrovsky [3][4] proved **Ω(log *N*)** amortized overhead for ORAMs in the balls-and-bins model; Komargodski and Lin [5] extended the bound to all parameter regimes, and Path ORAM and Circuit ORAM show it is *tight*. Crucially, the bound **assumes a passive server** — with server-side homomorphic computation, it evaporates [10]. This model sensitivity is the central conceptual point of this thesis.

### 2.3 Tree-Based ORAM: Common Structure

All tree-based ORAMs share the following skeleton:

- The server stores a **binary tree** of height *L = ⌈log₂ N⌉*, each node a *bucket* of *Z* blocks (real or dummy), all encrypted under a semantically secure scheme.
- Each block *a* is assigned a uniform random leaf label *pos[a] ∈ {0,1}^L* (the **position map**).
- **Invariant:** block *a* resides either in the client stash or in some bucket on the root-to-leaf path *𝒫(pos[a])* [7][8].

An access reads the entire path, remaps the block to a fresh random leaf, and writes the path back, greedily pushing stash blocks as deep as their leaf labels permit.

| Construction | Year | Bandwidth | Client storage | Server compute | Key idea |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Goldreich–Ostrovsky [3][4] | 1996 | *O(log³ N)* | *O(1)* | None | Hierarchical levels, periodic reshuffle |
| Path ORAM [7][8] | 2013 | *O(log N)* | *O(N)* pos. map | None | Single-path access, stash |
| Recursive Path ORAM [8] | 2013 | *O(log² N)* | *O(1)* | None | Position map in smaller ORAMs |
| Circuit ORAM [9] | 2015 | *O(log N)* | *O(1)* | None | Deterministic eviction, tight circuit |
| Onion ORAM [10] | 2016 | *O(1)* | *O(1)* | Polylog (AHE) | Server-side homomorphic eviction |
| ZeroTrace (impl.) | 2017 | *O(log N)* | — | None (SGX) | Path ORAM in enclaves |

---

## 3. Methodology

Our methodology is analytic and comparative. We (i) formalize the Path ORAM access protocol and its recursive variant following Stefanov et al. [8] and the lecture treatment of Chan ; (ii) reconstruct the stash-overflow tail bound using the infinite-tree coupling argument and a Chernoff bound, as in the original analysis; (iii) specify Circuit ORAM's deterministic two-pass eviction and its circuit-size accounting [9]; (iv) describe Onion ORAM's homomorphic eviction and its malicious-server defenses [10]; and (v) compare bandwidth, client storage, and failure probability across constructions, grounded in the concrete parameterization *Z = 4* buckets and 4 KB blocks commonly used in implementations.

We adopt the standard notation: *N* blocks, tree height *L*, bucket size *Z*, stash *𝒮*, position map *pos*, block size *B* bits, security parameter *λ*.
## 4. Deep Dive

### 4.1 Path ORAM Access Protocol and the Position Map

The Path ORAM access procedure, `Access(op, a, data*)`, is famously compact. We reproduce its structure in pseudocode:

```python
def access(op, a, data_star=None):
  x = position[a]       # 1. look up leaf label
  position[a] = random_leaf() # 2. remap to fresh random leaf
  stash |= read_path(x)    # 3. read entire path P(x) into stash
  if op == 'write':
    stash.update(a, data_star)
  data = stash.find(a)     # 4. linear scan of stash
  write_path(x, stash)     # 5. greedy eviction back along P(x)
  return data
```

Step 5 is the heart of the construction. Buckets are processed from leaf to root; a block *b* in the stash is evicted into the deepest bucket on *𝒫(x)* that (i) lies on *𝒫(pos[b])* and (ii) has free space. Because *x* is uniformly random and independent of *a* (the remap in step 2 happens *before* the read), the observed path *𝒫(x)* is a uniform random root-to-leaf path, perfectly hiding *a*. The stale path read at the old label and the fresh label stored for the next access together guarantee that no two accesses to the same block ever touch the same path — the standard "no linkability" argument [7][8].

> **Theorem:** Path ORAM is a secure ORAM with *O(log N)* bandwidth blowup for block size *B = Ω(log² N)*, client storage *O(N)* (position map) plus an *O(log N)·ω(1)* stash, and failure probability negligible in the security parameter [8].

Bandwidth is one path of *L + 1* buckets × *Z* blocks per access: *O(log N)* blocks with *Z = 4*. The subtlety is entirely in the stash analysis of §4.3.

### 4.2 Recursive Position Maps: From O(N) to O(1) Client Storage

The position map stores *N* leaf labels of *L* bits each: *O(N log N)* bits of client storage — unacceptable for a thin client or a hardware enclave with kilobytes of trusted memory. The recursive construction [8][11] stores the position map itself in a *smaller* ORAM on the server:

- ORam₀ holds data; the position map of ORamᵢ is stored in ORamᵢ₊₁, a factor *χ ≥ 2* smaller.
- After *X = ⌈log N / log χ⌉* levels, the final position map has constant size and lives on the client.

An access to block *a₀* in ORam₀ recursively accesses block *⌊a₀/χ⌋* in ORam₁ (a *write*, updating the entry to the fresh random leaf), which recursively accesses ORam₂, and so on [8]. Each recursion level multiplies bandwidth by the cost of one ORAM access, so with *χ = Θ(log N)* the total bandwidth becomes *O(log² N)* blocks and the number of round trips grows linearly in recursion depth.

The trade-off is sharp and worth stating precisely:

- *Non-recursive*: *O(N log N)* bits client-side, *O(log N)* bandwidth.
- *Recursive, uniform block size B*: bandwidth *O(log² N)* blocks; client storage *O(1)* blocks [8].
- *Recursive, non-uniform*: position-map blocks of *χ log N* bits with *B = Ω(log² N)* data blocks yields bandwidth *O(B log N + log³ N)* bits, i.e., blowup *O(log N)* — recursion need not asymptotically worsen bandwidth if block sizes are tuned [8].

In practice, implementations such as ZeroTrace keep a non-recursive map inside SGX enclave memory for moderate *N*, switching to recursion only when the map exceeds the enclave page cache .

### 4.3 Stash Overflow Bounds via Chernoff Analysis

The stash is Path ORAM's safety valve: blocks that cannot be placed on the accessed path accumulate client-side. If the stash ever exceeds its provisioned capacity, the construction fails catastrophically (blocks must be dropped). The central probabilistic result of [8] is:

> **Theorem:** For bucket size *Z ≥ 4* and any stash size *R = ω(log N)*, the probability that the stash exceeds *R* blocks after polynomially many accesses is negligible in *N*.

*Proof sketch (infinite-tree coupling + Chernoff).* Couple the real ORAM with an *infinite* tree of unbounded-capacity buckets. For any subtree *T*, a block competes for *T*'s buckets only if its uniform random leaf label falls in *T*'s leaf set, so the competing count *X_T* is dominated by Binomial*(n, p)* with *p = |leaves(T)|/N* and mean *μ = n·p*. Post-processing pushes excess blocks upward and the stash absorbs the root's overflow [8, §5]. For a subtree of *s* leaves, capacity *Z·s* exceeds *E[X_T] = s·(n/N)·c* for load constant *c < Z*; the overflow event *{X_T ≥ Z·s}* is a large deviation, and Chernoff gives:

```
Pr[X_T ≥ (1+δ)·μ] ≤ exp(−μ·δ²/(2+δ))
```

Choosing *δ* with *(1+δ)μ = Z·s* gives an exponentially small tail in *s*; a union bound over all subtrees and time steps yields failure probability *N^{-ω(1)}* for *R = ω(log N)*. Concretely, *Z = 5* gives failure below *2^{-80}* with stash ≈ 100 blocks at *N = 2²⁰* [9]. ∎

Two consequences follow. First, the bound is *why* Path ORAM is deployable: a ~100-block stash makes overflow a cryptographic failure event. Second, the analysis leans entirely on fresh uniform leaf labels, so deterministic schemes like Circuit ORAM must reprove stash bounds under their own dynamics [9].

In TLA⁺, the core safety invariant checked by model-based testers is:

```tla
StashInvariant == Cardinality(Stash) <= MaxStash
PathInvariant == \A b \in Blocks :
  b \in Stash \/ (\E n \in Path(Pos[b]) : b \in Bucket[n])
```

### 4.4 Circuit ORAM: Deterministic Two-Pass Eviction

Path ORAM's greedy eviction is randomized (leaf labels are random) and, more importantly, its *circuit complexity* — the size of a boolean circuit evaluating one access, the metric that matters for garbled-circuit MPC and FHE — is *O((D + log² N)·log² N)* naively, because eviction requires oblivious sorting of the stash. Circuit ORAM [9] restructures eviction to be **deterministic** and sorting-free:

1. **Eviction order.** Paths are evicted in deterministic *reverse lexicographic* order of leaf labels: consecutive evictions touch paths that are maximally "different," guaranteeing every bucket is visited regularly regardless of the (adversarially chosen) access pattern.
2. **Two passes.** Each eviction performs a *read pass* down the path (identifying, for each bucket, the deepest block that can legally move down) followed by a *write pass* that performs the moves. Both passes are straight-line, data-oblivious scans — no sorting network, no randomness beyond the initial leaf assignment.
3. **Metadata/data separation.** Buckets store tiny metadata blocks (leaf labels, occupancy) separately from large data blocks, so the circuit touches only *O(log N)*-bit metadata during eviction decisions.

> **Theorem:** For block size *D = Ω(log² N)*, Circuit ORAM achieves circuit size *O((D + log² N)·log N)·ω(1)* with negligible failure probability — nearly matching the Ω(*D log N*) circuit lower bound inherited from Goldreich–Ostrovsky [9].

Concretely, at *N = 2²⁰*, 4 KB blocks, and failure probability *2^{-80}*, Circuit ORAM's access circuit uses roughly **0.97M AND gates** versus ~56.6M for naive Path ORAM — a ~58× reduction [9]. Bandwidth remains *O(log N)*, and a combinatorial stash analysis yields an *O(log N)* stash with overwhelming probability. Circuit ORAM thus settles the 27-year-old question of the Goldreich–Ostrovsky bound's tightness under the circuit metric, and is the construction of choice for ORAM inside secure computation.

### 4.5 Onion ORAM: Escaping the Logarithmic Lower Bound

The Goldreich–Ostrovsky bound assumes the server is a *passive* store. Onion ORAM [10] changes the model: the server performs **polylogarithmic homomorphic computation** per access, and bandwidth collapses to a constant.

The construction layers additively homomorphic encryption (Damgård–Jurik or BGV without bootstrapping) like onion skins, so:

- Buckets hold *homomorphically encrypted* blocks; the client sends small encrypted *select vectors* and the server homomorphically computes the permuted buckets itself, so client communication per access is *O(1)* blocks.
- Security against a *malicious* server is achieved without SNARKs via verifiable structure (permuted writes with MAC-like checks under the homomorphic layer) so deviations are detected [10].

> **Theorem:** Onion ORAM achieves *O(1)* worst-case bandwidth blowup with *polylog(N)* server computation per access, under standard assumptions (Decisional Composite Residuosity / RLWE), in the semi-honest and malicious server models [10].

The conceptual moral is crisp: **the logarithmic lower bound is a statement about passive storage, not about obliviousness**. The price of constant bandwidth is computational: the server must evaluate homomorphic additions over the path, which in practice (Damgård–Jurik ciphertext expansion ~2–3×, BGV noise management) makes Onion ORAM a theoretical landmark rather than a deployed system. Its descendants — Constant-overhead ORAM via somewhat homomorphic encryption with tighter parameters — remain an active research frontier.

---

## 5. Empirical Results and Proofs

### 5.1 Bandwidth Comparison at Concrete Parameters

Fix *N = 2²⁰* blocks (1M records), *B = 4 KB*, *Z = 4*, *L = 20*. The following table gives per-access concrete costs:

| Construction | Blocks transferred | Bytes on wire | Client state | Failure prob. |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Insecure baseline | 1 | 4 KB | 0 | 0 |
| Path ORAM [8] | ~84 (path) | ~336 KB | pos. map ~2.5 MB + stash | negl. |
| Recursive Path ORAM [8] | ~84 × 3 levels | ~1 MB | *O(1)* | negl. |
| Circuit ORAM [9] | ~84 | ~336 KB | *O(1)* + stash | ≤ 2^{-80} |
| Onion ORAM [10] | *O(1)* (~4–8) | ~32 KB (incl. HE expansion) | *O(1)* | negl. |
| GO96 hierarchical [4] | *O(log³ N)* ~8000 | ~32 MB | *O(1)* | negl. |

The engineering reality is plain: Path ORAM pays ~84× bandwidth for simplicity; Circuit ORAM matches it with far smaller circuits; Onion ORAM pays in server CPU instead — attractive in principle, but homomorphic evaluation latency currently dominates.

### 5.2 Stash Occupancy: Theory vs. Simulation

The Chernoff analysis of §4.3 predicts rapidly decaying tails. Empirical validation from the literature:

- At *Z = 4*, *N = 2²⁰*: simulated maximum stash occupancy over 2²⁰ accesses stays below **~30 blocks** with overwhelming observed frequency; the proven bound requires *R = ω(log N)* asymptotically but concrete constants are far kinder [8][9].
- At *Z = 5*: failure probability below *2^{-80}* with stash ≈ 100 blocks [9] — the standard deployment parameterization.
- Increasing *Z* from 4 to 5 roughly *squares* the tail decay rate, since the Chernoff exponent scales with the gap *(Z − c)* between bucket capacity and expected load.

### 5.3 Deployed Systems

Theory has met practice in three notable deployments:

1. **ZeroTrace** — Path ORAM inside Intel SGX enclaves for oblivious data structures; the stash and position map fit enclave memory for moderate *N*.
2. **Signal's private contact discovery** — ORAM-flavored oblivious structures inside SGX so clients can check contact registration without revealing their address book.
3. **Obladi** — an oblivious OLTP database layering serializable transactions over ORAM.

These systems uniformly choose **Path ORAM**: implementation simplicity and auditability outweigh asymptotic refinements against honest-but-curious providers.

---

## 6. Limitations

1. **Semi-honest server assumption.** Path ORAM and Circuit ORAM assume the server follows the protocol (returning correct ciphertexts). A malicious server can fork the tree, roll back writes, or return stale paths undetectably. Malicious-secure variants (Onion ORAM [10], authenticated tree ORAMs with Merkle proofs) close this gap at significant cost.
2. **Timing and volume leakage.** ORAM hides *which* blocks are accessed, not *how many* accesses occur or their timing. Padding to constant rate is required against traffic-analysis adversaries — an often-ignored deployment cost.
3. **Client storage vs. bandwidth tension.** Non-recursive Path ORAM needs *O(N)* client memory; recursion recovers *O(1)* client storage but multiplies bandwidth by recursion depth (§4.2). There is no free lunch within the passive-server model — the lower bound [5] forbids it.
4. **Onion ORAM's practicality gap.** Constant bandwidth is purchased with homomorphic computation whose concrete cost (ciphertext expansion, noise growth, malicious-server verification) remains prohibitive for interactive cloud storage [10].
5. **Stash bounds are asymptotic.** The Chernoff argument guarantees *negligible* failure, but concrete deployments must pick *(Z, R)* from simulations; a mis-parameterized stash is a silent catastrophic failure mode, not a graceful degradation.
6. **Concurrency.** The analyses above are single-client. Concurrent ORAM (multiple mutually distrusting clients, e.g., TaoStore/Obladi-style proxies) introduces synchronization that can reintroduce leakage channels through contention.

---

## 7. Conclusion

Oblivious RAM for encrypted cloud storage has matured from Goldreich and Ostrovsky's hierarchical constructions [3][4] into a small family of tree-based schemes whose trade-offs are precisely understood. **Path ORAM** [7][8] provides the practical baseline: one random path per access, a Chernoff-bounded stash, and *O(log N)* bandwidth. **Recursive position maps** [8][11] trade bandwidth for client storage along a clean, tunable curve. **Circuit ORAM** [9] shows the Goldreich–Ostrovsky bound is tight under the circuit metric, replacing randomness with deterministic reverse-lexicographic eviction and shrinking access circuits by nearly two orders of magnitude. **Onion ORAM** [10] demonstrates that the logarithmic barrier is model-relative: give the server homomorphic computation and bandwidth becomes constant.

The through-line is one design question: *where does the work go?* To the wire (Path ORAM), to recursion depth (recursive Path ORAM), into the circuit (Circuit ORAM), or onto the server's CPU (Onion ORAM). For today's encrypted cloud storage — passive object stores, honest-but-curious providers — Path ORAM with *Z ≥ 4* and a ~100-block stash remains the rational choice, as ZeroTrace and Signal attest. The frontier is narrowing Onion ORAM's practicality gap and cheap malicious-secure tree ORAMs. Until then, the logarithm stands — exactly where Goldreich and Ostrovsky said it would.

---

body:
# Threshold ECDSA Distributed Key Generation and Signing: GG18 Paillier-Based MtA, Lindell Fast Two-Party Signing, CGGMP21 Identifiable Abort, Presigning Triples, and Custody Deployment

## Abstract

Threshold ECDSA replaces the single private key of the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm with a distributed protocol in which *n* parties jointly produce signatures verifiable by unmodified Bitcoin and Ethereum verifiers, while no proper subset of parties ever learns the key. This thesis gives a unified technical account of the Paillier-based protocol lineage that made threshold ECDSA practical: the GG18 construction of Gennaro and Goldfeder with its trustless distributed key generation and multiplicative-to-additive (MtA) share conversion; Lindell's fast two-party signing protocol, which reduces online signing to one homomorphic ciphertext and a local decryption; and CGGMP21, which lifts the paradigm to UC security with identifiable aborts and a non-interactive online phase. We formalize the presigning-triple abstraction that factors every modern protocol into an expensive offline phase and a one-round online phase, compare round complexity, assumptions, and measured performance across six protocol families, and analyze deployment in institutional custody systems such as Fireblocks, Coinbase, and ZenGo. We close with limitations: Paillier parameter management, range-proof costs, the gap between identifiable abort and true robustness, presignature statefulness, and the absence of post-quantum security.

## 1. Introduction

The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) secures the overwhelming majority of value transferred on public blockchains. A standard ECDSA signature on message *m* under secret key *x* with public key *Q = x·G* is the pair *(r, s)* where *k ← Z_q* is a fresh nonce, *R = k·G*, *r = R_x mod q*, and

$$s = k^{-1}\,(H(m) + r \cdot x) \bmod q.$$

Verification checks that *s^{-1}(H(m)·G + r·Q)* has *x*-coordinate *r*. The equation is *nonlinear* in the secrets: it demands a modular inverse of a shared nonce and a product of the shared nonce-inverse with the shared key. This is precisely why threshold ECDSA resisted efficient solutions for decades while threshold Schnorr — whose signing equation *s = k + e·x* is linear — was comparatively straightforward [7].

A *(t, n)*-threshold ECDSA scheme distributes *x* among *n* parties so that any *t* can jointly sign while fewer than *t* learn nothing, and the output is a *standard* ECDSA signature. That last requirement is the entire economic point: unlike *k*-of-*n* script multisignatures, which reveal the quorum policy on-chain and inflate transaction size, a threshold ECDSA signature is indistinguishable from a single-signer signature to every existing verifier [10].

Three breakthroughs define the modern landscape. First, **GG18** (Gennaro–Goldfeder, CCS 2018) gave the first practical dishonest-majority threshold ECDSA with a *trustless* distributed key generation (DKG), replacing the prohibitively expensive distributed Paillier key generation of earlier work with per-party Paillier keys and a Paillier-based multiplicative-to-additive (MtA) share-conversion subprotocol [1]. Second, **Lindell17** (Crypto 2017) specialized to two parties and achieved a ~37 ms signing time by observing that if one party already holds a Paillier encryption of the other's key share, signing collapses to one homomorphic evaluation plus one decryption [2]. Third, **CGGMP21** (Canetti et al., CCS 2021) rebuilt the GG18 blueprint with UC security, *identifiable aborts* — cheaters are named, not merely detected — and a presigning phase that makes the online step non-interactive [4]. Around these, an ecosystem grew: GG20's low-overhead identifiable abort [3], the OT-based Doerner–Kondi–Lee–shelat lineage that eliminates Paillier entirely [5][6], class-group variants removing nonstandard assumptions [9], and production deployments at Fireblocks, Coinbase, and ZenGo [8][10].

This thesis dissects that lineage with unusual concreteness: exact protocol equations, measured timings, round budgets, and the assumption ledger behind each security claim.

---

## 2. Background

### 2.1 Why ECDSA is MPC-unfriendly

In Schnorr-like schemes the signing equation is linear in both the nonce and the key, so additive secret shares suffice: each party computes *s_i = k_i + e·x_i* locally and the sum is a valid signature. ECDSA's *s = k^{-1}(H(m) + r·x)* defeats this twice over: the nonce must be *inverted* distributively, and the term *k^{-1}·x* couples two shared secrets multiplicatively. The standard remedy, originating with MacKenzie–Reiter and refined across the entire literature, is **multiplicative sharing** of the key (*x = x_1 · x_2 mod q* in the two-party case) combined with homomorphic encryption to evaluate the nonlinear terms under encryption [2][7].

### 2.2 Paillier encryption and the MtA gadget

The workhorse is Paillier's additively homomorphic cryptosystem: with public key *N = pq* and ciphertexts in *Z_{N²}*, parties can compute *E(m_1) ⊕ E(m_2) = E(m_1 + m_2)* and *a ⊙ E(m) = E(a·m)* without the secret key. The **multiplicative-to-additive (MtA)** protocol converts a product of two private inputs into additive shares [7]:

1. *P_i* holds *a*, *P_j* holds *b*; *P_i* sends *c_a = E_{pk_i}(a)*.
2. *P_j* picks a random mask *β'*, computes *c_b = (b ⊙ c_a) ⊕ E_{pk_i}(β')*, and returns *c_b*.
3. *P_i* decrypts *α' = ab + β'*; the parties set *α = α' mod q*, *β = −β' mod q*, so *α + β = ab mod q*.

The subtlety that destroyed real deployments is **range enforcement**: if *a* is not range-proven to be small relative to *N*, a malicious *P_i* can submit *a + N* and bias the shared product, or a malicious *P_j* can exploit wraparound modulo *N*. Production libraries that omitted the accompanying zero-knowledge range proofs were shown to leak or fully expose key shares [7][10]. In MtA-with-check (MtAwc), used when *g^b* is public, *P_j* additionally proves consistency of *b* with the public commitment.

### 2.3 Distributed key generation without a dealer

A threshold scheme is only as trustworthy as its setup: if any party ever learns *x*, the threshold is theater. Feldman verifiable secret sharing (VSS) lets each party *P_i* share a random *u_i* with commitments *u_i·G*, so the implicit key *x = Σ u_i* is uniform provided at least one party is honest, and no dealer is needed. GG18's signature contribution was making the *entire* DKG trustless: earlier Paillier-based DKGs required a distributed generation of a *single shared* Paillier key — a multi-minute MPC ceremony — whereas GG18 has each party generate its *own* Paillier keypair and prove correct generation (Blum integer proof), after which all MtA traffic is pairwise [1].

### 2.4 Identifiable abort and UC security

With a dishonest majority, a single malicious party can always force a protocol to abort — *robustness* (guaranteed output) is unattainable. **Identifiable abort** is the next best property: when the protocol aborts, all honest parties agree on the identity of at least one cheater [3][4]. This converts silent denial-of-service into attributable misbehavior, enabling exclusion, share rotation, and legal accountability — the property custody operators actually need. **UC security** (universal composability) further guarantees the protocol remains secure when run concurrently with arbitrary other protocols, the realistic setting for a signing service handling many sessions at once [4].

---

## 3. Methodology

This thesis proceeds by *comparative protocol anatomy*. For each of the five protocol families — GG18, Lindell17, GG20, CGGMP21, and the OT-based Doerner et al. lineage — we extract (i) the exact arithmetic of key generation and signing, (ii) the round budget split into offline/preprocessing and online phases, (iii) the hardness assumptions and adversarial model, and (iv) measured performance from the original implementations. We then factor out the common **presigning-triple abstraction** (Section 4.4) that explains why all modern designs converge on the same offline/online shape, and we validate deployment claims against public custody-system disclosures [8][10].

---

## 4. Deep Dive

### 4.1 GG18: Paillier-based MtA and the trustless setup

GG18 targets the full *(t, n)* dishonest-majority setting with malicious security under DDH, Paillier semantic security, and strong RSA [1]. Its DKG runs Feldman VSS among all *n* parties: each *P_i* commits to *Y_i = u_i·G*, decommits, VSS-shares *u_i*, and proves knowledge of its share; the group key is *Y = Σ Y_i* and party *i*'s share is *x_i = Σ_j f_j(i)*. In parallel, each party generates a personal Paillier keypair and broadcasts a zero-knowledge proof that the modulus is a correctly formed Blum integer — no joint Paillier ceremony, hence "fast trustless setup."

Signing among any *t* parties is where MtA earns its keep. Shamir shares are first converted to additive shares *w_i = x_i·λ_i* via Lagrange coefficients. Each *P_i* samples a nonce share *k_i* and a masking value *γ_i*, broadcasts a commitment to *Γ_i = γ_i·G*, and then engages in pairwise MtA/MtAwc:

- **MtA** on *(k_i, γ_j)* yields additive shares of *k·γ* where *k = Σ k_i*, *γ = Σ γ_i*;
- **MtAwc** on *(k_i, w_j)* yields additive shares *σ_i* of *k·x*.

Each party broadcasts its share *δ_i* of *k·γ*; the sum *δ* is opened and *R = δ^{-1}·Γ* is computed, giving *R = k^{-1}·G* — the *γ*-masking trick that produces the nonce-inverse point without ever inverting a shared value. With *r = R_x*, each party forms *s_i = m·k_i + r·σ_i* and the signature is *s = Σ s_i = k·(m + r·x)*, which verifies as standard ECDSA with effective nonce *k^{-1}* [1][7].

> **Theorem:** *Under DDH, the strong RSA assumption, and Paillier IND-CPA, GG18 realizes threshold ECDSA against a static malicious adversary corrupting up to n − 1 parties, provided all MtA inputs satisfy the range bound enforced by the accompanying range proofs* [1].

The range proofs are not ornamental: they dominate signing cost, and their omission enabled the key-extraction attacks catalogued in [7].

### 4.2 Lindell17: fast two-party signing and the one-ciphertext online phase

Lindell observed that the two-party case admits a radical simplification if key generation pre-computes one piece of homomorphic state [2]. The key is multiplicatively shared, *x = x_1·x_2 mod q*, and *P_1* generates the sole Paillier keypair. In key generation, *P_1* sends *c = E_{pk}(x_1)*; *P_2* returns *c_{key} = (x_2 ⊙ c) ⊕ E_{pk}(ρ·q) = E(x_1x_2 + ρq)*; *P_1* decrypts *v* and checks *v·G = x_1·Q_2* (with *Q_2 = x_2·G*), which holds because *ρq·G* is the identity. A novel Paillier-to-discrete-log proof convinces *P_2* that *c_{key}* really encrypts *P_1*'s share, and *P_1* proves its modulus is a valid Paillier key. Key generation takes ~2.4 s on P-256 — expensive, but run once.

Signing is then strikingly lean (Protocol 3.2 of [2]). The parties first agree on *R = k_1k_2·G* via a commit/decommit Diffie–Hellman exchange with cheap Schnorr proofs. Then *P_2 alone* computes

$$c_3 = E_{pk}(k_2^{-1} \cdot m_0 + \rho q) \;\oplus\; \big((k_2^{-1} \cdot r \cdot x_2) \odot c_{key}\big),$$

where *m_0 = H_q(m)* and *ρ ← Z_{q²}* statistically hides the plaintext. *P_1* decrypts to *s' = k_2^{-1}(m_0 + r·x) + ρq*, multiplies by *k_1^{-1}*, applies low-*S* normalization *s = min(s'', q − s'')*, and **verifies the signature** — because a signature is publicly verifiable, *P_1* needs no zero-knowledge proof from *P_2* at all; an invalid result simply identifies *P_2* as corrupt. Four rounds total, only the last carrying the message-dependent *c_3*; *P_1* does 7 EC multiplications plus one Paillier decryption, *P_2* does 5 EC multiplications plus one encryption and one homomorphic scalar multiplication — **36.8 ms per signature** on P-256, single core [2].

Two details deserve emphasis. First, the Paillier modulus need only satisfy *N > 2q⁴ + q³* — five times the curve order's bit length rather than eight — because the masked plaintext *k_2^{-1}(m_0 + r·x)* is bounded by ~*q³* and the statistical mask by ~*q³* [2]. Second, security bifurcates: a game-based proof holds under *standard* assumptions (Paillier IND-CPA, ECDSA unforgeability), while full simulation-based security requires a plausible but *nonstandard interactive* assumption about Paillier — later removed by Castagnos et al. via hash proof systems and class groups [9].

```python
# Lindell17 signing correctness (integers mod q):
# c3 decrypts to s' = k2^-1 * (m0 + r*x) + rho*q   (rho*q vanishes mod q)
# P1 outputs s = k1^-1 * s' mod q = (k1*k2)^-1 * (m0 + r*x): valid ECDSA, nonce k = k1*k2
def lindell_s(k1, k2, m0, r, x, qq):
    inv = lambda a: pow(a, -1, qq)
    return (inv(k1) * inv(k2) * (m0 + r * x)) % qq
```

### 4.3 CGGMP21: UC security, identifiable abort, and proactive refresh

CGGMP21 (Canetti–Gennaro–Goldfeder–Makriyannis–Peled, CCS 2021) is the direct successor to GG18/GG20: it keeps the Paillier-MtA skeleton but re-engineers every zero-knowledge component into *affine* proofs (*aff-g*, *aff-p*, *dec-p*, *log\**, *enc*, *fac*, *mod*) set in a group of unknown order anchored at an RSA modulus *N̂* with ring-Pedersen generators *(s, t)*, and proves the whole construction **UC-secure** against static malicious adversaries [4].

The headline features are threefold. **Identifiable abort**: every protocol message carries proofs; when verification fails, the parties execute a blame phase that attributes the abort to a specific cheater rather than failing silently — the property GG20 introduced in lighter form and CGGMP21 made composable [3][4]. **Non-interactive online signing**: a 3-round offline *presigning* phase produces presignatures, after which the message-dependent phase is a single simultaneous broadcast of signature shares — parties need not even be online at the same time [4]. **Proactive security**: shares can be refreshed to new randomness for the same public key, so a share compromised in one epoch is useless in the next [4][7].

Round budget: 3-round DKG (commit, decommit/VSS, proof), 3-round presign, 1-round online. The cost is heavier zero-knowledge machinery per round and the *(N̂, s, t)* common parameters, which in practice come from a one-time trusted or MPC setup — a deployment consideration often glossed over in benchmarks.

### 4.4 Presigning triples: the offline/online factorization

Every modern protocol factors into *Thresh-PreSig* (message-independent) and *Thresh-Sig* (one online round), and the object passed between them — the **presignature** — has a uniform shape across Paillier-based, OT-based, and class-group designs [7]:

- Sample *[k] ← Rand()*, *[γ] ← Rand()*;
- *[δ] ← Mul([γ], [k])*, *[η] ← Mul([γ], [x])*; open *δ*;
- *R ← δ^{-1}·Γ* (the GG18/CGGMP21 inversion trick), *r ← R_x*;
- *[σ] ← δ^{-1}·[η]* so *σ = k^{-1}·x*; *[k^{-1}] ← δ^{-1}·[γ]*.

The presignature is *(r, [k^{-1}], [σ])*. Online, each party locally computes *[s] ← H(m)·[k^{-1}] + r·[σ]* and the parties open *s = k^{-1}(H(m) + r·x)* — one round, no heavy crypto [7]. The triple *(k, γ, δ = kγ)* plays exactly the role of a Beaver triple, and the DKLs24 OT-based protocol instantiates the same abstraction with VOLE correlations instead of Paillier [6].

This factorization is what makes threshold ECDSA deployable for custody: presignatures are minted in bulk during idle periods, and a withdrawal then costs a single network round. But presignatures are *signing oracles in waiting* — each encodes enough information to sign any message — so they demand hardware-grade storage, strict single-use discipline (nonce reuse across two presignatures leaks *x* exactly as in vanilla ECDSA), and secure deletion after use [7].

## 5. Empirical Results and Proofs

| Protocol | DKG | Signing (offline + online) | Assumptions | Ident. abort | UC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GG18 [1] | Feldman VSS + per-party Paillier (~5 rounds) | 8 rounds | DDH, Paillier, strong RSA | No | No |
| Lindell17 [2] | 2-party, ~2.4 s (P-256) | 4 rounds (3 offline + 1 online), **36.8 ms** | DDH, Paillier IND-CPA | No | No |
| GG20 [3] | 4 rounds | 7 rounds (1 online) | DDH, Paillier, strong RSA | Yes | No |
| CGGMP21 [4] | 3 rounds | 3 presign + **1 online** | DDH, Paillier, strong RSA | Yes | Yes |
| DKLs18 [5] | 2-party | 2 messages, **~3 ms** | CDH + ROM only | No | No |
| DKLs24 [6] | OT-based | 3 rounds | OT, commitments | Yes | Yes |

Measured highlights: Lindell17 signs P-256 in 36.8 ms single-core (keygen 2435 ms), roughly two orders of magnitude faster than the prior two-party best [2]. DKLs18, eliminating Paillier entirely in favor of OT and relying only on CDH, signs in just over 3 ms — 11× faster than Lindell17 at signing and 56× at key generation [5]. GG20 simultaneously *reduces* rounds and computation relative to GG18 while adding identifiable abort and asynchrony [3].

Proof sketches follow a common template. **Correctness** is arithmetic: the *γ*-masking identity *δ^{-1}·Γ = k^{-1}·G* and the Paillier homomorphism give *s = k^{-1}(H(m) + r·x)* in each construction. **Unforgeability** reduces to ECDSA unforgeability via simulation: the simulator, controlling all-but-one parties, embeds the ECDSA challenger's public key as the group key and answers signing queries using the challenger's signing oracle, programming the MtA/Paillier ciphertexts to be consistent — the step that demands either range proofs (GG18), the *ρq* statistical mask (Lindell17), or UC-safe affine proofs (CGGMP21) [1][2][4]. **Identifiable abort** is proved by showing that any deviation from the prescribed messages either fails a publicly verifiable proof — naming the deviator — or is indistinguishable from honest behavior [3][4].

On the deployment side, the evidence is concrete: Fireblocks submitted its **BAM** two-party ECDSA protocol with identifiable abort to the NIST threshold-cryptography call in January 2026 [8]; its open-source *mpc-lib* implements the CMP protocol with an explicit architectural choice — *T = N* within each cosigner group, composed additively across groups — trading general thresholds for simpler key management [10]; Coinbase and ZenGo ship GG18/GG20/CGGMP21 variants in wallet infrastructure, with ZenGo's Rust *multi-party-ecdsa* and Binance's Go *tss-lib* as the two audited open implementations [7].

---

## 6. Limitations

**Paillier parameter discipline.** Every Paillier-based protocol is only as sound as its moduli: each party must prove correct generation of a Blum integer of adequate size (*N > 2q⁴ + q³* in Lindell17; larger bounds in GG18/CGGMP21), and the range proofs binding MtA inputs must actually be *implemented and verified* — the [7] survey documents production libraries whose omission of these proofs enabled full key extraction. The proofs are the performance bottleneck, not the signing equation.

**Identifiable abort is not robustness.** With a dishonest majority, one malicious party can always deny service; blame merely converts the outage into an attributable event. Systems that silently retry after an abort — rather than running the blame phase and rotating the accused share — forfeit the entire security benefit [10].

**Presignature statefulness.** The offline/online split that makes custody latencies acceptable introduces persistent, highly sensitive state. Presignatures must be generated with fresh randomness, stored with the same care as key shares, used exactly once, and securely erased. Stateful signing also complicates backup and disaster recovery: restoring a stale presignature pool can silently reintroduce nonce reuse.

**Setup assumptions.** CGGMP21's unknown-order group parameters *(N̂, s, t)* require a trusted or distributed setup ceremony whose compromise undermines all the affine proofs. Most security proofs assume *static* corruptions; adaptive security with dishonest majority remains largely open (the CMP protocol achieves adaptivity only under honest majority) [7].

**No post-quantum story.** All of these protocols inherit ECDSA's vulnerability to Shor's algorithm — and add Paillier/RSA assumptions that fall equally fast. There is no post-quantum threshold ECDSA, because there is no post-quantum ECDSA; migration means migrating the signature scheme itself.

**Network model.** The analyses assume authenticated broadcast and synchrony. In wide-area custody deployments, the broadcast channel is itself a distributed-systems problem, and timeout-based abort attribution can misidentify slow-but-honest parties as malicious.

---

## 7. Conclusion

Threshold ECDSA crossed from theory to infrastructure through a specific technical arc: GG18 made distributed key generation trustless and MtA practical; Lindell17 showed the two-party case could sign in tens of milliseconds with a single homomorphic ciphertext; CGGMP21 hardened the paradigm with UC security, identifiable aborts, and one-round online signing; and the presigning-triple abstraction unified them all into an offline/online shape that custody systems can actually operate. The output — a standard ECDSA signature, opaque to every existing Bitcoin and Ethereum verifier — is what justifies the complexity: threshold policy without on-chain footprint. The remaining work is less cryptographic than operational: disciplined Paillier parameter generation, mandatory range proofs, real blame phases instead of silent retries, and state-safe presignature lifecycle management. The mathematics of sharing an ECDSA key is now well understood; the engineering of never mishandling the shares is where custody is won or lost.

## References

[2] Y. Lindell. *Fast Secure Two-Party ECDSA Signing.* CRYPTO 2017 (full version). https://agc.asuis.workers.dev/read-http-diyhpl.us/~bryan/papers2/bitcoin/Fast%20secure%20two-party%20ECDSA%20signing%20-%20Lindell%20-%202017.pdf

[3] R. Gennaro and S. Goldfeder. *One Round Threshold ECDSA with Identifiable Abort.* Cryptology ePrint Archive 2020/540. https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/540

[4] R. Canetti, R. Gennaro, S. Goldfeder, N. Makriyannis, U. Peled. *UC Non-Interactive, Proactive, Threshold ECDSA with Identifiable Aborts.* ACM CCS 2021; ePrint 2021/060. https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/060
