body:
# Measure-Theoretic Foundations and Inference Engines of Probabilistic Programming Languages: From Quasi-Borel Semantics to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Amortized Variational Inference

## Abstract

Probabilistic programming languages unify Bayesian modeling and general-purpose computation by treating program executions as *random variables* and denotations as *probability measures*. This thesis spans (i) the measure-theoretic and categorical semantics of higher-order probabilistic programs, (ii) the inference engines that exploit program structure, and (iii) compilation techniques that amortize inference. We start from Aumann's obstacle — the failure of cartesian closure in measurable spaces — and show how *quasi-Borel spaces* [1] and *quasi-Borel predomains* [2] furnish a commutative probability monad over a cartesian closed category, yielding adequate semantics for higher-order languages with soft conditioning. We contrast universal *trace-based* languages (Church [3], Anglican [4]) supporting arbitrary stochastic recursion against *differentiable* languages (Stan [7]) that trade universality for gradients. We treat Hamiltonian Monte Carlo [5] and the No-U-Turn sampler [6] geometrically, derive stochastic variational inference [10] as natural-gradient ELBO optimization, show how Pyro [9] embeds guides in effect-handler transformations, and analyze *inference compilation* [11] as amortized trace-space importance sampling with a precise correctness characterization.

## 1 Introduction

A probabilistic program is a program that denotes a probability distribution. The slogan is crisp; its realization is not. A language designer must answer three interlocking questions: *what does a program mean?* (semantics), *how do we compute with that meaning?* (inference), and *how do we make inference fast enough to matter?* (compilation and amortization). Each question exposes a deep fault line.

The semantic question collides with a classical negative result: the category **Meas** of measurable spaces and measurable maps is *not* cartesian closed [1][3], so higher-order programs — functions that accept or return random functions — admit no naive denotation as measurable maps. The inference question collides with geometry: posteriors over hundreds of dimensions concentrate on thin, curved manifolds (typical sets), defeating random-walk Metropolis–Hastings whose proposal variance must scale as *O*(1/*d*). The engineering question collides with universality: a Turing-complete language admits programs with unbounded, data-dependent randomness, for which no single inference algorithm is both correct and efficient.

This thesis is organized around the three traditions that advanced each frontier: **semantics** via quasi-Borel spaces [1] and predomains [2]; **gradient-based inference** via Stan [7] with HMC [5] and NUTS [6]; and **universal inference** via Church [3], Anglican [4], Pyro [9], and inference compilation [11]. We derive trace-based MCMC, geometric HMC, and variational objectives from a single measure-theoretic foundation, and characterize when inference compilation preserves posterior correctness.

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Probability as a computational monad

Following Moggi's computational metalanguage, a probabilistic program of type *A* denotes a *computation* producing values in *A*. The Giry monad *P* maps a measurable space *X* to the space *P(X)* of probability measures on *X*; `return` is the Dirac measure and bind integrates a kernel [12]. The Giry monad is commutative — marginalization order is irrelevant — which semantically justifies the *commutativity* program equivalence that lets inference reorder independent samples [2].

The Giry construction breaks at higher order: there is no measurable structure on the function space *Y^X* making evaluation measurable in general [3]. The **quasi-Borel space (QBS)** model [1] resolves this by shifting the primitive from measurable *subsets* to admissible *random elements*: a QBS is a set *X* with a designated family *M_X ⊆ X^ℝ* of functions ℝ → *X* closed under precomposition with measurable maps and under countable gluing. The probability monad then takes the elegant form *P(X) = {[α, μ]}* where *α: ℝ → X* is a random element and *μ* a probability measure on ℝ, quotiented by change-of-variables equivalence [1]. The category **Qbs** is cartesian closed, and *P* is a commutative monad on it — the first model of higher-order probability with both properties.

### 2.2 Recursion, soft conditioning, and predomains

Real PPLs need *recursion* (stochastic memoizers, unbounded loops) and *soft constraints* (`observe` with densities, or `factor` scoring arbitrary log-weights). **Quasi-Borel predomains** [2] — chain-complete partial orders with compatible QBS structure — model both, yielding adequacy for recursive types and commutativity of the probabilistic powerdomain. Soft conditioning is handled by Staton's *s-finite* kernel semantics [12]: `observe d v` multiplies the trace weight by the density of *d* at *v*, allowing conditioning on measure-zero events that naive disintegration cannot express.

### 2.3 The two language families

| Feature | Universal trace-based (Church [3], Anglican [4], WebPPL) | Differentiable (Stan [7]) |
|---|---|---|
| Program class | Turing-complete; stochastic recursion, higher-order | Fixed-dimension continuous models; constrained types |
| Randomness model | Execution *traces*: sequences of addressed `sample` calls | Joint log-density ∇-differentiable over ℝⁿ |
| Conditioning | `observe` at arbitrary program points; soft factors | Observed data as inputs; log-density evaluation |
| Default inference | Trace-space MCMC, SMC, particle MCMC | NUTS [6] (HMC), ADVI [8] |
| Gradient access | None (black-box) | Reverse-mode AD through log-density |
| Memoization | Stochastic memoizer `mem` for nonparametrics [3] | Not supported |

This dichotomy — *universal but gradient-free* versus *differentiable but restricted* — organizes everything that follows. Pyro [9] and inference compilation [11] are attempts to dissolve it.

---

## 3 Methodology

Our method is *semantic derivation*: we fix the trace/measure semantics first, then derive each inference algorithm as a concrete Monte Carlo method on the semantic domain, and finally analyze its correctness and complexity. Concretely:

1. **Semantic core (§4.1).** Formalize traces and the QBS probability-monad semantics of `sample`/`observe`, fixing the target distribution each algorithm must approximate.
2. **Geometric inference (§4.2).** Derive HMC from symplectic geometry on the cotangent bundle, with NUTS [6] adaptively selecting trajectory length by recursive doubling.
3. **Variational inference (§4.3).** Derive SVI [10] as stochastic natural-gradient ascent on the ELBO, and show how Pyro [9] implements guides as effect-handler transformations.
4. **Amortized compilation (§4.4).** Formalize inference compilation [11] as learning a trace-space proposal *q_φ(x | y)* from prior traces, and characterize its correctness.

We validate each derivation against the primary literature [1]–[12] and the documented behavior of the Stan [7], Pyro [9], and Anglican [4] implementations.

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Trace semantics: evaluation histories as the fundamental object

The operational heart of universal PPLs is the **trace**. In Church [3], program evaluation is sampling: each random choice (`flip`, `gaussian`, ...) extends an *evaluation history*. A trace *t* is a finite map from *addresses* (syntactic call sites, distinguished by their dynamic call stack) to sampled values, plus a weight *w(t)* accumulating the product of prior densities and likelihood factors from `observe` statements.

> **Theorem (Trace correctness, Wingate–Stuhlmüller–Goodman 2011).** For a Church program with finitely many addresses per execution, the distribution over return values induced by prior-weighted traces, conditioned on all observations, equals the denotational semantics in the s-finite kernel model [12].

*Proof sketch.* By induction on evaluation derivations: `sample d` extends the trace with a draw from *d* (kernel composition); `observe d v` multiplies the weight by the density *d(v)* (score). The normalization constant is the model's marginal likelihood. ∎

**Single-site Metropolis–Hastings on traces** is the canonical universal inference algorithm. A proposal selects one address uniformly, resamples its value from the prior (or a local kernel), and *re-executes* the program deterministically from that point: downstream addresses whose control flow is unchanged are *reused* (their values persist), while addresses that vanish or appear are added or removed with the appropriate dimension-changing Jacobian-free acceptance ratio:

```
α = min(1,  (w(t') · q(t|t')) / (w(t) · q(t'|t)) )
```

where *q* includes the address-selection and resampling probabilities. Because only the *suffix* of the trace is re-executed, proposals are cheap in practice — the key engineering insight of the "lightweight" MH implementations [3].

**Coroutines and continuations in Anglican.** Anglican [4] compiles its Clojure-like language via continuation-passing style so execution can be *suspended and resumed* at `sample`/`observe` checkpoints, yielding particle filters (SMC), particle MCMC (PMMH, particle Gibbs), and trace MH for free. The CPS/coroutine design makes inference *generic*: the algorithm never sees the model program, only the stream of checkpoints — a precursor to Pyro's effect handlers [9].

The **stochastic memoizer** `mem` [3] deserves special mention: `(mem f)` returns a *stochastically memoized* function that draws its return value once per distinct argument and reuses it — semantically, an infinite random table. This single construct expresses Dirichlet processes, Chinese restaurant processes, and infinite mixture models in a few lines, demonstrating that *universality plus memoization subsumes nonparametrics*.

### 4.2 Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and the No-U-Turn sampler in Stan

When the log-density is differentiable, geometry beats randomness. **Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)** augments the *d*-dimensional position *θ* with momentum *ρ ∼ N(0, M)* and defines the Hamiltonian

```
H(θ, ρ) = -log π(θ) + ½ ρᵀM⁻¹ρ = U(θ) + K(ρ)
```

Hamilton's equations *θ̇ = M⁻¹ρ*, *ρ̇ = ∇log π(θ)* generate a flow that (a) preserves volume (Liouville), (b) is reversible, and (c) conserves energy — so proposals along the flow are accepted with probability ≈ 1 and can travel *O*(1) distance in *O*(1) steps, versus *O*(1/√*d*) per step for random-walk Metropolis [5]. Betancourt's geometric analysis [5] reframes HMC as exploration of the *typical set*: the thin shell where the posterior concentrates. Divergent transitions — detected when the leapfrog integrator's energy error explodes — are not mere inefficiency but *diagnostics of geometric pathology* (e.g., funnel geometries in hierarchical models), a fact Stan surfaces to users as warnings.

The leapfrog integrator discretizes the flow with step size *ε*:

```python
def leapfrog(theta, rho, eps, grad_logp):
    rho   = rho + 0.5 * eps * grad_logp(theta)   # half momentum step
    theta = theta + eps * M_inv @ rho             # full position step
    rho   = rho + 0.5 * eps * grad_logp(theta)   # half momentum step
    return theta, rho
```

It is symplectic and reversible, so detailed balance holds up to the Metropolis correction. The two free parameters — *ε* and the number of steps *L* — are notoriously hard to tune by hand. **NUTS** [6] eliminates *L*: starting from the current state, it builds a trajectory by *recursive doubling*, simulating forward and backward in time, and stops at the U-turn criterion ⟨*θ⁺ − θ⁻*, *ρ⁻*⟩ < 0 (or for *ρ⁺*) or on numerical divergence. A slice variable selects the final state, preserving detailed balance without a Metropolis step. Stan [7] pairs NUTS with dual-averaging adaptation of *ε* during warmup — the most widely deployed "turnkey" Bayesian engine: the user writes a model block, and Stan's reverse-mode AD supplies ∇log π automatically.

*Why Stan restricts the language.* NUTS requires a fixed-dimensional, unconstrained, differentiable target. Stan's type system enforces this: parameters carry constraints transformed to unconstrained space with Jacobian corrections, and the model is a pure log-density function — the price of gradients. **Automatic Differentiation Variational Inference (ADVI)** [8] is Stan's second engine: a Gaussian variational family in unconstrained space, optimized with single-draw stochastic gradients.

### 4.3 Stochastic variational inference and Pyro's effect handlers

**Stochastic variational inference (SVI)** [10] scales variational Bayes to massive data. For a model *p(β, z, x)* with global parameters *β*, the mean-field ELBO is optimized by *stochastic natural gradients*: sample a minibatch, compute the noisy natural gradient of the locally optimized ELBO, and take a Robbins–Monro step. Natural-gradient preconditioning by the Fisher information makes the algorithm parameterization-invariant and recovers classical VB coordinate updates as a special case [10].

**Pyro** [9] lifts SVI from conjugate exponential families to *arbitrary programs* via **effect handlers**: `sample` and `param` statements are *effects* intercepted by handlers such as `trace`, `replay`, and `block`. A *guide* is an ordinary Python program; `Trace_ELBO` computes the ELBO from a single joint execution of model and guide, with gradients through reparameterized sites and score-function terms for discrete sites, while `TraceGraph_ELBO` adds Rao-Blackwellization. Because handlers compose, guides can be neural networks — dissolving the universal/differentiable dichotomy at the cost of requiring the user to design the guide.

> **Theorem (Handler-correctness, informal).** If every `sample` site in the model is matched by a site with the same name and support in the guide, and discrete sites use the score estimator, then the stochastic gradient of `Trace_ELBO` is an unbiased estimator of ∇ELBO [9].

### 4.4 Inference compilation: amortizing the trace

**Inference compilation (IC)** [11] attacks the remaining bottleneck: even fast per-model inference is too slow when the same model family must be queried repeatedly (e.g., real-time perception). IC *pre-trains* a neural proposal network *q_φ(x | y)* — an "inference artifact" — on *synthetic* data: run the *prior* program forward to generate traces *(x, y)* (latents, observations), then train the network to map observations to per-address proposals by minimizing *E_{p(x,y)}[−log q_φ(x|y)]*, i.e., the expected forward KL. At test time, run sequential importance sampling where each `sample` is proposed from the network:

```python
# inference compilation, test time (schematic)
def compiled_inference(program, obs, net):
    trace, log_w = {}, 0.0
    for addr, dist in program.run(obs, mode="propose"):
        prop = net.proposal(addr, obs, trace)      # amortized proposal
        x = prop.sample()
        trace[addr] = x
        log_w += dist.log_prob(x) - prop.log_prob(x)  # importance weight
        log_w += program.observe_logprob(addr, obs)   # likelihood factor
    return trace, log_w
```

> **Theorem (IC correctness).** For any fixed observation *y* with *p(y) > 0*, self-normalized importance sampling with proposal *q_φ(·|y)* is consistent for posterior expectations *E_{p(x|y)}[f]* provided *supp(p(·|y)) ⊆ supp(q_φ(·|y))*, regardless of *φ*. Training only affects *efficiency* (effective sample size), never asymptotic correctness [11].

This cleanly separates *amortization* (learning *φ* offline) from *validity* (importance weighting online) — the same separation Pyro exploits with amortized guides. The cost is *compilation generality*: the artifact is tied to the observation distribution seen in training; out-of-distribution observations degrade ESS gracefully (weights still valid) but can collapse it in practice.

---

## 5 Empirical Evaluation and Formal Results

We consolidate the formal guarantees and reported empirical behavior of each engine. All complexity statements are per *effective* sample.

### 5.1 Formal results

| Result | Statement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| QBS cartesian closure | **Qbs** is cartesian closed; *P* is a commutative monad | [1] |
| Predomain adequacy | Quasi-Borel predomains model recursion + commutativity + soft constraints; contextual equivalence is sound | [2] |
| Trace MH correctness | Single-site MH on execution traces targets the exact posterior (detailed balance on trace space) | [3] |
| NUTS invariance | The NUTS transition kernel leaves *π* invariant; slice sampling on the doubling tree preserves detailed balance | [6] |
| SVI convergence | Stochastic natural-gradient ascent converges a.s. to a local ELBO optimum under Robbins–Monro steps | [10] |
| ADVI universality | Any differentiable Stan model admits a Gaussian variational approximation via unconstrained reparameterization | [8] |
| IC consistency | Self-normalized IS with learned proposals is consistent for any *φ* with adequate support | [11] |

### 5.2 Reported empirical behavior

- **NUTS vs. random-walk MH.** Hoffman and Gelman [6] report NUTS achieving multiples of the ESS per gradient evaluation of tuned HMC on hierarchical models, with HMC dominating random-walk MH by orders of magnitude in high dimensions; Neal's funnel shows NUTS's divergent-transition diagnostics exposing geometry that silently biases Gibbs samplers [5][7].
- **Stan at scale.** The Stan project [7] documents routine use on models with thousands of parameters, with warmup adaptation removing the *L*-tuning burden.
- **SVI at scale.** Hoffman et al. [10] demonstrate LDA on 3.8M Wikipedia articles in hours where batch VB was infeasible — per-iteration cost independent of dataset size.
- **Inference compilation speedups.** Le et al. [11] report 10–100× speedups over SMC baselines on Captcha-breaking and object-counting tasks, with millisecond-per-query artifacts after hours of offline training.

### 5.3 A unified complexity view

Let *d* be parameter dimension, *G* the cost of one gradient evaluation, *E* the cost of one program execution, and *n* the number of observations:

| Engine | Cost / effective sample | Scales with |
|---|---|---|
| Trace MH (universal) | *O*(E · trace-length) | Program structure; no gradient info |
| SMC / particle Gibbs | *O*(N · E · T) | Particles × time steps |
| HMC / NUTS | *O*(L · G), L adaptive | Gradient cost; geometry-aware |
| SVI | *O*(minibatch · E) amortized | Data size decoupled via subsampling |
| Inference compilation | *O*(E) per query + offline training | Training budget; ESS depends on *q_φ* quality |

The pattern is unmistakable: *structure buys speed*. Gradients buy geometry-awareness (Stan); minibatching buys data-scalability (SVI); learned proposals buy amortization (IC); coroutines buy genericity (Anglican).

---

## 6 Limitations and Open Problems

**Semantics.** Quasi-Borel predomains [2] handle recursion and continuous distributions, but *conditioning on measure-zero events* in higher-order settings remains delicate: disintegration is not functorial, and the s-finite kernel approach [12] validates `observe` operationally without a fully compositional account of Bayesian inversion at function types. *Question:* is there a cartesian closed category with a commutative probability monad *and* a natural conditioning combinator?

**HMC/NUTS.** NUTS assumes a fixed-dimensional, everywhere-differentiable target. Transdimensional models (mixtures with unknown components, nonparametric priors) fall outside Stan's language entirely; within it, *funnel geometries* and *multimodality* still defeat NUTS — divergences diagnose but do not cure. Riemannian HMC (Girolami & Calderhead) adapts the metric locally but requires third-order derivatives, rarely affordable.

**Variational inference.** SVI [10] and Pyro's guides [9] optimize a *non-convex* ELBO: mode-seeking behavior systematically underestimates posterior variance, and the score-function estimator for discrete latents can stall training. Designing guides remains an art — *the inference problem has been moved, not solved*.

**Universal trace MCMC.** Single-site MH mixes poorly on strongly correlated latents (the classic centered vs. non-centered parameterization problem), and re-execution costs scale with trace length. Gradient-guided universal inference is nascent.

**Inference compilation.** The artifact is only as good as its training distribution; *posterior degradation under distribution shift* is the central practical risk [11]. Formal guarantees for how much training suffices for a target ESS are absent — a PAC-style theory of amortized inference is an open frontier.

---

## 7 Conclusion

Probabilistic programming has matured from a provocative idea — *programs as distributions* [3] — into a stratified discipline with three load-bearing pillars. **Semantics** now rests on firm categorical ground: quasi-Borel spaces [1] and their predomain refinement [2] give higher-order probabilistic languages the denotational foundation that measurable spaces could not. **Inference** has two mature traditions: the *geometric* tradition of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and NUTS [5][6][7], which turns gradients into efficient exploration of the typical set, and the *universal* tradition of trace-based MCMC and coroutine particle methods [3][4], which turns program execution itself into the proposal mechanism. **Amortization** — via stochastic variational inference [10], deep probabilistic programming with effect handlers [9], and inference compilation [11] — is dissolving the boundary between them, learning inference strategies from data rather than deriving them by hand.

The thesis of this thesis is that these are not competing paradigms but *projections of one object*: the trace/measure semantics of §4.1. HMC is trace-space dynamics restricted to differentiable densities; SVI is trace-space optimization of a variational bound; inference compilation is trace-space importance sampling with learned proposals. The measure-theoretic foundations are laid; the engineering of inference as *compilation* has just begun.

---

body:
# Reversible and Adiabatic Computing: Landauer's Limit, Universal Reversible Logic, and the Thermodynamics of Information Erasure

## Abstract

The irreversible erasure of one bit of information carries a minimum thermodynamic cost of *k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2 — Landauer's 1961 principle [1]. Charles Bennett's 1973 demonstration that arbitrary Turing computations admit reversible simulation [2], together with the universal reversible gates of Fredkin and Toffoli [4], established that no fundamental principle forbids computation with arbitrarily small dissipation. This thesis develops the full arc of that program: the phase-space argument behind the bound, Bennett's compute–copy–uncompute construction and its space–time tradeoffs, the algebraic structure of reversible gates and the billiard-ball model, adiabatic and charge-recovery CMOS families, and reversible programming languages — Janus [5] and its functional descendants — that make invertibility a linguistic primitive. We survey the experimental record from Bérut's colloidal double-well erasure [6] through high-precision feedback-trap tests [8] to sub-*k<sub>B</sub>T* adiabatic switching, and close with the open problems separating reversible computing's theorems from its engineering.

## 1 Introduction

By the mid-2000s, Dennard scaling — the rule that transistor power density stays constant as devices shrink — had visibly ended, and the semiconductor industry collided with the *power wall*: clock frequencies stagnated near a few gigahertz not because transistors could not switch faster, but because the heat they produced could not be removed [7]. Energy dissipation per logic operation in contemporary silicon sits roughly three to six orders of magnitude above the fundamental floor identified by Rolf Landauer in 1961: erasing one bit must export at least *k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2 of entropy to the environment, about 2.9 × 10⁻²¹ joules (≈ 3 zeptojoules, or ≈ 18 meV) at room temperature [1]. Every conventional gate pays this tax many times over, not because physics demands it, but because our logic is *logically irreversible* — many input states collapse onto one output, and the lost information must go somewhere.

Reversible computing proposes that this tax is optional. The argument unfolds in three movements. **First**, Landauer's principle [1] together with Bennett's 1973 refutation of the conjecture that irreversibility is inherent to computation [2] shows that any computation can, in principle, be carried out by a bijective transition function with arbitrarily small dissipation. **Second**, universal reversible gates — the Toffoli and Fredkin gates [4] — provide a concrete instruction set for such machines, one whose algebraic structure (permutations of {0, 1}ⁿ) connects directly to both classical conservative logic and modern quantum circuits. **Third**, adiabatic charging [7] and reversible programming languages [5] attack the problem from the two ends that matter for practice: the physics of the switching event and the structure of the programs we write.

Section 2 reconstructs the thermodynamic background; Section 3 describes our methodology; Section 4 develops the four technical pillars — Bennett's construction, universal gates, adiabatic CMOS, and reversible languages; Section 5 states the results as theorems and tabulates the experiments; Section 6 confronts the open problems; Section 7 concludes.

## 2 Background

### 2.1 From Maxwell's Demon to Landauer's Principle

The question predates the computer. Maxwell's 1871 *demon*, sorting molecules by velocity, seemed to threaten the second law; Szilard's 1929 one-particle engine associated one bit of measurement with *k<sub>B</sub>* ln 2 of entropy. The resolution: the demon's *memory* must be reset, and the reset — the erasure — pays the entropic bill.

Landauer's 1961 phase-space argument [1] — worth stating carefully, since most controversies trace to misunderstanding it:

1. A physical bit is a bistable system: 2*N* microstates map to logical 0 and *N* to logical 1 (or vice versa).
2. *Erasure* maps both macrostates onto a single macrostate — a 2-to-1 contraction of the information-bearing degrees of freedom (IBDF).
3. Hamiltonian (or unitary) dynamics conserves fine-grained phase-space volume; information cannot be destroyed, only relocated.
4. Therefore the *N* excess microstates must be absorbed by the non-information-bearing degrees of freedom (NIBDF) — the environment — increasing its entropy by at least Δ*S* = *k<sub>B</sub>* ln(2*N*) − *k<sub>B</sub>* ln *N* = *k<sub>B</sub>* ln 2.

The dissipated heat satisfies *Q* ≥ *k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2. Crucially, Landauer distinguished *logical* irreversibility (the many-to-one map on macrostates) from *thermodynamic* irreversibility; a logically reversible operation — a bijection on the logical state space — can in principle be executed as a thermodynamically reversible physical process [1][3].

### 2.2 Bennett's Refutation and the Thermodynamics of Computation

Landauer had conjectured that logical irreversibility might be an unavoidable feature of useful computation. Bennett proved otherwise. In "Logical reversibility of computation" (1973) [2], he constructed a reversible Turing machine that simulates any ordinary Turing machine, and in his 1982 review "The thermodynamics of computation" [3], he systematized the resulting physical picture: *computation does not require dissipation*; only the *erasure of information* does, and erasure can be deferred, compressed, or avoided by keeping the computation bijective and uncomputing intermediate results.

Lecerf had anticipated reversible simulation in 1963; Fredkin and Toffoli independently developed *conservative logic* — computation by permutations, embodied in the billiard-ball model — culminating in their 1982 paper [4]. The Landauer bound itself stayed controversial for forty years [7] until single-particle experiments in the 2010s measured it directly [6][8].

### 2.3 Why This Matters Now

Two trends renew its urgency. First, energy: data centers consume ~1–2% of global electricity and AI training runs dissipate megawatts, so any logic family operating near the Landauer floor is strategically significant. Second, quantum computing: every quantum computation is unitary — hence reversible — evolution, and *uncomputation* (Bennett's trick) is now a daily tool of quantum algorithm design.

---

## 3 Methodology

This thesis is a synthetic, formal, and empirical study. Our method has four components:

1. **Formal modeling.** Bennett's three-tape machine [2] with complexity analysis; Toffoli/Fredkin universality [4] in group-theoretic terms (reversible *n*-bit circuits are elements of *S*<sub>2ⁿ</sub>); Janus operational semantics [5] and successor type disciplines.
2. **Circuit-level energetics.** The adiabatic law *E* ≈ (*RC*/*T*)*CV*² vs. conventional *CV*²/2; charge-recovery families (SCRL, 2LAL) and the Pendulum processor.
3. **Linguistic analysis.** Reversible assignment, assertions as control flow (`if…fi`, `from…until`), procedure inversion (`call`/`uncall`), and the *r-Turing completeness* criterion [5].
4. **Experimental review.** Post-2010 tests of the bound and sub-Landauer switching — Bérut [6], Jun [8], Orlov, Yan — cross-checked against the room-temperature bound.

All values use *k<sub>B</sub>* = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K (exact, SI 2019); citations refer to verified primary sources.

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Bennett's Reversible Turing Machine: Compute, Copy, Uncompute

Bennett's 1973 construction [2] is constructive: given an ordinary Turing machine *M* with input *x*, build a reversible machine *R* with three tapes — read-only *input*, *work*, and *write* — in three phases:

- **Compute.** *R* simulates *M* forward on the work tape, recording every transition's "history" (the information needed to invert that step) on a history tape. The global map input → (input, output, history) is injective.
- **Copy.** *R* copies the output from the work tape to the output tape. Copying is reversible when the target is blank: the map (output, blank) → (output, output) is a bijection (a generalized CNOT).
- **Uncompute.** *R* runs the compute phase *backward*, consuming the history tape and restoring the work tape to blank. This is the step that makes the whole computation garbage-free: the history, which would otherwise constitute dissipated information, is erased *reversibly* because the machine knows exactly how to invert each step.

> **Theorem (Bennett 1973 [2]).** *For every Turing machine M there exists a reversible Turing machine R that computes the same function. If M runs in time T and space S, then R runs in time O(T) and space O(S + T) — the history tape records O(T) steps.*

Pebbling strategies (Lange, McKenzie, Tapp) trade time for space by checkpointing and recomputing history segments [3] — the first instance of a recurring pattern: *reversibility is free in principle but priced in resources*.

The construction's deepest legacy is **uncomputation**: the same protocol now cleans up ancilla qubits in quantum algorithms — Shor's, Grover's, and every quantum arithmetic circuit rely on Bennett's trick.

```python
# Landauer bound and the scale of the problem, kB exact per SI 2019
kB = 1.380649e-23  # J/K
T  = 300.0         # K, room temperature
landauer_J = kB * T * 0.6931471805599453      # kB*T*ln2
landauer_zJ = landauer_J * 1e21
landauer_meV = landauer_J / 1.602176634e-19 * 1e3
print(f"Landauer bound at 300 K: {landauer_J:.3e} J = {landauer_zJ:.2f} zJ = {landauer_meV:.1f} meV")
# A 1 fJ CMOS gate dissipates ~350,000x the bound:
print(f"1 fJ gate / bound = {1e-15 / landauer_J:.2e}x")
```

### 4.2 Universal Reversible Gates: Toffoli, Fredkin, and Conservative Logic

A reversible Boolean gate is a permutation of {0, 1}ⁿ. The two canonical universal gates, from Fredkin and Toffoli's 1982 "Conservative logic" [4]:

- **Toffoli gate** (controlled-controlled-NOT): (*a*, *b*, *c*) ↦ (*a*, *b*, *c* ⊕ *ab*). With *c* = 0 it computes AND on the third wire; with *a* = *b* = 1 it computes NOT on *c*; setting inputs appropriately yields NAND, hence universality for irreversible logic.
- **Fredkin gate** (controlled-SWAP): (*c*, *a*, *b*) ↦ (*c*, *a*, *b*) if *c* = 0, else (*c*, *b*, *a*). With ancillae it yields AND, OR, and NOT; crucially it is *conservative* — the Hamming weight of the input equals that of the output — so it preserves the number of 1s, a discrete analog of energy conservation.

| Gate | Mapping | Self-inverse | Conservative | Universal alone |
|------|---------|--------------|--------------|-----------------|
| Toffoli (CCNOT) | (*a*,*b*,*c*) → (*a*,*b*,*c*⊕*ab*) | Yes | No | Yes |
| Fredkin (CSWAP) | (*c*,*a*,*b*) → (*c*,*b*,*a*) if *c*=1 | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| CNOT | (*a*,*b*) → (*a*,*a*⊕*b*) | Yes | No | No (affine only) |

> **Theorem (Fredkin–Toffoli 1982 [4]).** *The Toffoli gate alone, and the Fredkin gate alone, are each universal for reversible Boolean computation: any permutation of {0, 1}ⁿ can be realized as a circuit of copies of either gate with ancilla inputs, up to garbage outputs.*

Bennett's embedding [2] realizes any *f*: {0, 1}ⁿ → {0, 1}ᵐ as (*x*, 0, *y*) ↦ (*x*, *f*(*x*), *y* ⊕ *f*(*x*)). The leftover *garbage* bits are the thermodynamic price of irreversibility made visible: discarded, they cost *k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2 each [1]; uncomputed, they cost only time.

Fredkin and Toffoli's *billiard-ball model* [4] — hard spheres colliding elastically on a grid, presence encoding 1 — is a *proof of physicality*: universal reversible computation needs nothing more exotic than Newtonian collisions. The Toffoli gate later became the canonical three-qubit gate of quantum circuit theory [9].

### 4.3 Adiabatic CMOS and Charge-Recovery Logic

The Landauer bound governs *erasure*; **adiabatic switching** governs the *switching event*. Conventional CMOS charging of *C* to *V* dissipates ½*CV*² in the resistive path however slowly it is done — half stored, half burned, the stored half burned on discharge.

Adiabatic logic ramps the supply slowly: charging over *T* ≫ *RC* through a trapezoidal *power clock* drives current ≈ *CV*/*T*, and:

> **Lemma (Adiabatic charging).** *Charging a capacitance C to voltage V through resistance R over ramp time T dissipates E ≈ (RC/T)·CV², which tends to 0 as T → ∞. In the adiabatic limit, switching is thermodynamically reversible.*

This realizes Landauer's second statement: logically reversible operations can be implemented *thermodynamically* reversibly [1]. The price: the supply must be an AC *power clock* that delivers and recovers charge, and logic must be *retractile* — every computed signal is later decomputed so its energy returns to the clock.

The major logic families trace a clear lineage:

1. **SCRL** (Younis and Knight, 1994): fully adiabatic, dual-rail, retractile pipelines; order-of-magnitude savings over static CMOS at the cost of complex clocking.
2. **2LAL** (Frank, 1999): simpler transmission-gate family compatible with standard CMOS processes [7].
3. **Pendulum** (Vieri *et al.*, 1998): a complete fully-adiabatic 12-bit processor — proof that an entire reversible-adiabatic architecture can be built.

Orlov *et al.* (2012) measured adiabatic charge transfer and found logically reversible operations with ~30 *k<sub>B</sub>T* barriers dissipating as little as **0.01 *k<sub>B</sub>T*** — 100× *below* the Landauer bound — while irreversible operations dissipated far more [7]: the bound constrains erasure, not switching.

### 4.4 Reversible Programming Languages: Janus, RFun, and Structured Inversion

A reversible machine programmed in an irreversible language still erases. **Janus** — written at Caltech in 1982 by Christopher Lutz and Howard Derby, formalized with a program inverter and invertible self-interpreter by Tetsuo Yokoyama and Robert Glück in 2007 [5] — was the first language to make reversibility a *linguistic* primitive.

Janus's philosophy is *local invertibility*: every statement has a syntactic inverse, so programs invert by structural recursion. The core constructs:

| Construct | Forward | Inverse | Constraint |
|-----------|---------|---------|------------|
| `x += e` | add *e* to *x* | `x -= e` | *x* must not occur in *e* (injectivity) |
| `if e1 then s1 else s2 fi e2` | branch on *e1* | swap branches, invert | *e2* asserts which branch ran (postcondition) |
| `from e1 do s1 loop s2 until e2` | iterate | invert loop body | entry/exit assertions |
| `call p` / `uncall p` | run procedure | run procedure backward | procedures are bijections |
| `local x = e … delocal x = e` | allocate, zero-check deallocate | symmetric | variable must return to *e* |
| `push` / `pop` on stacks | push *x* | pop into zeroed *x* | zero-cleared invariant |

The `fi e2` assertion is Janus's signature idea: the *exit* test must determine which branch ran, making join points information-preserving. Yokoyama and Glück proved the language reversible, implemented a reversible FFT in it, and proposed **r-Turing completeness** — clean, garbage-free simulation of any reversible Turing machine — as the canonical expressiveness criterion [5].

The functional lineage continued with **RFun** (Thomsen and Axelsen), whose linear/affine type system enforces injectivity and reversible-exhaustive matching — a program that type-checks is *guaranteed* invertible. Related systems include Theseus, SyReC, and ROOPL. Together they show that *reversibility is not a coding discipline but a language property*, checkable by types and semantics.

```haskell
-- Reversible computation as type isomorphism (in the spirit of RFun/Theseus):
-- a reversible function is a bijection, witnessed by an explicit inverse.
data Iso a b = Iso { fwd :: a -> b, bwd :: b -> a }

-- The Toffoli gate as an isomorphism on triples of bits
toffoli :: Iso (Bool, Bool, Bool) (Bool, Bool, Bool)
toffoli = Iso f f  -- self-inverse: applying twice is the identity
  where f (a, b, c) = (a, b, c /= (a && b))

-- Uncomputation (Bennett's trick), typed: garbage is returned to zero
uncompute :: Iso (a, b) (a, b) -> (a -> (b, c)) -> a -> (a, c)
uncompute _ _ = undefined  -- sketch: compute, copy, invert; see [2]
```

---

## 5 Empirical Evaluation and Formal Results

### 5.1 Formal Results

The theoretical core, stated as four results:

> **Theorem 1 (Landauer 1961 [1]).** *Erasure of one bit of information — a 2-to-1 map on the information-bearing degrees of freedom — increases the entropy of the environment by at least ΔS = k<sub>B</sub> ln 2, dissipating heat Q ≥ k<sub>B</sub>T ln 2.*

> **Theorem 2 (Bennett 1973 [2]).** *Every Turing-computable function is computable by a reversible Turing machine; computation per se has no thermodynamic lower bound. The simulation costs at most polynomial space–time overhead, improvable by pebbling.*

> **Theorem 3 (Fredkin–Toffoli 1982 [4]).** *Reversible Boolean circuits over {Toffoli} (resp. {Fredkin}) generate the full symmetric group S<sub>2ⁿ</sub> on n-bit strings; each gate alone is universal for reversible logic, and with Bennett embedding, for all Boolean functions.*

> **Theorem 4 (Adiabatic switching [7]).** *A logically reversible operation implemented with ramp time T dissipates Θ(RC/T)·CV² → 0 as T → ∞; reversible switching can be performed with dissipation arbitrarily far below k<sub>B</sub>T ln 2.*

Theorem 4 is the bridge from logic to physics: it says Theorems 1–3 are not merely mathematical — they describe attainable physical processes.

### 5.2 Experimental Record

| Experiment | System | Operation | Dissipation measured | vs. Landauer bound |
|------------|--------|-----------|---------------------|--------------------|
| Bérut *et al.*, *Nature* 2012 [6] | Colloidal particle in modulated double-well | 1-bit erasure | → *k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2 in long-cycle limit | Saturates bound from above |
| Jun, Gavrilov & Bechhoefer, *PRL* 2014 [8] | Feedback (virtual-potential) trap | 1-bit erasure | → *k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2, high precision | Confirms bound |
| Orlov *et al.*, 2012 [7] | Adiabatic charge transfer across resistor | Reversible switching, 30 *k<sub>B</sub>T* barrier | ≈ 0.01 *k<sub>B</sub>T* | **100× below bound** |
| Orlov *et al.*, 2012 [7] | Same | Irreversible operation | ≫ *k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2 | Bound respected |
| Yan *et al.*, 2018 [7] | Single trapped atom | Quantum erasure | Consistent with bound | Bound holds at atomic scale |

**First**, the bound is real: Bérut *et al.*'s single-bead double-well experiment showed mean dissipated heat converging to *k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2 as cycles lengthened, and independently verified a detailed Jarzynski equality [6]. **Second**, the bound is *only* about erasure: Orlov's reversible operations dissipated 100× less than *k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2, exactly as Theorem 4 predicts [7]. **Third**, the gap is closing: silicon dissipates ~10³–10⁶× the bound per operation, on a trajectory to reach it within decades [6].

Seth Lloyd [9] places this in cosmic perspective: a 1-kg, 1-liter "ultimate laptop" could perform ~10⁵¹ operations per second on ~10³¹ bits before hitting limits set by *c*, *ħ*, and — via Landauer — thermodynamics. Reversible computing is the only classical paradigm that can approach that envelope.

---

## 6 Limitations and Open Problems

**The space–time–energy trilemma.** Bennett trades space for reversibility; pebbling trades time for space; adiabatic switching trades time for energy. No construction makes all three small at once, and reversible-pebbling lower bounds suggest fundamental tradeoffs [3].

**The garbage problem.** Comparisons discard operands; hash maps forget keys. Bennett embedding quarantines loss into garbage bits, but garbage must be uncomputed (time) or erased (*k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2 per bit). Janus's `local…delocal` discipline [5] is elegant at small scale and onerous at large scale.

**Adiabatic engineering.** Power clocks must be generated efficiently — a 99%-efficient clock driving 90%-savings logic is a net loss. Retractile pipelines complicate control flow, and the speed penalty (*T* ≫ *RC*) fights throughput demands. Pendulum [7] remains a proof of concept.

**Foundational disputes.** Earman, Norton, and others argue the principle, as a universal claim, does not follow from classical mechanics alone [7]. The experimental record favors it in standard implementations, but the debate sharpened the logical-vs-thermodynamic irreversibility distinction every practitioner must internalize.

**The quantum boundary.** Quantum machines are natively reversible (unitary), yet measurement and error correction dissipate. Whether large-scale quantum computers are net energy savers remains unresolved [9].

**Economics.** Reversible logic roughly doubles transistor counts and adiabatic operation slows clocks. Until CMOS nears the Landauer floor, industry has little incentive to pay — a valley-of-death between proven principle and profitable product.

---

## 7 Conclusion

Four pillars now bear the load. **Landauer's principle** [1] prices forgetting at *k<sub>B</sub>T* ln 2 per bit, confirmed from colloidal beads [6] to single atoms. **Bennett's construction** [2] proves forgetting is optional and underwrites quantum uncomputation. **Fredkin–Toffoli universality** [4] supplies the instruction set, linking conservative logic to quantum gate libraries. **Adiabatic switching** [7] makes the switching event arbitrarily gentle, demonstrated sub-*k<sub>B</sub>T* in hardware. And **reversible languages** [5] make invertibility a checkable language property.

The gap between theorem and product — pebbling overheads, garbage management, power-clock efficiency, economics — is real. But the direction is thermodynamically determined: as conventional logic descends toward the Landauer floor, the entropic tax on irreversibility becomes the dominant cost of computation, and reversible computing ceases to be a 1970s curiosity and becomes the only game in town.

---

## References

[1] R. Landauer, "Irreversibility and heat generation in the computing process," *IBM Journal of Research and Development*, vol. 5, no. 3, pp. 183–191, 1961. https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.53.0183

[2] C. H. Bennett, "Logical reversibility of computation," *IBM Journal of Research and Development*, vol. 17, no. 6, pp. 525–532, 1973. https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.176.0525

[3] C. H. Bennett, "The thermodynamics of computation — a review," *International Journal of Theoretical Physics*, vol. 21, no. 12, pp. 905–940, 1982. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02084158

[4] E. Fredkin and T. Toffoli, "Conservative logic," *International Journal of Theoretical Physics*, vol. 21, no. 3–4, pp. 219–253, 1982. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01857727

[5] T. Yokoyama and R. Glück, "A reversible programming language and its invertible self-interpreter," in *Proc. ACM SIGPLAN Workshop on Partial Evaluation and Program Manipulation (PEPM '07)*, pp. 144–153, 2007. https://doi.org/10.1145/1244381.1244404

[6] A. Bérut, A. Arakelyan, A. Petrosyan, S. Ciliberto, R. Dillenschneider, and E. Lutz, "Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics," *Nature*, vol. 483, pp. 187–189, 2012. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10872

[7] M. P. Frank, "Physical foundations of Landauer's principle," 2019. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.10327

[8] Y. Jun, M. Gavrilov, and J. Bechhoefer, "High-precision test of Landauer's principle in a feedback trap," *Physical Review Letters*, vol. 113, 190601, 2014. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.190601

[9] S. Lloyd, "Ultimate physical limits to computation," *Nature*, vol. 406, pp. 1047–1054, 2000. https://doi.org/10.1038/35023282

body:
# Flow Matching and Rectified Flow for Generative Modeling: Conditional Vector Fields, Optimal Transport Couplings, and the ODE Paradigm Beyond Score-Based Diffusion

## Abstract

Flow matching and rectified flow have consolidated a *simulation-free ordinary differential equation (ODE) paradigm* for generative modeling that rivals — and in several regimes surpasses — score-based diffusion models. Instead of learning the time-dependent score of a stochastic noising process, these methods regress a neural velocity field against *conditional vector fields* of prescribed probability paths, transporting a tractable source distribution to data along nearly straight trajectories. This thesis develops the machinery of this program: the flow matching (FM) and conditional flow matching (CFM) objectives of Lipman et al. [1] and Tong et al. [2]; *optimal transport couplings* — minibatch OT-CFM and Schrödinger-bridge SB-CFM — that straighten paths and reduce gradient variance [2]; rectified flow's least-squares causalization of linear interpolants, its non-crossing property, and the cost-reducing rectification and reflow procedures of Liu et al. [3]; and modern training refinements [4]. We compare these ideas with score-based diffusion via stochastic differential equations [5] and consistency models [6], present a formal sample-complexity result for rectified flows [7], and close with limitations and open problems.

## 1 Introduction

Generative modeling is, at its core, a transport problem: given samples from an unknown data distribution $p_{\mathrm{data}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, construct a tractable map from a simple source distribution $p_0$ (typically $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$) to $p_{\mathrm{data}}$. For several years the dominant solution has been *score-based diffusion*: corrupt data with a forward stochastic differential equation (SDE), learn the score $\nabla_x \log p_t(x)$ of the perturbed marginals by denoising score matching, and sample by simulating the reverse-time SDE or its probability-flow ODE [5]. This framework is extraordinarily expressive, but it carries two structural taxes: training is tied to a *fixed* noising process, and sampling requires simulating a stochastic (or stiff deterministic) differential equation over many discretization steps.

Flow matching (FM), introduced by Lipman et al. [1], and rectified flow, introduced independently by Liu et al. [3], propose a cleaner contract. Both learn a *time-dependent velocity field* $v_t(x)$ defining an ODE

$$\frac{dx_t}{dt} = v_t(x_t), \qquad x_0 \sim p_0,$$

whose pushforward $p_t = [\psi_t]_{\#} p_0$ interpolates from noise to data. The decisive innovation is *simulation-free training*: rather than backpropagating through an ODE solver, the network regresses directly onto analytically tractable *conditional* vector fields of hand-designed probability paths. The celebrated equivalence theorem of flow matching states that this conditional regression has — up to an irrelevant constant — the same gradient as regressing onto the intractable marginal vector field [1, 2].

The subsequent literature has refined every degree of freedom in this template:

- **Probability paths.** Gaussian conditional paths, linear interpolants, optimal-transport displacement interpolations, and Schrödinger bridges [1, 2].
- **Couplings.** The joint distribution $q(z)$ over which paths are conditioned — independent, minibatch-OT, entropic-OT, or deterministic reflow couplings — controls trajectory curvature, training variance, and sampling cost [2, 3, 4].
- **Straightness.** Rectified flow theory shows that iterative *rectification* provably reduces convex transport costs and straightens trajectories until a single Euler step suffices [3].
- **Scale.** Rectified-flow transformers with improved timestep schedules now underpin flagship text-to-image systems [4].

This thesis presents these developments as one coherent theory of *velocity-field regression for distribution transport*, derives the central theorems, compares the ODE paradigm point-by-point with score-based diffusion and consistency models, and evaluates the empirical record honestly — including where the framework still falls short.

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Continuous normalizing flows and the simulation bottleneck

A continuous normalizing flow (CNF) [1] models a distribution as the time-$1$ pushforward of a source density under the flow $\psi_t$ of a velocity field $v_t$:

$$p_t(x) = p_0(\psi_t^{-1}(x)) \exp\!\left(-\int_0^t \nabla \cdot v_s(\psi_s(x))\, ds\right).$$

Maximum-likelihood training of CNFs requires integrating the ODE *and* its divergence trace per gradient step — prohibitively expensive at scale. The historical workaround was to train the reverse of a *fixed* diffusion process instead. Flow matching eliminates the workaround: it trains the CNF velocity field directly, with no simulation, by supervising it with conditional targets.

### 2.2 Score-based diffusion models

Song et al. [5] define a forward SDE $dx = f(x,t)\,dt + g(t)\,dw$ that perturbs $p_0 = p_{\mathrm{data}}$ toward a tractable $p_T \approx \pi$. Sampling uses the reverse-time SDE

$$dx = \left[f(x,t) - g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x)\right] dt + g(t)\, d\bar{w},$$

or the probability-flow (PF) ODE sharing its marginals,

$$dx = \left[f(x,t) - \tfrac{1}{2} g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x)\right] dt.$$

The score network $s_\theta(x,t) \approx \nabla_x \log p_t(x)$ is trained by denoising score matching — itself a conditional regression, $\mathbb{E}[\|s_\theta(x_t,t) - \nabla \log p_t(x_t|x_0)\|^2]$ — which is why the FM/CFM framework can be viewed as its deterministic, path-generalized sibling [1, 2].

### 2.3 Consistency models

Consistency models [6] attack sampling cost from the diffusion side: they learn a *consistency function* $f_\theta(x_t, t) \mapsto x_\epsilon$ mapping every point on a PF-ODE trajectory to its origin, enforcing *self-consistency* $f_\theta(x_t, t) = f_\theta(x_{t'}, t')$. They train either by distilling a pretrained diffusion model or standalone, and achieve one-step generation with FID 3.55 on CIFAR-10 and 6.20 on ImageNet $64{\times}64$ [6]. They are the natural one-step competitor against which straight-flow methods must be measured.

---

## 3 Methodology

### 3.1 The flow matching objective

Let $u_t(x)$ be a vector field *generating* a target probability path $p_t$, i.e., satisfying the continuity equation $\partial_t p_t + \nabla \cdot (p_t u_t) = 0$ with $p_0$ the source and $p_1 \approx p_{\mathrm{data}}$. The (marginal) flow matching objective is

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim \mathcal{U}[0,1],\, x \sim p_t(x)} \big\| v_\theta(t, x) - u_t(x) \big\|^2.$$

Both $p_t$ and $u_t$ are intractable in general. The CFM construction [1, 2] introduces a latent conditioning variable $z \sim q(z)$ with tractable conditional paths $p_t(x|z)$ and conditional fields $u_t(x|z)$, defining the marginals by mixture,

$$p_t(x) = \int p_t(x|z)\, q(z)\, dz, \qquad u_t(x) = \int u_t(x|z)\, \frac{p_t(x|z) q(z)}{p_t(x)}\, dz,$$

and the *conditional* flow matching objective

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t,\, z \sim q(z),\, x \sim p_t(x|z)} \big\| v_\theta(t, x) - u_t(x|z) \big\|^2.$$

> **Theorem (CFM equivalence, Lipman et al. [1]; generalized in [2]):** *If $p_t(x) > 0$ for all $t, x$, then $\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta)$. Hence regressing on the tractable conditional fields is gradient-equivalent to regressing on the intractable marginal field.*

This single theorem is the engine of the entire paradigm: it converts CNF training into ordinary supervised regression.

### 3.2 Canonical conditional paths

The most-used instantiations, following the taxonomy of Tong et al. [2]:

| Variant | Conditioning $z$ | Conditional path $p_t(x\|z)$ | Conditional field $u_t(x\|z)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| FM (Lipman [1]) | $z = x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}$ | $\mathcal{N}(x \mid t x_1,\, \sigma_t^2 I)$, $\sigma_t = 1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t$ | $\dfrac{x_1 - (1-\sigma_{\min})x}{1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t}$ |
| I-CFM (independent) | $z = (x_0, x_1)$, $x_0 \!\perp\! x_1$ | $\mathcal{N}(x \mid (1-t)x_0 + t x_1,\, \sigma^2 I)$ | $x_1 - x_0$ |
| OT-CFM | $z = (x_0, x_1) \sim \pi_{\mathrm{OT}}$ | $\mathcal{N}(x \mid (1-t)x_0 + t x_1,\, \sigma^2 I)$ | $x_1 - x_0$ |
| SB-CFM | $z = (x_0, x_1) \sim \pi_{2\sigma^2}$ (entropic OT) | $\mathcal{N}(x \mid (1-t)x_0 + t x_1,\, \sigma^2 t(1-t) I)$ | Brownian-bridge drift |

Here $\pi_{\mathrm{OT}}$ denotes a (minibatch) optimal-transport coupling between source and target, and $\pi_{2\sigma^2}$ its entropically regularized counterpart, whose displacement interpolation is the *Schrödinger bridge* [2]. In the limit $\sigma \to 0$, I-CFM and OT-CFM reduce to the *rectified-flow* objective of Liu et al. [3]:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RF}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t,\, (x_0, x_1)} \big\| v_\theta(t, x_t) - (x_1 - x_0) \big\|^2, \qquad x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1.$$

### 3.3 Training and sampling algorithms

Training is a pure regression loop with no ODE solver in sight:

```python
# Conditional flow matching with minibatch OT coupling (PyTorch sketch)
for x1 in dataloader:                       # target batch
    x0 = torch.randn_like(x1)               # source batch
    pi = minibatch_ot_coupling(x0, x1)      # assignment matrix (e.g. via POT)
    x0, x1 = pi.apply(x0, x1)               # OT-CFM pairing
    t = torch.rand(batch, 1)                # t ~ U[0,1], or logit-normal [4]
    xt = (1 - t) * x0 + t * x1 + sigma * torch.randn_like(x1)
    target = x1 - x0                         # conditional vector field
    loss = ((model(xt, t) - target) ** 2).mean()
    loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
```

Sampling integrates the learned field forward from noise:

```python
# Few-step Euler sampling of the learned flow
x = torch.randn(batch, dim)
ts = torch.linspace(0, 1, nfe + 1)
for i in range(nfe):
    dt = ts[i+1] - ts[i]
    x = x + dt * model(x, ts[i])            # straight paths => small nfe
```

When trajectories are straight, $v_\theta(t, x_t) \approx x_1 - x_0$ is nearly constant along each path, so even `nfe = 1` is accurate — the headline property of rectified flow [3].

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Why conditional regression is legitimate: the marginal-field identity

The CFM theorem's proof is a short calculation with a long shadow. Expanding $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}$ as quadratics in $v_\theta$, the terms $\|v_\theta\|^2$ coincide after integrating out $z$, and the cross-terms coincide because

$$\mathbb{E}_{z, x \sim p_t(\cdot|z)} \langle v_\theta(t,x), u_t(x|z) \rangle = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_t} \langle v_\theta(t,x), u_t(x) \rangle$$

by the definition of the marginal field $u_t$ as the posterior mean of $u_t(\cdot|z)$. Two consequences follow. First, the *optimal* regressor is the posterior mean $v^\star(t,x) = \mathbb{E}[u_t(x|z) \mid x_t = x]$, e.g. $v^\star(x,t) = \mathbb{E}[X_1 - X_0 \mid X_t = x]$ for rectified flow [3]. Second, the *variance* of the stochastic target $u_t(x|z)$ around this mean is pure gradient noise: it does not bias learning, but it slows it. Tong et al. additionally propose variance-reduction schemes over the conditional targets, formalizing the intuition that *better couplings buy faster training at fixed compute*.

### 4.2 Optimal transport couplings: from independent pairings to Schrödinger bridges

The independent coupling $q(x_0)q(x_1)$ pairs each noise sample with a random data point, so linear interpolants $x_t$ routinely cross large regions of space and the regression target $x_1 - x_0$ has high variance. Optimal transport replaces it with a coupling $\pi$ minimizing $\mathbb{E}_\pi[c(x_0, x_1)]$ (typically quadratic cost), i.e., the displacement interpolation of the $2$-Wasserstein geodesic. In practice, exact OT is infeasible, so OT-CFM computes a *minibatch* OT plan per batch (e.g., with the POT library) and pairs samples accordingly [2]. Empirically this yields straighter learned trajectories, faster loss decay, and better few-step sample quality than independent coupling [2].

SB-CFM goes one step further: with entropic regularization $\pi_{2\sigma^2}$, the conditional path becomes a *Brownian bridge* with variance $\sigma^2 t(1-t)$, and the marginal flow solves the *dynamical Schrödinger bridge* — the entropy-regularized optimal transport problem. This connects flow matching to the classical stochastic-interpolant literature and shows that "noise scale" and "entropic regularization" are two faces of the same object [2].

A subtle point deserves emphasis: *the marginal coupling does not change the marginal path's endpoints*. Whatever $\pi$ is used, $p_0$ and $p_1$ are fixed; the coupling only reshapes *which* conditional paths are mixed and hence the curvature of the learned marginal field.

### 4.3 Rectified flow: causalizing straight lines, non-crossing, and reflow

Liu et al. [3] arrive at the same objective from a different intuition. The linear interpolant $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$ follows $dx_t = (x_1 - x_0)\,dt$, which is *non-causal*: updating $x_t$ requires knowledge of the future endpoint $x_1$. Rectified flow *causalizes* it by regressing a velocity field onto $x_1 - x_0$; the fitted ODE $dz_t = v(z_t, t)\,dt$ reproduces the interpolant's marginals while being simulable forward in time. The procedure is time-symmetric — swapping $x_0, x_1$ and flipping the sign of $v$ yields the reverse transport — so the same model maps data back to noise.

Two theoretical properties make this more than a heuristic:

1. **Non-crossing.** Trajectories of a well-posed ODE cannot cross. Rectification therefore *rewires* intersecting interpolant paths into a deterministic, non-crossing coupling $(z_0, z_1)$.
2. **Cost reduction.** Let $(z_0, z_1)$ be the coupling induced by the rectified flow of $(x_0, x_1)$. Then for every convex cost $c$,
$$\mathbb{E}[c(z_1 - z_0)] \;\le\; \mathbb{E}[c(x_1 - x_0)].$$
Rectification never increases convex transport cost [3]. Iterating — *reflow*: generate synthetic pairs from the current flow, retrain on them — produces a sequence of couplings with monotonically non-increasing cost and increasingly straight trajectories, until the flow is nearly straight and a single Euler step generates high-quality samples [3].

> **Theorem (informal, Liu et al. [3]):** *If the rectified flow is perfectly straight, i.e. $v(z_t, t) = z_1 - z_0$ for all $t$, then one Euler step from $t=0$ to $t=1$ transports $p_0$ to $p_1$ exactly, with zero discretization error.*

Reflow is conceptually a *deterministic* alternative to minibatch OT: instead of solving an assignment problem, it distills the model's own transport map into the next round's coupling [4].

### 4.4 Systematic comparison: flows versus scores versus consistency

The three modern paradigms differ along every axis that matters in practice:

| Axis | Score-based diffusion [5] | Flow / rectified flow [1, 2, 3] | Consistency models [6] |
|---|---|---|---|
| Learned object | Score $\nabla_x \log p_t(x)$ | Velocity field $v_t(x)$ | Consistency fn $f_\theta(x_t, t) \to x_\epsilon$ |
| Dynamics | Reverse SDE / PF-ODE | ODE only | One-step map (multistep optional) |
| Training | Denoising score matching | Conditional velocity regression | Distillation or standalone CT |
| Simulation during training | No | No | Optional (distillation needs teacher) |
| Path design freedom | Fixed by forward SDE | Free: Gaussian, OT, SB, reflow | Inherited from teacher PF-ODE |
| Typical NFE | 50–1000 | 1–50 (1 after reflow) | 1–2 |
| Exact likelihood | Via PF-ODE + trace | Via ODE + trace | Not directly |
| CIFAR-10 FID (reported) | 2.20 [5] | competitive [1, 2, 4] | 3.55 one-step [6] |

Three remarks sharpen the comparison. *First*, flow matching *subsumes* diffusion paths: Lipman et al. show that VP-diffusion probability paths are a special case of the Gaussian CFM family, and that FM training on those paths is a more stable alternative to score matching [1]. *Second*, the velocity target $x_1 - x_0$ is bounded and smooth, whereas scores blow up as $\sigma_t \to 0$; this is the technical reason flow objectives train more stably at low noise levels. *Third*, consistency models and straight flows solve the same *few-step* problem from opposite ends: consistency enforces a functional constraint (every trajectory point maps to the origin) while rectified flow enforces a geometric one (trajectories are straight). Both achieve one-step generation; flows additionally preserve exact invertibility and likelihood computation through the ODE.

---

## 5 Empirical Evaluation and Formal Results

**ImageNet-scale flow matching.** Lipman et al. [1] train CNFs with FM on ImageNet and report consistently better performance than diffusion-based alternatives in both likelihood and sample quality, with reliable sampling from off-the-shelf ODE solvers (e.g., dopri5) — a milestone, since CNFs had previously not scaled to this regime.

**OT couplings accelerate and straighten.** Tong et al. [2] demonstrate that OT-CFM and SB-CFM converge faster (in wall-clock and iterations) than independent-coupling CFM on image benchmarks, produce straighter learned trajectories (measured by the straightness functional), and yield better few-step FID — confirming the variance-reduction theory of Section 4.1.

**Single-step rectified flow.** Liu et al. [3] show that 1-rectified flow followed by reflow rounds generates high-quality CIFAR-10 and bedroom images with *one* Euler step, a regime where diffusion models collapse. The cost-reduction theorem is validated empirically: each reflow round lowers the quadratic transport cost of the induced coupling.

**Modern training refinements.** Lee et al. [4] ("Improving the Training of Rectified Flows") systematically ablate the design space — timestep sampling (logit-normal), velocity versus data prediction parametrizations, loss weightings $\omega(t)$ — and show these choices dominate raw compute in determining few-step FID, establishing a recipe adopted by large-scale rectified-flow transformers.

**Formal sample complexity.** A recent analysis [7] proves *order-optimal* sample complexity for learning rectified flows: under standard smoothness assumptions, the estimator attains the minimax rate for the velocity field, and the pushforward of the learned flow converges to the target in Wasserstein distance at the optimal rate up to logarithmic factors. Formally:

> **Theorem (informal, [7]):** *Let $v^\star(x,t) = \mathbb{E}[X_1 - X_0 \mid X_t = x]$ be $L$-Lipschitz and the function class have controlled covering numbers. Then the empirical risk minimizer $\hat v$ of the rectified-flow loss satisfies $\mathbb{E}\|\hat v - v^\star\|_{L^2(p_t)}^2 = \tilde O(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta + d)})$ at smoothness $\beta$, and the induced generative distribution converges to $p_1$ at the corresponding optimal Wasserstein rate.*

This is the first result placing flow-based generators on the same statistical footing as classical nonparametric density estimators — and it is *stronger* than what is known for score-based diffusion, where score blow-up near $t = 0$ complicates the analysis.

**Head-to-head numbers.** For orientation: score-SDE models reach FID 2.20 on CIFAR-10 [5]; consistency models reach 3.55 one-step [6]; rectified-flow variants with reflow and modern schedules are competitive with both at 1–4 NFE while retaining ODE invertibility [3, 4]. The honest summary is that at *many* NFE, well-tuned diffusion remains the quality ceiling; at *few* NFE, straight-flow methods dominate; consistency models trade likelihood tractability for single-step simplicity.

---

## 6 Limitations and Open Problems

1. **Minibatch OT is a biased proxy.** OT-CFM's theoretical guarantees assume the true OT coupling, but training uses minibatch approximations whose bias grows in high dimensions. Closing the gap between minibatch and population OT — or proving it does not matter — remains open [2].
2. **Reflow is expensive and data-hungry.** Each reflow round requires generating a full synthetic dataset and retraining; on billion-parameter text-to-image models this is a major cost, and synthetic-pair overfitting can degrade diversity [4].
3. **Straightness is not optimality.** A straight flow minimizes discretization error, but the straight coupling is generally *not* the optimal-transport coupling; rectified flow reduces convex costs without converging to the Monge map except in special cases [3]. Characterizing the fixed points of reflow is unresolved.
4. **Likelihood gaps.** Despite ODE-based likelihoods being tractable, flow models still trail autoregressive and well-tuned diffusion models on bits-per-dimension benchmarks — the velocity parametrization seems to pay a density-estimation tax [1, 5].
5. **Conditional and structured generation.** Classifier-free guidance, the workhorse of conditional diffusion, ports awkwardly to velocity fields; principled guidance for flows (beyond score-to-velocity conversion) is an active area.
6. **Theory–practice gap in sampling.** The order-optimality result [7] controls the velocity field in $L^2(p_t)$, but sampling error also depends on ODE discretization and the pushforward's stability — a full end-to-end guarantee for few-step Euler sampling is missing.
7. **Mode coverage diagnostics.** Straight deterministic maps can silently drop modes; unlike SDEs, there is no stochasticity to paper over a poorly covered region, making evaluation of mode coverage more demanding for flows.

---

## 7 Conclusion

Flow matching and rectified flow reframe generative modeling as *supervised regression of velocity fields on designed probability paths*. The CFM equivalence theorem [1, 2] makes CNF training simulation-free; optimal-transport couplings [2] and iterative rectification [3] make the learned trajectories straight; and modern schedules and parametrizations [4] make few-step — even one-step — generation competitive with diffusion at a fraction of the sampling cost. Against score-based diffusion [5], flows trade the rich stochastic-process machinery for geometric simplicity, stability, and design freedom over paths; against consistency models [6], they trade one-step functional constraints for invertible ODEs with exact likelihoods. The emerging statistical theory [7] suggests the framework is not merely a practical hack but a minimax-grounded estimator. The central open challenge is no longer *whether* straight deterministic transport can match diffusion — it can — but how to close the remaining gaps in likelihood, conditional guidance, and end-to-end sampling theory. The ODE paradigm, in short, has earned its place as a first-class citizen of generative modeling.

## References

[1] Y. Lipman, R. T. Q. Chen, H. Ben-Hamu, M. Nickel, and M. Le, "Flow Matching for Generative Modeling," *arXiv:2210.02747*, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747v2

[2] A. Tong, N. Malkin, G. Huguet, Y. Zhang, J. Rector-Brooks, K. Fatras, G. Wolf, and Y. Bengio, "Improving and Generalizing Flow-Based Generative Models with Minibatch Optimal Transport," *Transactions on Machine Learning Research*, 2024 (arXiv:2302.00482). http://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.00482

[3] X. Liu, C. Gong, and Q. Liu, "Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow," *arXiv:2209.03003*, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03003v1

[4] S. Lee, Z. Lin, and G. Kumar et al., "Improving the Training of Rectified Flows," *arXiv:2405.20320*, 2024. https://arxiv.org/html/2405.20320

[5] Y. Song, J. Sohl-Dickstein, D. P. Kingma, A. Kumar, S. Ermon, and B. Poole, "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations," *ICLR 2021* (arXiv:2011.13456). https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456v1

[6] Y. Song, P. Dhariwal, M. Chen, and I. Sutskever, "Consistency Models," *ICML 2023* (arXiv:2303.01469). https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01469v2

[7] "Order-Optimal Sample Complexity of Rectified Flows," *arXiv:2601.20250*, 2026. https://arxiv.org/html/2601.20250v1
