title: Leaderless Consensus Protocols: Dependency-Graph Ordering, Commutativity Exploitation, and Fast-Path Design in Generalized Paxos, EPaxos, CURP, and Tempo
abstract: Leaderless consensus protocols eliminate the distinguished proposer of classical Paxos and Raft, distributing the coordination burden across all replicas. This thesis presents a unified treatment of four landmark designs: Lamport's Generalized Paxos (2005), which relaxed consensus to agreement on *command-structure sets* ordered only modulo commutativity; Egalitarian Paxos (2013), which made every replica a leader and orders commands through explicit dependency graphs committed in one round trip; CURP (2019), which decouples durability from ordering by replicating commutative operations to witnesses in a single wide-area RTT; and Tempo (2021), which replaces explicit dependencies with scalar timestamps and decentralized *timestamp stability* to defeat the dependency-chain blocking that plagued earlier designs. We derive the theoretical foundations, formalize the fast-path and quorum geometry of each protocol, compare their commit latencies, message complexity, and execution blocking behavior, and synthesize a quantitative evaluation across contention regimes. The central finding is a persistent trilemma among fast-path commit latency, execution delay under contention, and recovery complexity — one that dependency-free timestamping approaches address most completely, though at the cost of subtler recovery machinery.
body:
# Leaderless Consensus Protocols: Dependency-Graph Ordering, Commutativity Exploitation, and Fast-Path Design in Generalized Paxos, EPaxos, CURP, and Tempo

## Abstract

## 1 Introduction

State machine replication (SMR) is the standard mechanism for building fault-tolerant services: a set of replicas agrees on a sequence of commands and applies them deterministically, so that a quorum of survivors preserves service despite crashes [1]. Classical Paxos achieves this by funneling every decision through a distinguished leader — a single proposer whose prepare and accept phases impose *two message delays* before any learner can execute a command [1]. Multi-Paxos amortizes the leader's prepare phase, but the leader remains the load hotspot, the latency gate, and the availability bottleneck: clients far from the leader pay trans-oceanic round trips for every write, and a leader failure halts ordering until a new view is established [4].

The *leaderless* program (2005–2021) asks whether the leader is essential. Lamport's Generalized Paxos [2] showed full consensus is stronger than necessary: learners need only agree on *equivalent* command sequences, so commutative commands may be learned in *two message delays*. EPaxos [3] made every replica a leader, ordering commands through *explicit dependency graphs* committed in one round trip. CURP [5] decoupled durability from ordering, letting commutative operations complete in one RTT via witnesses. Tempo [6] closed the circle: dependency graphs block execution under contention, and scalar timestamps with decentralized *timestamp stability* restore predictable execution latency without a leader.

This thesis unifies the four designs in a common formal framework, reconstructs each fast path with TLA+-style precision, and compares them quantitatively on latency, execution blocking, and recovery — identifying a persistent trilemma among fast commit, contention-robust execution, and simple recovery.

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Classical consensus and the leader bottleneck

In single-decree Paxos [1], a proposer drives a *ballot* through two phases: `Prepare(n)` collects promises from a majority, and `Accept(n, v)` replicates the chosen value. The **quorum-intersection lemma** guarantees safety: any two majorities overlap in at least one acceptor, so the highest-ballot accepted value observed in phase 1 necessarily includes any previously chosen value. In the leader-based steady state (Multi-Paxos), phase 1 is executed once per leader, and each command costs *two message delays* from client to leader to majority: one round trip (RTT).

> **Theorem: Fast-path lower bound.** No fault-tolerant asynchronous consensus algorithm can guarantee execution of two concurrently issued commands in fewer than *two message delays*, and even in the absence of faults, no algorithm can guarantee two-delay execution of *interfering* concurrent commands. Classical consensus additionally requires *three* message delays as practically deployed [2].

The practical cost of the leader is threefold. First, **load imbalance**: the leader handles every proposal while followers are underutilized [3]. Second, **latency inflation in wide-area deployments**: a client in Asia contacting a leader in Virginia pays the intercontinental RTT plus the replication fan-out. Third, **availability interruption**: leader failure suspends ordering until a view change completes, even when a majority of replicas remains reachable.

### 2.2 Mencius: rotating the leader

Mencius [4] partitions the log's instance space round-robin across all replicas, so each replica leads its own slots and clients contact the nearest leader. Because the log stays totally ordered, slot *s* cannot execute until all slots *< s* are decided, forcing idle replicas to broadcast *skip messages*. Mencius shortens the client-to-leader distance but is not *generalized*: gaps block execution, skip traffic is all-to-all, and latency stays at two message delays.

### 2.3 Generalized consensus and command-structure sets

Lamport's Generalized Paxos [2] redefines the target of agreement. Instead of a *sequence* of commands, learners agree on a **command-structure set (cstruct)**: a partially ordered set of commands where two cstructs are *equivalent* if they extend to the same sequences modulo commutativity of non-interfering commands. The specification weakens classical consensus in three clauses:

- **Nontriviality.** A learner's cstruct contains only proposed commands.
- **Stability.** The learned cstruct grows monotonically; once `v` is learned, all later learned values have `v` as an *eq-prefix*.
- **Consistency.** Any two correct learners' cstructs can be extended to equivalent sequences.

The algorithmic consequence: concurrently issued *non-interfering* commands are each learned in exactly two message delays, since acceptors accept them independently and learners take the union. But when commands *interfere*, ballots conflict and a classical leader must serialize them — Generalized Paxos "demotes" to ordinary Paxos under contention [7], leaving fully leaderless design to EPaxos.

---

## 3 Methodology

Our analysis proceeds in three stages. First, we extract each protocol's *system model* and *ordering invariant* — the property letting replicas execute commands in an identical, application-consistent order. Second, we formalize each *fast path* as a TLA+-style transition, making explicit the preconditions for one-round commitment. Third, we compare the protocols on five axes: (i) commit latency, (ii) message complexity, (iii) execution blocking — the commit-to-execute gap, (iv) fast-path availability under contention, and (v) recovery complexity. Numerical claims come from the original evaluations [3][5][6]; we reproduce their figures and flag workload differences.

A recurring distinction is **commit** versus **execution**: a command is *committed* when its fate is fixed at a quorum, but *executed* only when a replica can place it in the global order. Leaderless protocols routinely commit fast and execute slowly — EPaxos's dependency graphs [3] and CURP's witness lag [5] both defer execution, while Tempo's timestamp stability [6] was designed to close the gap.

### 3.1 Protocol anatomy: roles and quorums

We fix terminology used throughout:

- **Coordinator / command leader**: the replica that receives a client command and drives its commit. In leaderless protocols every replica can play this role simultaneously for different commands.
- **Fast quorum** (size `⌊3n/4⌋` in EPaxos, `⌊n/2⌋ + f` in Tempo): the set of replicas that must agree for a one-round commit [3][6].
- **Classic quorum** (majority, `⌊n/2⌋ + 1`): the fallback used in slow paths and recovery.
- **Fast path**: commitment in a single RTT (two message delays). **Slow path**: commitment requiring a second round.

### 3.2 Commutativity as the common currency

All four protocols are parameterized by a binary *interference* relation `∼`: `c₁ ∼ c₂` iff executing `c₁;c₂` differs observably from `c₂;c₁`. Non-interfering commands commute and may appear in either order. Lamport called this *non-interference* [2], EPaxos *interference* [3], CURP *commutativity* [5]. The relation must be specified conservatively by the application — a misspecification silently breaks linearizability.

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Generalized Paxos: weakening the problem

Generalized Paxos keeps the classic two-phase ballot structure but changes what ballots *propose*: instead of a single value, a ballot proposes an extension of a command-structure set [2]. Acceptors vote for cstructs, and a ballot is won when a quorum accepts the same cstruct. The critical innovation is in phase 2: an acceptor may accept a proposed cstruct even if it has seen a *different* cstruct for the same ballot, provided the two are *compatible* (their union is a valid cstruct). Compatible but distinct cstructs arise exactly when concurrent commands do not interfere.

> **Theorem: Generalized fast execution.** If commands `c₁ … cₖ` are pairwise non-interfering and each is proposed to a distinct ballot that reaches a quorum, then every learner learns a cstruct containing all of them within *two message delays* of each proposal, with no coordination between proposers [2].

The proof follows from compatibility: acceptors accept each proposal independently, and the union of accepted cstructs is itself accepted, so learners observe all commands after one round trip to a quorum. The limitation is equally sharp: interfering commands force a fallback to a classical leader round. Generalized Paxos is thus a possibility result; the engineering of a *fully* leaderless design is EPaxos's contribution.

### 4.2 EPaxos: egalitarian ordering through dependency graphs

EPaxos [3] assigns every replica the full set of roles — proposer, acceptor, learner — simultaneously. When replica `R` receives command `c`, it becomes `c`'s *command leader* and executes:

1. **Pre-accept phase.** `R` sends `PreAccept(c)` to a *fast quorum* of size `⌊3n/4⌋`. Each recipient computes `dep(c)` — the set of *interfering* commands it has already seen — and replies with its local dependency set.
2. **Fast path.** If all fast-quorum replies return *identical* dependency sets, `R` broadcasts `Accept(c, dep(c))`; upon a majority of acknowledgments, `c` is committed. Total: **one round trip** (two message delays).
3. **Slow path.** If replies disagree, `R` takes the union of reported dependencies and runs a classic Paxos accept phase on `(c, dep(c))` — two round trips.

Ordering is recovered *after* commitment by building a directed graph whose vertices are committed commands and whose edges point from `c` to each `d ∈ dep(c)`. Replicas execute commands in an order consistent with the graph: a command executes once all commands it (transitively) depends on have executed, with strongly connected components (SCCs) — which arise from concurrent interference — executed in a deterministic tie-broken order (e.g., by command ID).

```tla
---- MODULE EgalitarianOrdering ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS Replicas, Commands
VARIABLES committed, deps, executed
Interferes(c1, c2) == c1 /= c2 /\ ~(Commute(c1, c2))
Commit(c) == /\ c \notin committed
             /\ committed' = committed \cup {c}
             /\ deps' = deps @@ (c :> {d \in committed : Interferes(c, d)})
             /\ UNCHANGED executed
Execute(c) == /\ c \in committed
              /\ \A d \in deps[c] : d \in executed
              /\ executed' = executed \cup {c}
              /\ UNCHANGED <<committed, deps>>
====
```

EPaxos targets (i) uninterrupted availability while a majority is reachable, (ii) uniform load balancing with no special roles, and (iii) optimal wide-area commit latency for `f = 1, 2` via the one-RTT fast path [3]. Its evaluation reports throughput up to an order of magnitude above Mencius and Multi-Paxos under uniform load, since every replica is an entry point.

The price is **execution blocking**: a committed command cannot execute until its dependency closure is committed, so under contention a single slow replica transitively stalls everything interfering with its pending commands. Graph storage, traversal, and deterministic SCC resolution add further cost. These are performance, not correctness, flaws — but they are the cliff that motivated Tempo [6].

| Property | EPaxos fast path | EPaxos slow path |
|---|---|---|
| Message delays | 2 (1 RTT) | 4 (2 RTTs) |
| Quorum | `⌊3n/4⌋` (fast) | majority |
| Trigger | Identical `dep(c)` across fast quorum | Disagreement → union + Paxos round |
| Execution | After dependency graph resolves | After dependency graph resolves |

### 4.3 CURP: separating durability from ordering

CURP [5] observes that the two-RTT cost of consistent replication conflates two distinct obligations: **durability** (the operation must survive crashes) and **ordering** (replicas must agree on the sequence). Only ordering requires coordination; durability merely requires the operation to be recorded at enough replicas. CURP therefore supplements any primary-backup (or consensus) system with lightweight, *unordered* replication to **witnesses**:

1. The client sends the operation to the primary *and*, in parallel, to `f` witnesses.
2. Each witness records the operation durably and replies.
3. The primary executes the operation and replies to the client — **without waiting for normal replication**, which proceeds asynchronously.
4. Before the primary may execute, it checks that all *witnessed-but-not-yet-replicated* operations commute with the new one. If any does not commute, the operation waits for normal replication: **2 RTTs**.

Result: commutative operations complete in **1 RTT** — like an unreplicated system — while non-commutative ones pay 2 RTTs. On primary crash, witness records merge with backup state during recovery [5]. In RAMCloud, CURP halved write latency (13.8 → 7.3 µs) and quadrupled throughput; in Redis, it added durability and consistency to a non-durable cache for ~12% latency overhead.

CURP is not a consensus protocol but a *replication accelerator* that still relies on a primary for ordering: nearly free when operations commute, ordinary primary-backup under hot-key contention. It is the clearest demonstration that commutativity can be monetized *without* redesigning consensus.

### 4.4 Tempo: timestamps and decentralized stability

Tempo [6] starts from EPaxos's weakness: explicit dependencies couple execution to the slowest replica in the dependency closure. Its radical simplification is to order commands by **scalar timestamps** and to execute a command once its timestamp is *stable* — i.e., once the replica knows that no future command can receive a smaller timestamp.

Each command's timestamp is the *maximum* of proposals from a fast quorum (`⌊n/2⌋ + f` replicas), each proposal being the replica's clock advanced past all timestamps seen. If enough replicas propose the same maximum, the fast path commits in one RTT; otherwise a slow path (classic Paxos on the timestamp) fixes it [6].

Execution uses **promise tracking**: committing a command with timestamp `t` attaches promises `⟨replica, clock⟩` recording clocks advanced past `t`. Timestamp `t` is *stable* once a replica holds such promises from a majority — every future command must then take a timestamp `> t`. A command executes as soon as its timestamp is stable, *without waiting for any other command to commit*.

> **Theorem: Timestamp stability.** If a replica has received, for timestamp `t`, promises `⟨p, c_p⟩` with `c_p ≥ t` from a majority of replicas, then no command subsequently committed can have timestamp `≤ t`. Hence executing all commands with timestamp `≤ t` in timestamp order is safe [6].

This dissolves EPaxos's blocking: stability is a property of *clocks*, not of the dependency closure. Tempo's evaluation [6] shows it outperforming EPaxos, Atlas, Caesar, and Janus in geo-distributed deployments, with far better tail latency under contention — exactly where dependency graphs choke. It also generalizes to *partial replication* (per-partition timestamps for multi-partition commands), extending leaderless SMR beyond full replication.

### 4.5 The fast-path design space: a synthesis

The four protocols occupy distinct points in a space parameterized by *what is agreed upon* and *what the fast path assumes*:

| Protocol | Agreed object | Fast-path assumption | Commit (fast) | Execution gating |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Generalized Paxos | Command-structure set | Non-interference | 2 delays | Immediate (compatible cstructs) |
| EPaxos | `(command, dependencies)` | Identical dep sets at `⌊3n/4⌋` | 2 delays (1 RTT) | Dependency-graph closure committed |
| CURP | (durability ∥ ordering) | Commutativity w/ witnessed ops | 1 RTT | Primary executes immediately |
| Tempo | `(command, timestamp)` | Timestamp quorum agreement | 2 delays (1 RTT) | Timestamp stability |

Two patterns emerge. First, fast-path quorums exceed a majority wherever recovery must reconstruct commit metadata without a leader (EPaxos's `⌊3n/4⌋`, Tempo's `⌊n/2⌋ + f`). Second, execution gating migrates from *explicit* (dependency edges) to *implicit* (clock stability) — trading modest clock logic for a large reduction in contention-induced tail latency.

---

## 5 Empirical Evaluation / Formal Results

### 5.1 Latency: the one-RTT frontier

All three consensus protocols converge on the same fast-path latency — **one round trip** — the information-theoretic floor identified in [2]. The differentiator is *who* the client contacts: fixed in Multi-Paxos, nearest-replica in EPaxos and Tempo, so the RTT itself shrinks. EPaxos reports optimal wide-area latency for `f = 1, 2` [3]; Tempo matches it with stability-gated execution. CURP reaches 1 RTT *total* for commutative workloads, but only by delegating ordering to an underlying replication layer [5].

### 5.2 Throughput and load balance

EPaxos's evaluation shows the payoff of egalitarianism: with clients spread uniformly, aggregate throughput scales with replica count, exceeding Multi-Paxos by up to an order of magnitude [3]. CURP's RAMCloud deployment shows a different law: write throughput rose ~4× (184 → 728 kops/s) because the primary no longer waits for synchronous replication [5]. Tempo's contribution is steadiness: removing dependency-graph traversal from execution avoids the throughput collapse explicit-dependency protocols suffer as contention rises [6].

### 5.3 Execution blocking under contention

The decisive experiment in [6] varies the interference rate and measures the *commit-to-execute* gap. Dependency tracking exhibits a long tail: one uncommitted command at a slow replica transitively blocks everything interfering with it. Tempo's stability mechanism bounds this gap by clock progress rather than graph closure — *clocks summarize knowledge; graphs enumerate it*.

### 5.4 Formal verification status

All four designs carry proved safety arguments with uneven coverage. Generalized Paxos inherits the TLA+ treatment of the Paxos family [2]. The EPaxos authors shipped a machine-readable TLA+ specification [3], and independent model-checking has probed its intricate recovery paths — a sign of complexity, not of any published flaw. Tempo's safety is proved by hand against its PSMR specification [6]; CURP's is a refinement proof validated by its RAMCloud and Redis integrations [5]. Fast-path optimism *concentrates* correctness risk in recovery — the path exercised least in testing.

---

## 6 Limitations and Open Problems

1. **The interference relation is trusted, not verified.** Every protocol assumes a correct commutativity specification from the application. An overly permissive relation silently violates linearizability; an overly conservative one forfeits the fast path. No production system *infers* commutativity soundly from code — the largest adoption barrier.

2. **Recovery complexity grows with optimism.** EPaxos's slow path and coordinator recovery entangle fast-quorum and classic-quorum state; Tempo's recovery reconstructs timestamp proposals across partitions [6]. Leader-based protocols concentrate recovery in one view-change path; leaderless protocols distribute it, multiplying the states that must be correct.

3. **Clocks have failure modes.** Tempo's execution liveness depends on clock progress at a majority. A replica whose clock stalls can stall stability detection — a liveness coupling that explicit-dependency designs lack, since they gate only on message delivery.

4. **Partial replication is only partially solved.** Tempo extends to multi-partition commands [6], but cross-partition timestamp agreement reintroduces coordination costs reminiscent of two-phase commit. Scalable geo-replicated transactions over leaderless SMR remain open.

5. **Byzantine leaderless consensus is nascent.** All four protocols assume crash faults. Extending dependency-graph or timestamp-stability ordering to Byzantine replicas — where a faulty coordinator can equivocate on dependencies or timestamps — is largely unexplored.

6. **The trilemma persists.** No known protocol simultaneously achieves (a) one-RTT commit, (b) contention-independent execution latency, and (c) simple recovery. Tempo optimizes (a) and (b); CURP optimizes (a) for commutative workloads by punting (c) to the underlying protocol; EPaxos optimizes (a) and common-case simplicity at the cost of (b). Whether the trilemma is fundamental is the central open question.

---

## 7 Conclusion

The leaderless consensus program — Generalized Paxos, EPaxos, CURP, Tempo — is best understood as progressive *decoupling*: ordering from total order (commutative commands need no sequence position), coordination from a distinguished replica (every replica may lead), durability from ordering (witnesses suffice for commutative writes), and execution from dependency enumeration (clock stability replaces graph closure). Each step preserved the one-round-trip commit latency theory permits while attacking a different source of tail latency or imbalance.

The enduring insight: **consensus is a bundle of coupled obligations** — proposing, ordering, durability, execution, recovery — and the leader was load-bearing for all of them at once. Removing it forces each obligation to be re-solved on its own terms, which is why leaderless protocols are individually more complex than Raft yet collectively more robust to planetary-scale failure and latency profiles. Practical guidance: use CURP-style witness replication for commutative workloads on primary-backup systems; EPaxos-style dependency ordering for general workloads with modest contention; Tempo-style timestamp stability when tail latency under contention is the binding constraint. Byzantine tolerance, inferred commutativity, and cross-partition transactions will decide whether leaderless designs displace the leader entirely.

---

## References

[1] L. Lamport, "The Part-Time Parliament," *ACM Transactions on Computer Systems*, vol. 16, no. 2, pp. 133–169, May 1998. https://doi.org/10.1145/279227.279229

[2] L. Lamport, "Generalized Consensus and Paxos," Microsoft Research Technical Report MSR-TR-2005-33, March 2005. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/generalized-consensus-and-paxos/

[3] I. Moraru, D. G. Andersen, and M. Kaminsky, "There is More Consensus in Egalitarian Parliaments," in *Proc. 24th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '13)*, Farmington, PA, USA, 2013. http://dl.acm.org/ft_gateway.cfm?id=2517350&ftid=1403953&dwn=1

[4] Y. Mao, F. P. Junqueira, and K. body:
# From Semi-Naive Fixpoints to Worst-Case Optimal Joins: Datalog Evaluation, the AGM Bound, Leapfrog Triejoin, Generic Join, and Factorized Execution

## Abstract

Datalog evaluation reduces to two tightly coupled problems: computing the least fixpoint of recursive rules, and evaluating each rule's conjunctive body as fast as the output size allows. Semi-naive evaluation solves the first by deriving each tuple exactly once [10], but per-rule joins were long stuck with binary plans whose intermediates can asymptotically dwarf the output. The 2008 AGM bound proved the worst-case output size of a full conjunctive query is governed by the fractional edge cover number of its hypergraph, with Ngo, Porat, Ré, and Rudra giving the first join algorithm attaining it [3]. Veldhuizen's leapfrog triejoin — a strikingly simple variable-at-a-time multiway join over trie iterators — is also worst-case optimal, and strictly sharper on projection-constrained instances [1]. The generic join skeleton unifies both [8]. Meanwhile, factorized databases sidestep materialization, representing join results as algebraic expressions exponentially smaller than flat relations [5]. This thesis develops the full pipeline — fixpoint semantics, fractional edge covers, leapfrog intersections, factorized representations, and the Soufflé engine — with proofs and pseudocode.

## 1 Introduction

Datalog occupies a rare position in computer science: a declarative language simple enough to admit a clean least-fixpoint semantics, yet expressive enough to power industrial program analyses over code bases with millions of lines of code [6]. Every Datalog engine, from research prototypes to the Soufflé compiler, confronts the same two-level optimization problem. At the *outer* level, the engine must iterate rules to a fixpoint without redundant derivation. At the *inner* level, each rule body is a conjunctive query whose evaluation cost must be controlled. For decades these two levels were treated with asymmetric sophistication: semi-naive evaluation, which avoids re-deriving known facts, has been standard since the 1980s [10], while the inner join problem relied on binary join plans — sequences of pairwise joins — that are provably suboptimal on cyclic queries such as the triangle query

> `Q(a, b, c) ← R(a, b), S(b, c), T(a, c)`.

Given `|R| = |S| = |T| = N`, any binary plan materializes an intermediate of size `Θ(N²)` even though the output can never exceed `N^{3/2}`. The gap between `N²` and `N^{3/2}` is not a constant-factor engineering detail: it is polynomial, and it is precisely what the modern theory of worst-case optimal joins eliminates.

The theoretical breakthrough came in two steps. First, Atserias, Grohe, and Marx [2] proved a *tight* upper bound on the output size of any full conjunctive query in terms of the input relation sizes, via the fractional edge cover of the query hypergraph — the AGM bound. Second, Ngo, Porat, Ré, and Rudra [3] designed the first join algorithm whose running time matches this bound, establishing the notion of *worst-case optimality*: an algorithm is worst-case optimal if it runs in time proportional to the maximum possible output size over all instances consistent with the input cardinalities. Veldhuizen [1] then showed that leapfrog triejoin — the algorithm already deployed in the commercial LogicBlox Datalog system — achieves the same guarantee with a far simpler design, and in fact a sharper one. The subsequent generic join abstraction [8] revealed that NPRR's algorithm and leapfrog triejoin are instances of one recursive skeleton: pick a variable order, intersect, recurse.

Orthogonally, the factorized databases programme of Olteanu and Závodný [5] attacks the *output* rather than the *algorithm*: join results are represented as algebraic expressions over unions and products whose size can be exponentially smaller than the flat relation. The two ideas compose: worst-case optimal joins bound the time to enumerate, while factorization bounds the space to represent.

Section 2 reviews Datalog semantics, semi-naive evaluation, and conjunctive queries as hypergraphs. Section 3 presents leapfrog join, leapfrog triejoin, and generic join with pseudocode. Section 4 develops the deep theory; Section 5 the formal complexity results and the Soufflé case study; Section 6 limitations and open problems.

---

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Datalog and the least fixpoint

A Datalog program is a finite set of Horn rules of the form

> `p(X̄) ← q₁(Ȳ₁), …, qₙ(Ȳₙ).`

where the head predicate `p` is intensional (IDB) or extensional (EDB), and each body atom is a relation over variables and constants. The standard semantics is the *least fixpoint* of the immediate consequence operator `T_P`: starting from the EDB facts, `T_P` applies all rules once, adds derived facts, and repeats until no new facts appear. The number of iterations equals the height of the derivation trees, and termination is guaranteed because the Herbrand universe is finite.

Naive evaluation recomputes `T_P` from scratch each iteration, re-deriving every previously known fact. *Semi-naive evaluation* [10] avoids this by maintaining, for each IDB predicate `p`, a *delta* relation `Δp` containing only facts derived in the most recent iteration. Each rule with `k` IDB body atoms is rewritten into `k` delta rules, each requiring at least one body atom to match the delta:

> `p(X̄) ← q₁(Ȳ₁), …, Δqᵢ(Ȳᵢ), …, qₙ(Ȳₙ).    (for each i)`

Every fact is then derived exactly once, and each derivation is *useful*: it consumes at least one newly discovered fact. This is the outer loop of every modern engine, including Soufflé, which compiles delta rules into specialized C++ loops over B-tree indexes [6, 9].

### 2.2 Conjunctive queries as hypergraphs

Each delta rule body is a *conjunctive query* (CQ): a conjunction of relational atoms. A *full* CQ has no projections — every body variable appears in the head. The query is modeled as a hypergraph `H = (V, E)` where `V` is the set of variables and each hyperedge `F ∈ E` is the variable set of one atom, with relation `R_F` over it [4]. The join to compute is `Q = ⋈_{F∈E} R_F`.

A *fractional edge cover* of `H` is a weight assignment `x = (x_F)` with `x_F ≥ 0` such that every variable is covered:

> `Σ_{F: v ∈ F} x_F ≥ 1` for all `v ∈ V`.

The minimum-weight fractional edge cover `ρ*(Q)` is the optimum of a linear program, hence computable in polynomial time. The AGM bound states [2]:

> **Theorem (AGM bound):** For any fractional edge cover `x` and any instance, `|Q| ≤ Π_{F∈E} |R_F|^{x_F}`.

For the triangle query, `x = (1/2, 1/2, 1/2)` is a valid fractional cover, giving `|Q| ≤ N^{3/2}` — strictly better than the `N²` bound from any integral cover, and *tight*: instances with `Θ(N^{3/2})` triangles exist [2, 4].

### 2.3 Why binary joins fail

On the triangle query, every binary plan first computes some pairwise join, e.g. `R ⋈ S`, which can hold `N²` tuples even when the final output has only `N^{3/2}`. Since the plan must materialize this intermediate, its running time is `Ω(N²)` on instances where the AGM bound promises `O(N^{3/2})`. Binary plans are therefore *not* worst-case optimal for any cyclic query — a fact that motivated the entire line of work surveyed here [3, 7].

---

## 3 Methodology

We now present the three algorithmic pillars: leapfrog join (the inner intersection primitive), leapfrog triejoin (the variable-at-a-time multiway join), and generic join (the unifying recursive skeleton). The presentation follows Veldhuizen [1] and the free-join unification [8].

### 3.1 Leapfrog join: synchronized intersection

The primitive operation is the intersection of `k` sorted sets. Leapfrog join maintains one iterator per set and repeatedly advances the iterator currently positioned at the smallest key to the *least upper bound* of the largest key seen — "leapfrogging" over values that cannot belong to the intersection:

```python
def leapfrog_join(iters):
    """iters: list of sorted iterators supporting seek(key). Yields intersection."""
    k = len(iters)
    iters.sort(key=lambda it: it.key())
    while True:
        # find the maximum key among iterators
        hi = max(it.key() for it in iters)
        # advance every iterator to at least hi
        for it in iters:
            it.seek(hi)
            if it.at_end():
                return
        lo = min(it.key() for it in iters)
        if lo == hi:
            yield hi
            iters[0].next()  # advance past the match
            if iters[0].at_end():
                return
```

If the sets have sizes `m₁ ≤ m₂ ≤ … ≤ m_k`, leapfrog join runs in `O(m₁ log(m_k/m₁))` — proportional to the smallest set, up to a logarithmic factor — because each iterator is advanced at most once per distinct value of the smallest set [1]. The `seek` operation is the only data-structure requirement, satisfied by B-trees, sorted arrays, and hash tries alike.

### 3.2 Leapfrog triejoin

Leapfrog triejoin lifts this idea from sets to relations by organizing each relation as a *trie*: a tree whose depth equals the number of attributes, where every root-to-leaf path is a tuple, and each level's children are sorted. Given a variable order `v₁, …, vₙ`, the algorithm descends the tries in lockstep: at depth `d`, it leapfrog-joins the `v_d`-level iterators of precisely those relations containing `v_d`, binds `v_d` to each value in the intersection, and recurses:

```python
def leapfrog_triejoin(var_order, tries):
    """tries: dict atom -> trie iterator positioned at root."""
    if not var_order:
        yield ()            # all variables bound: emit tuple
        return
    v, rest = var_order[0], var_order[1:]
    iters = [tries[a].child_iter(v) for a in atoms if v in schema(a)]
    for a_val in leapfrog_join(iters):
        for a in atoms_containing(v):
            tries[a].open(a_val)     # descend one trie level
        yield from ((a_val,) + t for t in leapfrog_triejoin(rest, tries))
        for a in atoms_containing(v):
            tries[a].up()           # ascend
```

Veldhuizen proves that for *any* variable order, the total work is `O(AGM(Q) · log N)` — worst-case optimal up to a log factor [1]. The proof's key device is a *sum-min* bound: at each trie level, the leapfrog cost is charged against the minimum, over relations at that level, of a quantity controlled by the fractional cover.

### 3.3 Generic join

The generic join algorithm [8] abstracts the same recursion without committing to tries: it needs only the ability to compute `⋂ᵢ π_x(Rᵢ)` efficiently and to restrict relations by a binding (`σ_{x=a}(R)`), typically via hash tries:

```haskell
-- Generic join over variable order [x1..xn]
genericJoin :: [Var] -> [Relation] -> [[Value]]
genericJoin []     rs = [[]]
genericJoin (x:xs) rs = do
  a <- intersect [project x r | r <- rs, x `elem` schema r]
  let rs' = [restrict r x a | r <- rs]
  (a :) <$> genericJoin xs rs'
```

For the triangle query with order `[x, y, z]`, this becomes the familiar nested loop `for a in R.x ∩ T.x: for b in R[a].y ∩ S.y: for c in S[b].z ∩ T[a].z: output(a,b,c)` [8]. Both NPRR's algorithm and leapfrog triejoin are instances of this skeleton, differing only in the intersection data structure. Crucially, generic join is worst-case optimal for *every* variable order [8].

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 Trie iterators and the leapfrogging invariant

The trie iterator abstraction is what makes leapfrog triejoin both simple and general. A trie iterator supports `open(v)` (descend to the child labeled `v`), `up()` (ascend), `seek(k)` (advance to the least key `≥ k` at the current level), and `at_end()`. In practice one trie per index order of each relation suffices — supplied by B-tree indexes, which is why Soufflé's automatic index selection [9] accommodates the design. Veldhuizen shows the per-level leapfrog cost satisfies

> `cost(level v) ≤ Σ min_{F∋v} |π_{≤v}(R_F) ⋉ binding| · (log factor)`,

and summing over levels telescopes, via the fractional cover weights, into the AGM bound [1]. The elegance of the argument — a few pages versus the substantial machinery of NPRR — is a major reason for the algorithm's influence.

### 4.2 The AGM bound: statement, proof idea, tightness

Fix a fractional edge cover `x`. The AGM inequality `|Q| ≤ Π_F |R_F|^{x_F}` was originally proved by an entropy argument [2]: for the uniform distribution over output tuples, each variable's entropy is at most the weighted sum of relation entropies covering it, and subadditivity plus Shearer's lemma yields the bound. Ngo et al. gave an alternative inductive proof via Hölder's inequality, whose structure directly suggests the recursive join algorithm [3, 4].

*Tightness* is as important as the upper bound: for the optimal cover `x*`, there are infinitely many instances with `|Q| = Θ(Π_F |R_F|^{x*_F})` [2]. The extremal construction uses product distributions over the variable domains sized according to the dual LP (a fractional packing). Hence no algorithm can beat the AGM bound in the worst case, and worst-case optimality is a well-defined, attainable target.

| Query | Optimal fractional cover | AGM bound (|R|=N) | Binary plan cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Triangle `R(a,b),S(b,c),T(a,c)` | (½,½,½) | `N^{3/2}` | `Θ(N²)` |
| 4-cycle `R(a,b),S(b,c),T(c,d),U(d,a)` | (½,½,½,½) | `N²` | `Θ(N²)` |
| Lollipop / `R(a,b),S(b,c),T(b,c)` | (1,½,½) | `N²` | `Θ(N²)` |
| Star `R₁(x,y₁),…,R_k(x,y_k)` | (1,…,1) | `N^k` | `Θ(N^k)` |

### 4.3 Query decomposition and the NPRR algorithm

NPRR's algorithm is driven by the *query decomposition lemma* [3, 4]: for any partition of variables `V = I ⊕ J` and any fractional cover `x`,

> `Σ_{t_I ∈ L} Π_{F∈E_J} |R_F ⋉ t_I|^{x_F} ≤ Π_F |R_F|^{x_F}`,

where `L = ⋈_{F∈E_I} π_I(R_F)`. The algorithm recursively solves a subquery on a variable subset `I` and, per partial binding, the residual query; the lemma bounds total work by the AGM bound. This was the first worst-case optimal join, published at PODS 2012 [3]. Veldhuizen's refinement [1] shows leapfrog triejoin additionally achieves optimality under *projection cardinality* constraints — e.g., bounds on `|π_a(R)|` — where NPRR provably does not: a counterexample family makes leapfrog run in `O(n log n)` while NPRR needs `Θ(n^{1.375})`. Finer-grained instance classes thus separate the two algorithms even though both meet the coarse AGM bound.

### 4.4 Factorized databases: compressing the output

All the above algorithms *enumerate* flat tuples. Factorized databases [5] observe that the output itself is often highly redundant: a join result can be written as an algebraic expression over singleton relations using union (`∪`) and Cartesian product (`×`), applying distributivity of product over union. An *f-representation* of the triangle result might read

> `⟨a₁⟩ × (⟨b₁⟩ × ⟨c₁⟩ ∪ ⟨b₂⟩ × (⟨c₂⟩ ∪ ⟨c₃⟩)) ∪ ⟨a₂⟩ × …`,

whose *factorization tree* (ftree) nests unions inside products so shared prefixes are stored once. Olteanu and Závodný prove tight size bounds: every CQ result has an f-representation of size `O(|D|^{s(Q)})` where `s(Q) ≤ ρ*(Q)` is the *factorization exponent*, and the gap between `ρ*` and `s` can be as large as the query size — i.e., exponentially more succinct than any flat representation [5]. *D-representations* add explicit sharing of repeated subexpressions (DAGs instead of trees) for further compression. The FDB engine evaluates queries directly on factorized data, and aggregates and machine-learning tasks (e.g., linear regression over joins) can run on the compressed form without ever materializing the flat join [5]. Factorization is thus complementary to worst-case optimal enumeration: one minimizes *time*, the other *space*.

---

## 5 Empirical Evaluation / Formal Results

### 5.1 Formal complexity landscape

The results compose into a clean hierarchy. Let `N` be the input size and `Z = |Q(D)|` the output size:

1. **Semi-naive fixpoint:** each fact derived once; total rule firings proportional to the number of distinct derivations [10].
2. **AGM upper bound:** `Z ≤ Π_F |R_F|^{x_F}` for every fractional cover `x` [2]; tight in data complexity.
3. **NPRR:** runs in `O(AGM(Q))` — worst-case optimal [3].
4. **Leapfrog triejoin:** runs in `O(AGM(Q) log N)` for any variable order; optimal under projection constraints where NPRR is not [1].
5. **Generic join:** unifies (3) and (4); optimal for any variable order given optimal intersections [8].
6. **Factorization:** representation size `O(|D|^{s(Q)})` with `s(Q) ≤ ρ*(Q)`; worst-case optimal construction algorithms exist for equijoins [5].

Beyond the AGM bound, the *polymatroid bound* incorporates degree constraints and functional dependencies, and is achievable by backtracking search under acyclic degree constraints [7] — the current frontier of beyond-worst-case analysis.

### 5.2 The Soufflé case study

Soufflé compiles Datalog to parallel C++: rules become nested loops over trie-indexed relations, with semi-naive delta iteration, automatic index selection, and a specialized concurrent B-tree supporting lock-free evaluation [6, 9]. Its headline result remains the points-to analysis of the OpenJDK 7 class library — 1.4 million program variables, 350 thousand objects, 160 thousand methods — completed in under a minute on a single machine [6]. This is semi-naive evaluation at industrial scale: hundreds of recursive rules, each body a multiway join, evaluated to fixpoint. Integrating worst-case optimal multiway joins into Datalog materialization remains an active frontier, since per-rule variable orders interact non-trivially with shared index structures.

---

## 6 Limitations and Open Problems

**Variable orders are worst-case optimal but not instance optimal.** Every variable order attains the AGM bound, yet orders differ enormously in practice; choosing them is a cost-based optimization problem that current engines solve heuristically. Instance optimality — competing with the best algorithm on *every* instance — is known only for restricted cases such as acyclic queries over search-tree indexes [7].

**Aggregates, negation, and non-full queries.** The AGM theory targets full conjunctive queries. Projections (existential variables), aggregation, and stratified negation change the output-size landscape; the polymatroid bound [7] extends the theory to degree constraints, but practical worst-case optimal engines for aggregate queries remain rare.

**Factorization vs. enumeration trade-offs.** Factorized representations excel when the output is consumed by further algebraic operators (aggregates, learning), but many applications need flat tuples; converting back can cost the full output size. Characterizing which workloads benefit, and compiling Datalog fixpoints directly over factorized relations, is largely open.

**Dynamic and incremental settings.** Semi-naive evaluation handles insertions via delta rules, but deletions require heavyweight techniques (DRED, counting). Marrying worst-case optimal joins with incremental view maintenance and with differential dataflow-style retract propagation is unresolved.

**Parallelism and hardware.** Leapfrog triejoin's pointer-chasing trie descent is less SIMD-friendly than hash joins; scaling multiway joins to GPUs and distributed memory while preserving worst-case guarantees is an active area.

---

## 7 Conclusion

The arc from semi-naive evaluation to factorized databases tells a coherent story about the maturation of query evaluation theory. Semi-naive evaluation tamed the *outer* fixpoint loop by ensuring each fact is derived once [10]. The AGM bound then characterized exactly how large a rule body can be [2], and worst-case optimal joins — NPRR's decomposition algorithm [3], Veldhuizen's leapfrog triejoin [1], and their generic-join unification [8] — showed how to attain that bound, closing a polynomial gap that binary plans could never bridge. Factorized representations [5] completed the picture by compressing the output itself, and engines like Soufflé [6, 9] demonstrated that the classical ideas scale to million-line program analyses. The remaining frontiers — instance optimality, aggregates and degree constraints, incremental worst-case optimal maintenance, and hardware-conscious multiway joins — define the next decade of join processing research. What began as a curiosity about triangle queries has become the organizing principle of modern join evaluation: *never do asymptotically more work than the output size demands, and never store more output than its structure requires.*

body:
# Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machines: Proving General-Purpose Computation via RISC-V Constraint Systems, Continuations, and STARK Recursion

## Abstract

Zero-knowledge virtual machines (zkVMs) have displaced hand-crafted arithmetic circuits as the dominant frontend for succinct verifiable computation: a program compiled to an instruction set architecture (ISA) — most commonly RISC-V — is executed by a prover, and the execution is attested by a succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge. This thesis develops the design theory of modern zkVMs end to end. We formalize the arithmetization pipeline that converts RISC-V execution traces into algebraic intermediate representation (AIR) constraints over small-characteristic prime fields, analyze the FRI-based STARK proof system that attests trace correctness without trusted setup, and prove how *continuations* — segmenting long executions and recursing over segment proofs — yield amortized constant verification cost. We compare three engineering generations: RISC Zero with its recursion and STARK-to-SNARK composition, SP1 with its precompile-centric Plonky3 backend, and Valida's ISA co-designed for proving efficiency. Finally we contrast the AIR paradigm with the lookup-singularity approach of Jolt/Lasso [2,3], quantify empirical prover bottlenecks from recent head-to-head benchmarks [7,9], and enumerate the open problems — memory proving, proving economics, and formal ISA-verification gaps — that bound current practice.

---

## 1 Introduction

The classical formulation of succinct zero-knowledge arguments assumes a *circuit*: the witness-checking procedure is flattened into a fixed acyclic network of gates, and the prover attests that the network is satisfiable. This formulation is expressive but ergonomically catastrophic. Real software is loops, recursion, dynamic dispatch, and heap allocation; expressing a modern program as a monolithic circuit forces the developer to become a cryptographer, and the audit surface of hand-rolled circuits is notorious for soundness bugs.

A zero-knowledge virtual machine inverts the relationship. The statement to be proved is *the program*: the developer writes ordinary code — Rust, C++, or any language with an LLVM frontend — compiles it to a target ISA, and the zkVM proves correct execution of the resulting machine code. The verifier learns nothing beyond the declared public outputs and the fact that execution was faithful. The frontend/backend separation is now canonical: the *frontend* reduces execution to a set of algebraic constraints, and the *backend* — a polynomial interactive oracle proof (PIOP) combined with a polynomial commitment scheme (PCS) — compiles those constraints into a succinct argument [1,2].

This thesis is a systematic treatment of that pipeline. We answer three questions: (i) how is a general-purpose ISA arithmetized into constraints that are *cheap* to prove, (ii) how do long executions scale beyond the memory and time limits of a single prover, and (iii) where do the remaining costs concentrate, and which architectural choices — precompiles, field selection, lookup arguments — attack them. Our analysis is grounded in deployed systems: RISC Zero's RISC-V zkVM [8], Succinct's SP1 [7], and the Delendum/Lita Valida design [5], together with the Jolt/Lasso lookup-singularity line of work [2,3,4] and the first independent multi-zkVM benchmarking studies [9].

## 2 Background

### 2.1 From circuits to execution traces

A zkVM replaces the circuit's gate network with an *execution trace*: a matrix $T \in \mathbb{F}^{N \times w}$ whose rows are successive machine states (program counter, registers, memory ports, instruction fields) and whose columns are *registers* of the arithmetization. Correct execution is expressed as a set of *transition constraints* $C_j$ such that $C_j(T_t, T_{t+1}) = 0$ for every row $t$, plus boundary constraints on the first and last rows. This is the Algebraic Intermediate Representation (AIR): a uniform constraint system in which the same transition polynomial applies to every row, so the constraint degree stays small while $N$ grows with program length [1].

> **Theorem (AIR soundness reduction).** Let $T$ be an $N \times w$ execution trace and $\{C_j\}_{j=1}^{m}$ transition polynomials of degree at most $d$. If all $C_j$ vanish on consecutive rows and boundary constraints hold on $T_0, T_{N-1}$, then $T$ is a faithful execution of the specified machine, provided each machine transition is uniquely determined by the constraint set. The STARK protocol then reduces the claim "$T$ satisfies all constraints" to a low-degree test on a composed polynomial, with soundness error bounded by the FRI proximity gap [1].

Concretely, the prover interpolates each column into a polynomial over a domain $D$ of size $N$, forms the *composition polynomial* $Q(x) = \sum_j \alpha_j C_j(\cdot) / Z_H(x)$ where $Z_H$ is the vanishing polynomial of $D$, and commits to $Q$ using a Merkle tree over a Reed–Solomon codeword with blowup factor $\beta$ (typically 2–4). The FRI protocol [1] then proves that $Q$ has degree below the required bound; a handful of queries yields $\approx 100$–128 bits of conjectured security, with grinding adding further bits [6].

### 2.2 Small fields and the cost model

Proving cost is dominated by finite-field arithmetic on trace columns and by hashing inside the PCS. Early systems used the 64-bit Goldilocks field; the modern generation uses 31-bit fields — Baby Bear ($p = 2^{31} - 2^{27} + 1$) in RISC Zero's stack [8], Mersenne31 ($p = 2^{31} - 1$) in Valida's design [5] — because 31-bit limbs fit in native 64-bit multiplies without overflow, vectorize cleanly under AVX2/AVX-512/NEON, and still provide a large smooth multiplicative subgroup for FFTs. The Plonky3 toolkit [6] exposes exactly this menu (BabyBear, Mersenne31, Goldilocks), FRI-based and Brakedown-based commitment schemes, and Poseidon2/BLAKE3/Keccak hashing, and both SP1 and Valida build on it.

### 2.3 SNARKs, STARKs, and recursion

A STARK [1] is transparent (no trusted setup) and plausibly post-quantum, but its proofs are large — tens to hundreds of kilobytes — because FRI opening proofs carry Merkle paths per query. A *recursion* step proves, inside the arithmetization itself, the verification of one or more STARK proofs, compressing many segment proofs into one; repeating this yields a single constant-size proof for an arbitrarily long execution. Finally, a *wrapping* step embeds the recursion verifier in a pairing-based SNARK such as Groth16, producing a $\approx 200$-byte proof verifiable on-chain for roughly 275k EVM gas [7]. RISC Zero open-sourced exactly these three primitives — high-speed recursion, proof composition, and a STARK-to-SNARK wrapper — under Apache-2.0 in 2023 [8].

---

## 3 Methodology

Our method is comparative-architectural: we fix a common evaluation frame and instantiate it across the major zkVM designs, validating each claim against primary sources (protocol specifications, peer-reviewed papers, and reproducible benchmarks).

**Frame.** A zkVM design is decomposed along five axes:

1. *ISA choice*: RISC-V (RISC Zero, SP1, Jolt) versus a proving-native ISA (Valida), and the resulting cycle-count inflation for cryptographic workloads.
2. *Arithmetization*: AIR transition constraints over small fields versus lookup-centric (Jolt) representations.
3. *Memory model*: how reads/writes are proved consistent — offline memory checking via permutation/multiset arguments, or Merkleized memory — and its share of trace width.
4. *Scaling*: continuations (segmented proving) and recursion topology for long executions.
5. *Acceleration*: precompiles — dedicated constraint "chips" for SHA-256, Keccak, secp256k1, ed25519 — versus naive instruction-by-instruction execution.

**Evidence.** Performance claims are taken from (a) Succinct's reproducible SP1 vs. RISC Zero and SP1 vs. Jolt benchmark suites (Tendermint light client, Merkle SSZ withdrawal proofs, and Reth executing real Ethereum blocks) [7]; (b) the first peer-reviewed head-to-head study of six zkVMs presented at zkProof 2025, measuring CPU/memory bottlenecks and continuation parallelization [9]; and (c) the Zeth Type-0 zkEVM report, the first production-scale demonstration of continuation-based proving on RISC Zero [8]. Theoretical claims rest on the STARK [1], Jolt [2], and Lasso [3] papers and the a16z crypto engineering write-ups [4].

---

## 4 Deep Dive

### 4.1 ISA design: why RISC-V won, and what it costs

Choosing RISC-V as the proving ISA is an *ecosystem* decision, not a cryptographic one. The RISC-V toolchain — `rustc`/`clang` targets, `cargo prove`, standard libraries — lets developers compile unmodified programs, including full Ethereum clients (Reth) and light clients (Tendermint), and prove their execution [7,8]. The cost is arithmetization inefficiency: a RISC-V ISA was designed for silicon, not for field arithmetic. A single SHA-256 compression executed instruction-by-instruction costs tens of thousands of cycles; an ECDSA verification, millions. Cycle count is the fundamental cost driver, because the trace has one row per cycle and proving work scales (at least) linearly in trace length.

Valida [5] takes the opposite bet: a RISC-inspired but proving-native ISA with no general-purpose registers (the machine operates directly on memory), constraints of degree at most 3, minimal instruction decoding, and an extensible instruction set in which cryptographic accelerators are first-class instructions rather than bolted-on precompiles. Its authors argue that co-designing the ISA for the constraint system beats retrofitting RISC-V — at the price of abandoning the mature RISC-V toolchain (their LLVM-IR-to-Valida backend was still under development, and the repository has since moved to Lita's stewardship). The tradeoff is therefore *toolchain maturity vs. constraint efficiency*, and every production zkVM today sits somewhere on this spectrum: SP1 keeps RISC-V but surrounds it with precompiles; RISC Zero keeps RISC-V and relies on recursion economics.

```rust
// SP1-style guest program: ordinary Rust, compiled to RISC-V, proven by the zkVM [7]
use sp1_sdk::{ProverClient, SP1Stdin};

fn main() {
    let client = ProverClient::from_env();
    let mut stdin = SP1Stdin::new();
    stdin.write(&block_header);          // public input: Ethereum block
    let (pk, vk) = client.setup(ELF);    // one-time setup for the program
    let proof = client.prove(&pk, &stdin).run().expect("proving failed");
    client.verify(&proof, &vk).expect("verification failed");
}
```

### 4.2 STARK constraint systems over small fields

In the AIR paradigm, each RISC-V instruction family becomes a set of transition constraints. A representative 32-bit ADD in a Baby Bear AIR looks schematically like:

```python
# Schematic AIR transition constraint for ADD rd, rs1, rs2 (Baby Bear field)
def transition_add(row, nxt, F):
    # decode: opcode selects the ADD chiplet
    is_add = row["opcode"] - OPCODE_ADD
    # register file consistency is enforced by a separate memory argument
    a = row["rs1_val"]; b = row["rs2_val"]; c = nxt["rd_val"]
    # 32-bit addition with carry, constrained limb-wise over a 31-bit field
    carry = row["carry"]
    return [
        is_add * (a + b - c - carry * 2**32),   # arithmetic correctness
        is_add * carry * (carry - 1),            # carry is boolean
        is_add * (nxt["pc"] - row["pc"] - 4),    # pc advances by 4
    ]
```

Because the field is only 31 bits, 32-bit values are handled limb-wise (e.g., two 16-bit limbs), and range checks — ubiquitous in decoding, memory addressing, and carry handling — are proved with *lookup arguments* such as LogUp, the log-derivative construction SP1 uses to avoid Merkleized-memory overhead [7]. The composition polynomial is committed with a blowup factor of 2 in SP1 (versus 4 in some RISC Zero configurations), halving the Reed–Solomon domain and the hashing work that dominates FRI [7]. This is where Plonky3 [6] matters as infrastructure: its FRI variant commits to tables of *different sizes*, improving trace-area utilization, and its field/hash menu lets each zkVM tune the field-to-hashing cost ratio.

> **Theorem (Preprocessing-free soundness).** A STARK over a 31-bit field with FRI soundness parameters $(\rho, s, \zeta)$ — code rate $\rho$, $s$ queries, $\zeta$ grinding bits — achieves $\lambda \geq \min(\zeta + s\log_2 \rho^{-1},\, \cdot)$ bits of conjectured security, where the second term is the field-size bound; with $s = 28$ queries, $\rho^{-1} = 4$, and $\zeta = 16$ the standard configuration targets $\approx 100$ bits [6].

### 4.3 Continuations and STARK recursion

A single STARK proof over a billion-cycle trace is infeasible: the prover's memory grows with the trace, and latency grows superlinearly. *Continuations* solve this by executing the program once in a fast native emulator, snapshotting machine state at configurable intervals, and proving each segment independently — typically capped near $2^{20}$–$2^{21}$ cycles per shard. Segments are assigned to a pool of workers and proved in parallel; a recursion layer then proves the verification of pairs of segment proofs, and the recursion tree collapses to one constant-size proof [8]. The Zeth Type-0 zkEVM demonstrated this at production scale: each shard stays small (a few seconds of proving), and with enough workers the wall-clock time for the whole execution approaches the time for a single shard [8].

Recursion depth is logarithmic in the number of segments, and each recursion node re-runs the STARK verifier *inside* the constraint system — which is why the verifier's arithmetization must itself be proving-friendly, and why the recursion field is usually the same small field as the base layer. The empirical study [9] measured continuation scaling directly: on 8 cores, SP1 showed the highest parallel speedup among the tested zkVMs, and logarithmic extrapolation predicts saturation near $\approx 10.6\times$ for SP1 and $\approx 9.9\times$ for Ceno at 40 cores — continuations scale well but sublinearly, bounded by aggregation and commitment-generation overhead.

| Stage | Input | Output | Asymptotic cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Execution + trace gen | RISC-V ELF, public input | Trace $T \in \mathbb{F}^{N \times w}$ | $O(N)$ |
| Sharding (continuations) | Trace of $N$ cycles | $k$ shards of $\le 2^{21}$ cycles | $O(N)$ |
| Core proving (parallel) | $k$ shards | $k$ STARK proofs | $O(N \log N)$ total, $O(N/k)$ wall-clock |
| Recursion | $k$ segment proofs | 1 aggregated proof | $O(k \log k)$ |
| SNARK wrap (Groth16) | Aggregated STARK proof | $\approx 200$-byte proof | Constant; $\approx 275$k EVM gas [7] |

### 4.4 Precompile-accelerated proving

Precompiles are the single largest performance lever in deployed zkVMs. Instead of executing SHA-256 or secp256k1 as thousands of RISC-V instructions, the VM traps to a dedicated AIR *chiplet* whose constraints natively express the primitive — e.g., a Keccak-$f$ permutation chiplet with one row per round. SP1's precompile-centric architecture reports 5–10$\times$ cycle-count reductions on blockchain workloads [7], and the effect is visible in the benchmarks: on the Tendermint light client and Reth programs, SP1's cycle counts are dramatically lower than RISC Zero's precisely because of first-class precompile support [7]. The Jolt line makes the same point from the other direction: its subtables *are* the precomputations, and structured tables of size $2^{128}$ cost no more than the subtables actually touched [2].

Designing a precompile is a constraint-engineering problem. The chiplet must (i) express the primitive in low-degree AIR, (ii) interface with the main trace through bus/memory arguments so that inputs and outputs are consistent, and (iii) be cheap enough in the recursion layer, since the verifier will re-verify chiplet-heavy proofs. The payoff compounds: fewer cycles means fewer shards, less recursion, and lower aggregation cost.

```haskell
-- Schematic: precompile dispatch as an AIR bus constraint
-- main trace posts (opcode, inputs) on the bus; the chiplet consumes them
dispatch :: Trace -> Chiplet -> Constraint
dispatch trace chiplet =
  busLookup (opcodeOf trace) (inputsOf trace)   -- main -> bus
  <> busLookup (opcodeOf chiplet) (outputsOf chiplet)  -- bus -> chiplet
  <> boundary (pcNext trace == pcOf trace + trapCost)
```

### 4.5 The lookup-singularity alternative: Jolt and Lasso

Jolt [2] rejects the AIR-per-instruction paradigm. Every RISC-V instruction is expressed as *lookups* into a small set of structured tables; the tables are indexed by chunked operands (e.g., 8-bit limbs of 32-bit words), and the full $2^{128}$-entry virtual table is never materialized — Lasso [3] commits only to the subtables actually accessed plus per-entry access counts, all of them *small* field elements, which makes the polynomial commitments (MSM-based, e.g., Hyrax/KZG) dramatically cheaper than committing to random field elements [4]. For 64-bit RISC-V datatypes, the dominant prover cost is committing to roughly six 256-bit field elements per CPU step, with no FFTs anywhere in the pipeline [2].

The tradeoff is subtle. Jolt's prover is arithmetically lean but its per-step constant is paid on *every* step, and its memory-checking still requires an offline argument. In head-to-head benchmarks [7], SP1 outperformed Jolt on proving time (1.66–3.23$\times$) and proof size (1.29–3.60$\times$ smaller) at comparable cycle counts — the AIR+precompile approach currently wins on real workloads, though Jolt's auditability (constraints are *just lookups*) and its avoidance of hash-heavy FRI remain attractive. An independent ACL2 formalization has now machine-checked Jolt's RV32I semantics against its Rust implementation, finding and fixing real inefficiencies (removing redundant lookups, shrinking three subtables by 87.5%) — a sign that ISA-level formal verification is becoming a practical engineering tool.

---

## 5 Empirical Evaluation / Formal Results

**Benchmark design.** The most careful public comparisons fix hardware (AWS `r7i.16xlarge`, 64 vCPUs), enable precompiles on both sides, and measure end-to-end proving: witness generation plus core proving plus recursion to constant size, excluding one-time setup [7]. Workloads are real programs — Merkle SSZ withdrawal proofs, a Tendermint light client, and Reth executing Ethereum blocks — rather than synthetic loops.

**Headline results.**

1. *SP1 vs. RISC Zero (v1.1.1 vs. v1.0.0):* SP1 is faster end-to-end on all three workloads, with the gap largest where precompiles apply; both use constant-size proofs via recursion, but SP1's Groth16 wrapper adds a $\approx 50$-second "shrinking" stage absent from RISC Zero's pipeline [7].
2. *SP1 vs. Jolt:* at matched proof size and cycle count, SP1 proves 1.66$\times$ (SHA-256 chain), 3.23$\times$ (Fibonacci), and 1.93$\times$ (loop) faster, with proofs 1.29–3.60$\times$ smaller [7].
3. *Six-way study [9]:* across SP1, RISC Zero, Jolt, Nexus, and Ceno, the dominant CPU bottlenecks are proof aggregation and commitment generation (SP1, RISC Zero), Lasso's sumcheck (Jolt), and folding (Nexus); the dominant memory bottleneck is Merkle tree construction. No zkVM scales linearly with cores; continuations help all of them, most for SP1.
4. *Real-time Ethereum proving:* Succinct's Hypercube backend (multilinear, GPU-oriented) reports proving $\approx 93\%$ of Ethereum blocks in under 12 s (average $\approx 10.3$ s) — the threshold for L1-slot proving, though these vendor-demonstration figures await independent replication.

**Formal results.** Beyond benchmarks, two proof-theoretic facts anchor the field. First, the STARK IOP+FRI composition gives transparent, plausibly post-quantum succinct arguments with prover time $O(N \log N)$ and verifier time polylogarithmic in $N$ [1]. Second, the Jolt/Lasso analysis shows that for *decomposable* tables the prover commits to only $O(cm + cN^{1/c})$ field elements for $m$ lookups into a size-$N$ table — sublinear in the table size — which is what makes the "lookup singularity" (circuits that only perform lookups) asymptotically viable [2,3].

---

## 6 Limitations and Open Problems

---

## 7 Conclusion

The zero-knowledge virtual machine has matured from a research curiosity into infrastructure: compile ordinary code to RISC-V, execute, shard via continuations, prove each shard with a FRI-based STARK over a 31-bit field, recurse to constant size, and wrap in Groth16 for on-chain verification. Each layer of this stack exists because the layer below it was too expensive — AIR replaced monolithic circuits, continuations replaced monolithic traces, recursion replaced linear-size proofs, and precompiles replaced instruction-by-instruction cryptography. The empirical record [7,9] shows the strategy working: order-of-magnitude speedups from precompiles, near-real-time block proving on the horizon, and a healthy competition between the AIR paradigm (RISC Zero, SP1, Valida) and the lookup paradigm (Jolt/Lasso). The remaining problems — memory proving, cost transparency, precompile governance, and end-to-end formal verification — are now engineering and economic rather than purely cryptographic, which is itself the strongest signal that zkVMs have arrived.
